en: The First Chapter of the *Sarvārthasiddhi*, composed by the venerable teacher Śrī Pūjyapāda:
[Salutation] to the leader of the path to liberation and the destroyer of the mountains of karma.
I bow to the knower of all principles in order to attain those same qualities.

A certain fortunate person (*bhavya*), whose liberation was near at hand, being wise and desiring his own welfare, approached a preeminent teacher of the Nirgranthas in a certain secluded and most delightful hermitage—a resting place for noble beings. This teacher sat in the midst of an assembly of sages like liberation itself incarnate, manifesting in physical form the path to emancipation without the utterance of words. Skilled in logic and scripture, solely intent on the task of establishing the welfare of others, and worthy of being served by the noble, he was approached with humility and questioned as follows.
“Blessed One, what indeed would be for the benefit of the self? He replied, “Liberation.

He then asked again: “What is the nature of this liberation, and what is the means for its attainment? The Teacher said: “Liberation is the ultimate, unassailable state of supreme bliss and inconceivable innate qualities such as knowledge, belonging to the bodiless self whose stains of the impurity of karma have been entirely eliminated.

Because that [Self] is absolutely beyond the senses, the disputants who are still under the veil of ignorance and who consider themselves Tīrthaṅkaras conceptualize the consciousness of the Puruṣa in a completely different way through words that do not touch its true nature and which are based on fallacious reasoning. They hold that the nature of the Puruṣa is consciousness turned away from the discernment of the forms of objects; thus, even though it exists, it is as if non-existent because it lacks form. Furthermore, they maintain that liberation for the Puruṣa consists in the total cessation of specific qualities such as intellect (*buddhi*) and the rest.
That conceptualization, too, is indeed non-existent, because that which is devoid of specific characteristics is not a real entity. Furthermore,

the notion that the extinction of the self is like the extinguishing of a lamp has been explicitly refuted by those very same [authorities], who have demonstrated that it is like the conceptualization of a donkey’s horn.
And so forth.
We shall explain its faultless essential nature later on.

They also contradict [the truth] regarding the means for attaining that [liberation], asserting that its attainment occurs through knowledge alone, independent of conduct; or through mere faith alone; or through conduct alone, independent of knowledge.

Just as for one overcome by disease, there is no possibility of success through fragmented means such as knowledge regarding a medicine that is the remedy for that illness, so too fragmented knowledge and the other factors do not constitute the means for attaining liberation.
What then? He says that those three combined constitute it:
right vision, right knowledge, and right conduct are the path to liberation.
The word *samyak* is either unanalyzed (*avyutpanna*) or analyzed (*vyutpanna*).
When derived from the root *añc* with the suffix *kvip*, it becomes *samyak* in the sense of "moving together" (*samañcati*).
Its meaning is praise (*praśaṃsā*).
Each of these is completed individually:
right vision, right knowledge, and right conduct.
We shall explain their essential nature in detail later, according to their characteristics and their prescriptions.

This, however, is stated merely as a summary: for the purpose of gathering together the faith that takes as its object the realization of the true nature of the categories of existence, the qualification "correct" (*samyak*) is applied to "vision" (*darśana*).
Correct knowledge is the comprehension of the categories—such as the soul (*jīva*) and so forth—in whatever manner they are established.
The qualification "correct" is used for the purpose of eliminating delusion, doubt, and error.
Right conduct (*samyakcāritra*) is the cessation of activity that causes the undertaking of karma for one who possesses knowledge and is intent upon the cessation of the causes of *saṃsāra*.
The qualifier "right" (*samyak*) is used for the purpose of excluding conduct preceded by ignorance.

It sees, it is seen by it, or it is mere seeing—this is vision (*darśana*). It knows, it is known by it, or it is mere cognition—this is knowledge (*jñāna*). It moves, it is moved by it, or it is mere movement—this is conduct (*cāritra*).
But surely, in this way, it follows that the agent is the very same as the instrument, and that is contradictory.
True; however, such a statement is made with the intention of expressing a distinction between the substance undergoing transformation and its specific modification.

Just as fire burns fuel through the process of combustion, so too has the status of being an agent (*kartṛ*) and other factors of action been explained. Since the non-absolutist position (*anekānta*) is established regarding the identity and difference between a mode (*paryāya*) and the substratum (*paryāyin*), and since the intention to express either independence or dependence is possible, this is not contradictory even with respect to a single entity—
just as the status of being an agent and other factors of action exists in the case of the act of burning and so forth in fire.
It would be logical to mention "knowledge" (*jñāna*) first, because vision (*darśana*) is preceded by it and because [the word] has fewer syllables.
This is not correct, because they arise simultaneously.

When, through the subsidence, destruction, or destruction-cum-subsidence of this delusion regarding vision (*darśana-moha*), the self manifests in the form of right vision (*samyag-darśana*), at that very moment, preceded by the cessation of wrong cognition (*matyajñāna*) and wrong scriptural knowledge (*śrutājñāna*), right cognition (*mati-jñāna*) and scriptural knowledge (*śruta-jñāna*) manifest—just as the heat and light of the sun become manifest upon the clearing away of thick clouds. [In the compound *mati-śruta-jñāna*,] that which has fewer syllables or is more venerable (*abhyarhita*) is placed first. Why is it more venerable? Because cognition is the cause for the correct designation [of the self].
Knowledge is applied prior to conduct, because conduct is preceded by it.
Liberation is the complete release from all karma.
The path is the means for attaining that [nirvāṇa].

The use of the singular number in the term "path" is intended to indicate that it exists as a unified whole; by this, the status of being a "path" is precluded for its individual components taken separately.
Therefore, this triad— right vision, right knowledge, and right conduct— should be understood as the collective direct path to liberation.
Regarding that, for the purpose of defining the characteristic of right vision, which was mentioned first, this is said:
Right vision is faith in the meaning of the principles (*tattvārthaśraddhāna*). The word *tattva* denotes existence in general.
How so? The word *tat* is a pronoun (*sarvanāman*). A pronoun functions in a general sense.
The state of being that is its "reality" (*tattva*).

Of what is that [the object]? It means the existence of that object exactly as it is situated. "Object" (*artha*) means that which is sought after; in other words, it is that which is determined. An object in its true state is the "object of reality" (*tattvārtha*).
Alternatively, there is the designation of the possessor of a state by means of the state itself, because of their non-difference.
Reality itself is the object; thus, "the object of reality" (tattvārtha).
Faith in the object of reality is "faith in the object of reality" (tattvārtha-śraddhāna), which is to be understood as right view (samyagdarśana).
And the meaning of reality (*tattvārtha*) consists of the living beings (*jīva*) and so forth, which will be explained hereafter. [Objection:
Since the root *dṛś* has the sense of "illumination," its transition to the sense of "faith" is not logical. [Response: There is no fault, because verbal roots possess multiple meanings.
If it is asked, "Why abandon the well-known meaning? [the answer is: because this is a treatise on the path to liberation (*mokṣamārga*).

For it is logical that faith in the true nature of reality (*tattvārtha-śraddhāna*), as a modification of the self (*ātma-pariṇāma*), is the means to liberation, since its object is the *bhavya* (capable) soul.
However, illumination (*āloka*) caused by the eyes and so forth is not logically the path to liberation, because it is common to all transmigrating souls (*saṃsārin*).
If it is argued that [faith] is faith in objects (*artha*), then it would follow that there is faith in all objects.
If it is argued that it is faith in reality (*tattva*), then it would follow that it is merely faith in existence (*bhāva*).
Some imagine that "reality" (*tattva*) consists of existence, substantiality, quality-ness, action-ness, and so forth;
however, this leads to the undesirable consequence of grasping everything as a single unity.
Others imagine that "this whole world is indeed the Person" (*puruṣa*) and so on.
This being the case, there would be a contradiction with what is seen and what is accepted.
Therefore, both are mentioned for the sake of non-deviation.

That [object] is of two kinds, distinguished by the objects of those with passion and those free from passion; the first is characterized by the manifestation of tranquility, spiritual urgency, compassion, faith, and so forth.
The other [is] merely the purification of the self.
Now, as to how this right vision (*samyagdarśana*) regarding the categories of existence such as the soul (*jīva*) arises, he says:
That [is acquired] either through innate nature or through realization;
"innate nature" means one's own inherent disposition.
Realization is the comprehension of the meaning.
These two are taught as being the causes of what? Of activity.
And what is the action? The word "arises" (*utpadyate*) is supplied, because the sūtras contain ellipses.
Thus, this right view arises either from innate disposition (*nisarga*) or from realization (*adhigama*).
Here it is asked: In the case of innate right vision (*samyagdarśana*), would there be the realization of the object or not?
If there is, then that too is born of realization and is not something distinct from it.

If there is not, how can there be faith in the object for one who has not awakened to reality? This is not a fault; in both cases of right vision, the internal cause is the same: the subsidence (*upaśama*), destruction (*kṣaya*), or partial destruction and subsidence (*kṣayopaśama*) of the delusion regarding vision (*darśanamoha*).

When that [nescience] exists, that which manifests without the aid of external instruction is innate (*naisargika*). That which is preceded by the instruction of another and has the soul (*jīva*) and so forth as its object is the subsequent (*uttara*).
This is the distinction between these two.
For what purpose is that mention [of "tat"]? It is for the purpose of indicating what has been immediately preceded.
By this word "tat," right view (*samyagdarśana*) is indicated as being immediate.
Otherwise, since the path to liberation (*mokṣamārga*) is also under discussion, there would be a connection with that [path] as well.

If it is argued that—according to the principle “a rule or a prohibition applies to what is immediately preceding”—the reference to right vision (*samyagdarśana*) is established as being the immediate predecessor, we say no; because “proximity is weaker than the primary factor,” it would instead connect only with the path to liberation.
Therefore, that statement is made.
§ 17. It has been stated that "right view is faith in the meaning of reality. Now, what is reality? To this, he says the following:
The principles are the soul (jīva), the non-soul (ajīva), influx (āsrava), bondage (bandha), stoppage (saṃvara), dissociation (nirjarā), and liberation (mokṣa).
Among these, the soul is characterized by consciousness (cetanā).
And that [consciousness] is divided into many types according to the distinctions of knowledge and so forth.
Non-soul (ajīva) is characterized as the opposite of that.
Influx (āsrava) consists of the gateways through which auspicious and inauspicious karma enters.
Bondage consists of the mutual penetration of the spatial points of the self and karma.
Restraint (saṃvara) is characterized by the cessation of the influx (āsrava).
Dissociation (nirjarā) is characterized by the partial destruction of karma.
Liberation is characterized by the total dissociation from karma.
An elaboration of these points will be discussed later.
Because every fruit is dependent upon the self (ātman), the living being (jīva) is mentioned first.
Because it serves as a support for that [jīva], the designation of *ajīva* (non-living matter) follows immediately after it.
Because it is the object of both of those, the inclusion of *āsrava* (influx) follows immediately after that.
Because it is preceded by that [influx], the designation of *bandha* (bondage) follows immediately after that.
Because there is an absence of bondage for one who is restrained (*saṃvr̥ta*), the term "restraint" (*saṃvara*) is stated immediately after that, for the purpose of practicing its opposite.
Since shedding (*nirjarā*) occurs when restraint exists, the term "shedding" is stated following that.
Because liberation (*mokṣa*) is what is ultimately attained, it is mentioned at the end.
Here, the inclusion of merit and demerit must be made,
because others have also stated that "there are nine categories."
It need not be mentioned, because it is included within the influx (*āsrava*) and bondage (*bandha*).
If this is so, then the mention of influx and the rest is purposeless, since they are included within the categories of the soul (*jīva*) and the non-soul (*ajīva*).
It is not purposeless.
Here, liberation is the subject under discussion;
it must necessarily be defined,
and it is preceded by cyclic existence (saṃsāra).
Influx (*āsrava*) and bondage (*bandha*) are the primary causes of *saṃsāra*,
while restraint (*saṃvara*) and dissociation (*nirjarā*) are the primary causes of liberation (*mokṣa*).
Therefore, they have been taught separately for the purpose of demonstrating the relationship between the primary causes and their resulting effects.
For it is observed that even a particular, though included within a general category, may be mentioned separately for a specific purpose, as in:
“The kṣatriyas have arrived; Sūravarmā also.
It has been stated that the word *tattva* denotes a state (*bhāva*).

How, then, does it attain grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with terms such as *jīva*, which denote substances (*dravya*)? Coreferentiality occurs because there is no distinction [between the substance and its state] and because the state is superimposed upon it.
For example: "The self is precisely upayoga."

If this is so, would it not follow that the gender and number of each respective term should persist? [The answer is: "Even when there is a relationship between a qualifier and a qualified, there is no deviation from the gender and number already expressed, due to the requirements of the word's own expressive power (*śabdaśakti*). This principle should also be applied to the opening sūtra.

Thus, in order to eliminate confusion regarding specific conventional usage among these aforementioned categories—namely, right vision (*samyagdarśana*) and the rest, as well as the soul (*jīva*) and the rest—he says:
Its placement [is performed] by way of name, representation, substance, and state.
Name (*nāma*) is the act of designation applied to an object that does not possess those qualities, for the purpose of conventional usage, which directs human effort toward it.
*Prasthāpanā* is the act of establishing that "this is that very thing" in relation to objects such as wood, clay, paintings, or the casting of dice.
*Dravya* is so called because it is quickly approached (*druta-gata*) by its qualities (*guṇa*), or because it will be approached by qualities, or because it will approach qualities.
*Bhāva* is the substance (*dravya*) characterized by its current mode (*paryāya*).
To explain: the meaning of the term *jīva* is established in four ways—as *nāmajīva*, *sthāpanājīva*, *dravyajīva*, and *bhāvajīva*.
A *nāmajīva* is the name given to anyone whatsoever, regardless of whether they possess the quality of living (*jīvana*).
A *sthāpanājīva* is that which is designated as "jīva" or "human jīva" in the casting of dice and similar contexts.
The substantial soul (*dravyajīva*) is of two kinds: the substantial soul in the sense of scripture (*āgamadravyajīva*) and the substantial soul not in the sense of scripture (*noāgamadravyajīva*).
Among these, one who knows the *Jīvaprābhṛta* or the *Manuṣyajīvaprābhṛta*, but whose self is currently not engaged in that cognition, is a substantial soul in the sense of scripture.

The substantial soul not in the sense of scripture is established as threefold, through the distinctions of the cognizer’s body (*jñāyakaśarīra*), the body occupied by it (*bhāvitaśarīra*), and that which is distinct from both (*tadvyatirikta*).
In this context, that body of the knower which pertains to the three periods of time is the "body of the knower" (*jñāyaka-śarīra*).

With respect to the general [category], there is no "living being existing through non-scriptural [knowledge]" (*noāgamabhāvijīva*), because the generality of "living" (*jīvana-sāmānya*) is always present. However, with respect to the specific [category], it does exist.
A living being situated in another state of existence (gatyantara), facing toward the attainment of human birth, is a "potential human being" (manuṣyabhāvijīva).
Apart from that, there is the distinction between karmic and non-karmic [beings].
The "ontological being" (bhāvajīva) is twofold: the ontological being consisting of scripture (āgamabhāvajīva) and the ontological being not consisting of scripture (noāgamabhāvajīva).

In that regard, the self (ātman) which is occupied with the object of the "gift of life" (*jīvaprābhṛta*) or endowed with the cognitive engagement (*upayoga*) regarding the object of the "gift of human life" is the *āgamabhāvajīva*.
The self which is permeated by the state (*paryāya*) of being alive or by the state of being a human life is the *noāgamabhāvajīva*.
In this same manner, the method of applying the categories of naming and so forth (*nāmādinikṣepavidhi*) should be applied to the other categories of objects as well.

What is its purpose? It is for the sake of setting aside what is irrelevant and for the sake of defining what is relevant. Through the method of formal presentation (*nikṣepavidhi*), the meaning of the word is laid out.
What is the purpose of that mention of the word? It is for the sake of including everything.

For if that word were absent, there would be a connection through the placement [of the suffix] only with the primary elements, such as right vision (*samyagdarśana*) and so forth; it would not apply to the non-primary elements, such as the individual soul (*jīva*) and so forth, which are grasped as being the objects of those [primary elements].
However, when that word is indeed employed, the inclusion of both the primary and the non-primary elements is established by implication.
If one asks, "How can those who are thus introduced by means of names and so forth attain the realization of reality? it is for this reason that it is said:
"Realization is attained through the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the viewpoints (*naya*).

The reality (*tattva*) of the living beings (*jīva*) and other categories, which have been introduced by means of the method of the fourfold designation (*nikṣepa*) beginning with names, is apprehended through the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the viewpoints (*naya*).
The characteristics and divisions of the means of valid cognition and the viewpoints will be explained below.
Among them, the means of valid cognition is of two kinds: for one's own sake (*svārtha*) and for the sake of others (*parārtha*).

In this context, with the exception of scripture (*śruta*), valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is for one's own sake (*svārtha*). Scripture, however, is both for one's own sake and for the sake of others (*parārtha*):
that which consists of knowledge is for one's own sake, while that which consists of speech is for the sake of others.
The *nayas* are the conceptualizations thereof.
Here, one might object: "Since the word *naya* has fewer syllables, it ought to be placed first [in the compound].
This is not a fault.
The term "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) is placed first because it is more highly esteemed;
and being more highly esteemed is stronger than anything else.
Why is it more highly esteemed? Because it is the source from which the exposition of the method (*naya*) originates.

For it has been stated thus: "Naya is the determination of an object by grasping it through the specific transformation [of the perspective] according to the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). And because the pramāṇa has the entirety [of reality] as its object, it has likewise been said: "The complete description (sakalādeśa) is dependent on the pramāṇa; the partial description (vikalādeśa) is dependent on the naya."
The *naya* is twofold: the substantial (*dravyārthika*) and the modal (*paryāyārthika*).

The reality of existence (*bhāvatattva*) is to be understood through the modal standpoint (*paryāyārthikanaya*), while for the other three [standpoints], it is understood through the substantial standpoint (*dravyārthikanaya*), because they consist of the universal (*sāmānya*).

That for which substance (*dravya*) is the object (*artha*) or purpose (*prayojana*) is the substantialist (*dravyārthika*). That for which mode (*paryāya*) is the object or purpose is the modalist (*paryāyārthika*).
All of that, taken together, is to be apprehended through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Thus, in order to further demonstrate other means for the comprehension of the living beings (*jīva*) and so forth, which have already been understood through the instruments of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the methods of reasoning (*naya*), he says: "By way of description, ownership, proof, locus, duration, and mode."
Exposition (*nirdeśa*) is the designation of essential nature (*svarūpa*).
Sovereignty (*svāmitva*) is lordship (*ādhipatya*).
The means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) is the cause of origination. The locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
Duration (*sthiti*) is the delimitation by time.
"Method" (vidhāna) means "manner.
In response to the question "What is right vision? there is the instruction: "Faith in the true nature of reality," or [the definition] beginning with "name" and so forth.
When it is asked "Of what?", it is stated generally: "of the soul" (jīva).

Specifically, according to the enumeration of destinies (*gati*), among the hell-beings in all the hells who are fully developed (*paryāptaka*), there exists the subsidential (*aupaśamika*) and the subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣāyopaśamika*) [right belief].
In the first hell, among those both fully developed and not yet fully developed, there exists the destructive (*kṣāyika*) and the subsidence-cum-destruction [right belief].
In the animal destiny, among the animals who are fully developed, there exists the subsidential [right belief].
The kṣāyika and kṣāyopaśamika [faculties] exist for those who are both complete (paryāpta) and incomplete (aparyāptaka).
Among animals, the kṣāyika does not exist.
The aupaśamika and kṣāyopaśamika exist only for those who are complete, not for those who are incomplete.

In the human realm, among humans—both those who are fully developed (*paryāpta*) and those who are not yet fully developed (*aparyāpta*)—there exists that which is produced by destruction (*kṣāyika*) and that which is produced by the subsidence of karma along with its destruction (*kṣāyopaśamika*).
That which is produced by subsidence alone (*aupaśamika*) exists only for those who are fully developed, not for those who are not yet fully developed.
Among human females, all three types exist, but only for those who are fully developed, not for those who are not yet fully developed.
In the celestial realm (*devagati*), all three types [of right vision] exist among both the fully developed (*paryāptaka*) and the undeveloped (*aparyāptaka*) gods.

If it is asked how the subsidential (*aupaśamika*) type exists among the undeveloped, it is because it applies to those who die while the delusion of conduct (*cāritramoha*) is in a state of subsidence.
Among the gods of the *bhavanavāsin*, *vyantara*, and *jyotiṣka* classes, as well as the goddesses residing in the *saudharma* and *aiśāna* heavens, the destructive (*kṣāyika*) type does not exist.

Among those who have attained full development, there exists that which is characterized by tranquility (*aupaśamika*) and that which is characterized by the subsiding of defilements (*kṣāyopaśamika*).
According to the classification by faculties, all three types exist for those with five faculties who possess perception (*saṃjñin*), but not for others.
In terms of classification by body, all three types exist for those belonging to the mobile class of beings, but not for others.
In terms of classification by yoga, all three types exist for those possessing the three yogas;
for those without yoga, there is only that which is exhaustively purified (kṣāyika).

With respect to the Vedas, all three types exist for those possessing the three Vedas. For those from whom the Vedas have departed, there exists the acquired (*aupāśamika*) and the destructive (*kṣāyika*) [right belief].
With respect to the passions (*kaṣāya*), all three types exist for those possessing the four passions.
For those free from passions (*akaṣāya*), there exists both the subsidential (*aupaśamika*) and the destructive (*kṣāyika*) [knowledge].

According to the classification by knowledge (*jñāna-anuvāda*), those possessing sensory cognition (*ābhinibodhika*), scriptural knowledge (*śruta*), clairvoyance (*avadhi*), and mind-reading knowledge (*manaḥparyaya*) possess all three types.
For those possessing omniscience (*kevalajñāna*), there is only the destructive type.

With reference to restraint (*saṃyama*), all three types [of right vision] exist for those who are restrained by means of equanimity (*sāmāyika*) and those who are restrained by means of re-institution (*chedopasthāpanā*).

For those restrained by means of purification through penance (*parihāraviśuddhi*), the subsidential (*aupaśamika*) does not exist, but the other two do exist. For those restrained by means of subtle-passion (*sūkṣmasāṃparāya*) and those with perfect conduct (*yathākhyāta*), both the subsidential and the destructive (*kṣāyika*) exist. For those who are partially restrained (*saṃyatāsaṃyata*) and for those who are unrestrained (*asaṃyata*), all three also exist. With reference to perception (*darśana*), all three exist for those possessing visual perception (*cakṣurdarśana*), non-visual perception (*acakṣurdarśana*), and limited perception (*avadhidarśana*). For those possessing omniscient perception (*kevaladarśana*), only the destructive exists.
With reference to *leśyā*, all three [types of right vision] exist for those possessing the six *leśyās*, whereas for those without *leśyā* (the *aleśyas*), there is only that which is *kṣāyika*.
With reference to *bhavyatva* (the capacity for liberation), all three exist for those who are *bhavya*, but not for those who are *abhavya*.
With reference to rightness (*samyaktva*), one should understand that wherever a particular type of right vision exists, it is that very one [which applies].

With respect to cognition (*saṃjñā*), all three [types of knowledge] exist for those possessing cognition, but not for those lacking cognition; for those devoid of both designations, there is only the knowledge resulting from destruction (*kṣāyika*).

With respect to nutrition (*āhāra*), all three exist for those who take food; all three also exist for non-feeding *chadmastha* (non-omniscient) beings; and for omniscients (*kevalin*) who have entered the process of total dissolution (*samudghāta*), there is only that which results from destruction.
The means of attainment (sādhana) is twofold: internal and external.

The internal is the subsidence, destruction, or partial destruction-cum-subsidence of delusion regarding right vision (darśanamoha). The external means of attaining right vision for hell-beings up to the fourth [hell] consists, for some, of the recollection of past births (jātismaraṇa), for others, of hearing the Dharma, and for others, of the overcoming of intense suffering (vedanā).
From the fourth up to the seventh [bhūmi], the denizens of hell possess the recollection of their past births and the overcoming of their suffering.
Among animals, some possess the recollection of their past births, some hear the Dharma, and some behold the images of the Jinas.
It is the same for humans as well.

Among the gods, some possess the recollection of their past births (*jātismaraṇa*), some the hearing of the Dharma (*dharmaśravaṇa*), some the vision of the majesty of the Jinas (*jinamahimadarśana*), and some the vision of divine prosperity (*devardhidarśana*). This remains the case up to the Ānata heaven. For the gods of the Ānata, Prāṇata, Āraṇa, and Acyuta heavens, with the exception of the vision of divine prosperity, all three other [faculties] also exist.
Among those dwelling in the nine *graiveyaka* heavens, some possess the recollection of their past lives (*jātismaraṇa*) and others hear the Dharma.

This conceptualization does not apply to those dwelling in the *anudiśa* and *anuttara* vimānas; for it is precisely because they have previously attained right view (*samyaktva*) that they are born there.
The locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is twofold: internal and external.

The internal is the self (*ātman*) alone, which is capable of the relationship between owner and owned, since the application of grammatical factors (*kāraka*) proceeds according to the speaker's intention.
The external is the channel of the world (*lokanāḍī*).
How large is it? It is one *rajju* in width and fourteen *rajjus* in length.
The duration of the subsidential (*aupaśamika*) [state] is, both minimum and maximum, within a *muhūrta*.
For one in saṃsāra who possesses [karma] that is subject to destruction, the minimum duration is one antarmuhūrta.
The maximum is thirty-three sāgaropamas, plus two pūrvakoṭis less eight years and one antarmuhūrta.
For one who is liberated, it has a beginning but no end.
The minimum duration of the [state] resulting from destruction-cum-subsidence is one antarmuhūrta, and the maximum is sixty-six sāgaropamas.
The classification, in general, is one: right vision (samyagdarśana).
The twofold [division] is by way of the distinction between innate (*nisargaja*) and acquired (*adhigamaja*).
The threefold [division] is by way of the distinction between the subsidential (*aupaśamika*), the destructive (*kṣāyika*), and the subsidential-destructive (*kṣāyopaśamika*).
Thus, there are numerable varieties according to terminology.
They are innumerable and infinite due to the distinction between the believer and the object of belief.

Thus, this method of exposition and so forth should be applied, according to the scripture, to knowledge and conduct, as well as to the categories of the living (jīva) and the non-living (ajīva), and the rest.

Is the comprehension of the soul and the other categories achieved by these means alone, or is there another means of comprehension? He says that there is one which has been observed: "And by means of existence, number, field, contact, time, interval, presence, and smallness or greatness.
"Sat" is an indication of existence. That [term], when used in the sense of praise and so forth, is not what is intended here.
"Number" (saṃkhyā) is the calculation of distinctions.

The field (*kṣetra*) and the dwelling (*nivāsa*) pertain to the present time; that same contact (*sparśana*), however, has the three times as its object. Time is of two kinds: primary (*mukhya*) and conventional (*vyāvahārika*).
The determination of these two will be explained later.
*Antara* means the period of separation.
*Bhāva* is characterized by the subsidential (*aupaśamika*) and other types of states.
Alpabahutva (the state of being few or many) is the comprehension of distinctions through mutual comparison.
Furthermore, by means of these [categories], the understanding of right vision (*samyagdarśana*) and so forth, as well as of the souls (*jīva*) and other categories, is to be known.
Now, one might object: is not the inclusion of "existence" (*sat*) already established by the very definition?
From the mention of "method" (vidhāna), the understanding of number is obtained; from the mention of "location" (adhikaraṇa), the comprehension of field and contact is obtained;
and from the mention of "duration" (sthiti), the inclusion of time is obtained.
Existence (*bhāva*) is already included within [the categories] beginning with name (*nāman*).
Why, then, are these mentioned again?
It is established by way of truth (*satya*).
The presentation of reality and so forth is according to the dispositions of those to be trained.
Some have a preference for brevity, some for detail,
and others are to be instructed neither too concisely nor too extensively.
For the exertion of the virtuous is for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings; thus, the enumeration of the different means for attaining realization has been made.

Otherwise, since realization would already be established by the phrase "realization through the means of valid cognition and the methods of reasoning" alone, the inclusion of the others would be purposeless.
Therein, the exposition of the doors of inquiry (anuyogadvāra) beginning with existence (sat) is undertaken with reference to the substance of the soul (jīvadravya).
Souls are established within the fourteen stages of spiritual development (guṇasthāna).

They are: wrong view (mithyādṛṣṭi), right view with delusion (sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi), right-and-wrong view (samyagmithyādṛṣṭi), right view without self-restraint (asaṃyatasamyagdṛṣṭi), the partially restrained (saṃyatāsaṃyata), the careless restrained (pramattasaṃyata), the careful restrained (apramattasaṃyata), the one in the stage of unprecedented action who is a pacifier (upaśamaka) or an annihilator (kṣapaka), the one in the stage of subtle passion who is a pacifier or an annihilator, the one in the stage of subsided passions who is free from attachment but still possessed of the physical body (upaśāntakaṣāyavītarāgachadmastha), the one whose passions are destroyed who is free from attachment but still possessed of the physical body (kṣīṇakaṣāyavītarāgachadmastha), the omniscient with activity (sayogakevalī), and the omniscient without activity (ayogakevalī).
For the purpose of defining these very same classes of souls (*jīvasamāsa*), fourteen loci of inquiry (*mārgaṇāsthāna*) are to be known:

[1] gati (destiny), [2] indriya (senses), [3] kāya (body), [4] yoga (activity), [5] veda (sexuality), [6] kaṣāya (passion), [7] jñāna (knowledge), [8] saṃyama (restraint), [9] darśana (vision), [10] leśyā (purity of thought-coloration), [11] bhavya (capacity for liberation), [12] samyaktva (right conviction), [13] saṃjñā (ideation), and [14] āhāraka (assimilation).
In that regard, the exposition of existence (*satprarūpaṇā*) is twofold: by way of generality and by way of particularity.
By way of generality, there exists false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), the view of one who has attained right vision after falling back (*sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi*), and so forth.
By way of particularity, according to the enumeration of the destinies (*gati*), in the hellish destiny, across all the earths, the first four stages of spiritual development (*guṇasthāna*) exist.
In the three lower realms, those same [categories] exist, with the addition of the states of the restrained and the unrestrained.
In the human realm, all fourteen exist.
In the celestial realm, it is as in the case of the hell-beings.
According to the enumeration by faculties (*indriya*), from those with one faculty up to those with four faculties, there is only one station of wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭisthāna*).
Among those with five faculties, all fourteen [stations] exist.
According to the enumeration by bodies (*kāya*), from the earth-body up to the plant-body, there is only one station of wrong view.
In the mobile bodies (trasakāya), all fourteen stages are present.
According to the enumeration by yoga, there are thirteen stages of spiritual development (guṇasthāna) within the three types of yoga;
beyond that is the state of the one liberated from yoga (ayogakevalin).

In the three Vedas, following the recitation of the Vedas, there exist [stages] beginning with the non-cessation of false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and ending with the subtle non-cessation (*anivṛttibādara*).
Among those who have departed from the Vedas, there exist [stages] beginning with the subtle non-cessation and ending with the ayogakevalin.

With reference to the passions (*kaṣāya*): in the case of anger, pride, and deceit, there are [the stages] beginning with wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and ending with the stage of non-restraint-cum-gross-passion (*anivṛttibādara*).
In the passion of greed (*lobha-kaṣāya*), those same [stages] exist, with the addition of the stage of subtle-passion (*sūkṣmasāṃparāya*).

The state without passion (*akaṣāya*) consists of the subsided-passion (*upaśāntakaṣāya*), the destroyed-passion (*kṣīṇakaṣāya*), the omniscient with activity (*sayogakevalin*), and the omniscient without activity (*ayogakevalin*).
In terms of knowledge (*jñāna*), among *mati-ajñāna*, *śruta-ajñāna*, and *vibhaṅga-jñāna*, there exist the states of wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and right view with delusion (*sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi*).

Among *ābhinibodhika-jñāna*, *śruta-jñāna*, and *avadhi-jñāna*, there exist the states from the uncontrolled right view (*asaṃyatasamyagdṛṣṭi*) up to the state of one whose passions are exhausted (*kṣīṇakaṣāya*).

In the case of *manaḥparyaya-jñāna* (mind-reading knowledge), there are those from the stage of the *pramatta-saṃyata* (the heedful self-restrained) up to the *kṣīṇakaṣāya* (one whose passions are exhausted).
In the case of *kevala-jñāna* (perfect knowledge), there are both the *sayoga* (with-vibration) and the *ayoga* (without-vibration) [stages].

With reference to restraint (*saṃyama*), those who are restrained range from the "negligent" (*pramatta*) up to the "isolated ones without yoga" (*ayogakevalin*). Those restrained by the purity of equanimity (*sāmāyika*) and the purity of re-establishment (*chedopasthāpanā*) range from the "negligent" up to the "unwavering" (*anivṛtti*).

Those restrained by the purity of avoidance (*parihāraviśuddhi*) consist of both the "negligent" and the "non-negligent. Those restrained by the purity of subtle passion (*sūkṣmasāṃparāya*) exist in only one place: the stage of subtle passion.
Those who dwell in purity as described—ranging from those with restrained passions (*upaśāntakaṣāya*) to the omniscient ones without yoga (*ayogakevalin*)—are the "restrained" (*saṃyata*).
Those who are both restrained and unrestrained (*saṃyatāsaṃyata*) occupy only the single stage of being both restrained and unrestrained.
The "unrestrained" (*asaṃyata*) occupy the first four of these stages of spiritual development (*guṇasthāna*).

According to the enumeration by way of vision (*darśana*), false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and the others up to the destruction of the passions (*kṣīṇakaṣāya*) exist in both the visual vision (*cakṣurdarśana*) and the non-visual vision (*acakṣurdarśana*).
In the clairvoyant vision (*avadhidarśana*), those from the uncontrolled right-viewed (*asaṃyatasamyagdṛṣṭi*) up to the destruction of the passions exist.
In the case of *kevala-darśana* (omniscient perception), there are the *sayoga-kevalin* (those with active yoga) and the *ayoga-kevalin* (those without active yoga).

According to the enumeration of *leśyās* (karmic tints), in the *kṛṣṇa*, *nīla*, and *kapota* *leśyās*, there exist [categories] beginning with *mithyādṛṣṭi* (false view) and ending with *asaṃyata-samyagdṛṣṭi* (right view without restraint).
In the *tejaḥ* and *padma* leśyās, there are the stages beginning with *mithyādṛṣṭi* and ending with *apramattasthāna*.
In the *śukla* leśyā, there are the stages beginning with *mithyādṛṣṭi* and ending with *sayogakevalin*. Those without leśyā (*aleśya*) are the *ayogakevalins*.
By way of reference to those who are capable, all fourteen [categories] exist among the capable.
Those who are incapable exist only in the first station.

With reference to rightness (*samyaktva*), in the case of rightness that is exhaustively destroyed (*kṣāyika-samyaktva*), there exist states beginning with the right-viewed non-restrained (*asaṃyata-samyagdṛṣṭi*) and ending with the non-yoked perfected one (*ayoga-kevalin*).

In the case of rightness that is partially destroyed and partially subsided (*kṣāyopaśamika-samyaktva*), there exist states beginning with the right-viewed non-restrained and ending with the non-negligent (*apramatta*).

In the case of rightness through subsidence (*aupaśamika-samyaktva*), there are the stages beginning with the non-restrained right-viewer (*asaṃyata-samyagdṛṣṭi*) and ending with the one whose passions are subsided (*upaśāntakaṣāya*).
The rightness-attaining (*sāsādana-samyagdṛṣṭi*), the right-wrong (*samyagmithyādṛṣṭi*), and the wrong-viewer (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) each reside in their own respective places.

By way of reference to those with perception (*saṃjñin*), there are twelve stages of spiritual development (*guṇasthāna*) among them, ending with the stage of one whose passions are exhausted (*kṣīṇakaṣāya*).
Among those without perception (*asaṃjñin*), there is only one: the stage of false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
Those devoid of both designations are the one possessed of omniscience with activity (*sayogakevalin*) and the one without activity (*ayogakevalin*).
According to the classification by nutriment (*āhāra*), among those possessing nutriment, there are the stages beginning with wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and ending with the omniscient (*kevalin*).

Among those without nutriment—namely, those undergoing the state of transition (*vigrahagati*)—there are three stages of spiritual development (*guṇasthāna*): wrong view, the view of one who is attaining rightness (*sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi*), and the view of one who is right but unrestrained (*asaṃyatasamyagdṛṣṭi*).
Those who have reached total eradication are the Kevalins with activity (sayogakevalin) and the Kevalins without activity (ayogakevalin).
The perfected ones (siddhas), the supreme beings (parameṣṭhins), have transcended the stages of spiritual development (guṇasthāna).
Thus, the detailed exposition of existence has been stated.
The exposition of number is now stated.
It is twofold: general and specific.
In general, first of all, souls with false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) are infinite-infinite (*anantānanta*).

Those with right view with delusion (*sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi*), those with mixed right-and-wrong view (*samyagmithyādṛṣṭi*), those with right view but not yet restrained (*asaṃyatasamyagdṛṣṭi*), and those who are partially restrained (*saṃyatāsaṃyata*) are measured by an incalculable fraction (*asaṃkhyeyabhāga*) of a *palyopama*.
Those who are restrained but with negligence (*pramattasaṃyata*) are numbered in the range of several tens of millions (*koṭīpṛthaktva*).
"Distinctness" (*pṛthaktva*) is the designation in the scriptures for the interval above three *koṭis* and below nine [of the *sāgaropamas*]. The *apramattasaṃyata*s are numerable.
Regarding the four types of *upaśamaka*s, by way of entry, there is one, two, or three;
at most, forty-four.
Those who have arisen at their own time are countable.
At most, four *kṣapaka*s and *ayogakevalin*s enter [into liberation] simultaneously—either one, two, or three;
at the maximum, they number one hundred and eight.
Those who have attained perfection at their own time are countable.
Through the entry of those possessing both yoga and absolute knowledge (*sayogakevalin*), there may be one, two, or three;
at the maximum, they number one hundred and eight.
At their respective times, they arise in numbers reaching hundreds of thousands of distinct units.

Specifically, according to the enumeration of destinies (*gati*), in the destiny of hell, on the first earth, the hell-beings who hold wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) are incalculable; they measure incalculable series (*śreṇī*) and incalculable portions of a plane (*pratara*).
From the second up to the seventh [hell], the *mithyādṛṣṭis* (those with false views) are measured by an incalculable fraction (*asaṃkhyeyabhāga*) of the [total] series;
and that incalculable fraction consists of incalculable millions of millions of *yojanas*.

In all the earths, the *sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭis* (those with right view who have just descended), the *samyagmithyādṛṣṭis* (those with mixed right-and-wrong views), and the *asamyatasamyagdṛṣṭis* (those with right view but lacking self-restraint) are measured by an incalculable fraction of a *palyopama*.
Among the animals in the animal realm, those with false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) are infinite-infinite (*anantānanta*).

Those with right-views-inclination (*sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi*) and so forth, up to those who are partially restrained (*saṃyatāsaṃyata*), are measured by an incalculable fraction (*asaṃkhyeyabhāga*) of a *palyopama*.
In the human realm, humans with false views are measured by an incalculable fraction of a *śreṇī*.
And that incalculable portion consists of incalculable millions of millions of *yojanas*.
Those beginning with the right-viewed-in-attainment (*sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi*) and ending with the partially restrained (*saṃyatāsaṃyata*) are numerable.
The general number for those beginning with the negligent (*pramatta*) has already been stated.
In the realm of gods (*devagati*), those with false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) are as numerous as incalculable series (*śreṇi*), measured by an incalculable fraction of a plane (*pratara*).

Those with right view attained through subsidence (*sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi*), those with right-and-wrong view (*samyagmithyādṛṣṭi*), and those who are right-viewed but not restrained (*asaṃyatasamyagdṛṣṭi*) are measured by an incalculable fraction of a *palyopama*.
According to the enumeration by sense-faculties (*indriya-anuvāda*): those with one sense-faculty who possess false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) are infinite-infinite (*anantānanta*).

Those with two, three, and four sense-faculties are innumerable (*asaṃkhyeya*) rows (*śreṇi*), measuring a portion of an innumerable plane (*pratarāsaṃkhyeyabhāga*). Among those with five sense-faculties, those with false view are innumerable rows, measuring a portion of an innumerable plane.
From those with "attaining right view" (*sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi*) up to the "omniscient without activity" (*ayogakevalin*), their numbers are as stated generally.
According to the classification by body: those belonging to the earth-body, water-body, fire-body, and air-body are incalculable worlds;
those belonging to the plant-body are infinitely infinite.
The numerical measure of the mobile-bodied beings is like that of those possessing five sense-faculties.

According to the exposition of yoga, those with mental yoga and those with vocal yoga who hold wrong views are innumerable; they are measured by incalculable series (*śreṇi*) and an incalculable fraction of a plane (*pratara*).
The wrong-viewed souls among the body-yogis are infinite-infinite.

Among all three types of yogis, those beginning with the right-viewed-with-attenuation (sāsādana-samyagdṛṣṭi) and ending with the partially restrained (saṃyatāsaṃyata) are measured by an incalculable fraction of a *palyopama*.
Those beginning with the restrained-but-negligent (pramatta-saṃyata) and ending with the omniscient-with-yoga (sayoga-kevalin) are numerable.
The *ayogakevalins* have the number stated generally.

According to the enumeration of genders, those with female gender (*strīveda*) and male gender (*puṃveda*) who are of false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) are innumerable; they are measured by innumerable rows (*śreṇi*) and innumerable parts of a plane (*pratara*).
Those with the neuter gender and false view are infinite-infinite.

Those with the female gender and those with the neuter gender—beginning from the right-viewed-in-the-sense-of-falling-backward (sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi) up to the partially restrained (saṃyatāsaṃyata)—have the numbers as stated generally.
Those beginning from the careless restrained (pramattasaṃyata) up to the non-subtle-uninterrupted (anivṛttibādara) are numerable.

Those with male gender are those beginning from the right-viewed soul with subsidence (sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi) up to the stage of gross passion with cessation (nivṛttibādara), numbering as stated generally. Those free from gender are those beginning from gross passion without cessation (anivṛttibādara) up to the stage of the omniscient one without activity (ayogakevalin), numbering as stated generally.

With reference to the passions (*kaṣāya*), regarding anger, pride, and deceit, the categories beginning with false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and ending with the partially restrained (*saṃyatāsaṃyata*) have the number stated generally.
From the careless restrained (*pramattasaṃyata*) up to the non-subtle (*anivṛttibādara*), they are numerable (*saṃkhyeya*).
Regarding the passions of greed (*lobhakaṣāya*), the sequence is exactly as stated.
However, this is the distinction: those who are restrained with subtle passion (*sūkṣmasāṃparāyasaṃyata*) are as numerous as stated in the general enumeration.

Those free from passion (*akaṣāya*), beginning with those whose passions are suppressed (*upaśāntakaṣāya*) and ending with those who possess omniscience without activity (*ayogakevalin*), are as numerous as stated in the general enumeration.

In terms of knowledge, those with sensory-cognition-based ignorance (*matyajñānin*) and scriptural-cognition-based ignorance (*śrutājñānin*)—namely, the false-viewed (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and the right-viewed-in-attainment (*sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi*)—are of the number stated generally.
Those with distorted-cognition (*vibhaṅgajñānin*) who are false-viewed are innumerable *śreṇī*s, measured by an innumerable fraction of a *pratara*.
Those who are right-viewed-in-attainment are measured by an innumerable fraction of a *palyopama*.

Those possessing sensory knowledge (*mati-jñāna*) and scriptural knowledge (*śruta-jñāna*)—ranging from the unrestrained right-viewed (*asaṃyata-samyagdṛṣṭi*) up to those whose passions are exhausted (*kṣīṇakaṣāya*)—are of the number stated generally.

Those possessing clairvoyant knowledge (*avadhi-jñāna*)—the unrestrained right-viewed, the restrained-unrestrained (*saṃyatāsaṃyata*), and the restrained (*saṃyata*)—are of the number stated generally.
From the restrained-with-heedlessness (*pramatta-saṃyata*) up to those whose passions are exhausted, they are numerable (*saṃkhyeya*).

Those possessing mind-pervading knowledge (*manaḥparyaya-jñānin*)—ranging from the partially restrained with negligence (*pramatta-saṃyata*) up to those whose passions are exhausted (*kṣīṇakaṣāya*)—are numerable.
Those possessing omniscience (*kevala-jñānin*), both with activity (*sayoga*) and without activity (*ayoga*), have the numbers as stated generally.

With reference to restraint (*saṃyama*), the *sāmāyika* and *chedopasthāpana* pure restrained souls—ranging from the *pramatta* (negligent) up to the *anivṛttibādara* (subtle-passion-without-turning-back)—possess the number stated generally.
The *parihāraviśuddhi* pure restrained souls are both *pramatta* and *apramatta* (non-negligent), and they are numerable (*saṃkhyeya*).

The *sūkṣmasāmparāya* pure restrained souls, the *yathākhyāta-vihāra-śuddhi* pure restrained souls, the restrained-unrestrained (*saṃyatāsaṃyata*), and the unrestrained (*asaṃyata*) possess the number stated generally.

According to the enumeration by vision (*darśana*), those with eye-vision (*cakṣurdarśanin*) who hold false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) are incalculable in number, measuring an incalculable fraction of a *pratara*.
Those without eye-vision (*acakṣurdarśanin*) who hold false views are infinitely infinite (*anantānanta*).
Both [categories]—beginning with the *sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi* and ending with those whose *kaṣāyas* are exhausted—possess the numbers stated generally.
Those possessing *avadhidarśana* are like those possessing *avadhijñāna*; those possessing *kevaladarśana* are like those possessing *kevalajñāna*.

By way of the *leśyās*: those with black (*kṛṣṇa*), blue (*nīla*), and grey (*kāpota*) *leśyās* range from the false-viewed (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) up to the unrestrained right-viewed (*asaṃyata-samyagdṛṣṭi*), and their numbers are as stated generally.
Those with fiery (*tejas*) and lotus (*padma*) *leśyās* range from the false-viewed up to the restrained-unrestrained (*saṃyatāsaṃyata*), like those of the female gender (*strīveda*).
Among them, the restrained ones who are either negligent (*pramatta*) or non-negligent (*apramatta*) are numerable (*saṃkhyeya*).
Those with white *leśyā*, from those with false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) up to the partially restrained (*saṃyatāsaṃyata*), are measured by an incalculable fraction of a *palyopama*.
The careless (*pramatta*) and non-careless (*apramatta*) restrained are numerable.
Those from the stage of unprecedented action (*apūrvakaraṇa*) up to the omniscient with activity (*sayogakevalin*), as well as those without *leśyā* (*aleśya*), have the numbers stated generally.

With reference to those capable of liberation (bhavya), among the capable souls, the categories beginning with wrong view (mithyādṛṣṭi) and ending with the omniscient without activity (ayogakevalin) have the numbers stated generally. Those incapable of liberation (abhavya) are infinite.

According to the classification by rightness (*samyaktva*), among those with right vision that is exhaustively destroyed (*kṣāyika-samyagdṛṣṭi*), the partially restrained with right vision (*asaṃyata-samyagdṛṣṭi*) are measured by an incalculable fraction of a *palyopama*.
Those from the restrained-and-unrestrained (*saṃyatāsaṃyata*) up to those whose passions are subsided (*upaśāntakaṣāya*) are numerable.
There are four types of *kṣapaka*s: those with *sayoga-kevala* (omniscience with activity) and those with *ayoga-kevala* (omniscience without activity), whose numbers are as stated generally.

Among those with *kṣāyopaśamika-samyaktva* (right vision through subsidence-cum-destruction), from the *asaṃyata-samyagdṛṣṭi* (right-viewed non-restrained) up to the *apramatta* (diligent), their numbers are as stated generally.

Among those with *aupaśamika-samyaktva* (right vision through subsidence), the *asaṃyata-samyagdṛṣṭi*s and the *saṃyatāsaṃyata*s (restrained-non-restrained) are measured by an incalculable fraction of a *palyopama*.
The partially restrained and the fully restrained who are heedless or not heedless are numerable.
The four types of those characterized by subsidence have the numbers stated generally.
Those with right vision accompanied by delusion, those with right-and-wrong vision, and those with wrong vision also have the numbers stated generally.

By way of restating the designations (saṃjñā), among those possessing designations, [the categories] beginning with wrong view (mithyādṛṣṭi) and ending with those whose passions are exhausted (kṣīṇakaṣāya) are like those with visual perception (cakṣurdarśin).
Among those without designations, those with wrong view are infinite-infinite.
Those devoid of both designations have the number stated generally.

With reference to the enumeration of those who possess nourishment (*āhāraka*), from those with wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) up to those possessing omniscience with activity (*sayogakevalin*), they have the number stated generally.
Among those who do not take food, those with wrong view, those with right view accompanied by delusion, and those with right view who are unrestrained have the numbers stated generally.
Those who are omniscient with active yoga are numerable. Those who are omniscient without yoga have the numbers stated generally.
The enumeration has been determined.
The field is now being explained.
That [obstruction] is twofold: by way of generality and by way of particularity.
First, by way of generality: for those with false views, it is the entire world;
for those from the stage of "attaining right view" up to the "omniscient ones without activity" (ayogakevalin), it is an incalculable fraction of the world.

For those with complete omniscience while still in the state of embodied existence (*sayogakevalin*), [the space occupied] is an innumerable part of the world, or innumerable parts of the world, or the entire world.

Specifically, according to the classification by destiny (*gati*): in the hellish destiny, on all the earths, for the denizens of hell in the four stages of spiritual development (*guṇasthāna*), [the space occupied] is an innumerable part of the world.

In the animal realm, the field for animals—ranging from those with wrong view up to those who are partially restrained—is as generally stated. In the human realm, for humans ranging from those with wrong view up to those possessing ayoga-kevala-jñāna, the field is an innumerable part of the universe. For those possessing yoga-kevala-jñāna, the field is as generally stated. In the celestial realm, for all gods across the four spiritual stages (guṇasthānas), the field is an innumerable part of the universe.
According to the enumeration of faculties (*indriya*), the field of those with one faculty is the entire world. The field of those with incomplete faculties is an incalculable fraction of the world.
Regarding the five faculties, it is like that of humans.
According to the classification by body, the entire world constitutes the realm for those ranging from the earth-body up to the plant-body.
For those belonging to the mobile class [of beings], it is like that of those possessing five sense-faculties.

According to the exposition of yoga, for those possessing yoga of speech and mind—ranging from those with false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) up to those with pure yoga (*sayogakevalin*)—it is an incalculable fraction of the world.

For those possessing the yoga of the body—ranging from those with false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) up to those with omniscience accompanied by activity (*sayogakevalin*), as well as those without activity (*ayogakevalin*)—the field is that which has been stated generally.

According to the enumeration of the genders, for those with female and male gender (*strī-puṃveda*) ranging from false view up to the "not-yet-returned-to-subtlety" (*anivṛttibādara*) stage, it is an innumerable part of the world (*loka*).

For those with neuter gender-feeling (*napuṃsakaveda*)—ranging from those with wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) up to those at the stage of non-refinement (*anivṛttibādara*)—and for those who have eliminated gender-feeling (*apagataveda*), the field is as stated generally.

According to the enumeration of passions (*kaṣāya*): for those with the passions of anger, pride, and deceit—from those with wrong view up to those at the stage of non-refinement—as well as for those with the passion of greed, for those at the stage of subtle-passion (*sūkṣmasāṃparāya*), and for those without passions (*akaṣāya*), the field is as stated generally.

In terms of knowledge (*jñāna*), the field for those with sensory cognition (*matyajñānin*) and scriptural cognition (*śrutājñānin*) who possess either false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) or the right view of the approaching stage (*sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi*) is as stated generally. For those with divided cognition (*vibhaṅgajñānin*) who possess either false view or the right view of the approaching stage, it is an incalculable fraction (*asaṃkhyeyabhāga*) of the world-system (*loka*).

The field as generally described applies to those possessing sensory knowledge (ābhinibodhika), scriptural knowledge (śruta), and clairvoyant knowledge (avadhi)—ranging from the undisciplined with right view (asaṃyata-samyagdṛṣṭi) up to those whose passions are exhausted (kṣīṇakaṣāya); to those possessing mental-paryaya knowledge (manaḥparyaya-jñāna)—ranging from the negligent (pramatta) up to those whose passions are exhausted; and to those possessing omniscience (kevala-jñāna), both while still in possession of the physical body (sayoga) and when free from it (ayoga). § 68.

By way of reference to restraint (*saṃyama*), the field previously mentioned in general applies to the four types of pure-restrained souls (*śuddhi-saṃyata*)—namely, those with equanimity (*sāmāyika*), those with re-establishment (*chedopasthāpanā*), those with purity through avoidance (*parihāraviśuddhi*), and those who are either *pramatta* or *apramatta*; to the pure-restrained souls with subtle-passion (*sūkṣmasāṃparāya*); to the four types of pure-restrained souls abiding in the state of perfect conduct (*yathākhyāta-vihāra*); to the partially restrained (*saṃyatāsaṃyata*); and to the four types of unrestrained (*asaṃyata*).

By way of reference to vision (*darśana*), for those possessing visual vision (*cakṣurdarśanin*), from those with wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) up to those whose passions are exhausted (*kṣīṇakaṣāya*), the field is an innumerable part of the world.
For those with non-visual perception (acakṣurdarśana), from those with false view up to those whose passions are exhausted (kṣīṇakaṣāya), the field is as generally stated.
For those with limited perception (avadhidarśana), it is like that for those with limited knowledge (avadhijñāna).
For those with perfect perception (kevaladarśana), it is like that for those with perfect knowledge (kevalajñāna).

According to the enumeration by *leśyā*: for those with black (*kṛṣṇa*), blue (*nīla*), and grey (*kāpota*) *leśyās*, ranging from those with false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) up to those who are non-restrained right-viewed (*asaṃyata-samyagdṛṣṭi*), the field is as stated generally.

For those with fiery (*tejas*) and lotus (*padma*) *leśyās*, ranging from those with false view up to those who are non-negligent (*apramatta*), it is an incalculable fraction (*asaṃkhyeyabhāga*) of the world.
For those with white leśyā, ranging from the false-viewed to those whose passions are exhausted (kṣīṇakaṣāya), the space is an incalculable fraction of the world.
For those who are omniscient yet still possessed of activity (sayogakevalin) and for those without leśyā, the field is as previously stated in general.
By way of restating the category of those capable [of liberation], the field common to the fourteen types of those capable has been stated;
for those incapable, it is the entire world.

With reference to rightness (*samyaktva*): for those with right vision that is kṣāyika—ranging from the non-restrained right-viewed (*asaṃyata-samyagdṛṣṭi*) up to the omniscient without activity (*ayogakevalin*)—and for those with right vision that is kṣāyopaśamika—ranging from the non-restrained right-viewed up to the non-negligent (*apramatta*)—and for those with right vision that is aupaśamika—ranging from the non-restrained right-viewed up to the one whose passions are pacified (*upaśāntakaṣāya*)—and for those with false-right vision (*sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi*), those with mixed vision (*samyagmithyādṛṣṭi*), and those with wrong vision (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), the field is as stated generally.
With reference to ideation (*saṃjñā*): for those possessing ideation (*saṃjñin*), it is like [the case of] visual perception (*cakṣurdarśana*).
The entire world consists of those who are without perception. For those who are devoid of both designations, the field is that which has been described in general terms.

With respect to the classification by nutriment (*āhāra*), the field for those who take nutriment—ranging from those with wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) up to those whose passions are exhausted (*kṣīṇakaṣāya*)—is as generally stated.
For those with vibratory omniscience (*sayogakevalin*), it is an incalculable fraction of the universe (*loka*).

For those who do not take nutriment—namely, those with wrong view, those with the right view of the approaching stage (*sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi*), those with the right view of the unrestrained stage (*asaṃyatasamyagdṛṣṭi*), and those with vibratory omniscience—the field is as generally stated.
For those possessing omniscience while still in the state of embodied existence (sayogakevalins), the space occupied is either an incalculable number of parts of the universe or the entire universe.
Thus, the determination of their spatial extent is completed.
Contact is being explained.
It is of two kinds: general and specific.
First, in its general sense, the entire world is touched by those with wrong views.

For those with right view who are still in the state of progression (*sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi*), [the space occupied] is an incalculable fraction of the world, or eight, twelve, or fourteen parts minus a small portion.

For those with right-and-wrong view (*samyagmithyādṛṣṭi*) and for those with right view who are not yet restrained (*asaṃyatasamyagdṛṣṭi*), [the space occupied] is an incalculable fraction of the world, or eight or fourteen parts minus a small portion.
For those who are partially restrained (*saṃyatāsaṃyata*), [the space occupied] is an incalculable fraction of the world, or six parts of fourteen minus a small portion.
The contact [of the soul] for those ranging from the *pramattasaṃyata* (the heedful self-restrained) up to the *ayogakevalin* (the kevalin without yoga) is like that of the field (*kṣetra*).

Specifically, according to the classification by *gati* (destiny), in the hellish destiny, on the first earth (*pṛthivī*), a portion of the world (*loka*) equal to an innumerable part (*asaṃkhyeyabhāga*) is touched by the hell-beings belonging to the four stages of spiritual development (*guṇasthāna*).

In the second and subsequent [levels], prior to the seventh, by means of wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and the right view of those who have attained the state of "entering the stream" (*sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi*), an incalculable fraction (*asaṃkhyeyabhāga*) of the world is occupied—specifically one, two, three, four, or five parts, or fourteen parts less a fraction.

By means of the mixed right-and-wrong view (*samyangmithyādṛṣṭi*) and the right view of those who are not yet self-restrained (*asaṃyatasamyagdṛṣṭi*), an incalculable fraction of the world is occupied.
On the seventh earth (*pṛthivī*), by means of wrong view, an incalculable fraction of the world is occupied—specifically six parts out of fourteen, or fourteen parts less a fraction.
By the remaining three [categories], an incalculable fraction of the world is touched.
In the animal realm, the entire world is touched by animals with wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
By those with right view who are in the state of "entering the stream" (*sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi*), an incalculable fraction of the world is touched, or seven-fourteenths minus a portion.
By those with right and wrong views, an incalculable fraction of the world is touched.

By those with right view who are neither restrained nor unrestrained, and by those who are both restrained and unrestrained, an incalculable fraction of the world is touched, or six-fourteenth parts minus a portion.
Within the human realm, by humans with wrong views, an incalculable fraction of the world is touched, or the entire world is touched.

For those with right vision while still subject to downfall (*sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi*), the contact is an incalculable part of the world or seven-fourteenths less a portion. For those from those with right-and-wrong vision (*samyagmithyādṛṣṭi*) up to those with perfect knowledge and activity (*ayogakevalin*), the contact is like that of the [right] field.
In the celestial realm, for the gods who possess wrong vision or right vision while subject to downfall, the contact is an incalculable part of the world or eight or nine-fourteenths less a portion.
By those with right view, wrong view, and those who are unrestrained yet possess right view, an incalculable fraction of the world is touched, or eight-fourteenths less a portion.
According to the enumeration of faculties, the entire world is touched by those with a single faculty.
By those with deficient faculties, an incalculable portion of the world or the entire world [is touched].
Among those with five faculties, by those with wrong view, an incalculable portion of the world or eight-fourteenths—or slightly less than the entire world—is touched.
For the remaining [faculties], the contact is as stated generally.
According to the classification by body, the entire world is touched by those belonging to the stationary bodies;
for those belonging to the mobile bodies, there is contact through the possession of five sense faculties.

According to the enumeration by yoga, for those possessing yoga of speech and mind who hold false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), the contact is either an incalculable fraction of the world, or eight-fourteenths less a part, or the entire world.
For those beginning with the *sāsādana-samyagdṛṣṭi* up to those whose passions are exhausted (*kṣīṇakaṣāya*), the contact is as stated generally.
For those with vibrational omniscience (sayogakevalins), the space touched is an innumerable part of the universe (loka).

For those with physical vibration (kāyayogins)— ranging from those with wrong view up to those with vibrational omniscience— as well as for those without vibration (ayogakevalins), the space touched is as stated generally.

By those with wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) who possess the female, male, or neuter sexual dispositions (*strī-puṃ-veda*), an incalculable fraction (*asaṃkhyeya-bhāga*) of the world is touched, or eight or fourteen parts minus a fraction, or the entire world. By those with right view with fallibility (*sāsādana-samyagdṛṣṭi*), an incalculable fraction of the world is touched, or eight or nine parts minus a fraction.
For those from the stage of right view with fallibility up to the stage of non-refinement of gross passions (*anivṛtti-bādara*), the contact is as stated generally.
Regarding those with neuter gender, the contact for those with wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and those with the view of rightness-inclination (*sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi*) is as stated generally.
For those with right-and-wrong view (*samyagmithyādṛṣṭi*), it is an incalculable fraction (*asaṃkhyeyabhāga*) of the world.

For those with unrestrained right view (*asaṃyatasamyagdṛṣṭi*) and those who are restrained-unrestrained (*saṃyatāsaṃyata*), it is an incalculable fraction of the world, or six-fourteenths minus one part.
For those from the stage of the negligent up to the end of the subtle-passion (bādarānivṛtti) who are free from gender-attachment (vedas), the contact is as stated generally.
According to the enumeration of passions (kaṣāya), for those with the four passions and for those without passions, the contact is as stated generally.

In terms of knowledge (*jñāna*), the contact (*sparśana*) for those with sensory ignorance (*matyajñānin*) and scriptural ignorance (*śrutājñānin*)—namely, the false-viewed (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and those with right view who have not yet attained stability (*sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi*)—is as stated generally.
For those with deluded knowledge (*vibhaṅgajñānin*) who hold false views, it is an incalculable fraction of the world, or eight or fourteen parts less a portion, or the entire world.
The contact of those with right view who are in the state of "attaining" (sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi) is as stated generally.

The contact of those possessing sensory knowledge (ābhinibodhika), scriptural knowledge (śruta), clairvoyance (avadhi), mental clairvoyance (manaḥparyaya), and perfect knowledge (kevalajñāna) is as stated generally.
By way of reference to restraint (*saṃyama*), the contact common to all—whether restrained, partially restrained, or unrestrained—is stated.

By way of reference to vision (*darśana*), for those possessing visual vision (*cakṣurdarśanin*) ranging from those with wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) up to those whose passions are exhausted (*kṣīṇakaṣāya*), it is like that of five-sensed beings.

Regarding those with non-visual perception (*acakṣurdarśanin*), from those with wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) up to those whose passions are exhausted (*kṣīṇakaṣāya*), as well as those with pure visual perception (*kevaladarśanin*), the contact is as stated generally.
According to the enumeration of *leśyās*, the entire world is touched by those with wrong view who possess black, blue, or grey *leśyās*.

For those with right view who are still in the state of attainment (*sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi*), [the space occupied] is an incalculable fraction of the world, or five, four, or two parts of fourteen minus a small portion.
For those with wrong view and those with right view who are not yet restrained (*asaṃyatasamyagdṛṣṭi*), it is an incalculable fraction of the world.

For those with fiery radiance (*tejoleśya*) who have wrong view or are in the state of attainment, it is an incalculable fraction of the world, or eight, nine, or [up to] fourteen parts minus a small portion.
By those with right view, wrong view, and those who are neither restrained nor unrestrained, there is an incalculable fraction of the world, or eight-fourteenths less a portion.

By those who are both restrained and unrestrained, there is an incalculable fraction of the world, or one and a half fourteenths less a portion. By those who are negligent and those who are not negligent, there is an incalculable fraction of the world.

Those with *padmaleśyā* (lotus-leśyā), from those with false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) up to those who are partially restrained with right view (*asaṃyatasamyagdṛṣṭi*), occupy an innumerable fraction of the world, or eight fourteenth-parts minus a fraction. Those who are partially restrained and fully restrained (*saṃyatāsaṃyata*) occupy an innumerable fraction of the world, or five fourteenth-parts minus a fraction. Those who are negligent (*pramatta*) and non-negligent (*apramatta*) occupy an innumerable fraction of the world.

For those with white *leśyā*, ranging from the false-viewed (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) up to the partially restrained (*saṃyatāsaṃyata*), the contact is an incalculable fraction of the world, or six, fourteen, or slightly less than fourteen parts.
For those from the careless (*pramatta*) up to the omniscient with active yoga (*sayogakevalin*), as well as for those without *leśyā* (*aleśya*), the contact is as stated generally.

By way of restating the possibility [of attainment], the general contact previously mentioned applies to those capable [of liberation], ranging from those with wrong view up to those possessing omniscience free from attachment (*ayogakevalin*).
By those incapable [of liberation], the entire world is contacted.

With reference to rightness (*samyaktva*), that which was stated generally applies to those with right vision resulting from destruction (*kṣāyika-samyagdṛṣṭi*), ranging from the undeveloped right-visioned (*asaṃyata-samyagdṛṣṭi*) up to the omniscient ones who have ceased all activity (*ayogakevalin*).
However, for those who are partially restrained (*saṃyatāsaṃyata*), it is an incalculable fraction of the world (*loka*).
That which was stated generally also applies to those with right vision resulting from subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣāyopaśamika-samyagdṛṣṭi*).

For those with right view through subsidence (*aupaśamika-samyaktva*) who are unrestrained yet possess right view (*asaṃyata-samyagdṛṣṭi*), that which was stated generally applies. For the remaining categories—namely, those with right view through attainment (*sāsādana-samyagdṛṣṭi*), those with right-and-wrong view (*samyagmithyādṛṣṭi*), and those with wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*)—that which was stated generally applies.
As for the rest of the world, it is an incalculable fraction (*asaṃkhyeya-bhāga*).
For those with right view through attainment, right-and-wrong view, and wrong view, that which was stated generally applies.
By way of restating the designations (saṃjñā), [the state of] those possessing designations is like the seeing with the eye.
The entire world is touched by those who are without designations (asaṃjñin).
For those who are devoid of both designations, that which was stated generally applies.
By way of restating the types of nourishment, for those who possess nourishment—ranging from those with false view up to those whose passions are exhausted—that which was stated generally applies.
For those with complete omniscience while still in a state of physical activity (sayogakevalins), it is an incalculable fraction of the universe.
Among those who do not take food (anāhārakas), the entire universe is touched by those with wrong view (mithyādṛṣṭis).
By those with right view but prone to regression (sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭis), it is an incalculable fraction of the universe, or eleven or fourteen parts minus a portion.
For those with right view who are not yet self-restrained (asaṃyata-samyagdṛṣṭi), [the space occupied] is an innumerable part of the world, or six or fourteen parts minus a fraction.
For those possessing perfect knowledge while still in union with matter (sayogakevalin), it is an innumerable part of the world or the entire world.
For those who have attained perfect knowledge without the union of matter (ayogakevalin), it is an innumerable part of the world.
Contact has been explained.
Now, time is being introduced.
It is of two kinds: general and specific.
First, generally speaking, with respect to false view (mithyādṛṣṭi), it exists at all times in relation to multiple living beings (nānājīva).
In relation to a single living being (ekajīva), there are three permutations (bhaṅga).

[It is] beginningless and endless, beginningless but with an end, and with both a beginning and an end. Among these, that which has both a beginning and an end is, at minimum, an antarmuhūrta; at maximum, it is slightly less than half a pudgalaparivarta.
With respect to multiple living beings (*nānājīva*), the minimum duration for a right view with partial realization (*sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi*) is one moment;
the maximum is an incalculable fraction of a *palyopama*.
With respect to a single living being (*ekajīva*), the minimum is one moment.
At the maximum, it lasts for six āvalikās.
For a right-wrong view (*samyagmithyādṛṣṭi*), with respect to various living beings (*nānājīva*), the minimum duration is one antarmuhūrta;
at the maximum, it is an incalculable fraction (*asaṃkhyeyabhāga*) of a *palyopama*.
For a single soul, both the minimum and maximum duration is one antarmuhūrta.
For an uncontrolled right-viewed being (asaṃyata-samyagdṛṣṭi), with respect to multiple souls, the duration is the entire period of time;
for a single soul, it is at least one antarmuhūrta.
At the maximum, it is slightly more than thirty-three sāgaropamas.
For one who is both restrained and unrestrained, with respect to all living beings, the duration is for all time;
with respect to a single being, the minimum is an antarmuhūrta.
At its maximum, it is slightly less than a *pūrvakoṭī*.
