With respect to various beings, both those who are heedless and those who are heedful, it exists at all times.
With respect to a single being, at its minimum, it is one moment.
At the maximum, it is an antarmuhūrta.

For the four types of upaśamakas, with respect to various living beings (*nānājīva*) and with respect to a single living being (*ekajīva*), it is at the minimum one moment (*samaya*) and at the maximum an antarmuhūrta.
For the four types of *kṣapaka*s and for the *ayogakevalins*, both the minimum and maximum duration—considering multiple souls as well as a single soul—is one *antarmuhūrta*.
For *sayogakevalins*, considering multiple souls, it is for all time;
with respect to a single soul, the minimum is one *antarmuhūrta*.
At its maximum, it is slightly less than a *pūrvakoṭī*.

Specifically, according to the enumeration of destinies (*gati*), among hell-beings in the hellish destiny across the seven earths, for one with wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), it is for all time when considering various individual beings (*nānājīva*).
With respect to a single soul, the minimum duration is one antarmuhūrta.
At the maximum, it is respectively one, three, seven, ten, seventeen, twenty-two, and thirty-three sāgaropamas.
For the sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi and the samyagmithyādṛṣṭi, the duration is as stated generally.
For one with right view who is not yet self-restrained, [the duration] is at all times when considering various living beings.
With respect to a single living being, it is at minimum an antarmuhūrta;
at maximum, it is exactly as stated for the highest [duration], minus a fraction.
In the animal realm, for animals with wrong view, [the duration] is at all times when considering multiple beings;
with respect to a single being, it is at minimum one antarmuhūrta.
At the maximum, it is an infinite duration consisting of incalculable *pudgalaparivartas*.

The time stated generally applies to those with right view of the approaching stage (*sāsādana-samyagdṛṣṭi*), those with right-and-wrong view (*samyagmithyādṛṣṭi*), and those who are restrained-unrestrained (*saṃyatāsaṃyata*).
For one with right view who is unrestrained (*asaṃyata-samyagdṛṣṭi*), considering all individual souls (*nānājīva*), the duration is for all time.
With respect to a single soul, the minimum duration is one antarmuhūrta;
the maximum is three palyopamas.
In the human realm, among humans, with respect to wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) from the perspective of various living beings (*nānājīva*), it exists at all times.
With respect to a single living being (*ekajīva*), the minimum duration is one *antarmuhūrta*;
the maximum is three *palyopamas* increased by a plurality of *pūrvakoṭīs*.
With respect to multiple souls, the duration of the right-viewed-in-attainment (sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi) is, at minimum, one moment and,
at maximum, an antarmuhūrta. With respect to a single soul, it is, at minimum, one moment.
At the maximum, it is six āvalikās.

For right-cum-wrong view (samyagmithyādṛṣṭi), with respect to various living beings (nānājīva) and with respect to a single living being (ekajīva), both the minimum and the maximum duration is one antarmuhūrta.
For the partially restrained right-viewed (asaṃyatasamyagdṛṣṭi), with respect to various living beings, it is for all time.
With respect to a single soul, the minimum duration is an antarmuhūrta;
the maximum is slightly more than three palyopamas.
For the remaining [karmas], the duration is as stated generally.
In the celestial realm, among the gods, for one with wrong view, [the duration] in relation to various living beings is at all times;
with respect to a single living being, it is at minimum an antarmuhūrta.
At the maximum, it is thirty-one sāgaropamas.
The duration for the sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi and the samyagmithyādṛṣṭi is as stated generally.
For the asaṃyatasamyagdṛṣṭi, with respect to multiple living beings (nānājīva), the duration is all time.
With respect to a single soul, the minimum is an antarmuhūrta;
the maximum is thirty-three sāgaropamas.
According to the enumeration of the sense-faculties (*indriya*), for those with one sense-faculty, with respect to various living beings, it is all time.
With respect to a single living being, at the minimum it is the duration of a minor birth;
at the maximum, it is an infinite period of incalculable *pudgala-parivartas*.
For those with deficient sense-faculties, the duration is all time when considering various living beings;
for a single being, it is at minimum a minor birth and at maximum a countable number of thousands of years.

Regarding the five sense-faculties (*pañcendriya*), for false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), from the perspective of various living beings (*nānājīva*), it exists for all time. With respect to a single being (*ekajīva*), at the minimum it lasts for an antarmuhūrta;
at the maximum, it lasts for a thousand *sāgaropama* plus several tens of millions of years (*pūrvakoṭī*).
For the remaining [beings], the time is as stated generally.

According to the classification by body (*kāya*), for those belonging to the bodies of earth, water, fire, and air, the time is all time (*sarvakāla*) with respect to various individual lives (*nānājīva*).
With respect to a single living being, the minimum is the duration of a minor birth; the maximum is incalculable world-ages (*asaṃkhyeya-loka*),
as is the case for one-sensed beings belonging to the vegetable body (*vanaspati-kāyika*).
Among the mobile-bodied beings, for one with wrong view, the duration is all time when considering various living beings.
With respect to a single living being, it is at minimum an antarmuhūrta;
at maximum, two thousand *sāgaropamas* plus a plurality of *pūrvakoṭīs*.
The remaining [categories] are like those of the five senses.

According to the enumeration by yoga, among those possessing speech and mind—namely, those with wrong view, the uncontrolled, those with right view who are neither controlled nor uncontrolled, the controlled, the careless, the non-careless, and the embodied omniscients (sayogakevalins)—with respect to multiple living beings, [this duration] exists at all times.
With respect to a single soul, the minimum duration is one moment (*samaya*), and the maximum is an antarmuhūrta.

For the right view with delusion (*sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi*), the duration is as stated generally; for the right-and-wrong view (*samyagmithyādṛṣṭi*), with respect to multiple souls, the minimum is one moment.
At the maximum, it is an incalculable fraction of a *palyopama*. With respect to a single living being, at the minimum it is one moment;
at the maximum, it is an *antarmuhūrta*.

For the four types of suppressors (upaśamaka) and destroyers (kṣapaka), with respect to multiple living beings (*nānājīva*) and with respect to a single living being (*ekajīva*), the minimum duration is one moment (*ekasamaya*). The maximum is an antarmuhūrta.
Among those possessing bodily yoga (*kāyayogin*), for the false-viewed (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), with respect to multiple living beings, it lasts for all time.

With respect to a single living being, the minimum duration is one moment; the maximum is an infinite time consisting of incalculable cycles of matter (pudgalaparivarta). For the remaining [yogas], it is the same as for the mental yoga (manoyoga).
Like [the duration] of those without yoga (*ayoga*), it is common to all.
According to the recitation of the Vedas, with respect to female gender (*strīveda*) and false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), from the perspective of various living beings (*nānājīva*), it is for all time.
With respect to a single soul, the minimum duration is an antarmuhūrta;
the maximum is a few hundred palyopamas.
For those beginning with the sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi and ending with the anivṛttibādara, the duration is as stated generally.
However, for the unrestrained right-viewed being (*asaṃyata-samyagdṛṣṭi*), with respect to all living beings (*nānājīva*), it is for all time.
With respect to a single living being (*ekajīva*), it is at minimum one *antarmuhūrta* and at maximum slightly less than fifty-five *palyopamas*.
Regarding the male gender, for a wrong view (mithyādṛṣṭi), considering multiple living beings (nānājīva), the duration is all time.
For a single being (ekajīva), it is at minimum an antarmuhūrta and at maximum several hundreds of sāgaropamas.
The duration for those from the *sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi* up to the *anivṛttibādara* stage is as stated generally.
Regarding the neuter gender, for a *mithyādṛṣṭi*, the duration in relation to multiple living beings (*nānājīva*) is the entire period;
with respect to a single living being (*ekajīva*), it is at minimum one *antarmuhūrta*.
At the maximum, the duration is infinite, consisting of incalculable *pudgalaparivartas*.
This is the same for those from the *sāsādana-samyagdṛṣṭi* up to the *anivṛtti-bādara*.
However, with respect to all individual souls (*nānājīva*), the duration for the *asaṃyata-samyagdṛṣṭi* is the entirety of time.
With respect to a single soul, the minimum duration is one antarmuhūrta;
the maximum is thirty-three sāgaropamas less a fraction.
For those who have transcended the passions (apagatavedas), it is as in the general case.

According to the classification by *kaṣāyas*, the duration for those with the four *kaṣāyas*—from those with wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) up to those who are *apramatta*—is like that of those with mental activity (*manoyogi*).

For the two types of *upaśamaka* (suppression-attainers), the two types of *kṣapaka* (destruction-attainers), those with only greed (*lobha*), and those without *kaṣāyas*, the duration is as stated generally above.

In terms of knowledge, for those with sensory-cognition-based ignorance (*matyajñānin*) and scriptural-ignorance-based ignorance (*śrutājñānin*), it is as in the general case for the wrong-viewed (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and the right-viewed-with-attachment (*sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi*).
For those with distorted cognition (*vibhaṅgajñānin*), from the perspective of multiple living beings (*nānājīva*), it is all time for the wrong-viewed.
With respect to a single soul, the minimum duration is one antarmuhūrta;
the maximum is thirty-three sāgaropamas less a fraction.
For the sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi, the duration is as stated generally.

The duration for those possessing sensory knowledge (*ābhinibodhika*), scriptural knowledge (*śruta*), clairvoyance (*avadhi*), mind-reading knowledge (*manaḥparyaya*), and omniscience (*kevalajñāna*) has been stated in general terms.

With reference to restraint (*saṃyama*), the duration stated in general terms applies to the four types of restrained ones—those with total restraint (*sāmāyika*), those with occasional restraint (*chedopasthāpana*), those with purity through careful movement (*parihāraviśuddhi*), and those with subtle passion (*sūkṣmasāṃparāya*)—as well as to those who are partially restrained (*saṃyatāsaṃyata*) and those who are unrestrained (*asaṃyata*).

According to the exposition by way of vision (*darśana*), among those possessing visual perception (*cakṣurdarśin*), with respect to all living beings (*nānājīva*), [the duration] for wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) is all time.
With respect to a single living being (*ekajīva*), it is at minimum one antarmuhūrta.
At the maximum, it is two thousand *sāgaropamas*.
For those beginning with the *sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi* and ending with the *kṣīṇakaṣāya*, the duration is as stated generally.
Among those with non-visual perception (*acakṣurdarśana*), for those beginning with the *mithyādṛṣṭi* and ending with the *kṣīṇakaṣāya*, the duration is as stated generally.
For those possessing limited and complete perception, it is like [the duration] for those possessing limited and complete knowledge.
According to the enumeration of *leśyās*, for a false believer (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) within the black, blue, and grey *leśyās*, with respect to multiple living beings (*nānājīva*), the time is all time.
With respect to a single soul, the minimum duration is one antarmuhūrta;
the maximum is slightly more than thirty-three, seventeen, and seven sāgaropamas respectively.
For the sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi and samyaṅmithyādṛṣṭi, the duration is as stated generally.
For one with right view who is not yet self-restrained (*asaṃyata-samyagdṛṣṭi*), considering all living beings, the duration is for all time.
With respect to a single being, it is at minimum an *antarmuhūrta*,
and at maximum slightly less than thirty-three, seventeen, and seven *sāgaropamas* respectively.

For the *tejas* and *padma* leśyās, in relation to false-viewed (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and unrestrained-right-viewed (*asaṃyata-samyagdṛṣṭi*) souls respectively, the duration is all time when considering multiple souls (*nānājīva*).
With respect to a single soul (*ekajīva*), it is at minimum one *antarmuhūrta*;
at maximum, two *sāgaropamas* and eighteen *sāgaropamas* plus a fraction more.
The duration for those with right view while falling away (sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi) and those with right-and-wrong view (samyagmithyādṛṣṭi) is as stated generally.

For those who are partially restrained (saṃyatāsaṃyata), those who are negligent (pramatta), and those who are non-negligent (apramatta), the duration, in relation to multiple souls (nānājīva), is all time;
with respect to a single soul (ekajīva), it is at least one moment (samaya).
At the maximum, it is an antarmuhūrta.
For those with white leśyā who hold wrong views, with respect to multiple living beings, the duration is the entire period of time;
with respect to a single living being, it is at the minimum an antarmuhūrta.
At the maximum, it is slightly more than thirty-one sāgaropamas.
For those beginning with the *sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi* and ending with the *sayogakevalin*, as well as for those without *leśyā*, the duration is as stated generally.
However, regarding the *saṃyatāsaṃyata* (the partially restrained), the entire duration is in reference to multiple living beings (*nānājīva*).
With respect to a single living being, the minimum duration is one moment;
the maximum is an antarmuhūrta.
With reference to those capable [of liberation], regarding the false view among the capable, from the perspective of multiple living beings (*nānājīva*), it exists for all time.
From the perspective of a single living being (*ekajīva*), there are two possibilities: beginningless with an end, and having a beginning and an end.
Among these, that which has a beginning and an end is at its minimum one *antarmuhūrta*.
At the maximum, it is slightly less than half a pudgala-parivarta.
This is the general duration stated for those beginning with the *sāsādana-samyagdṛṣṭi* up to the *ayogakevalin*.
For those who are incapable of liberation (*abhavya*), it is without beginning and without end.

With reference to rightness (*samyaktva*), the time for those with right vision resulting from destruction (*kṣāyika-samyagdṛṣṭi*)—ranging from the unrestrained right-viewed (*asaṃyata-samyagdṛṣṭi*) up to the omniscient without activity (*ayoga-kevalin*)—is as stated generally.
The time for the four types of those with right vision resulting from subsidence and destruction (*kṣāyopaśamika-samyagdṛṣṭi*) is also as stated generally.

Regarding the states of right view through subsidence (*aupaśamika-samyaktva*), for the categories of the unrestrained right-viewed (*asaṃyata-samyagdṛṣṭi*) and the restrained-unrestrained (*saṃyatāsaṃyata*), with respect to multiple living beings (*nānājīva*), the minimum duration is one antarmuhūrta;
the maximum is an incalculable fraction of a *palyopama*.
With respect to a single living being (*ekajīva*), both the minimum and the maximum are one antarmuhūrta.

For the two [stages of] the careless and the careful, and for the four types of those practicing subsidence, with respect to multiple living beings as well as a single living being, the minimum duration is one moment (*samaya*),
and the maximum is an antarmuhūrta.
For the sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi, samyaṅmithyādṛṣṭi, and mithyādṛṣṭi, the duration is as stated generally.

By way of restating the designations (*saṃjñā*), regarding those possessing the designations (*saṃjñin*), the non-cessation of wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and so forth up to the gross [passions] is like male gender (*puṃveda*).
For the remaining [passions], it is as stated in the general [section].

For those without perception (*asaṃjñin*), with respect to various living beings (*nānājīva*), the duration is all time. With respect to a single living being (*ekajīva*), it is at minimum a minor birth (*kṣudrabhavagrahaṇa*) and at maximum an infinite period consisting of incalculable *pudgalaparivartas*.
For those who lack the designation of either [of these two], the duration is as stated for the general case.
With reference to the enumeration of those who possess nutriment, for those with false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), the entire period of time applies in relation to various living beings (*nānājīva*).
With respect to a single soul, the minimum duration is an antarmuhūrta;
the maximum is an incalculable fraction of an angula, or incalculably incalculable numbers of utsarpiṇīs and avasarpiṇīs.
For the remaining [categories], the duration is as stated generally.

Among those who do not take food, with respect to false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), all time [is possible] from the perspective of multiple living beings (*nānājīva*). With respect to a single living being (*ekajīva*), it is at least one moment (*samaya*) and at most three moments. With respect to multiple living beings, for the state of right view with partial realization (*sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi*) and the state of right view without self-restraint (*asaṃyatasamyagdṛṣṭi*), it is at least one moment.
At the maximum, it is an incalculable fraction of an *avalikā*.
With respect to a single living being, at the minimum it is one moment (*samaya*),
and at the maximum it is two moments.
With respect to multiple souls, the minimum duration for those possessing omniscience with residual karma (sayogakevalin) is three time-units (samayas),
and the maximum is a countable number of time-units.
With respect to a single soul, both the minimum and the maximum duration is three time-units.
The duration for those who possess pure, non-attached knowledge has been described in general terms.
The time [of their existence] has been explained.
The *antara* (interval) is now defined.
When a desired quality has transitioned into another quality, the interval is that which occurs in the interim before the original quality is regained.
This is twofold: general and particular.
Generally speaking, with respect to various living beings (*nānājīva*), there is no interval for wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).

With respect to a single living being (*ekajīva*), it is at minimum one *armuhūrta* and at maximum slightly less than two sixty-sixths of a *sāgaropama*. For right view with subsidence (*sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi*), with respect to various living beings, the interval is at minimum one moment (*samaya*).
At the maximum, it is an incalculable fraction of a *palyopama*.
With respect to a single living being, at the minimum, it is an incalculable fraction of a *palyopama*;
at the maximum, it is slightly less than half a *pudgalaparivarta*.

The interval for right-cum-wrong view (samyagmithyādṛṣṭi), with respect to various living beings, is like that of the state of being a "sāsādana. With respect to a single living being, it is at minimum one antarmuhūrta; at maximum, it is slightly less than half a pudgala-parivarta.
For those ranging from the unrestrained right-viewed (asaṃyata-samyagdṛṣṭi) up to the heedful (apramatta), there is no interval when considering multiple living beings (nānājīva).
With respect to a single living being (ekajīva), the minimum is an antarmuhūrta;
the maximum is slightly less than half a pudgala-parivarta.

Regarding the four types of those who attain tranquility (*upaśamaka*), with respect to various living beings (*nānājīva*), the minimum duration is one moment (*samaya*) and the maximum is a separation of years (*varṣapṛthaktva*). With respect to a single living being (*ekajīva*), the minimum is an antarmuhūrta.
At the maximum, it is slightly less than half a pudgala-parivarta.
For the four types of kṣapaka-s and for the ayogakevalin-s, with respect to multiple souls, the minimum duration is one moment;
at the maximum, it is six months.
There is no interval with respect to a single soul.
For those who possess omniscience while still in the state of embodied existence (sayogakevalins), there is no interval whether with respect to multiple souls or with respect to a single soul.

Specifically, according to the description of the destinies (*gati*), among hell-beings in the hellish destiny across the seven earths, there is no interval (*antara*) between those with wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and those with non-restrained right view (*asaṃyata-samyagdṛṣṭi*) when considering multiple beings (*nānājīva*).
With respect to a single being (*ekajīva*), the minimum is an antarmuhūrta;
the maximum is slightly less than one, three, seven, ten, seventeen, twenty-two, and thirty-three *sāgaropamas* respectively.

With respect to multiple living beings (*nānājīva*), for those with right view with partial realization (*sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi*) and those with mixed right-and-wrong view (*samyagmithyādṛṣṭi*), the minimum duration is one moment (*samaya*).
At the maximum, it is an incalculable fraction (*asaṃkhyeyabhāga*) of a *palyopama*.
With respect to a single living being (*ekajīva*), the minimum is an incalculable fraction of a *palyopama* and an antarmuhūrta.
At the maximum, it is slightly less than one, three, seven, ten, seventeen, twenty-two, and thirty-three *sāgaropamas*.
Regarding the animal realm, for animals with wrong view, there is no interval when considering various individual beings.
With respect to a single soul, the minimum duration is one antarmuhūrta;
the maximum is three palyopamas less a fraction.
For the four [stages] beginning with sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi, the interval is as stated generally.

In the human realm, for humans, [the duration] of wrong view is as in the case of animals. For those with right view who are in the state of "entering" (sāsādana) and those with right-and-wrong view, it is as in the general case, with respect to various individual beings.
With respect to a single soul, the minimum duration is an incalculable fraction of a *palyopama* and an *antarmuhūrta*.
At the maximum, it is three *palyopamas* plus a plurality of *pūrvakoṭis*.
With respect to multiple souls, there is no interval for the unrestrained right-viewed (*asaṃyata-samyagdṛṣṭi*).
With respect to a single soul, the minimum duration is an antarmuhūrta;
the maximum is three *palyopamas* increased by a plurality of *pūrvakoṭis*.
With respect to multiple souls, there is no interval for those who are restrained-unrestrained (*saṃyatāsaṃyata*), the negligent (*pramatta*), and the non-negligent (*apramatta*).
With respect to a single soul, the minimum duration is an antarmuhūrta;
the maximum is several *pūrvakoṭīs*.
With respect to multiple souls, for the four types of *upaśamakas*, it is as in the general case.
With respect to a single living being, the minimum duration is one antarmuhūrta; the maximum is several koṭis of pūrvas. For the remaining [categories], it is as in the general case.
In the celestial realm, for the gods who possess either false view or non-restrained right view, there is no difference when considering multiple living beings (*nānājīva*).
With respect to a single living being (*ekajīva*), the minimum duration is an antarmuhūrta.
At the maximum, it is slightly less than thirty-one *sāgaropamas*.
For the *sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi* and *samyagmithyādṛṣṭi*, with respect to multiple beings (*nānājīva*), it is as in the general case.
With respect to a single being (*ekajīva*), at the minimum, it is an incalculable fraction of a *palyopama* and an *antarmuhūrta*.
At the maximum, it is slightly less than thirty-one *sāgaropamas*.
According to the classification by faculties (*indriya*), for those with a single faculty (*ekendriya*), there is no interval (*antara*) when considering various individual beings (*nānājīva*).
With respect to a single living being, the minimum duration is the duration of a minor birth;
the maximum is two thousand sāgaropamas increased by a plurality of pūrvakoṭīs.
With respect to multiple beings among those with incomplete sense-faculties, there is no interval.
With respect to a single living being, the minimum is a minor birth;
the maximum is an infinite period of time consisting of incalculable *pudgala-parivartas*.
Thus, the interval with respect to the faculties has been explained.
Regarding the quality [of intensity], there is no difference between the two cases.
Among the five faculties, this is like the general case for wrong view.
For the right-view-inclined and the right-wrong view, it is like the general case with respect to multiple living beings.
With respect to a single soul, the minimum duration is an incalculable fraction of a *palyopama* and an *antarmuhūrta*.
At the maximum, it is one thousand *sāgaropamas* plus several tens of millions of *pūrvakoṭis*.
With respect to multiple souls, there is no interval for those ranging from the unrestrained right-viewed (*asaṃyata-samyagdṛṣṭi*) up to the non-negligent (*apramatta*).
With respect to a single soul, the minimum duration is an antarmuhūrta;
the maximum is one thousand sāgaropamas plus several pūrvakoṭis.
With respect to multiple souls, for the four types of upaśamakas, it is as in the general case.
With respect to a single soul, the minimum duration is an antarmuhūrta;
the maximum is one thousand sāgaropamas increased by several pūrvakoṭis.
For the remaining [karmas], it is as stated generally.

According to the classification by body (*kāya*), there is no interval (*antara*) among those belonging to the bodies of earth, water, fire, and air when considered in relation to various individual living beings (*nānājīva*).
With respect to a single living being, the minimum duration is that of a minor birth (*kṣudrabhavagrahaṇa*).

At the maximum, the duration is infinite: incalculable cycles of individuals (*pudgalaparivarta*). For those belonging to the vegetable body (*vanaspatikāyika*), there is no interval when considering multiple living beings; however, with respect to a single living being, the minimum is the duration of a minor birth.
At the maximum, they are incalculable worlds.
Thus, regarding the body, an interval has been stated;
however, regarding their qualities, there is no interval whatsoever in either case.
Among the mobile-bodied beings, [the duration] for those with wrong view is as in the general case.
For those with right view with subsidence and those with right-and-wrong view, with respect to multiple living beings, it is as in the general case.
With respect to a single living being, the minimum is an incalculable fraction of a *palyopama* and an antarmuhūrta.
At the maximum, it is two thousand *sāgaropamas* increased by various multiples of a *pūrvakoṭi*.
For those ranging from the unrestrained right-viewed (*asaṃyata-samyagdṛṣṭi*) up to the heedful (*apramatta*), there is no interval (*antara*) when considering multiple living beings (*nānājīva*).
With respect to a single living being (*ekajīva*), the minimum is an *antarmuhūrta*.
At the maximum, it is two thousand *sāgaropamas*, increased by various multiples of a *pūrvakoṭi*.
For the four types of *upaśamakas*, this is the same as for [the *kṣapaka*] with respect to multiple living beings (*nānājīva*).
With respect to a single living being (*ekajīva*), it is at the minimum one *antarmuhūrta*.
At the maximum, it lasts for two thousand *sāgaropamas*, increased by various multiples of a previous limit (*pūrvakoṭī*).
For the remaining [faculties], it is like that of the five faculties.

In reference to yoga, for those possessing yoga of body, speech, and mind—namely, the false-viewed, the unrestrained right-viewed, the restrained-unrestrained, the careless, the non-careless, and the embodied omniscients (sayogakevalins)—there is no interval (antara), whether considering multiple souls or a single soul.

For the right-viewed-in-the-process-of-attainment (sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi) and the right-and-wrong-viewed (samyagmithyādṛṣṭi), considering multiple souls, it is as in the general case; with respect to a single soul, there is no interval.
For the four types of suppressors (*upaśamaka*), there is no interval with respect to a single soul, as there is for those considered across multiple souls.
For the four types of destroyers (*kṣapaka*) and for the non-possessing omniscients (*ayogakevalin*), it is as in the general case.
According to the Vedic tradition, regarding the female gender (*strīveda*), there is no interval (*antara*) for wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) when considering various living beings (*nānājīva*).
With respect to a single living being (*ekajīva*), it is at minimum one *antarmuhūrta*.
At the maximum, it is slightly less than fifty-five *palyopamas*.
For the *sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi* and *samyagmithyādṛṣṭi*, with respect to multiple living beings (*nānājīva*), it is as in the general case.
With respect to a single living being (*ekajīva*), at the minimum, it is an incalculable fraction of a *palyopama* and an *antarmuhūrta*.
At the maximum, it is a few hundred *palyopamas*.
For those ranging from the uncontrolled right-viewed (*asaṃyata-samyagdṛṣṭi*) up to the heedful (*apramatta*), there is no interval when considering multiple living beings (*nānājīva*).
With respect to a single living being (*ekajīva*), the minimum is an *antarmuhūrta*.
At the maximum, it is a distinct multiple of one hundred *palyopamas*.
For the two types of suppressors (*upaśamaka*), in relation to various living beings (*nānājīva*), it is as in the general case;
for a single living being, at the minimum, it is an *antarmuhūrta*.
At the maximum, it is a separate hundred *palyopamas*.
For two types of destroyers (*kṣapaka*), with respect to various living beings (*nānājīva*), at the minimum it is one moment;
at the maximum, it is a separate number of years.
There is no interval with respect to a single living being. In the case of male-vedanā, [the duration] for one of wrong view is like the general rule.
Regarding the *sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi* and *samyagmithyādṛṣṭi*, with respect to various souls (*nānājīva*), it is like the general case [of the *mithyādṛṣṭi*].
With respect to a single soul (*ekajīva*), the minimum is a fraction of an *asaṃkhyeya* part of a *palyopama* and an *antarmuhūrta*.
The maximum is a separate hundred *sāgaropamas*.
For those ranging from the unrestrained with right view up to the heedful, there is no interval when considering multiple living beings.
With respect to a single living being, the minimum is an antarmuhūrta;
the maximum is a distinct hundred pṛthaktvas of sāgaropamas.
Regarding the two types of subsidence (upaśamaka), with respect to various living beings (nānājīva), they are like the general case.
With respect to a single living being, the minimum duration is one antarmuhūrta;
the maximum is a few hundred sāgaropamas.
Regarding two [types of] destroyers (kṣapaka) with respect to different living beings (nānājīva), the minimum duration is one moment;
the maximum is a year plus a fraction.
With respect to a single living being, there is no interval.
Regarding those with the neuter gender who hold wrong views, there is no interval when considering multiple living beings.
With respect to a single living being, the minimum duration is one antarmuhūrta.
At the maximum, it is slightly less than thirty-three sāgaropamas.
For those beginning with the sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi and ending with the anivṛttyupaśamaka, the duration is as stated generally.
For the two types of kṣapakas, it is like that of the female gender (strīveda).

Regarding those who have departed from delusion (*apagataveda*), for both the non-returner with coarse subsidence (*anivṛttibādaropaśamaka*) and the one with subtle passion-subsidence (*sūkṣmasāṃparāyopaśamaka*), the general statement applies in relation to multiple living beings (*nānājīva*).
With respect to a single living being, however, both the minimum and maximum duration is one *antarmuhūrta*.
For one whose passions are subsided (*upaśāntakaṣāya*), it is as in the general case in relation to multiple living beings.
There is no interval with respect to a single living being;
for the rest, it is like the general case.

With reference to the passions (*kaṣāya*): for the passions of anger, pride, deceit, and greed—ranging from those with wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) up to those who have attained subsidence (*upaśamaka*)—the minimum duration, as in the case of mental activity (*manoyoga*), is one moment when considering multiple living beings (*nānājīva*) during the two types of destruction (*kṣapaka*). The maximum is slightly more than a year.
For one who has suppressed the subtle passions (sūkṣmasāṃparāyopaśamaka) while possessing only greed, with respect to multiple living beings, it is like the general case;
with respect to a single living being, there is no interval.
For one who is destroying those [passions] (kṣapaka), it is like the general case.
Among those without kaṣāya, for one whose kaṣāyas have been pacified, [the duration] is like the general rule with respect to various living beings;
with respect to a single living being, there is no interval.
For the remaining three, it is like the general rule.

In terms of knowledge, among those possessing sensory cognition (mati-ajñāna), scriptural cognition (śruta-ajñāna), and the deluded cognition (vibhaṅga-jñāna), there is no interval for a false believer (mithyādṛṣṭi), whether considering multiple living beings or a single living being.
For a right believer with partial realization (sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi), it is as in the general case when considering multiple living beings.
With respect to a single soul, there is no interval.

Among the types of knowledge consisting of sensory perception (*ābhinibodhika*), scriptural knowledge (*śruta*), and clairvoyance (*avadhi*), with respect to multiple souls, there is no interval for those who possess right view while being unrestrained (*asaṃyata-samyagdṛṣṭi*).
With respect to a single soul, the minimum duration is an antarmuhūrta.
At the maximum, it is slightly less than a *pūrvakoṭī*.
For one who is both restrained and unrestrained, there is no interval when considering various living beings (*nānājīva*).
With respect to a single living being (*ekajīva*), the minimum is an *antarmuhūrta*.
At the maximum, it is slightly more than sixty-six sāgaropamas.
With respect to various living beings among those who are both negligent and non-negligent, there is no interval.
With respect to a single living being, the minimum is an antarmuhūrta.
At the maximum, it is slightly more than thirty-three sāgaropamas.
For the four types of upaśamakas, with respect to various individual souls, it is as described generally. With respect to a single soul, at the minimum, it is an antarmuhūrta.
At the maximum, it is slightly more than sixty-six *sāgaropamas*.
For the four types of destroyers (*kṣapaka*), it is as in the general case;
however, among those possessing clairvoyant knowledge (*avadhijñānin*), with respect to multiple living beings (*nānājīva*), it is at the minimum one moment (*samaya*).
At the maximum, it is a separate year (*varṣapṛthaktva*).
With respect to a single soul, there is no interval.

Among those possessing mind-pervading knowledge (*manaḥparyaya-jñāna*), with respect to various souls, there is no interval between the *pramatta-saṃyata* (the heedful) and the *apramatta-saṃyata* (the unheedful).
With respect to a single soul, both the minimum and the maximum duration is one antarmuhūrta.
With respect to multiple souls, for the four types of upaśamakas, it is as in the general case.
With respect to a single soul, the minimum is one antarmuhūrta.
At the maximum, it is slightly less than a previous *koṭī*.
For the four types of destroyers (*kṣapaka*), it is like that of those with clairvoyant knowledge (*avadhijñānin*).
For the two types of possessors of omniscience (*kevalajñānin*), it is as in the general case.

With reference to restraint (*saṃyama*), among those with *sāmāyika* and *chedopasthāpana* purity of restraint, for both the *pramatta* (negligent) and *apramatta* (non-negligent), there is no interval when considering multiple living beings (*nānājīva*).
With respect to a single living being (*ekajīva*), the minimum and maximum duration is one *antarmuhūrta*.

Regarding the two types of subsidence (upaśamaka), with respect to different living beings (nānājīva), it is like the general case. With respect to a single living being, the minimum duration is one antarmuhūrta; the maximum is slightly less than a pūrvakoṭi.
The two types of *kṣapaka*s are as in the general case.
Among those restrained by purity through avoidance (*parihāra-śuddhi-saṃyata*), for both the *pramatta* and *apramatta*, there is no interval when considering multiple living beings (*nānājīva*).
With respect to a single living being, the minimum and maximum duration is an *antarmuhūrta*.

Among those who are pure-restrained with subtle passion (*sūkṣmasāmparāya-śuddhisaṃyata*), for one who is in the state of subsidence (*upaśamaka*), [the duration] is as in the general case with respect to multiple living beings (*nānājīva*).
With respect to a single living being (*ekajīva*), there is no interval (*antara*).
For that same person in the state of destruction (*kṣapaka*), it is as in the general case.
In the case of the *yathākhyāta* [caritra], it is like that of one without *kaṣāya*.
For the *saṃyatāsaṃyata*, there is no interval (*antara*) either with respect to multiple living beings (*nānājīva*) or with respect to a single living being (*ekajīva*).
Among the *asaṃyata*, for the *mithyādṛṣṭi*, there is no interval with respect to multiple living beings.
With respect to a single soul, the minimum duration is one antarmuhūrta;
the maximum is thirty-three sāgaropamas less a fraction.
For the remaining three [karmas], it is as in the general case.
According to the enumeration by vision (*darśana*), among those with visual vision (*cakṣurdarśanin*), [the duration] of false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) is like the general case.
For the right-attaining view (*sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi*) and the right-wrong view (*samyagmithyādṛṣṭi*), it is like the general case when considering multiple living beings (*nānājīva*).
With respect to a single soul, the minimum duration is an incalculable fraction of a *palyopama* and an *antarmuhūrta*.
At the maximum, it is two thousand *sāgaropamas* less a portion.
With respect to multiple souls, there is no interval for those from the unrestrained right-viewed (*asaṃyata-samyagdṛṣṭi*) up to the non-negligent (*apramatta*).
With respect to a single soul, the minimum duration is one antarmuhūrta, and the maximum is two thousand sāgaropamas less a fraction.
For the four types of upaśamakas, the general duration stated with respect to multiple souls applies;
however, with respect to a single soul, the minimum is one antarmuhūrta.
At the maximum, it is slightly less than two thousand sāgaropamas.
For the four types of *kṣapaka*, the general rule has been stated.

Regarding those with non-visual perception (*acakṣurdarśanin*), the general interval between those starting from the wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) up to those whose passions are destroyed (*kṣīṇakaṣāya*) has been stated.
Those with limited vision are like those possessing limited knowledge;
those with perfect vision are like those possessing perfect knowledge.

According to the classification by *leśyā* (psychic tint), among those with black, blue, and grey *leśyās*, there is no difference between those with false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and those with right view but lacking self-restraint (*asaṃyata-samyagdṛṣṭi*) when considering multiple living beings (*nānājīva*).
With respect to a single living being (*ekajīva*), the minimum duration is an *antarmuhūrta*;
the maximum is slightly less than thirty-three, seventeen, and seven *sāgaropamas* respectively.
Regarding the *sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi* and *samyagmithyādṛṣṭi*, with respect to various living beings (*nānājīva*), it is like the general case.
With respect to a single living being (*ekajīva*), the minimum duration is an incalculable fraction (*asaṃkhyeyabhāga*) of a *palyopama* and an antarmuhūrta;
the maximum is slightly less than thirty-three, seventeen, and seven *sāgaropamas* respectively.

Regarding the *tejoleśyā* and *padmaleśyā*, there is no interval between those with wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and those who are partially restrained with right view (*asaṃyata-samyagdṛṣṭi*) when considering multiple living beings (*nānājīva*).
With respect to a single living being (*ekajīva*), the minimum [interval] is an *antarmuhūrta*.
At the maximum, it is two *sāgaropamas* and eighteen *sāgaropamas* plus a fraction.
For the *sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi* and *samyagmithyādṛṣṭi*, with respect to various souls (*nānājīva*), it is as in the general case.
With respect to a single soul (*ekajīva*), at the minimum, it is an incalculable fraction of a *palyopama* and an *antarmuhūrta*.
At the maximum, it is two *sāgaropamas* and eighteen *sāgaropamas* plus a fraction.
For those who are restrained, unrestrained, negligent, and non-negligent, there is no interval [of time] when considering multiple beings or a single being.

Among those with white radiance (*śuklaleśya*), for both the false-viewed (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and the unrestrained right-viewed (*asaṃyata-samyagdṛṣṭi*), there is no difference when considering multiple living beings (*nānājīva*).
With respect to a single living being (*ekajīva*), the minimum is an antarmuhūrta;
the maximum is thirty-one *sāgaropamas* less a fraction.

Regarding the right-view-with-attenuation (*sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi*) and the mixed-right-and-wrong-view (*samyagmithyādṛṣṭi*), with respect to multiple beings (*nānājīva*), it is like the general case [of the right-view].
With respect to a single being (*ekajīva*), the minimum is an incalculable fraction of a *palyopama* and an antarmuhūrta;
the maximum is thirty-one *sāgaropamas* less a portion.
The restrained-unrestrained (*saṃyatāsaṃyata*) and the careless-restrained (*pramattasaṃyata*) possess the fiery radiance (*tejo-leśyā*).
For the careful-restrained (*apramattasaṃyata*), with respect to multiple living beings (*nānājīva*), there is no interval.
With respect to a single living being, both the minimum and the maximum [duration] is an antarmuhūrta.
Regarding the three types of those who are pacifying (*upaśamaka*), with respect to multiple living beings (*nānājīva*), it is as in the general case.

With respect to a single living being (*ekajīva*), both the minimum and the maximum duration is one *antarmuhūrta*. Regarding the one whose passions are pacified (*upaśāntakaṣāya*), with respect to multiple living beings, it is as in the general case.
There is no difference with respect to a single soul.
It is the same for the four types of *kṣapaka*s, for those possessing *sayogakevali* omniscience, and for those free from *leśyā*.

By way of restating the category of the capable (*bhavya*), among the capable, the intervals for those ranging from false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) up to the state of omniscience (*kevalin*) are as in the general case.
For the incapable (*abhavya*), there is no interval, whether considering multiple souls or a single soul.

With reference to rightness (samyaktva), among those with right view that is exhaustible (kṣāyika-samyagdṛṣṭi), there is no interval for the unrestrained one with right view (asamyata-samyagdṛṣṭi) when considering multiple living beings (nānājīva).
With respect to a single living being, it is at minimum an antarmuhūrta; at maximum, slightly less than ten million years (pūrvakoṭī).
With respect to multiple living beings (*nānājīva*), there is no difference between those who are restrained, unrestrained, heedless, or non-heedless restrained.
With respect to a single living being (*ekajīva*), the minimum duration is an *antarmuhūrta*,
and the maximum is slightly more than thirty-three *sāgaropamas*.
Regarding the four types of suppressors (*upaśamaka*), with respect to various living beings, it is like the general case.
With respect to a single living being, the minimum is one *antarmuhūrta*;
the maximum is thirty-three *sāgaropamas* plus a fraction more.
For the remaining [categories], it is like the general case.

Among those with right vision resulting from the subsidence-cum-destruction of karma (*kṣāyopaśamika-samyagdṛṣṭi*), there is no interval (*antara*) for the uncontrolled one with right vision (*asaṃyata-samyagdṛṣṭi*) when considering multiple living beings (*nānājīva*).
With respect to a single soul, the minimum duration is an antarmuhūrta; the maximum is slightly less than ten million pūrvas.
With respect to multiple souls, there is no interval for those who are partially restrained (saṃyatāsaṃyata).
With respect to a single soul, the minimum duration is an antarmuhūrta;
the maximum is sixty-six sāgaropamas less a fraction.
With respect to multiple souls, there is no interval between the *pramatta-saṃyata* (careless self-restrained) and *apramatta-saṃyata* (unperturbed self-restrained) stages.
For a single soul, the minimum duration is one antarmuhūrta;
the maximum is slightly more than thirty-three sāgaropamas.

Among those with right view through subsidence (*aupaśamika-samyagdṛṣṭi*), for one who possesses right view while being unrestrained (*asaṃyata-samyagdṛṣṭi*), with respect to various living beings (*nānājīva*), the minimum duration is one moment (*samaya*) and the maximum is seven days and nights. With respect to a single living being (*ekajīva*), both the minimum and the maximum are an antarmuhūrta.
For one who is both restrained and unrestrained, with respect to various living beings, the minimum duration is one moment (*samaya*),
and the maximum is fourteen days and nights.
With respect to a single living being, both the minimum and the maximum are an antarmuhūrta.

With respect to multiple living beings (*nānājīva*), for both the negligent (*pramatta*) and non-negligent (*apramatta*) self-restrained, the minimum duration is one moment (*samaya*) and the maximum is fifteen days and nights.
With respect to a single living being (*ekajīva*), both the minimum and the maximum duration is an antarmuhūrta.

For the three types of suppressors (*upaśamaka*), with respect to multiple living beings (*nānājīva*), the minimum duration is one moment (*samaya*) and the maximum is a separate year (*varṣapṛthaktva*).
With respect to a single living being (*ekajīva*), both the minimum and the maximum are an antarmuhūrta.
For one whose passions (*kaṣāya*) have been pacified, [the interval] is like that of the general case with respect to multiple living beings (*nānājīva*);
with respect to a single living being (*ekajīva*), there is no interval.

For the right-viewed-in-the-process-of-falling (*sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi*) and the right-and-wrong-viewed (*samyagmithyādṛṣṭi*), with respect to multiple living beings, the minimum is one moment (*samaya*).
At the maximum, it is an incalculable fraction of a *palyopama*.
With respect to a single living being (*ekajīva*), there is no interval (*antara*).
With respect to various living beings (*nānājīva*) and with respect to a single living being, there is no interval for those of wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
By way of restating the designations (*saṃjñā*), [the states] among those possessing designations (*saṃjñin*) are like the general case for wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
For the right-approaching view (*sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi*) and the right-and-wrong view (*samyagmithyādṛṣṭi*), they are like the general case with respect to various living beings (*nānājīva*).
With respect to a single soul, the minimum duration is an incalculable fraction of a *palyopama* and an *antarmuhūrta*;
the maximum is a few hundred *sāgaropamas*.
With respect to multiple souls, there is no interval for those ranging from the uncontrolled right-viewed (*asaṃyata-samyagdṛṣṭi*) up to the non-negligent (*apramatta*).
With respect to a single soul, the minimum duration is an antarmuhūrta;
the maximum is a few hundred sāgaropamas.
With respect to multiple souls, for the four types of upaśamakas, it is the same as in the general case.
With respect to a single soul, the minimum duration is an antarmuhūrta;
the maximum is a few hundred sāgaropamas.
For the four types of *kṣapaka*s, it is as described generally.
For those without perception, there is no interval, whether with respect to many individual lives or with respect to a single individual life;
this is like the case of those who lack both designations and possess commonality.
In terms of the classification by food, regarding those who consume food, it is like the general rule for wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).

Regarding the right view with partial realization (*sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi*) and the mixed right-and-wrong view (*samyagmithyādṛṣṭi*), from the perspective of multiple living beings (*nānājīva*), it is like the general rule.
With respect to a single living being (*ekajīva*), the minimum duration is an incalculable fraction of a *palyopama* and an antarmuhūrta.
In terms of increase, it is an incalculable fraction of a finger-breadth; [in terms of time,] there are incalculable upon incalculable *utsarpiṇīs* and *avasarpiṇīs*.
For those from the unrestrained right-viewed (*asaṃyata-samyagdṛṣṭi*) up to the non-negligent (*apramatta*), with respect to multiple living beings (*nānājīva*), there is no interval.
With respect to a single living being (*ekajīva*), the minimum is an *antarmuhūrta*.
In terms of increase, it is an incalculable fraction of a finger-breadth; in terms of time, it is incalculable *utsarpiṇīs* and *avasarpiṇīs*.
Regarding the four types of suppressors (*upaśamaka*), this is the same as for the general case when considering multiple living beings (*nānājīva*).
With respect to a single living being (*ekajīva*), the minimum duration is one *antarmuhūrta*.
At the maximum, it lasts for an incalculable portion of a finger-breadth (aṅgula), spanning incalculable upon incalculable aeons of increase and decrease (utsarpiṇī-avasarpiṇī).
For the four types of destroyers (kṣapaka) and those possessing omniscience with activity (sayogakevalin), it is the same as in the general case.
Among those who do not take food, there is no interval for false view (mithyādṛṣṭi), whether considering multiple living beings or a single living being.
For right view with partial realization (sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi), considering multiple living beings, the minimum is one moment;
the maximum is an incalculable fraction of a palyopama.
With respect to a single soul, there is no interval.
With respect to multiple souls, for one who possesses right view but is not restrained, the minimum duration is one moment;
the maximum is a few months.
With respect to a single soul, there is no interval.
With respect to multiple souls who are *sayogakevalins*, the minimum duration is one moment (*samaya*),
and the maximum is a separate year (*varṣapṛthaktva*).
With respect to a single soul, there is no interval.
With respect to multiple souls, for an Ayogakevalin, the minimum duration is one moment;
the maximum is six months.
There is no interval with respect to a single living being. An interval has been understood.
An entity (bhāva) is analyzed;
it is twofold: by way of generality and by way of particularity.
First, by way of generality, "false view" (mithyādṛṣṭi) is an entity arising from the manifestation of karma (audayika).
"Right view with partial realization" (sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi) is a transformative state (pāriṇāmika-bhāva).
"Right-cum-wrong view" (samyaṅmithyādṛṣṭi) is a state resulting from subsidence and destruction (kṣayopaśamika-bhāva).
"Unrestrained right view" (asaṃyatasamyagdṛṣṭi) is a state that is either subsidential (aupaśamika), destructive (kṣāyika), or resulting from subsidence and destruction (kṣāyopaśamika).
Furthermore, the uncontrolled state is due to the quality of arising (*audayika*).
The controlled-uncontrolled state—namely, the careless controlled (*pramatta-saṃyata*) and the careful controlled (*apramatta-saṃyata*)—is the quality of subsidence-exhaustion (*kṣāyopaśamika*).
The quality of subsidence (*aupaśamika*) belongs to the four types of those who are effecting subsidence (*upaśamaka*).
The state of destruction (*kṣāyika-bhāva*) exists in the four types of *kṣapaka*s, as well as in the *sayogakevalin* and *ayogakevalin*.

Specifically, according to the enumeration of destinies (*gati*), among the hell-beings in the first earth (*pṛthivī*) of the hellish destiny—ranging from those with wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) up to those who are unrestrained yet right-viewed (*asaṃyata-samyagdṛṣṭi*)—it is the same as in the general case.

From the second stage up to the seventh, the states of wrong view (mithyādṛṣṭi), the view of one who has attained right vision (sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi), and the mixed view (samyagmithyādṛṣṭi) are like those in the general case.
For the unrestrained right-viewed (asaṃyatasamyagdṛṣṭi), there is either a state resulting from subsidence (aupaśamika) or a state resulting from subsidence-cum-destruction (kṣāyopaśamika).
The unrestrained, however, [possesses] a state resulting from the rise of karma (audayika).
In the animal realm, for animals ranging from those with false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) up to those who are partially restrained (*saṃyatāsaṃyata*), it is as in the general case.
In the human realm, for humans ranging from those with false view up to those who possess the omniscience of the non-attached (*ayogakevalin*), it is as in the general case.
In the celestial realm, for gods ranging from those with false view up to those with right view but who are unrestrained (*asaṃyatasamyagdṛṣṭi*), it is as in the general case.
According to the enumeration by faculties (*indriya*), there is the state of arising (*audayika-bhāva*) for those with one faculty and those with incomplete faculties.
Among those with five faculties, it is as in the general case for those ranging from those with wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) up to the omniscient ones free from attachment (*ayogakevalin*).
According to the classification by body (*kāya*), for those belonging to the stationary body (*sthāvara-kāyika*), there is the state of arising (*audayika-bhāva*);
for those belonging to the mobile body (*trasa-kāyika*), it is the same as the general case.

According to the exposition of yoga, there is only a general similarity among those possessing yoga of body, speech, and mind, and among those ranging from those with false view up to those with pure omniscience (sayogakevalin).
By way of enumeration according to the *vedas* (sexual dispositions), there is a general similarity between those with female, male, and neuter *vedas*, and those without a *veda*.
By way of enumeration according to the *kaṣāyas* (passions), there is a general similarity between those with the *kaṣāyas* of anger, pride, deceit, and greed, and those without *kaṣāyas*.

According to the classification by knowledge (*jñāna*), it is the same as the general case for those possessing sensory cognition (*mati-ajñānin*), scriptural cognition (*śruta-ajñānin*), and partial-cognition (*vibhaṅga-jñānin*), as well as for those possessing sensory cognition, scriptural cognition, clairvoyance (*avadhi*), mental-penetration (*manaḥparyaya*), and omniscience (*kevala-jñānin*).

§ 141. According to the classification by restraint (*saṃyama*), it is the same as the general case for all those who are restrained (*saṃyata*) and those who are both restrained and unrestrained (*saṃyatāsaṃyata*).

According to the enumeration by vision (*darśana*), [the number of] those possessing eye-vision (*cakṣurdarśana*), non-eye-vision (*acakṣurdarśana*), clairvoyant vision (*avadhidarśana*), and omniscient vision (*kevaladarśana*) is like that of the general [categories].
By way of *leśyā*, for those with the six *leśyās* and for those without *leśyā*, it is as in the general case.

By way of *bhavyatva* (the state of being capable of liberation), for those who are *bhavya*, ranging from those with wrong view up to those possessing the *ayogakevalin* stage, it is as in the general case.
The transformative state (*pāriṇāmika-bhāva*) belongs to those incapable [of liberation].

Regarding the enumeration of rightness (*samyaktva*), among those with right vision through destruction (*kṣāyika-samyagdṛṣṭi*), the state of destruction (*kṣāyika-bhāva*) belongs to the one with right vision who is not yet restrained (*asaṃyata-samyagdṛṣṭi*).
Right view is of the nature of destruction (kṣāyika).
The state of being uncontrolled is due to the state of emergence (audayika).

For those who are partially controlled, those who are fully controlled but heedless, and those who are fully controlled and non-heedless, the state is one of subsidence-cum-destruction (kṣāyopaśamika).
There is right conviction that is exhaustional.
There is the state of the four types of pacifiers that is pacificatory;
[there is also] right conviction that is exhaustional.
For the remaining [categories], it is as with the general case.

Among those with right vision resulting from subsidence-exhaustion (kṣāyopaśamika), for one who possesses right vision while being unrestrained (asaṃyata-samyagdṛṣṭi), there is a state resulting from subsidence-exhaustion;
that is, right vision resulting from subsidence-exhaustion.
The uncontrolled state, moreover, is due to the quality of arising (audayika).
For those who are controlled-uncontrolled, the careless-controlled, and the careful-controlled, there is the quality of subsidence-exhaustion (kṣāyopaśamika).
Right view (samyaktva) is of the nature of subsidence-exhaustion.

Among those with right view through subsidence (*aupaśamika-samyagdṛṣṭi*), there is the subsidential state (*aupaśamiko bhāva*) of the one with right view who is not yet restrained (*asaṃyata-samyagdṛṣṭi*).
This is subsidential rightness (*aupaśamika-samyaktva*).
However, that unrestrained person [also possesses] the state of arising (*audayika-bhāva*).
The state resulting from the subsidence-cum-destruction (kṣāyopaśamika) belongs to those who are restrained, unrestrained, heedless, and non-heedless restrained.
Right faith (samyaktva) is of the nature of subsidence (aupaśamika).
The state of subsidence belongs to the four types of those practicing suppression (upaśamaka).
Rightness through subsidence (*aupaśamika-samyaktva*).
It is the transformational state (*pāriṇāmika-bhāva*) of one with right vision accompanied by delusion (*sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi*);
it is the state resulting from destruction and subsidence (*kṣāyopaśmika-bhāva*) of one with right-cum-wrong vision (*samyagmithyādṛṣṭi*).
The state of false view is of the nature of arising.
By way of restating the designation, it is like the generality of those who possess that designation.
The state of those without perception is of the nature of arising;
it is like that of [beings] who possess generality, being devoid of designation as either of those two.
By way of the classification of nutriment, the general treatment of those who possess nutriment and those who do not has been completed. § 148.
The relative smallness and greatness [of numbers] is described.
That is twofold: general and specific.

First, in a general sense, those who are in the state of suppression (upaśamaka) are the fewest of all; they are equal in number because of their simultaneous entry into the stages of their own respective qualities.
Those with subsided passions (*upaśāntakaṣāya*) are exactly that many.
Those who are destroyers (*kṣapaka*) are a numerable multiple (*saṃkhyeyaguṇa*) more.
Those who are omniscient yet still in the state of a non-omniscient being with destroyed passions (*kṣīṇakaṣāyavītarāgacchadmastha*) are exactly that many.

The *sayogakevalins* (those with complete knowledge while still possessing activity) and the *ayogakevalins* (those with complete knowledge who have ceased all activity) are equal in number when considering their entry [into the state].
The *sayogakevalins*, when aggregated according to their own duration, are numerable-fold more numerous.
The *apramattasaṃyatas* (those restrained without negligence) are numerable-fold more numerous [than the *sayogakevalins*].
The partially restrained (pramatta-saṃyata) are numerable-fold [more numerous];
the restrained-unrestrained (saṃyatāsaṃyata) are innumerable-fold [more numerous];
the right-viewed-in-falling-back (sāsādana-samyagdṛṣṭi) are innumerable-fold [more numerous].
Those with right-and-wrong views are numerable-fold;
those with right view who are not restrained are incalculable-fold;
those with wrong views are infinite-fold.

Specifically, according to the enumeration of destinies (*gati*), among all the hells in all the earths within the hellish destiny, those with right view accompanied by inclination (*sāsādana-samyagdṛṣṭi*) are the fewest of all.
Those with right-and-wrong view (*samyagmithyādṛṣṭi*) are a numerable multiple (*saṃkhyeyaguṇa*) greater than that.
Those with right view who are not restrained are incalculable times more numerous.
Those with wrong view are incalculable times more numerous.
Within the animal realm, those animals who are both restrained and unrestrained are the fewest of all.
For the others, it is as with the general case.
Among human beings in the human realm—from those who have attained subsidence (upaśamaka) up to the partially restrained (pramatta-saṃyata)—it is as with the general case.
Beyond that, the partially restrained (saṃyatāsaṃyata) are numerically greater by a multiple.
Those with right view who are in the state of "attaining" (sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi) are numerically greater;
those with right-and-wrong view (samyagmithyādṛṣṭi) are numerically greater;
and those with right view who are not restrained (asaṃyatasamyagdṛṣṭi) are numerically greater.
False views are incalculable times greater [than the previous].
Among gods in the realm of gods, it is as with the hell-beings.

According to the enumeration by sense-faculties (*indriya*), there is no distinction of stages of spiritual development (*guṇasthāna*) among those with one sense-faculty or those with deficient faculties; thus, there is an absence of numerical comparison (*alpabahutva*).
This is similar to the case of five-sensed beings in general.
However, this is the distinction: those with wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) are infinitely greater in number.
According to the classification by body, because there is no distinction of stages of attainment among immobile bodies, there is no difference in their smallness or greatness.
Those belonging to the water-bodied class are like those possessing five sense-faculties.
According to the discourse on yoga, those possessing the yoga of speech and mind are like those possessing the five sense-faculties;
those possessing the yoga of the body are like the general case.
By way of analogy with the Vedas, the female and male faculties are like those possessing the five sense-faculties;
the neuter faculties and those without faculties are like the general case.
In terms of the passions (*kaṣāya*), the number of those with the passions of anger, pride, and deceit is like that of the male gender.

However, this is the distinction: those with wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) are infinitely greater [in number]. Regarding the passions of greed (*lobha-kaṣāya*), the number is equal for the two types of those who have attained subsidence (*upaśamaka*).
The *kṣapaka*s (those who destroy [the defilements]) are numerable-fold [in number].
The *sūkṣmasāṃparāya-śuddhyupaśamaka-saṃyata*s (those restrained by the subsidence of purity in the stage of subtle passion) are specifically greater.
The *sūkṣmasāṃparāya-kṣapaka*s (those destroying [the defilements] in the stage of subtle passion) are numerable-fold [in number].
For the remaining [categories], it is as with those possessing common characteristics.

According to the enumeration by knowledge, among those with sensory-cognition-based ignorance (*matyajñānin*) and scriptural-cognition-based ignorance (*śrutājñānin*), the sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭis are the fewest of all.
Those with wrong views are infinite in number.
Among those possessing analytical knowledge (*vibhaṅgajñānin*), those with right view who are in the state of "attaining" (*sāsādana*) are the fewest of all;
those with wrong views are incalculable times more numerous.

Among those possessing sensory cognition (*mati*), scriptural cognition (*śruta*), and clairvoyant cognition (*avadhi*), the four types of suppressors (*upaśamaka*) and the four types of destroyers (*kṣapaka*) are the fewest in all respects; the [next] four types are numerically greater.
The unrestrained self-controlled (*apramatta-saṃyata*) are numerically greater;
the restrained self-controlled (*pramatta-saṃyata*) are numerically greater.
The restrained-unrestrained possess innumerable qualities.
Those with right view who are unrestrained possess innumerable qualities.
Among those possessing mind-pervading knowledge (*manaḥparyāya-jñāna*), the four types of suppressors (*upaśamaka*) are the fewest of all.
The four types of practitioners who have exhausted [their defilements] are numerable-fold more numerous. The those who are restrained with vigilance are numerable-fold more numerous.
The those who are restrained but with negligence are numerable-fold more numerous.
Among those possessing kevalajñāna, the *sayogakevalins* (those with active yoga) are numerically greater than the *ayogakevalins* (those without yoga).

With reference to restraint (*saṃyama*), the number of those purified by *sāmāyika* and *chedopasthāpana* restraint is equal for both types of *upaśamakas* (those who have attained suppression of the passions).
Beyond that, the two types of destroyers (kṣapaka) are a numerable-fold increase.
The non-negligent (apramatta) are a numerable-fold increase. The negligent (pramatta) are a numerable-fold increase.

Among those restrained by purity of avoidance (*parihāra-śuddhi-saṃyata*), the heedless (*pramatta*) are numerically greater than the heedful (*apramatta*). Among those restrained by purity of subtle passion (*sūkṣma-saṃparāya-śuddhi-saṃyata*), the destroyers (*kṣapaka*) are numerically greater than the pacifiers (*upaśamaka*).

Among those restrained by purity of conduct as it is described (*yathā-khyāta-vihāra-śuddhi-saṃyata*), those whose passions are destroyed (*kṣīṇa-kaṣāya*) are numerically greater than those whose passions are pacified (*upaśānta-kaṣāya*).
The *ayogakevalins* are exactly that many.
The *sayogakevalins* are numerable-fold more.
Among the *saṃyatāsaṃyatas*, there is no smallness or greatness [in number].
Among those who are not restrained in every respect, the *sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭis* are few;
the *samyagmithyādṛṣṭis* are numerically greater;
and the *asaṃyatasamyagdṛṣṭis* are innumerable times greater still.
The views beginning with "I am" (asmimāna) possess infinite qualities.
According to the classification by vision (*darśana*), those possessing eye-vision (*cakṣurdarśanin*) are like those possessing mental yoga (*manoyogin*).
For those with non-visual vision, it is like the body-yoga;
for those with clairvoyant vision, it is like clairvoyant knowledge;
for those with perfect vision, it is like perfect knowledge.
According to the enumeration by *leśyā*: for those with black, blue, and grey *leśyās*, it is as in the case of the unrestrained (*asaṃyata*).
Among those with fiery and lotus *leśyās*, the *apramatta* (those who are vigilant) are the fewest of all.
Those who are heedless are numerable-fold [more].
Thus it is for the others as well, like those with five sense-faculties.
Among those with white *leśyā*, all the *upaśamakas* (those who have attained suppression) are fewest.
The *kṣapaka*s are numerable-fold;
the *sayogakevalin*s are numerable-fold;
the *apramattasaṃyata*s are numerable-fold.
The partially restrained (pramatta-saṃyata) are numerable-fold [more numerous].

The restrained-unrestrained (saṃyatāsaṃyata) are innumerable-fold [more numerous]. Those with right view who are in the state of attaining [right view] (sāsādana-samyagdṛṣṭi) are innumerable-fold [more numerous].
Those with right-and-wrong views are numerable-fold;
those with wrong views are incalculable-fold;
those with uncontrolled right views are numerable-fold.
By way of restating those who are capable, the case of the capable is like that of the general category.
For those who are incapable, there is no smallness or greatness [in number].

According to the exposition of rightness (*samyaktva*), among those with right view that has reached destruction (*kṣāyika-samyagdṛṣṭi*), the four types of suppressors (*upaśamaka*) are the fewest of all.
For the others, from the [unrestrained] up to the negligent (*pramatta*), they are as in the general case.
Next, those who are both restrained and unrestrained are incalculable times more numerous.
Those with right view who are unrestrained are incalculable times more numerous.
Among those with right view that is the result of the subsidence and destruction of karma (kṣāyopaśamika), the least numerous of all are the those who are heedless (apramatta).
Those who are heedless are numerable-fold;
those who are partially restrained and unrestrained are innumerable-fold;
those with right view who are unrestrained are innumerable-fold.
Among those with right view resulting from subsidence (*aupaśamika-samyagdṛṣṭi*), the four types of subsiders (*upaśamaka*) are the fewest of all.
Those who are heedful (*apramatta*) are numerically greater;
those who are heedless (*pramatta*) are numerically greater still.
Those who are both restrained and unrestrained possess incalculable qualities.
Those with right view who are unrestrained possess incalculable qualities.
Among the remaining categories, there is no distinction of fewness or manyness.

By way of restating the designations (saṃjñā), [the number] of those possessing designations is like that of visual perception; for those lacking designations, there is neither deficiency nor plurality.
Those devoid of both designations [of soul and body] are like those possessing kevalajñāna.
Regarding the classification by way of nutriment, those who take nutriment are like those with the bodily yoga (*kāyayoga*).
Among those who do not take food, the *sayogakevalins* (omniscient beings with activity) are the fewest of all;
the *ayogakevalins* (omniscient beings without activity) are numerable-fold more;
and the *sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭis* (those with right vision in the state of falling back) are innumerable-fold more.
Those with right view who are unrestrained are incalculable times more numerous;
those with wrong view are infinite times more numerous.
Thus, the investigation of false views and so forth regarding the destinies and other categories has been conducted in a general manner.
In this regard, the subtle distinctions should be pursued in accordance with the scriptures without contradiction.
Thus, regarding right vision (*samyagdarśana*), which was first mentioned, its definition, origin, possessor, object, application, and means of attainment have been explained.
In connection with that, the designations, dimensions, and so forth of the soul (*jīva*) and other categories have also been explained.
Following that, since right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) is now fit for investigation, he says:
Intellectual knowledge, scriptural knowledge, clairvoyant knowledge, mind-reading knowledge, and omniscience are the types of knowledge.
The word "knowledge" (jñāna) applies to each one individually.

Sensory knowledge (*mati-jñāna*), scriptural knowledge (*śruta-jñāna*), clairvoyance (*avadhi-jñāna*), telepathy (*manaḥparyaya-jñāna*), and omniscience (*kevala-jñāna*). That by which an object is thought according to its own nature through the senses and the mind, or which is merely the act of thinking—that is *mati*.
When there is the subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣayopaśama*) of the karma that obscures it, an object is perceived; that by which one hears, or which is merely the act of hearing—that is *śruta*.
The proximate definition of these two has been given because of their relationship as cause and effect;
and so it will be stated later: "What is heard is preceded by mati.
It is called *avadhi* (clairvoyance) because of its non-oral nature or because its objects are delimited.
An object residing in the mind of another is called "mind" (manas).
Because of their constant association, the thorough investigation or complete comprehension of that [object] is "mental-pervasion" (manaḥparyaya).
If it is argued that this would entail [the category of] sensory cognition (matijñāna), we say no; for [that objection] applies only in a relative sense.
For that which is manifested solely by the power of the subsidence-cum-destruction (kṣayopaśama) of karma is designated as "exclusive" (kevala) with respect to one's own or another's mind,
just as one says, "Look at the moon in the cloud.
That which seekers pursue as their goal through external and internal austerity— that alone is "exclusive."
Or [it is called] "without a companion.
It is designated as "at the end" because it is attained at the end.
Because of its proximity to that [omniscience], the term "knowledge of others' minds" (manaḥparyaya) is mentioned in its vicinity.
Whence is this proximity? Because it shares the same substratum as the restraint (saṃyama).
Its limit is remote.
Why? Because of the vast distance between them.
The indirect (parokṣa) was mentioned before the direct (pratyakṣa) because it is easier to understand.
For the path of cognition and scripture (*mati-śruta-paddhati*), consisting of what is heard, familiarized, and experienced, is generally attained by almost all classes of living beings.
Thus, this knowledge is fivefold;
its divisions and so forth will be explained further on.

It has been stated that "comprehension occurs through means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) and viewpoints (naya). Regarding this, for some, *pramāṇa* is intended to be knowledge (*jñāna*); for others, it is contact (*saṃnikarṣa*); and for others, it is the sense organ (*indriya*).
Therefore, in order to demonstrate that only memory and the other [cognitions] under discussion possess the status of valid cognition, he says: "That is valid cognition" (tatpramāṇe).
What is the purpose of that statement?
It is for the sake of precluding the postulation of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Some postulate that "contact" (*saṃnikarṣa*) is the means of valid cognition or that "the sense organ" (*indriya*) is the means of valid cognition; it is said "that" (*tat*) in order to preclude such views.
Therefore, that alone—namely, cognition (*mati*) and the other [faculties]—is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and nothing else.

Now, if contact (*saṃnikarṣa*) or the sense organ (*indriya*) were the means of valid cognition, what would be the fault? If contact were the means of valid cognition, it would follow as an undesirable consequence that subtle, obstructed, and distant objects could not be apprehended.
For those [objects] are not in contact with the sense faculties.
Therefore, there would be an absence of omniscience.
Even if the sense faculty were a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), that same fault would apply; for the eye and other senses have limited objects, whereas the knowable is immeasurable.
Furthermore, there is an absence of contact with all the sense-faculties; this is because the eye and the mind lack the capacity to function by reaching their objects.
That they lack such capacity will be explained later.
If cognition were the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there would be an absence of a result (*phala*).
For it is intended that the result is comprehension (*adhigama*), not some other distinct entity.
If that [cognition] is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it cannot have any other result (*phala*).
Furthermore, the means of valid cognition must possess a result.
Only when contact (*saṃnikarṣa*) or the sense faculty (*indriya*) is the means of valid cognition is it logical for comprehension (*adhigama*) to be the result as a distinct entity.
That is incorrect.

If contact (*saṃnikarṣa*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the apprehension of the object (*arthādhigama*) is the result (*phala*), then because that [contact] resides in two [entities], its result—the apprehension—must also reside in two. Consequently, it would follow that there is an apprehension of the object and so forth as well.
If you argue that because the self (*ātman*) is conscious, the apprehension inheres in that [self] alone; [we reply:]...

No; for if the nature of being a knower were absent, all things would be insentient. Alternatively, if the nature of being a knower were admitted, it would contradict your own tenet regarding the self.
But was it not said that if cognition is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), there would be no result (*phala*)?
This is not a fault; for satisfaction is observed upon the apprehension of an object.
For the self, whose nature is that of a knower but which is defiled by karma, satisfaction arises when there is a determination of an object through the mediation of the instruments [of sense].
That is called the fruit.
Equanimity or the destruction of ignorance is the fruit.
Equanimity is the absence of mental aspiration toward attachment and aversion.
Or rather, the fruit is said to be the destruction of ignorance, which is like darkness.
A means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that by which one cognizes, that which is cognized, or simply the act of cognition itself (*pramiti*).
What is cognized by this?
It is an object such as the living soul (jīva).

If a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is required for the apprehension of the living soul and other such objects, then another means of valid cognition must be postulated for the apprehension of that very means of valid cognition.
If that were so, there would be an infinite regress.
There is no infinite regress, as in the case of a lamp.

Just as a lamp is the cause for illuminating objects such as jars, and it is that very same lamp which illuminates its own nature, without another illumination being sought, so too it must necessarily be admitted regarding the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

If, like the object of cognition (*prameya*), the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) were to require the postulation of another means of cognition, there would be no attainment of its own [cognition], and thus no recollection.
Due to the absence of that [recollection], worldly discourse (*vyavahāra*) would come to an end.
The use of the dual number is in reference to the distinctions that are about to be stated;
for it will be said that "the first is indirect, while the other is direct. Furthermore, this use of the dual number is intended to exclude any other number of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Having established that the fivefold knowledge previously mentioned is included within the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he says—beginning with the first—in order to eliminate the conceptualization of a separate pair of means such as perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*): "The indirect [is the first]. (174)
The word "ādi" (beginning) expresses priority.
That which exists at the beginning is "ādya" (the first).
How can there be primacy for two? By means of the conceptualization of primary and metaphorical [status].
