First, sensory cognition (*matijñāna*) is primary according to the principal sense of the term.
Scriptural knowledge (*śruta*) is also figuratively designated as "first" due to its close proximity to the former.
By the force of the dual-number designation, the secondary [knowledge] is also included.
"Both the first and the first" means that the first two are cognition (*mati*) and scripture (*śruta*).
Both of these are connected with the term "indirect means of valid cognition" (*parokṣa-pramāṇa*). Why is this [cognition] indirect?

Because it depends on external factors, it will be stated that sensory cognition (*mati-jñāna*) has the sense organs and the mind as its causes, and that scriptural knowledge (*śruta*) belongs to the non-sensory [mind].

Therefore, depending on external causes such as other senses, the mind, light, instruction, and so forth, and requiring the subsidence and destruction of the karma obscuring it, the *mati* and *śruta* arising in the self are designated as indirect (*parokṣa*).
Consequently, comparison (*upamāna*), verbal testimony (*āgama*), and the like are included within these very two.
In order to demonstrate that everything other than that which is characterized as "indirect" (parokṣa) is "direct perception" (pratyakṣa), he says:
"The other is direct perception."
That which perceives (*akṣṇoti*), pervades (*vyāpnoti*), and knows (*jānāti*) is the *akṣa*, namely the self (*ātman*).

When that very [self] has attained the subsidence of karmic destruction (*kṣayopaśama*) or when its obscurations (*āvaraṇa*) have been destroyed, it is "direct" (*pratyakṣa*), being specific to each individual.

Limited vision (*avadhidarśana*) and omniscient vision (*kevaladarśana*) are also restricted to the sense-faculties (*akṣa*); therefore, they too would have to be included [in the definition of perception].
This is not a fault; for the term "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is understood to carry over [from the previous definition], and by that, vision is excluded.
Even so, false discernment (*vibhaṅgajñāna*) is also restricted to the sense-faculties, and thus it too would have to be included.
Because of the governing context of "rightly" (*samyak*), there is the cessation of that [wrong knowledge].
The term "rightly" carries over [from the previous definition]; by it, knowledge is qualified, whereby the exclusion of distorted knowledge (*vibhaṅgajñāna*) is established.
For that [distorted knowledge], due to the arising of false view (*mithyādarśana*), has as its object a perverted reality and is therefore not "right."

It might be thought that the definition of non-contradiction must be accepted as follows: knowledge produced by the operation of the sense faculties is *pratyakṣa* (perceptual), while that whose operation concerns objects beyond the senses is *parokṣa* (non-perceptual).

This is incorrect, because it would entail the consequence that an authoritative person (*āpta*) lacks perceptual knowledge. If knowledge is held to be *pratyakṣa* only when caused by the sense faculties, then in that case, an authoritative person would have no perceptual knowledge.
For his comprehension of objects is not preceded by the sense organs.
If it is then assumed that even his knowledge is preceded by an instrument, he would lack omniscience.
If it is argued that his perception is mental, since knowledge is preceded by the application of the mind, there is indeed an absence of omniscience.
If it is argued that its establishment is through scripture (*āgama*), we say no; for that [scripture] is preceded by perceptual knowledge (*pratyakṣajñāna*).
If it is argued that there is another type of knowledge, namely yogic perception, which is also divine, we reply:

it does not possess the status of perception (*pratyakṣatva*), because it lacks the sense organs as its cause; for it is accepted that perception is that which occurs in relation to each individual sense organ (*akṣam akṣaṃ prati*).

Furthermore, there would be either a lack of omniscience or a contradiction of one's own thesis. This is because the cognition of this yogi must either be restricted to each individual object or grasp multiple objects simultaneously. If it were restricted to each individual object, this yogi would not possess omniscience, because the objects of knowledge are infinite.

Now, if the thesis is that consciousness apprehends multiple objects— that consciousness does not [apprehend] two objects simultaneously just as it apprehends one object, nor do two consciousnesses [apprehend one object]— then that thesis is abandoned.
Just as consciousness does not cognize two objects simultaneously,
so too it does not cognize a single object with two consciousnesses.

Alternatively, the thesis that "all conditioned phenomena are momentary" would be abandoned, because one would be admitting that a single consciousness exists across multiple moments. For the apprehension of multiple objects occurs sequentially.
If it is argued that they occur simultaneously:

That which is its moment of birth is solely for the purpose of attaining its own self-nature (*ātmalābha*). For once it has attained its own self-nature, it engages in its own activity, like a lamp. If this is argued:
For even in that case, it is only when there is a state of having multiple moments as its object that the relationship between the illuminated and the illuminator can be admitted.
Furthermore, because it transcends conceptual construction, it would follow that it is empty.
In order to explain the specific distinctions within the first type of the two types of valid cognition (pramāṇa) already mentioned, he says:
"Cognition (mati), recollection (smṛti), recognition (saṃjñā), deliberation (cintā), and discernment (abhinibodha) are synonymous.

Those which were first mentioned as synonyms for the knowledge [in question] are to be understood as follows: because they are the objects of the cognitive application (*upayoga*) produced by the internal cause—the subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣayopaśama*) of the veil of sensory knowledge (*matijñānāvaraṇa*)—and because they do not apply to scriptural knowledge (*śruta*) and the other types.
*Manana* is *mati*; *smaraṇa* is *smṛti*; *saṃjñāna* is *saṃjñā*; *cintana* is *cintā*; and *abhinibodhana* is *abhinibodha*.
Other etymological analyses (*vigraha*) should be understood according to their respective possibilities.
Even though there is a difference in their etymological origins (*prakṛti*), they function as synonyms because they acquire conventional usage (*rūḍhi*).

For example, "Indra," "Śakra," and "Puraṃdara" are designations for the one and only Lord of Śacī, despite the difference in the actions denoted by the terms, such as "ruling" (*indana*) and so forth.

From the perspective of the *samabhirūḍha* (etymological) standpoint, if one were to conceive of them as having distinct meanings, that same sequence would indeed exist even in the case of *mati* and the others.

However, the intended meaning here is that they do not transcend the functional application (*upayoga*) caused by the subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣayopaśama*) of the veil of sensory knowledge (*matijñānāvaraṇa*).
The word "iti" signifies a manner; thus, these synonymous terms are of this particular kind.
Or rather, it is the object denoted:
that single object which is expressed by these terms—*mati*, *smṛti*, *saṃjñā*, *cintā*, and *abhinibodha*—is one and the same.
Now, as to what the cause for its acquisition of self-nature is, he says: "That has the sense-faculties and the non-sense-faculty as its cause. (185)
The term *indra* means "the sovereign," referring to the Self (*ātman*).

When there is the destruction or subsidence of the veil over that Self whose nature is consciousness, yet which is itself incapable of perceiving objects, that which serves as the sign for the apprehension of objects is called the *indriya*, the "sign of Indra.
Alternatively, it is a "sign" (*liṅga*) because it makes known an object that is otherwise hidden.
The sense organ is the mark for the realization of the existence of the subtle self (*ātman*).

Just as smoke here [on earth] is a mark of fire, so too this instrument of touch and the other senses cannot exist in the absence of an agent, the self; thus, the existence of the knower is understood.
Alternatively, "Indra" refers to the activity of naming; that which is created by him is the sense-faculty (*indriya*). Its function, such as touching and so forth, will be explained later.
"Non-faculty" (*anindriya*), "mind" (*manas*), and "inner instrument" (*antaḥkaraṇa*) are not different in meaning.
But how can the term "non-faculty" apply to the mind—which is indeed a mark of Indra (*indraliṅga*)—by way of negating its status as a faculty?
Because the negative particle *nañ* is used in the sense of "slight" (*īṣadartha*). Thus, "slight sense-faculty" (*īṣadindriya*) is called "non-sense-faculty" (*anindriya*),
just as a girl with a slight waist is called "waistless" (*anudarā*).
How is it used in the sense of "slight" (īṣadartha)?
These sense organs have objects restricted to specific locations and persist for a period of time;
the mind, however, is not like that—even though it is the mark (liṅga) of Indra, it does not have objects restricted to specific locations nor does it persist for a period of time.
That is also called the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

Because it does not depend on the sense organs in its operations such as the investigation of qualities and defects or recollection, and because it is not perceived externally like the eyes and other senses, it is called the "internal organ" (*antaḥkaraṇa*) since it is an organ situated within.
For what purpose is the word "that" (tat) used?
It is for the purpose of indicating sensory cognition (mati-jñāna).
But surely, according to the principle that "a rule or a prohibition applies to what immediately precedes," only that [preceding term] should be understood here.
It is said that this [term *jñāna*] is for the sake of the present context and for the sake of what follows:

that knowledge which is denoted by synonymous terms such as *mati* and so forth, and which is caused by the sense organs (*indriya*) and the non-sense organ (*anindriya*), is precisely what constitutes apprehension (*avagraha*), speculation (*īhā*), perceptual judgment (*avāya*), and retention (*dhāraṇā*).

Otherwise, having first stated that cognition denoted by terms such as "mati" is caused by the sense organs and the non-sense organ (the mind), it would lead to the undesirable conclusion that this very [cognition] is [identical to] avagraha, īhā, avāya, and dhāraṇā.

Thus, since the cause of its arising has been fully understood but its divisions have not yet been determined, he says the following in order to explain those divisions: "Apprehension (avagraha), speculation (īhā), perceptual judgment (avāya), and retention (dhāraṇā).
Immediately following the conjunction of the object and the sense-organ, the initial apprehension is *avagraha*.
When there is a conjunction of the object and the sense-organ, there occurs a mere perception (*darśana*);
immediately after that, the apprehension of the object's meaning is *avagraha*.
For example: the apprehension by the eye that "this is a white form" is *avagraha* (perception).
The desire to know the specific details of the object already grasped by *avagraha* is *īhā* (speculative inquiry).
For example: "This white form—what is it, a crane or a banner?"
*Avāya* is the comprehension of the true nature [of an object] through the discernment of its specific qualities;
for example, "This is indeed a crane, not a banner," based on its flying up, swooping down, and flapping its wings.
*Dhāraṇā* is the cause of not forgetting what has been understood at a later time.
"Just as this is that very same crane which I saw in the forenoon.
The sequence in which these [phonemes], beginning with the *avagraha*, are presented is determined by the order of their production.
In order to explain the subdivisions of the aforementioned types of sensory perception, such as *avagraha* and so forth, he says:
"Of many, manifold, quick, distinct, unexpressed, and constant [objects], together with their opposites.
(Sūtra 192)
The specific actions such as *avagraha* (seizure) and so forth have been introduced as the subject at hand.
This designation of the object (*karman*) is made with reference to them:
"of the words beginning with *bahu*, together with their opposites."
The term *bahu* is understood here as denoting both number and abundance, since there is no distinction made between them.
As an example of its denoting number: "one," "two," or "many.
As an example of its denoting abundance: "much rice" or "much soup."
The word *vidha* denotes a variety or mode.
The inclusion of the term *kṣipra* (swift) is for the purpose of indicating immediate comprehension.
The inclusion of the term *aniḥsṛta* (not emerged) is for the purpose of indicating that not all individuals have emerged [from the womb].
"Unstated" means apprehension by way of intention. "Constant" means continuous apprehension according to the object as it is.
"Together with its opposite" is for the purpose of including its counter-position.

Apprehension (*avagraha*) is of twelve varieties: apprehension of many [objects], apprehension of few, apprehension of many kinds, apprehension of one kind, apprehension quickly, apprehension after a long time, apprehension of the unmanifested, apprehension of the manifested, apprehension of the unspoken, apprehension of the spoken, apprehension of the permanent, and apprehension of the impermanent.
In this same way, inquiry (*īhā*) and the other stages of cognition are also [divided] accordingly.
These [perceptions] are manifested individually through the five sense-faculties and the mind.

Among them, the many types of apprehension (*avagraha*) and so forth arise from the excellence of the subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣayopaśama*) of the veil of sensory cognition (*mati-jñānāvaraṇa*), and not others.
Because they are the most venerable, they are mentioned first.

What is the specific distinction between "much" (*bahu*) and "of many kinds" (*bahuvidha*); for in both cases there is "muchness," whether it be among many things or among things of many kinds? The distinction is made by way of being of a single type or of various types.

What is the specific distinction between [the meditative absorptions] that have emerged from what has been taught (*uktaniḥsṛta*) and those that have emerged from all [the teachings] (*sakalaniḥsaraṇa*); for in both cases they have emerged from the entirety [of the teachings]?

Is it not already stated that it is of this very nature? There is this distinction: [in the former case] grasping was said to be preceded by the instruction of another; [here] grasping has emerged spontaneously by itself.
For others, the reading is *kṣipraniḥsṛtaḥ*.

They describe it thus: when a sound is being grasped by the auditory faculty, one person recognizes it as "that of a peacock" or "that of a curlew," while another does so by means of its essential form alone.

What is the specific distinction between *dhruvāvagraha* (constant apprehension) and *dhāraṇā* (retention)? It is said: at the time of attaining *kṣayopaśama* (subsidence-cum-destruction), due to the continuity of pure transformation resulting from that attained *kṣayopaśama*, the apprehension (*avagraha*) in the first moment is exactly as it is in the second and subsequent moments—neither less nor more—and thus it is called *dhruvāvagraha*.

Furthermore, when there is a subsidence of karma (*kṣayopaśama*) resulting from the mixture of pure transformation and defiled transformation, the apprehension (*avagraha*) arising therefrom sometimes pertains to many objects, sometimes to few, sometimes to many kinds, and sometimes to a single kind; because of this state of deficiency or excess, it is called "unsteady apprehension" (*adhruvāvagraha*).
Retention (*dharaṇā*), on the other hand, is the cause for not forgetting the object already apprehended; thus, there is a great difference between these two.

If [it is argued that] "restriction" (avagraha) and the other [phonetic elements] project actions such as "many" (bahu), but it remains unclear of what [the qualities] "many" and so forth are qualifiers, he says: "Of the object" (arthasya).§ 198.
The object is that which is the domain of the eye and the other sense organs.
The connection is made that *avagraha* and the other stages of cognition occur with respect to that [object] as qualified by attributes such as "many" and so forth.

Why is this stated, given that "many" and so forth are simply properties of the object itself? This is true; however, the term "of the object" (*arthasya*) is stated in order to exclude the conceptual constructions of rival disputants.
Some proponents maintain that it is only the qualities such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth that come into contact with the sense organs, and therefore only these are apprehended.
That is incorrect; for those qualities such as form are not incorporeal (*amūrta*), yet they cannot undergo contact with the sense organs.
If that is so, then how is it that one can say, "Form has been seen by me," or "Odor has been smelled"?
And it exists.

How so? That which moves through its modes (*paryāya*), or that by which [the soul] is moved, is the object (*artha*), namely substance (*dravya*). When that [substance] comes into contact with the sense organs, because they are not distinct from it, the conventional usage [of terms like "color" and so on] regarding color-form (*rūpa*) and the rest is also appropriate.
Are these stages beginning with apprehension (*avagraha*) common to all sense organs and the mind-organ (*anindriya*), or is there some specific distinction among their objects? To this, he says:
The apprehension of the *vyañjana*.
*Vyañjana* refers to the indistinct arising of sound and so forth; its apprehension occurs, but not [the apprehension] of *īhā* and the other stages.

For what purpose is this? It is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*), [meaning] that here only *avagraha* occurs and not *neha* and so forth. Should that particle *eva* then be employed? It need not be employed; according to the principle that "a rule being undertaken when [the matter] is already established is for the sake of restriction," it will serve as a restriction even without the particle *eva*. But surely the mention of *avagraha* is the same in both cases; what then is the basis for this distinction? The distinction between *arthāvagraha* and *vyañjanāvagraha* is one made on the basis of the manifest and the unmanifest.

How so? Like the drying of a fresh earthen bowl. Just as a fresh bowl does not become dry when sprinkled with only one or two drops of water, but that very same bowl gradually becomes moistened when sprinkled again and again; likewise, material particles (*pudgala*) transformed into sound and other objects, when apprehended by the sense organs such as the ear over two or three moments, do not become manifest. When there is repeated apprehension, they become manifest. Therefore, prior to the apprehension of the manifest is the apprehension of the non-manifest (*vyañjanāvagraha*), while the apprehension of the manifest is the apprehension of the object (*arthāvagraha*).
Consequently, because it is the apprehension of the non-manifest, no further stages such as *īhā* (speculation) occur.

Since it would follow that there is apprehension by way of the manifestation of all the sense organs without distinction, he states the prohibition of those objects for which such apprehension is impossible:
"Not by means of the eye or the non-sensory organ."
There is no apprehension of phonemes (*vyañjanāvagraha*) by means of the eye or the non-sensory faculty (*anindriya*). Why? Because they function without reaching their object (*aprāpyakāritva*).

Since the eye perceives an object that is not reached [by contact], yet is not distant, is suitable, situated within the range of proximity, and manifested by external light—and since the mind likewise does not reach its object—there is no *vyañjanāvagraha* (perception of the sign) for these two.
How is the fact that the eye functions without reaching its object (*aprāpyakāritva*) determined? Both from scripture (*āgama*) and from reasoning (*yukti*).
First, from scripture and also from reasoning: the eye does not act by reaching [its object], because it does not grasp what has been touched.

If it were to function by reaching its object, like the sense of touch, it would perceive the collyrium applied to the eye when touched; however, it does not perceive it. Therefore, it should be understood that, like the mind, it functions without reaching its object.
Consequently, with the exception of the eye and the mind, the remaining senses possess *vyañjanāvagraha* (perception of the manifesting sign).
It is thus established that all senses, both physical and mental, possess *arthāvagraha* (perception of the object itself).

It was said: "Cognitive knowledge (*matijñāna*) has been explained according to its characteristics and its classifications. Immediately following that, "scriptural knowledge" (*śruta*) was mentioned; its characteristics and classifications must now be stated. Therefore, he says:
"Scriptural knowledge is preceded by cognitive knowledge; it is of two kinds, many kinds, and twelve kinds."
Although this word *śruta* is derived based on the act of hearing (*śravaṇa*), by the force of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), it refers to a particular kind of knowledge.
Just as the word *kuśala*, although derived in relation to the work of clearing a forest (*kuśalavana-karman*), by the force of conventional usage, refers to that which is purified (*paryavadāta*).
What, then, is this specific kind of knowledge? To this he says: "Learning is preceded by intelligence.
Here, "preceding" (*pūrva*) means that which fulfills the validity of learning; thus, "preceding," "sign," and "cause" are synonymous.
Intelligence (*mati*) has already been defined.
“Preceded by intelligence” (*matipūrva*) means that its cause is intelligence; this is the meaning.
If scriptural learning (*śruta*) were preceded by intelligence, it would follow that it too consists of intelligence, for in the world an effect is seen to resemble its cause.
This, however, is not an absolute rule.
This jar has the staff and other such factors as its causes, but it does not consist of the staff and so forth.
Furthermore, because that [effect] is absent even when those [causes] are present.

Even when sensory cognition (*mati-jñāna*) exists and external conditions for scriptural cognition (*śruta-jñāna*) are present, there is an absence of scriptural cognition due to the arising of powerful obscuration to scripture (*śrutāvaraṇa*).

However, when there is an excellence in the destruction-cum-subsidence (*kṣayopaśama*) of the obscuration of scriptural knowledge (*śruta-āvaraṇa*), then scriptural knowledge (*śrutajñāna*) arises; thus, sensory knowledge (*matijñāna*) should be understood as merely the instrumental cause.
[An objector] says: "Scriptural knowledge is held to be without beginning or end."
If it were preceded by [human] intellect, those [qualities] would be absent from it; because that which has a beginning must have an end.

And consequently, since it would be a human composition, it would lack authority. This is not a fault; for, because it conveys the general categories such as substance and so forth, the Śruti is held to be without beginning or end.
Indeed, it was not conceived by any person, anywhere, at any time, or in any manner whatsoever.
It is said that [the Veda] is "preceded by intelligence" because, with respect to its specific instances, a beginning and an end are possible.
Just as a sprout is preceded by a seed, yet that [seed-lineage], in view of the continuum (*saṃtāna*), is without beginning or end.
Furthermore, being authorless (*apauruṣeyatva*) is not the cause of validity; for otherwise, the instruction of thieves and the like, whose authors are not remembered, would result in being valid.
And what contradiction is there in the validity of impermanent means of knowledge, such as direct perception?

[The opponent] asks: "At the first arising of right faith (*samyaktva*), since cognitions undergo transformation simultaneously, it is not possible for scriptural knowledge (*śruta*) to be preceded by mati. That is incorrect; for right faith is dependent upon that [mati].
Since the acquisition of the self occurs sequentially, there is no contradiction with its being preceded by cognition (*matipūrvaka*). [The opponent] says:
"The definition that 'learning (*śruta*) is preceded by cognition' is too narrow (*avyāpin*), for it is also accepted that learning can be preceded by [other instances of] learning."

For example—when a person who has mastered the conventions [of language] understands from a collection of aggregates (*skandha*) consisting of a person transformed into sound, which possesses the nature of phonemes, words, and sentences, and from objects such as the eyes and so forth that have become the objects of initial hearing, another related effect such as the holding of water by a jar, or a substance such as fire from smoke and so forth—at that time, is this not "comprehension of what was heard" (*śrutapratipatti*) based on what was heard? This is not a fault; for even that [understanding] is, by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), preceded by cognition (*mati*).
Furthermore, even "hearing" (*śruta*) is sometimes metaphorically designated as "cognition" (*mati*) because it is preceded by cognition.
The term "division" (*bheda*) applies to each [category] individually—as in "two divisions," "many divisions," or "twelve divisions.
First, regarding the two divisions: namely, "outside the limbs" (*aṅgabāhya*) and "entered into the limbs" (*aṅgapraviṣṭa*).
That which is outside the limbs is of many kinds, such as the *Daśavaikālika*, the *Uttarādhyayana*, and so forth.
The *aṅgapraviṣṭa* (canonical texts included in the limbs) is of twelve kinds.

Namely: *Ācāra*, *Sūtrakṛta*, *Sthāna*, *Samavāya*, *Vyākhyāprajñapti*, *Jñātṛdharmakathā*, *Upāsakādhyayana*, *Antakṛddaśa*, *Anuttaraupapādikadaśa*, *Praśnavyākaraṇa*, *Vipākasūtra*, and *Dṛṣṭivāda*.
The *Dṛṣṭivāda* is fivefold: *Parikarma*, *Sūtra*, *Pūrvam-anuyoga*, *Pūrvagata*, and *Cūlikā*.

Among these, the fourteen-fold *pūrvaga* consists of: *utpādapūrva*, *agrāyaṇīya*, *vīryānupravāda*, *astināstipravāda*, *jñānapravāda*, *satyapravāda*, *ātmapravāda*, *karmapravāda*, *pratyākhyānanāmadheya*, *vidyānupravāda*, *kalyāṇanāmadheya*, *prāṇāvāya*, *kriyāviśāla*, and *lokabindusāra*.
This sacred scripture (*śruta*) is divided into two types, many types, and twelve types.
What is the cause of this distinction? It is caused by the distinction among the speakers.
There are three types of speakers: the omniscient Tīrthaṅkara, another who is a Śrutakevalin (one possessing perfect scriptural knowledge), and one who is heterodox.
Among these, the Āgama was taught in its true sense by the omniscient Supreme Seer, through his extraordinary power of supreme, inconceivable, and absolute knowledge.
Its authority arises from the fact that he was a direct perceiver and his defects were completely destroyed.

His composition of texts—characterized as the *aṅgas* and *pūrvas*—was recorded by his immediate disciples, the *gaṇadharas*, who possessed supreme intellectual power and miraculous faculties and were *śrutakevalins*.
That is authoritative because of its authority.

Furthermore, by later teachers, for the sake of favoring disciples whose lifespan, intelligence, and strength were diminished due to the defects of the age, [the teachings] were compiled in works such as the *Daśavaikālika*. In terms of its substance, that is precisely this; it is like water from the ocean of milk taken up in a jar.
The indirect has been explained.
The direct must now be discussed.
It is of two kinds: direct with respect to place and direct with respect to all [objects].
Limited direct perception (*avadhi-pratyakṣa*) consists of the knowledge of limited range (*avadhi-jñāna*) and the knowledge of others' minds (*manaḥparyaya-jñāna*).
Universal direct perception (*sarva-pratyakṣa*) is the absolute knowledge (*kevala-jñāna*).

If this is so, then let this very limited knowledge (*avadhi-jñāna*), which is the first of the three types of direct perception, be explained first. To this it is said: limited knowledge is of two kinds—caused by birth (*bhava-pratyaya*) and caused by the subsidence-cum-destruction of karmic obstructions (*kṣayopaśama-nimitta*).
In that regard, the condition of existence (*bhavapratyaya*) is stated:
the condition of existence is the determinative limit (*avadhi*) for gods and hell-beings.
It is called "existence" (*bhava*). What is existence? Existence is a state (*paryāya*) of the self caused by the arising of the karma named "life-span.
"Condition," "cause," and "motive" (*nimitta*) are synonymous terms.
Existence (*bhava*) is its condition; thus, existence as a condition (*bhavapratyaya*) should be understood as the limit for gods and hell-beings.

If this is so, does it not follow that [the knowledge] there cannot have the subsidence of karmic obstructions (*kṣayopaśama*) as its cause? This is not a fault; for that [subsidence] is established by depending upon that [existence].
Since the subsidence of obstructions arises in dependence upon existence, existence is taught as the primary cause.

Just as the flight of birds in the sky is caused by their birth-nature (*bhava*) and not by any specific quality of training, so too, even in the absence of vows, restraints, and the like, [the experience] arises for gods and hell-beings; thus it is said to be "conditioned by birth" (*bhavapratyaya*).
For otherwise, since birth would be common [to all], there would be no distinction among them.
Yet, it is accepted that in those cases there occurs a variation in the intensity and lack of intensity of the limit [of experience].

Although the expression “of gods and hell-beings” is stated without qualification, it refers specifically to those with right view. Why? Because of the mention of “limitation” (avadhi), and because [the scripture] speaks of a “detailed analysis” (vibhaṅga) regarding those with false view.
And its occurrence in states of excellence or non-excellence is to be understood from scripture.

If the limitative cognition (avadhi) of gods and hell-beings is caused by their state of existence (bhava), then for whom is it caused by the subsidence-cum-destruction (kṣayopaśama)? To this he says:
The [knowledge] caused by subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣayopaśama*) has six varieties for the remaining [beings].

When there is the rising of the partial-obscuring (*deśaghāti*) *spardhakas* of the obscuration of clairvoyance (*avadhijñāna*), the non-arising of the total-obscuring (*sarvaghāti*) *spardhakas* is destruction (*kṣaya*); the state of existence of those very same [total-obscuring *spardhakas*] which have reached the stage of non-arising is subsidence (*upaśama*).
"Having that as its cause" means having the subsidence-cum-destruction (kṣayopaśama) as its cause.
That [attainment] is to be understood as belonging to the remaining [categories].
But who, then, are the remaining ones?
They are humans and animals.
Even among them, it should be understood that this applies only where there is the capacity [for such action].
For those who are without perception (asaṃjñin) and those who are not yet fully developed (aparyāptaka) lack that capacity.
It does not belong to all those who possess consciousness and are fully developed (paryāptaka).

To whom, then, does it belong? It is perceived by those whose karma has been pacified or destroyed, provided that the aforementioned causes such as right vision (samyagdarśana) and so forth are present.

If [karma] were the cause for everyone through its subsidence (kṣayopaśama), the specific mention of "subsidence" would be unnecessary; rather, the mention of "subsidence" is for the sake of restriction, to indicate that it is only subsidence that serves as the cause, and not [the mere presence of] karma.
This aforementioned limit (*avadhi*) is of six types.

Why? Because of the distinctions between that which follows [the object], that which does not follow, that which increases, that which decreases, that which remains stable, and that which is unstable.
A certain limit follows one who is moving, like the light of the sun.
One [kind of limit] does not follow along but perishes right there, like the words of a man who points out a question while looking upward.

Another limit is like a fire produced by rubbing fire-sticks together, which, once kindled by a heap of fuel accumulated from dry leaves, increases from its initial size until it reaches incalculable worlds due to the presence of the transformation of purity through qualities such as right vision (*samyagdarśana*).

The other limit [of avadhi] is such that, like the flame of a fire whose fuel is limited, it decreases from whatever magnitude it arose with—due to its connection with the decline of qualities such as right vision (*samyagdarśana*) and the transformation and increase of defilements—down to an incalculable fraction of a finger-breadth (*aṅgula*). The other limit, however, remains at the very same magnitude at which it arose due to the persistence of qualities such as right vision; it neither decreases nor increases, like a *liṅga* (the subtle body), until the destruction of existence (*bhava*) or the arising of omniscience (*kevalajñāna*).

The other type of *avadhi* arises through the increase or decrease of qualities such as right vision (*samyagdarśana*) and so forth; it expands from its initial magnitude as far as it is capable of expanding, and contracts as far as it is capable of contracting, like a wave of water driven by the force of the wind.
Thus, the *avadhi* is of six varieties.
Thus has clairvoyance (*avadhijñāna*) been explained; immediately following that, the knowledge of others' minds (*manaḥparyayajñāna*) must now be discussed.
Desiring to explain its definition preceded by its divisions, he says this:
"The knowledge of others' minds consists of the straight and the expansive intellect."
It is upright, accomplished, and straight.
Why is it accomplished? Because of the cognition of that which has been performed by speech, body, and mind, and which is intended for another's mind.
He whose mind is straight is "straight-minded" (*ṛjumati*).
It is unswerving and vast.
Why is it unswerving? Because he understands the objects produced by the speech, body, and mind of others as they exist within their own minds.
He whose intellect is vast is Vipulamati.
Both Ṛjumati and Vipulamati are referred to as Ṛjuvipulamatī.
Because the meaning of the word *mati* is already conveyed by the preceding term, one instance of it is not employed.
Alternatively, "straight" (*ṛju*) and "vast" (*vipula*) constitute "straight-and-vast" (*ṛjuvipula*).
Those whose intellects (*mati*) are straight-and-vast are called "those of straight-and-vast intellect" (*ṛjuvipulamatī*).
Thus, this knowledge of others' minds (*manaḥparyaya*) is twofold: that of straight intellect and that of vast intellect.

It is said: "The classification has been stated; now the definition must be stated. To this, it is replied: Manaḥparyaya is the functional application (*upayoga*) of the self, which—by virtue of the subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣayopaśama*) of the veil of energy (*vīryāntarāya*) and the veil of mind-reading knowledge (*manaḥparyayajñānāvaraṇa*), and by the support of the acquisition of the pure [karmic] matter of the limbs and sub-limbs (*aṅgopāṅga-nāma*)—attains its activity through connection with the minds of others.
If it is argued that this entails the consequence of it being sensory cognition (*matijñāna*), the answer has already been given previously.
The mind (*manas*) is the instrumental cause (*apekṣākāraṇa*).
Here, only this much is required as the object of dependence: that an object situated in another's mind is known by means of this [knowledge].

Regarding that, *manahparyaya* for one of straightforward intellect (*ṛjumati*), in terms of time, describes—at its minimum—the two or three births of living beings and oneself, and at its maximum, seven or eight [births], by way of their movements through various states of existence and so forth.
Regarding space, at the minimum it is a distinct interval of two *gavyūtis*, and at the maximum it is within a distinct interval of several *yojanas*, but not beyond.
Regarding time, the second [type] is described as being, at the minimum, seven or eight births, and at the maximum, an incalculable number through coming and going and so forth.
Regarding space, at the minimum it is a distinct interval of one *yojana*, and at the maximum it is within Mount Mānuṣottara, but not beyond.
Furthermore, in order to clarify the distinction between these two that have been mentioned, he says: "Their distinction is by way of purity and non-retrogression."
When there is the destruction and subsidence of those obscurations, the clarity of the self is purification (*viśuddhi*).
Falling back [to a lower state] is a relapse (*pratipāta*).

"Non-falling" means not falling back. For one whose passions (*kaṣāya*) have been stilled, there may be a falling back from the pinnacle of restraint due to the intensification of delusion regarding conduct (*cāritramoha*).
For one whose passions are destroyed, however, there is no falling back because of the absence of any cause for such a fall.
Purity and non-falling back are "purity and non-falling back.
By means of those two, purity and non-falling back, there is their distinction;
that is, the distinction between them.
Regarding purity therein: one of vast intellect (*vipulamati*) is purer than one of straight intellect (*ṛjumati*) by way of substance, space, time, and state.

How so? Here, the final infinitesimal part of the karmic matter (*kārmaṇadravya*) that is known by every limited cognition (*sarvāvadhi*) is further divided into infinite parts; the final part of that is the object of one of straight intellect.
The final part of that object of straight intellect, when further divided into infinite parts, is the object of one of vast intellect.
Because the infinite has infinite divisions,
purity has been described in terms of substance, space, and time.

Purity in terms of state (*bhāva*) is to be understood as having an even more subtle substance as its object, due to its association with the purity of supreme subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣayopaśama*).
Furthermore, Vipulamati is distinguished by his non-falling away, because for his masters there is an increase in the arising of right conduct (*cāritra*);
whereas Ṛjumati is subject to falling away, because for his masters there is a decline in the arising of right conduct due to the intensification of the passions (*kaṣāya*).
If this *manahparyaya* has such a specific characteristic for each individual soul, then from what does the distinction between these two—*avadhi* and *manahparyaya*—arise? To this he says:
"From purity, field, owner, and object, there is a distinction between *avadhi* and *manahparyaya*.
(Section 222)
Purity is clarity.
The field is that wherein one encounters phenomena.
The master is the agent.
The object is to be known.
Among these, the knowledge of the mind (manahparyaya) is more pure than the knowledge of limits (avadhi).
Why? Because its object is subtle.
The field has been explained;
the object will be explained next; and ownership is being addressed.
It exists among those endowed with the qualities of excellent conduct, ranging from the negligent (*pramatta*) up to those whose passions are destroyed (*kṣīṇakaṣāya*).
Furthermore, it arises among those whose conduct is increasing, not among those whose conduct is declining.
And arising among those whose conduct is increasing, it occurs in those who have attained any one of the seven kinds of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), but not in others.
[This applies] to some who have attained supernatural powers (ṛddhi), but not to all.
Thus, this is the distinction regarding the owner [of the knowledge], or rather, the mention of "distinguished self-restraint" (saṃyama) is the subject under discussion in the statement.
Furthermore, the limit [of its range] is "among those in the four states of existence" (cāturgatika); thus, there is a distinction between these two even due to the difference in their owners.
Now the time has come to state the definition of absolute knowledge (*kevalajñāna*). Yet, bypassing that, the connection between the objects of knowledge is examined.

Why? Because that [omniscience] will be explained later in the passage: "It is absolute due to the destruction of delusion, and the destruction of the veils of knowledge and perception and of the obstructive karma.
If this is so, then let the connection with objects be stated first for cognition (*mati*) and scriptural knowledge (*śruta*); therefore, he says:
"The connection of cognition and scriptural knowledge is with substances, but not with all their modes (*paryāya*)."
Binding is the act of binding.
Of what? Of the object.
Should the mention of "objects" (viṣaya) be made here? It need not be made.
The mention of "objects" is already under discussion.
Where was it mentioned? In the passage: "From the objects consisting of the field of purification and its owner."
Therefore, by the force of the meaning, there is a transformation of the case-ending for that [word], so that it is connected with “of the object” (*viṣayasya*).

The use of the plural number in “in substances” (*dravyeṣu*) is for the purpose of including all [substances]: living beings (*jīva*), merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), time (*kāla*), space (*ākāśa*), and matter (*pudgala*).
The inclusion of the term “not all modes” (*asarvaparyāya*) is for the purpose of qualifying those [substances].

Those substances, while becoming objects of sensory perception (*mati*) and scriptural knowledge (*śruta*), become objects through only a few of their infinite modes (*paryāya*), and not through all of them.

Here an objection is raised: "Since categories such as the *dharmāstikāya* are beyond the senses, sensory cognition (*matijñāna*) does not operate with respect to them. Therefore, the claim that sensory cognition operates with respect to all substances is incorrect? This is not a fault; for there exists a non-sensory instrument (*anindriya-karaṇa*), and based upon that, a mental application (*upayoga*)—preceded by the attainment of the subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣayopaśama*) of the non-sensory veil (*noindriyāvaraṇa*)—arises in the form of apprehension (*avagraha*) and so forth, even before [the operation of the physical senses].

Then, that previously mentioned scriptural knowledge (*śrutajñāna*) operates upon its own appropriate objects. Now, as for the connection regarding the object-domain of clairvoyance (*avadhi*), which is worthy of being mentioned immediately after sensory and scriptural knowledge (*mati* and *śruta*), he says:
Regarding the material [elements],
the term "bondage to the object" (*viṣayanibandha*) is understood to carry over.
By the term “in material things” (*rūpiṣu*), both persons (*pudgala*) and living beings (*jīva*) who are connected to the substance of a person are included.
A restriction is established that the objective connection of limited knowledge (*avadhi*) occurs only in relation to material things, and not in relation to non-material things.

Even among material things, it does not occur with respect to all modes (*paryāya*); rather, for the sake of emphasis, the phrase “not in all modes” is connected [to the previous statement] to indicate that it occurs only in those modes suitable to itself.

Now, as for the object-restriction (*viṣayanibandha*) of mind-reading (*manaḥparyaya*), which follows immediately after that [description], he says: "The object of mind-reading is one part of that [object of omniscience]."

Of this material substance which has been established as the object of all types of clairvoyant knowledge (*avadhijñāna*), when it is divided into infinite parts, the knowledge of others' minds (*manaḥparyaya*) operates upon only one part.
Now, regarding that *kevalajñāna* (perfect knowledge) which was mentioned at the end, what is its objective basis? To this he says:
"Of the perfect [knowledge], [the object] consists of all substances and all their modifications.
(Sūtra 230).
"Substances and modes" (*dravyaparyāyāḥ*) is a copulative compound (*dvandva*) characterized by mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*).

The qualifying term "all" (*sarva*) is connected with each [member] individually, meaning "in all substances and in all modes. First, the substances of living beings (*jīvadravya*) are infinitely infinite; the substances of matter (*pudgaladravya*), divided into atoms and aggregates, are even more infinitely infinite; the three—dharma, adharma, and space—are [each] one; and time (*kāla*) is innumerable. Their modes (*paryāya*), existing across the three periods of time, are infinitely infinite for each of them. In these [substances and modes], [the omniscient one knows everything].
Neither substance nor the collection of its modes transcends the state of being an object for kevalajñāna.
Indeed, it is said "in all substances and modes" in order to demonstrate that its majesty is immeasurable.
It has been established that cognition and the other faculties are restricted by their respective objects.
However, this remains to be determined: when several cognitions arise simultaneously in a single self through the proximity of their own respective causes, how many can there be?
It is said: one or more may occur simultaneously in a single self, up to four.
The word *eka* denotes number, and the word *ādi* denotes a part.
Those things of which "one" is the first are these "beginning-with-one" (*ekādi*) items.
The portions are to be divided;
simultaneously within a single self.
To what extent? Up to four.

For example, first, there is only one [type of] perfect knowledge (*kevalajñāna*); no other knowledge resulting from the subsidence and destruction of karma (*kṣāyopaśamika*) coexists with it simultaneously.
There are two: sensory cognition (*mati*) and scriptural knowledge (*śruta*).

There are three: sensory cognition, scriptural knowledge, and clairvoyant knowledge (*avadhijñāna*), or alternatively, sensory cognition, scriptural knowledge, and telepathic knowledge (*manaḥparyayajñāna*).
There are four types of knowledge: mati, śruta, avadhi, and manaḥparyaya.
There are not five, because kevala-jñāna exists without a companion.
Now, as for whether the aforementioned [cognitions] such as *mati* and so forth receive the designation "knowledge" (*jñāna*) exclusively, or otherwise as well, he says:
"Sensory cognition (*mati*), scriptural cognition (*śruta*), and clairvoyant cognition (*avadhi*), as well as error (*viparyaya*).
"Error" means "falsity.
Why? Because of the governing context of "correctly.
The word "and" (ca) has the sense of conjunction.
"And there is perversion as well as correctness.
But from what does their perversion arise? From their inherence in the same object as false view (*mithyādarśana*), like milk contained in a dusty, bitter gourd.
[Objection: But in that case, the perversion of the milk's taste is due to a defect in the container.
And there is no such reversal in the apprehension of objects by wrong cognition (*matyajñāna*) and the rest.

For instance, just as one with right vision perceives forms and so forth through the eyes and other senses, so too does one with wrong vision [perceive them] through wrong sensory cognition (*matyajñāna*).

And just as one with right vision knows and defines forms and so forth through scriptural knowledge (*śruta*), so too does one with wrong vision [know and define them] through wrong scriptural cognition (*śrutājñāna*).

Just as one with right view understands material objects through the knowledge of supernormal power (*avadhijñāna*), so too does one with wrong view understand them through the knowledge of analysis (*vibhaṅgajñāna*).
To this, it is said:
Because there is no distinction between the existent and the non-existent, perception occurs by chance, like that of a madman.
"Existent" means what is present; "non-existent" means what is absent. This is the meaning.
Because these two are perceived indistinctly by chance, a misconception arises.

Sometimes, even though form and so forth exist, one perceives them as non-existent; or even though they do not exist, one perceives them as existent. At other times, what exists is determined to be existent, and what does not exist is determined to be non-existent. This occurs due to the arising of false views, just as one whose intellect is agitated by the onset of bile might think "this is my wife" when it is his mother, or think "this is my mother" when it is his wife.

Even when one perceives a mother as merely a mother or a wife as merely a wife by chance, even then that is not correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*). In this same way, the error regarding cognition and the other [faculties] with respect to form and the other [objects] is to be understood.

For instance, a certain transformation of cognition (*mityādarśanapariṇāma*) residing in the self produces a reversal of causes, a reversal of difference and non-difference, and a reversal of essential nature, even while the perception of form and so forth is occurring.
First, regarding the inversion concerning causes: some postulate that there is a single cause for form and the other [sensory objects], which is immaterial and eternal.
Others hold that atoms—distinct in their species as earth and so forth, and possessing four, three, two, or one quality—are the originators of effects belonging to similar species.

Still others describe [the following]: the four elements, earth and so forth, and the elemental properties of color, odor, taste, and touch; the collection of these constitutes the "eightfold" atom of form (*rūpa-paramāṇu*), and so on.
Others describe it as follows: earth, water, fire, and air—possessing the qualities of solidity, fluidity, heat, and motion—are atoms distinct by genus that originate the effect.
This is the inversion of difference and non-difference, consisting of the conceptualization that the effect is either entirely different from its cause or entirely not different from it.
§ 239. The reversal of intrinsic nature [consists in this]: that form and the other [sense-objects] are either non-conceptual existents or simply do not exist at all;
rather, it is consciousness itself that has transformed into their aspect.
And that object which serves as the focal point is not external.
In this way, they also postulate other various types of conceptual constructions that contradict what is seen and what is accepted; these arise from false views, and they develop faith in them.
Consequently, there arises ignorance regarding those doctrines, ignorance resulting from hearing [them], and distorted knowledge (*vibhaṅgajñāna*).
Furthermore, right vision (samyagdarśana) produces faith regarding the realization of the true nature of reality (tattvārtha).
From that, there arises that cognition consisting of sensory knowledge (mati-jñāna), scriptural knowledge (śruta-jñāna), and clairvoyant knowledge (avadhi-jñāna).
He says: "The two types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) have been described.
Since the viewpoints (*naya*), which occupy a portion of valid cognition, must be explained immediately following them, he therefore says:
'The viewpoints are Naigama, Saṃgraha, Vyavahāra, Ṛjusūtra, Śabda, Samabhirūḍha, and Evambhūta.'"
The general and specific characteristics of these must be stated.

First, the general characteristic: a *naya* is an application that, by presenting a reason without contradiction regarding an entity whose nature is manifold, is inclined toward bringing about the true state of the particular property to be proven (*sādhyaviśeṣa*).

It is twofold: substantial (dravyārthika) and modal (paryāyārthika). Substance (dravya) means the universal (sāmānya), the general (utsarga), or persistence (anuvṛtti); that which has this as its object is the substantial standpoint.
“Paryāya” means synonym, distinction, negation, or exclusion. That which has these as its object is the *paryāyārthika* [standpoint].
The distinctions between those two are the *naigama* and the others.

Their specific characteristics are stated as follows: the *naigama* [type of cognition] grasps merely the conceptualization of an object that has not yet been actualized. For example, having observed a certain man walking along while carrying an axe, someone asks him, "For what purpose are you going?"
He said, "I shall bring a *prastha*.
At that time, the measure known as a *prastha* was not present;
the designation "a *prastha*" was used merely through the intention to produce it.
Similarly, when someone is engaged in the task of fetching fuel, water, and so forth, another person asks, "What are you doing?
He replies, "I am cooking rice. At that time, the word for "rice" (*odana*) is not present; rather, it is employed in reference to the activity intended for that purpose.
Worldly convention (*lokasaṃvyavahāra*) of this kind, which has as its object merely conceptualization regarding things that are not actually produced, is the domain of the empirical (*naigama*).

*Saṃgraha* (the synthetic mode) consists in bringing together various aspects (*paryāya*)—which possess distinct differences—into a single unity without contradiction to their own nature, by grasping them collectively without distinction.
"Existent," "substance," "pot," and so forth.

When "existent" is stated, there is an inclusive collection of all things without distinction, which serve as the substrata for existence, as inferred by the sign of the continuous operation of the verbal cognition "existent.

When "substance" is stated, there is likewise an inclusive collection of the soul (jīva), the non-soul (ajīva), and their various divisions and subdivisions, characterized by the fact that they "flow" or pass through their respective modes (paryāya).
Likewise, even when "pot" is uttered, there is a collection of all objects inferred by the mark (*liṅga*) of the conformity between the cognition and the designation of "pot.
Such other types as these are also the domain of the *saṃgraha-naya* (the inclusive perspective).
Vyavahāra (the conventional standpoint) is the systematic extraction of those objects implied by the saṃgraha (the synthetic standpoint).
What is this method? The method is that the vyavahāra proceeds precisely according to the sequence in which the object was grasped by the saṃgraha; this is the method.

For example: whatever existence is grasped by the universal saṃgraha is not capable of practical transaction (*saṃvyavahāra*) as long as its specific distinctions are disregarded; therefore, the vyavahāra-naya is resorted to.
Whatever exists is either a substance (*dravya*) or a quality (*guṇa*).

Since practical worldly discourse (*saṃvyavahāra*) cannot be carried out by means of "substance" alone—as that term, when employed through the principle of inclusion (*saṃgraha*), remains indifferent to the specific distinctions between living beings (*jīva*) and non-living things (*ajīva*)—one must resort to the discourse of "living substance" or "non-living substance.

Furthermore, since even "living being" and "non-living thing," when taken as mere inclusive categories, are insufficient for practical discourse, one must resort to specific instances in practice, such as gods, hell-beings, and so forth, for the former, and jars, and so forth, for the latter.
Thus this method proceeds as long as there is no further differentiation.
It is called *ṛjusūtra* because it strings together and extends that which is straight and upright.

Transcending objects belonging to the three times—namely those of the past and future—it grasps those belonging to the present time, because there is no conventional usage regarding the past and future due to their having perished and not yet arisen, respectively.
And that present [time] is merely a moment (samaya).
The *ṛjusūtra* [naya] grasps only the modes (paryāya) that have that [moment] as their object.
If it is argued that this would lead to the collapse of worldly convention (*saṃvyavahāra*), we say no; for this method merely demonstrates its specific scope.
Indeed, worldly convention is accomplished by the synthesis of all methods (*naya*).
The *śabdanaya* is intent upon the exclusion of deviation regarding gender, number, grammatical means (*sādhana*), and so forth.
Among these, deviation of gender is seen in such cases as *puṣyaḥ*, *tārakā*, and *nakṣatram*.
Deviation of number is seen in such cases as *jalam* and *āpaḥ*, *varṣāḥ* and *ṛtuḥ*, *āmrāḥ* and *vanam*, and *varaṇāḥ* and *nagaram*.
Deviation of the means (*sādhanavyabhicāra*): "The army dwells on the mountain.

Deviation of the person (*puruṣavyabhicāra*): "Come, I think you will go by chariot; you will not go, for your father has already gone. Deviation of time (*kālavyabhicāra*): "The son who has seen all shall be born."
"The action was to be performed" (*bhāvi kṛtyam āsīt*).
This is an inconsistency regarding the verbal suffix (*upagraha-vyabhicāra*), as in [the cases where one says] "it stands," "it is established," "it ceases," or "it desists.
He considers such usage to be improper, because there can be no connection between a word having one meaning and a word having another meaning.
If it is argued that this contradicts worldly convention, let it contradict;
for here we are investigating reality (*tattva*), not a medical treatment that conforms to the whims of the patient.
The *samabhirūḍha* [naya] is so called because of its ascent toward multiple meanings.
Since it transcends various meanings and ascends directly toward a single meaning, it is called *samabhirūḍha*.
For example, this word "cow" (*go*), while applicable to objects such as speech and so forth, is here fixed (*abhirūḍha*) specifically upon the animal.
Alternatively, the employment of words is for the purpose of conveying meaning.
In that case, since a single meaning is already conveyed by a single word, the employment of synonymous terms would be purposeless.
If there is a difference in words, there must necessarily also be a difference in meaning.
The *samabhirūḍha* [naya] is so called because it ascends to various distinct meanings.

For example, he is *indra* because of his ruling (*indana*), *śakra* because of his power (*śakana*), and *purandara* because of his shattering of cities (*pūrdāraṇa*); this applies everywhere in such cases.

Alternatively, that which is "ascended" (*abhirūḍha*) in a particular sense is the *samabhirūḍha*, because it ascends by meeting (*sametya*) with that specific meaning in a direct manner (*abhimukhena*).
For example: "Where do you reside? "In the self.
Why? Because there is no occurrence [of one thing] in another entity.
If the occurrence of one thing were possible in another, then knowledge and so forth, as well as form and so forth, would have occurrence in space.
"Evambhūta" (thus-occurred) means that by whatever nature [the object] has come to be, by that very same nature it causes determination;
thus, that word is appropriate only at the moment of the transformation of the action intended by itself, and not at any other time.
Just as when one intends, at that very moment one is Indra—not one who has been consecrated nor one who is worshipping;
and just as when one moves, at that very moment one is a cow—not one who is standing nor one who is lying down.
Or else, by whichever self and by whichever cognition one has become transformed, by that very same [self and cognition] one determines [the object].
Just as the self itself, when transformed through the cognition of Indra and Agni, is designated as both Indra and Agni.
The *naigama* and other modes of reasoning (*naya*) have thus been explained.

The sequence of these perspectives is due to their progressively subtler objects and because each preceding one serves as the cause for the subsequent. Thus, these perspectives—each having a larger object that contradicts the preceding one and a smaller object that accords with the following one—arise in many varieties, being differentiated according to each specific power of the infinite potency of substance (*dravya*). These perspectives, being mutually dependent through the predominance or subordination of their qualities, are the causes of right vision (*samyagdarśana*) by virtue of their capacity to accomplish the purposeful activity of the person (*puruṣārtha*). Like threads and other materials, they are designated as "cloth" and so forth when arranged according to the appropriate means; however, when independent, they are ineffective.
"Like threads and so forth" is an unequal comparison. Threads and the like produce some degree of an effect even when independent [of other conditions].
For indeed, there may be some individual thread capable of protecting against cold, and a single strand of balvaja grass capable of binding.

But these [Nayas], being independent [of one another], do not bring forth even a fraction of right vision (*samyagdarśana*). This is not a fault, because it arises from a failure to understand what has been stated.
Not understanding the point that was stated, the opponent objects as follows:
"It has been said that the effect, such as a cloth, does not exist in the threads and so forth when they are independent;
however, that which was pointed out by him is not the effect, such as a cloth."
What then? It is merely the effect of the threads and so forth.
Even the effect of the threads and so forth does not exist at all when the parts, such as the threads, are independent; thus, our own position is indeed established.
Now, if it is argued that the effect, such as the cloth, exists within the threads and so forth by way of potentiality (*śakti*).

Even though the means [of knowledge] are independent [of one another] and consist of cognition and verbal expression, because there exists a transformation into the cause of right vision by virtue of their causal power,
the statement that they exist as potentiality is indeed equivalent.
Thus ends the first chapter in the *Tattvārthavṛtti* titled *Sarvārthasiddhi*.
Now begins the second chapter.

It is asked: among the soul and other categories taught as the objects of right vision (*samyagdarśana*), what is the essential nature (*svatattva*) of the soul (*jīva*) which was introduced at the outset? This is now explained:
The subsidential (aupaśamika), the destructive (kṣāyika), the mixed (miśra), as well as the emergent (audayika) and the transformational (pāriṇāmika) states constitute the true nature of the soul.
Subsidence (upaśama) is the non-manifestation within the self of the inherent power of karma due to the influence of a cause.
Just as the subsiding of mud in water occurs through contact with substances such as *kataka*,
and its destruction is absolute cessation;
just as in that very same water, once it has been transferred into another clean vessel, there is the absolute non-existence of the mud.
The mixed state consists of both [aspects].
For example, in that very same water, due to contact with substances such as *kataka* (nutmeg), the activity of the mud is both diminished and not diminished.
The emergence (*udaya*) of karmas is the attainment of their fruit by virtue of causes such as substances and other factors.
Transformation has as its cause merely the acquisition of the substance's own nature.
That which has cessation (*upaśama*) as its purpose is "cessation-born" (*aupaśamika*).
Likewise, there are those that are "destruction-born" (*kṣāyika*), "destruction-and-cessation-born" (*kṣāyopaśamika*), "arising-born" (*audayika*), and "transformation-born" (*pāriṇāmika*).
These five states are called the unique, intrinsic nature (*svatattva*) of the soul (*jīva*).

Since right vision (*samyagdarśana*) is the subject under discussion, and because among its three modalities (*vikalpa*) the subsidential (*aupaśamika*) is obtained first, it is mentioned at the beginning.

Immediately after that, the mention of the *kṣāyika* (destructive) type is made; because it is its opposite, and because, in comparison with the transmigrating being (*saṃsārī*), it is numerically incalculable times greater than that.
Following that, the mention of the *miśra* (mixed) type is made; because it consists of both those natures, and because it is incalculable times greater than that.
Finally, the mention of the *audayika* (emergent) and *pāriṇāmika* (transformative) types is placed at the end, because all of those [preceding ones] are infinitely greater in number.
In this case, a dual compound (dvandva) should have been employed—namely, *aupaśamikakṣāyikamiśraudayikapāriṇāmikāḥ*.
Had that been done, the word "and" (*ca*) would not need to be repeated twice.
One should not entertain such a doubt; for it is understood [that the repetition] is with respect to other qualities (*anyaguṇāpekṣayā*).
Furthermore, when there is a single sentence, the word "and" (ca) serves to draw in both the topics under discussion.
If it is argued that, in that case, one should simply use the term "kṣāyopaśamika," we say no; for that would involve unnecessary complexity (gaurava).
The mention of "mixed" (miśra) is placed in the middle for the sake of referring to both cases:
the subsidential (aupaśamika) and destructive (kṣāyika) dispositions belong to one who is capable of liberation (bhavya);

furthermore, the mixed disposition occurs even in one incapable of liberation (abhavya), while it also occurs in one capable of liberation along with the emergent (audayika) and transformational (pāriṇāmika) dispositions.

If it is argued that, in view of the state [of the object], the gender and number of its own essence (*svatattva*) would follow [those of the object], we say no; because it possesses the gender and number already acquired [by the suffix].
Its state is its essence (*tattva*). "Its own essence" (*svatattva*) means its own nature.
Here it is asked: Are those states of that single self, such as tranquility and so forth, possessed of difference or devoid of difference?
To this it is replied: they are possessed of difference.
If this is so, let the divisions be stated; therefore he says: "There are, respectively, two, nine, eighteen, twenty-one, and three divisions. (255)

It should be understood that numeral compounds such as *dvi* (two) and so forth, when formed as dvandvas, function—either with reference to their own constituent members (*svapadārtha*) or with reference to another object (*anyapadārtha*)—together with the word *bheda* (division).
Thus: *dvau ca nava ca aṣṭādaśa ca ekaviṃśatiś ca trayaś ca* [is] *dvinavāṣṭādaśaikaviṃśatitrayaḥ*.
[The compound] *dvinavāṣṭādaśaikaviṃśatitribhedāḥ* functions either as "those which are divisions" (*te ca te bhedāś ca*), or as "those whose divisions are precisely these" (*ta eva bhedā yeṣām*).

When the compound is taken as having its own members (*svapadārtha*) as its referent, the connection is made as follows: "the states (*bhāva*) beginning with the subsidential (*aupaśamika*) have two, nine, eighteen, twenty-one, and three varieties respectively. This is because the case endings are transformed according to the sense (*arthavaśāt*).

When the compound is taken as having another member (*anyapadārtha*) as its referent, the words are connected exactly as they appear with their respective case endings: "the states beginning with the subsidential have two, nine, eighteen, twenty-one, and three varieties.
The expression "in due order" (*yathākrama*) is used for the purpose of ensuring that the items correspond to the numbers in their proper sequence.
The pacifying [attainment] is of two types;
the destructive [attainment] is of nine types;
the mixed [attainment] is of eighteen types.
The *audayika* [state] has twenty-one divisions;
the *pāriṇāmika* [state] has three divisions.
If this is so, then what are the two divisions of the subsidential (aupaśamika) [right belief]? To this he says: right belief and right conduct.
Right view and right conduct have already been explained by their characteristics.

If it is asked, "In what sense do they possess the quality of being 'subsidential' (aupaśamika)? it is said: Delusion regarding conduct (cāritramoha) is of two kinds—delusion pertaining to the passions (kaṣāyavedanīya) and delusion pertaining to the quasi-passions (nokaṣāyavedanīya). Among these, the subdivisions of that which pertains to the passions are the four infinite-bonding (anantānubandhin) types: anger, pride, deceit, and greed.
The delusion of vision (*darśana-moha*) has three divisions: rightness (*samyaktva*), falsity (*mithyātva*), and mixed right-and-falsity (*samyag-mithyātva*).
From the subsidence (*upaśama*) of these seven types of karma arises subsidential rightness (*aupaśamika-samyaktva*).

For one who is capable (*bhavya*) yet possesses beginningless false views, how can there be the subsiding of that [defilement] when turbidity has been produced by the rising of karma? It is because of causes such as the attainment of the proper time (*kālalabdhi*).

Regarding that, first, the attainment of the proper time is as follows: the soul (*ātman*), though permeated by karma, becomes fit for the acquisition of the first right conviction (*samyaktva*) only when the remaining duration of the *ardhapudgalaparivartana* has elapsed, and not when more remains.
This is the first kind of attainment of the proper time.
There is another acquisition of time regarding the duration of karma:
the attainment of the first right view (*prathamasamyaktva*) does not occur while karmas have either maximum or minimum durations.

Where, then, does it occur? It occurs when karmas with a duration of up to ten million times ten million *sāgaropamas* are being bound; through the power of pure transformation (*viśuddhapariṇāma*), those karmas are reduced by thousands of *sāgaropamas* that are numerable, and when they are established at a duration of less than ten million times ten million *sāgaropamas*, one becomes fit for the first right view.
There is another acquisition of time by way of dependence on existence (*bhava*).
A fortunate being (*bhavya*) who possesses the five faculties, is conscious (*saṃjñin*), is fully developed (*paryāptika*), and is completely purified, produces the first right view (*samyaktva*).
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the recollection of past lives (*jātismaraṇa*) and other such qualities are included.
Aupaśamika-cāritra (conduct of subsidence) arises from the subsidence of all deluding karma (*mohanīya*).
Among these [five types of conduct], right faith (*samyaktva*) is mentioned first, because conduct is preceded by it.

Regarding the ninefold nature of the state that is characterized by destruction (*kṣayika*), which has been previously mentioned, he speaks in order to explain its specific divisions and essential nature:
"Knowledge, vision, giving, acquisition, enjoyment, utilization, and energy."
The word "and" (*ca*) serves to include right view and right conduct.

Due to the absolute destruction of the veil of knowledge (*jñānāvaraṇa*), there is perfect knowledge (*kevalajñāna*), which is of the nature of destruction (*kṣāyika*); likewise, there is perfect perception (*kevaladarśana*).

The gift of fearlessness (*abhayadāna*) is that which is characterized by destruction (*kṣāyika*), because it brings about the ultimate cessation of obstacles to giving and bestows favor upon infinite multitudes of living beings.

Gain (*lābha*) is that which is characterized by destruction, because through the total removal of every obstacle to gain, there occurs at every moment an association with infinite, supremely pure, subtle *pudgala* (matter) particles—unshared by others—that serve as the cause for sustaining the bodily strength of the Kevalins who have abandoned the act of consuming morsel food.

Enjoyment (*bhoga*) is that which is characterized by destruction, because through the disappearance of all obstacles to enjoyment, there manifests an infinite, extraordinary, and preeminent enjoyment.
From which particular manifestations such as showers of flowers arise;
from the destruction of every obstacle to enjoyment, there arises infinite, exhaustible enjoyment (*kṣāyika*),
from which prosperities such as the lion-throne, chowries, and parasols emerge.
Infinite vigor is the exhaustible [quality] manifested through the absolute destruction of the karma that obstructs vigor.
Right conviction (samyaktva) is exhaustible through the absolute destruction of the seven previously mentioned types [of karma].
Conduct (cāritra) is likewise.

If fearlessness-giving and the like were produced by the destruction of the dispositions (bhāva) of giving and so forth, would that not entail their occurrence even in the perfected beings (*siddhas*)? This is not a fault, because [the manifestation of such qualities] depends upon the rising of karma related to the body-name (*śarīra-nāman*) and the Tīrthaṅkara-name (*tīrthaṅkara-nāman*).
Since those [types of karma] are absent in them, there is no such entailment.
How, then, does their activity exist among the perfected beings? Their activity therein exists solely in the form of supreme bliss and the absence of affliction.
Just as there is the manifestation of infinite energy in the form of *kevalajñāna* (omniscience).
Regarding that eighteen-fold state which was described as being of the nature of destruction-cum-subsidence (*kṣāyopaśamika*), he speaks in order to define its divisions:
The acquisitions of knowledge, non-knowledge, and vision consist of four, three, and five types respectively; as do right view, conduct, restraint, and non-restraint.
"Four, three, three, and five" means four, and three, and three, and five.
Those which have those divisions are "those with four, three, and five divisions.
The phrase "respectively" (yathākramam) is understood [from the previous context].
Through that connection, the [four] knowledges and so forth are connected with the [four] numbers beginning with four.
There are four types of knowledge, three types of non-knowledge, three types of vision, and five attainments.

Due to the destruction of the rise of all-pervading (sarvaghāti) spardhakas and the subsidence of those very same [spardhakas], and due to the rise of partial-pervading (deśaghāti) spardhakas, there occurs the state of destruction-cum-subsidence (kṣāyopaśamika).
In that regard, the functioning of knowledge and the others is to be explained as resulting from the destruction-cum-subsidence of their respective veils and obstructive karmas.
By the mention of "right belief" (*samyaktva*), "experiential right belief" (*vedakasamyaktva*) is included.

When there is the rise of a *deśaghāti* (partially obscuring) *sparddhaka* of right belief—due to the destruction or subsidence of the four infinite-bondage passions (*anantānubandhi-kaṣāya*) and of the delusion of falsehood (*mithyātva*) and mixed delusion (*samyagmithyātva*)—the faith in the true nature of reality is "right belief born of destruction-subsidence" (*kṣayopaśamika-samyaktva*).

The transformation of the self toward cessation (*nivṛtti-pariṇāma*), occurring through the destruction or subsidence of the twelve passions (*kaṣāya*)—namely the four infinite-bonding (*anantānubandhi*), the four non-renouncing (*apratyākhyāna*), and the four renouncing (*pratyākhyāna*)—and through the rise of any one of the partially-destructive (*deśaghāti*) *sparddhakas* of the four fuming (*saṃjvalana*) passions, as well as the rise of the nine quasi-passions (*nokaṣāya*) as far as possible, constitutes conduct (*cāritra*) that is both destructive-subsidential (*kṣāyopaśamika*).

Due to the destruction or subsidence of the eight passions (*kaṣāya*)—namely, the four *anantānubandhi* and the four *apratyākhyāna*—and due to the rise of the *pratyākhyāna* passions and the partial-destructive (*deśaghāti*) *sparddhakas* of the *saṃjvalana* passions, as well as the rise of the nine secondary passions (*nokaṣāya*) as far as possible, there arises a state of partial renunciation (*viratāvirata*). This *kṣāyopaśamika* modification is designated as "mixed conduct" (*saṃyamāsaṃyama*).
Regarding the twenty-one varieties of the *audayika* (operative) state that were previously mentioned, this is stated for the purpose of enumerating their specific divisions:

The destinies (*gati*), passions (*kaṣāya*), marks (*liṅga*), false view (*mithyādarśana*), ignorance (*ajñāna*), lack of self-restraint (*asaṃyata*), and non-perfection (*asiddha*), as well as the tints (*leśyā*), have four, four, two, one, one, one, one, and six divisions respectively.

The term "respectively" (*yathākramam*) carries over [from the previous section]; thus, by that connection, destiny has four divisions: the hellish destiny, the animal destiny, the human destiny, and the celestial destiny.

In that regard, because the state of being a hell-being arises from the manifestation (*udaya*) of the karma named "hellish destiny," the hellish destiny is of the nature of manifestation (*audayika*).
The same applies to the others as well.
Kaṣāya is of four types: anger, pride, deceit, and greed.
In that regard, anger is "arising" (*audayika*) because of the emergence of the karma that brings about anger;
the same applies to the others as well.
The gender (*liṅga*) is threefold: female gender, male gender, and neuter gender.
From the rise (*udaya*) of the karma of female-ness (*strīveda*), there is the "arisen" (*audayika*) female-ness.
The same applies to the others as well.
False view (*mithyādarśana*) has a single division.
Due to the arising of the karma of false vision (*mithyādarśana*), the transformation consisting of a lack of faith in the true nature of reality is the *audayika* state of false vision.
Due to the arising of the karma of knowledge-obscuration (*jñānāvaraṇa*), the failure to comprehend the categories of existence occurs; that is the *audayika* state of ignorance.
Due to the arising of the all-pervading (*sarvaghāti*) sub-type of the deluding karma of conduct (*cāritramoha*), one is unrestrained; this is the *audayika* state of non-restraint.
The *audayika* [state], which depends on the generality of the arising of karma, is unestablished [in this context].
*Leśyā* is twofold: material *leśyā* (*dravyaleśyā*) and spiritual *leśyā* (*bhāvaleśyā*).
Since the present discussion concerns the states of the soul (*jīva*), material *leśyā* is not the subject under consideration.
Bhāvaleśyā is said to be of the nature of *audayika* (arising from the rise of karma), because it is the activity of the *yogas* colored by the rise of the *kaṣāyas*.
It is sixfold: black leśyā (*kṛṣṇaleśyā*), blue leśyā (*nīlaleśyā*), grey leśyā (*kāpotaleśyā*), fiery leśyā (*tejoleśyā*), lotus leśyā (*padmaleśyā*), and white leśyā (*śuklaleśyā*).

But is it not the case that according to the scripture, white leśyā exists in one whose passions (*kaṣāya*) have subsided, in one whose passions are destroyed, and in an omniscient being with active yoga (*sayogakevalin*)?
