In those states, because of the absence of coloring by the passions, its status as an *audayika* (arising from fruition) would not be tenable.

This is not a fault; for, with reference to the perspective of the method of designating prior states, that very activity of the *yoga* which was colored by the passions is metaphorically called *audayika*.
Due to the absence of that [leśyā], it is determined that the *ayogakevalin* is "without leśyā" (*aleśya*).
Regarding the threefold transformative (*pāriṇāmika*) state that has been mentioned, he speaks in order to explain the nature of its specific divisions:
§ 268. Furthermore, the states of being a soul,

being capable of liberation, and being incapable of liberation— these three dispositions (*bhāva*), which are transformative (*pāriṇāmika*) and unique to the self as distinct from other substances, are to be understood.
Furthermore, why is this [soul] considered transformational?
Because it does not depend upon the emergence, subsidence, destruction, or destruction-cum-subsidence of karma.
And "jīvatva" (the state of being a soul) means consciousness.
One who will become [endowed] with the state of right vision and so forth is *bhavya* (capable);
one who is the opposite of that is *abhavya* (incapable).
These three states are the transformative (*pāriṇāmika*) qualities of the soul.

But surely there are also other states of being that are transformational (*pāriṇāmika*), such as existence, permanence, and spatial extension; should these not also be included here? They need not be included; they have already been included.
How so? Because they are conjoined by the word "and" (*ca*).
If this is so, does it not contradict the number "three"?
It does not contradict it, for there are exactly three uncommon states (*bhāva*) of the soul (*jīva*), which are transformational (*pāriṇāmika*).
Furthermore, existence and the other [categories] are categorized separately by the word "and" (*ca*), because they are common to both the soul (*jīva*) and the non-soul (*ajīva*).

An objection is raised: the states such as subsidence (*aupaśmika*) and so forth are untenable for the soul because it is formless (*amūrta*); for those states depend upon the bondage of karma, and it is not logical for that which is formless to have a bondage of karma.
That is not so; because it is inconclusive.
It is not the absolute rule that the self is exclusively formless.
In view of its states of being bound by karma, it may be considered possessed of form due to the penetration of those [karmic] influences.
With respect to its pure nature, it would be formless (*amūrta*).
If this were so, then because of the penetration of the bondage of karma, non-discrimination (*aviveka*) would follow despite its unity.
This is not a fault; for although there is unity with respect to bondage, its plurality is determined due to the difference in its characteristics (*lakṣaṇabheda*).
And it has been said: "With respect to bondage, there is unity; by virtue of its characteristic, there is its distinctness;
therefore, the immaterial nature of the soul is to be understood."
With respect to bondage, there is unity; by way of its characteristics, there is its distinctness.
Therefore, the immaterial nature of the soul is to be understood.
If this is so, then let that very characteristic be stated by which distinctness is determined; to this he says:
Upayoga is the defining characteristic.
Upayoga is a transformation that arises by virtue of both internal and external causes and conforms to consciousness (caitanya).

Therefore, although there is oneness with respect to their being bound, the self is characterized [as distinct], just as gold and silver, though they possess oneness with respect to their being bound, are distinguished by differences in color and so forth.
To demonstrate that distinction, he says:
That is of two kinds, with eight and four subdivisions.
That application (upayoga) is twofold: the application of knowledge (jñānopayoga) and the application of vision (darśanopayoga).

The cognitive application (*jñānopayoga*) is of eight types: sensory knowledge (*matijñāna*), scriptural knowledge (*śrutajñāna*), clairvoyance (*avadhijñāna*), telepathy (*manaḥparyayajñāna*), omniscience (*kevalajñāna*), sensory ignorance (*matyajñāna*), scriptural ignorance (*śrutājñāna*), and false clairvoyance (*vibhaṅgajñāna*). The perceptual application (*darśanopayoga*) is of four types: visual perception (*cakṣurdarśana*), non-visual perception (*acakṣurdarśana*), clairvoyant perception (*avadhidarśana*), and omniscient perception (*kevaladarśana*). How is there a distinction between these two? It is due to the distinction between being with form (*sākāra*) and without form (*anakāra*).
Cognition (*jñāna*) possesses an aspect (*sākāra*), while vision (*darśana*) is aspectless (*anākāra*). This occurs sequentially among those still subject to obscuration (*chadmastha*).
Among those free from obscuration (*nirāvaraṇa*), both occur simultaneously; however, because vision arises later, cognition is mentioned first, as it is more highly esteemed.

Prior to the section on right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), the fivefold application of knowledge (*jñānopayoga*) was explained. Here, however, because the term "application" (*upayoga*) is employed, error (*viparyaya*) is also included; thus, it is said to be eightfold.
Those characterized as "possessing utility" by means of this aforementioned transformation of what has been expressed, through a utilization common to all selves, are of two kinds:
those in the cycle of existence (saṃsārin) and those who are liberated (mukta).

*Saṃsaraṇa* means *saṃsāra*, which signifies revolving. Those who possess this are the *saṃsāriṇaḥ* (those subject to transmigration). That revolving is fivefold: revolving of substance (*dravya*), revolving of field (*kṣetra*), revolving of time (*kāla*), revolving of existence (*bhava*), and revolving of state (*bhāva*).
In that regard, the transformation of substance (dravya-parivartana) is of two kinds: the transformation of non-karma substance and the transformation of karma substance.

In this context, what is called the *nokarma-dravya-parivartana* (the cycle of non-karmic matter) is as follows: those *pudgala* particles suitable for the three bodies and the six capacities (*paryāpti*), which were grasped by a single soul at one moment and remain as they are through their smoothness, roughness, color, odor, and so forth, in states of intense, mild, or moderate intensity—when, after passing through infinite cycles of those [particles] already worn away (*nirjīrṇa*) and not yet grasped, and after passing through infinite cycles of mixed [particles], and after passing through infinite cycles of those grasped in the interim, those very same particles attain the state of *nokarma* for that very same soul in that very same manner; the sum total of all such instances constitutes the *nokarma-dravya-parivartana*.

The transformation of karmic matter (*karmadravyaparivartana*) is explained as follows: when, in a single moment, those *pudgala* particles which have been grasped by a single soul in the form of the eight types of karma pass beyond one additional *āvalikā* (a unit of time) and are discharged in the second and subsequent moments, they—by that very same sequence and in that very same manner—attain the state of being karma for that soul again. This continues until [the cycle is complete]; this is the transformation of karmic matter.
And it has been said:

The transformation of the field (kṣetraparivartana) is explained as follows: a subtle nigoda-jīva, being incomplete (aparyāptika) and possessing a body with the minimum number of spatial units (pradeśa), is born having placed eight central spatial units of the world within its own body; it lives out a brief existence and then dies.

That very same [being], having been born again in that very same place by that same process a second time, and likewise a third and a fourth time—in this manner, until as many times as there are space-points in an incalculable fraction of a *ghanāṅgula*—having been born in that very same place, he then proceeds by increasing one space-point at a time until the entire world has been brought to the state of his own birth-field (*janmakṣetra*). This is what constitutes a "turning of the field" (*kṣetraparivartana*). And it is said: § 277. [The verse: "Having been born in that very same place, in that very same way, two, three, four times, and so on, until the space-points of an incalculable fraction of a *ghanāṅgula* have been reached; then, by increasing one space-point at a time, the entire world is made his birth-field.
And it is said: [the prose commentary follows].
The transformation of time is described as follows: a certain living being born at the first instant of an *utsarpiṇī* dies upon the completion of its own lifespan.
That same being is then born again at the second instant of the second *utsarpiṇī* and dies upon the exhaustion of its lifespan.
That same being is then born again at the third instant of the third *utsarpiṇī*.
In this manner, the *utsarpiṇī* (ascending aeon) is completed;
likewise the *avasarpiṇī* (descending aeon).
Thus, the uninterrupted succession of births has been described.
The uninterrupted succession of deaths should likewise be understood in the same way.
This constitutes a complete cycle of time.
And it has been said:
The transformation of existence is now described: in the hell realm, the shortest lifespan is ten thousand years.
Having been born there with that lifespan, one wanders about and is born again with that very same lifespan.
Thus, for as many moments as there are in ten thousand years, he was born and died in that very same place that many times.
Then, by the addition of one moment at a time, thirty-three *sāgaropamas* were completed.
Having passed away from there, he was reborn in the animal realm with a lifespan of an *antarmuhūrta*.
In the same sequence previously described, three *palyopamas* were completed by him.
It is likewise in the human realm;
and in the divine realm, it is just as in the hell realms.
But this is the distinction: the cycle of existence (bhavaparivartana) lasts for as long as thirty-one *sāgaropama*s have been completed.
And it is said:

The transformation of state (*bhāvaparivartana*) is explained as follows: A certain soul (*jīva*) who possesses the five sense organs, is endowed with consciousness (*saṃjñin*), is fully developed (*paryāptaka*), and holds false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), undergoes the minimum duration (*sthitibandha*) of the knowledge-obscuring (*jñānāvaraṇa*) karma-prakṛti appropriate for itself, which is known as "inner ten million times ten million" (*antaḥ-koṭīkoṭī*).

For that soul, there are innumerable world-systems (*asaṃkhyeya-loka*) worth of degrees of intensity of passion (*kaṣāyādhyavasāyasthāna*), which fall into six categories and are suitable for that duration.
Among these, caused by the most minimal degree of passion-intensity, there are innumerable world-systems worth of degrees of intensity of fruition (*anubhāgādhyavasāyasthāna*).

Thus, for one who occupies the most minimal duration (*sthiti*), the most minimal degree of karmic intensity (*kaṣāyādhyavasāyasthāna*), and the most minimal degree of fruition-intensity (*anubhāgabandhasthāna*), there occurs the most minimal degree of vibratory activity (*yogasthāna*) suitable for those [three].

For those very same degrees of duration, karmic intensity, and fruition-intensity, there occurs a second degree of vibratory activity characterized by an increase of one innumerable part (*asaṃkhyeyabhāga*).

In this manner, in the third and subsequent [degrees], there arise degrees of vibratory activity that fall into four categories (*catuḥsthānapatita*) and are measured by innumerable parts of a series (*śreṇyasaṃkhyeyabhāgapramita*).
Likewise, for one who attains that very same state and that very same level of kashaya-intensity, there occurs a second level of experiential determination (*anubhavādhyavasāyasthāna*).
Its yoga-levels (*yogasthāna*) are to be understood as before.
In this manner, it continues through the third and subsequent levels of experiential determination until the completion of the incalculable world-cycle (*asaṃkhyeyaloka*).
Thus, for one who attains that very state, there occurs the second station of the intensity of the passions (*kaṣāyādhyavasāyasthāna*).
Its stations of experiential intensity and its stations of yoga (*yogasthāna*) are also to be understood as before.

In this manner, the sequence of increase is to be understood for the third and subsequent stations of the intensity of the passions, until the completion of the incalculable world-cycle (*asaṃkhyeyaloka*).
The locations of the *kaṣāya* and other factors for the minimum duration mentioned—which exceeds [the minimum] by one *samaya*—are as previously described.
In this manner, by increasing one *samaya* at a time up to the maximum duration of thirty *koṭī-koṭīs* of *sāgaropamas*, the locations of the *kaṣāya* and other factors are to be understood.

These six are the places of increase: infinite-fold increase (*anantabhāgavṛddhi*), innumerable-fold increase (*asaṃkhyeyabhāgavṛddhi*), numerable-fold increase (*saṃkhyeyabhāgavṛddhi*), numerable-fold multiplication (*saṃkhyeyaguṇavṛddhi*), innumerable-fold multiplication (*asaṃkhyeyaguṇavṛddhi*), and infinite-fold multiplication (*anantaguṇavṛddhi*).
Decrease is likewise.
There are four stages devoid of increase by an infinite fraction and increase by an infinite multiple.
In this manner, the sequence of transformation for all karmas—both root-natures (*mūlaprakṛti*) and sub-classifications (*uttaraprakṛti*)—is to be understood.
All this taken together constitutes the transformation of existence (bhāvaparivartana).
And it has been said:
Those who have turned away from the fivefold saṃsāra described above are liberated.
The mention of those in saṃsāra comes first because the designation of "liberated" is preceded by that [distinction].
Those who are transmigrating beings are of two kinds: those with minds and those without minds.
The mind is twofold: substantial mind (*dravyamana*) and mental state (*bhāvamana*).
Among these, substantial mind depends upon the emergence of karma that results in the maturation of a person (*pudgala-vipākika-karma*).

Mental state is the purity of the self (*ātman*), which depends upon the subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣayopaśama*) of the obstruction to energy (*vīryāntarāya*) and the obstruction to the senses (*no-indriya-āvaraṇa*).
Those who exist together with that mind are "possessing mind" (*samanaska*).
Those for whom no mind exists are these "mindless" (*amanaska*) ones.
Thus, by the presence and absence of the mind, transmigrating beings are divided into two kinds.
"Those with minds and those without minds are called 'those with minds and without minds.
The word *samanaska* (with mind) is placed first because it is more honored.
Why is it more honored? Because it possesses the capacity to investigate virtues and faults."
Furthermore, in order to explain the classification of transmigrating beings, he says:
"Transmigrating beings are mobile and immobile."

The inclusion of the term "saṃsārin" (the transmigrating being) is redundant, because it has already been introduced. Where was it introduced? In the statement: "The transmigrating being and the liberated one."
It is not purposeless; rather, it serves to refer back to what precedes: those mentioned as "with mind" (*samanaska*) and "without mind" (*amanaska*) are transmigrating beings (*saṃsārin*).
For if there were no qualification of the preceding [term], the mention of "with mind" and "without mind" would be connected respectively with the words "transmigrating beings" and "liberated ones.
By doing so, the placement of the term "transmigrating beings" at the beginning becomes logical.
That [classification], depending on what precedes it, also serves as the basis for what follows.
Those transmigrating beings are of two kinds: mobile (trasa) and immobile (sthāvara).
Mobile beings are those who are brought under the influence by the rising of the karma named *trasanāma*.
Those who are subject to the operation of the *nāmakarma* known as "stationary" (*sthāvara*) are the stationary beings.

They are called "mobile" (*trasa*) because they move; if it is argued that "stationary" refers to those whose nature is to remain fixed in one place, that is not so, because it contradicts the scriptures (*āgama*).
For in the scripture, when classifying by body, mobile beings are said to begin from the two-sensed organisms up to the *ayogakevalin*.
Therefore, the state of being mobile or immobile does not depend on movement or lack of movement;
it depends solely on the arising of karma.
The term "mobile" (trasa) is placed first because it has fewer syllables and because it is more venerable.
Because all [types of] utilization are possible [in their case], they possess a state of being highly esteemed.

Since there is very little to be said regarding those with a single sense-faculty (*ekendriya*), he bypasses the sequential order and speaks for the purpose of explaining the divisions of the stationary beings (*sthāvara*):
Earth, water, fire, air, and plants are the stationary beings;
they exist as the earth-body and so forth, which are specific types of karma-named stationary beings.
The designations "earth" and so forth should be understood as applied to living beings based on the emergence of those [qualities].

Although these terms are derived from their original nature—such as "expanding" (*prathana*) and so on—they function by virtue of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) without depending on that etymological derivation.
Regarding each of these elements, such as earth and the rest, a fourfold classification has been stated in the works of the Sages (*ārṣa*).
If one asks how that is so, it is said: "earth," "the earth-body," "one belonging to the earth-body," "the earth-soul," and so forth.
In this context, "earth" is that which is insentient, produced through natural transformation (*vaiśrasika-pariṇāma*), and characterized by the quality of solidity.
Because it is insentient, even in the absence of the manifestation of the karma named "earth-body," this [earth] is nevertheless characterized by the activity of expansion.
Alternatively, "earth" refers to the general category, because it exists throughout all three subsequent [categories].
"Body" means the physical frame.
An "earth-body" is that which has been abandoned by a living being belonging to the earth-body class, like the body of a deceased human or similar being.
One who possesses the earth-body is an "earth-bodied being" (*pṛthivīkāyika*).
The self is brought under control by its connection with that body.

A living soul of earth (*pṛthivījīva*) is one who has attained the emergence of the karma named "earth-body," who abides in the yoga of the kārmaṇa-body, and who for the time being does not yet grasp the earth as his body.
The same should be applied to water and the other elements as well.

These types of beings on the couches are stationary (sthāvara). How many vital breaths (prāṇas) do they possess? Four: the vital breath of the sense of touch, the vital breath of bodily strength, the vital breath of inhalation and exhalation, and the vital breath of life-span.
Now, as to what those mobile beings (*trasa*) are, it is said here: mobile beings are those with two or more sense-faculties (*dvīndriyādayas*).
One who possesses two faculties is "dvīndriyaḥ.
Those for whom the two faculties are the first are "dvīndriyādayaḥ. The word "ādi" (beginning/first) expresses a fixed order.
In what [order] are they fixed? In the scripture (*āgama*).
How so? [They are] those with two sense-faculties (*dvīndriya*), three, four, and five.
Because the term is used in a way that includes the possession of those qualities (*tadguṇasaṃvijñānavṛtti*), even those with two sense-faculties are included.

Furthermore, how many vital breaths (*prāṇa*) do they have? For those with two sense-faculties, there are six vital breaths: namely, the previously mentioned ones, plus the tongue and the organ of speech.
For a three-facultied being, there are those same seven, with the addition of the nose and the life-faculty.
For a four-facultied being, there are eight, with the addition of the eye and the life-faculty.
For a five-facultied animal that is non-sentient, there are nine, with the addition of the ear and the life-faculty.
Those same ten [types of beings] possessing perception (*saṃjñin*) are further distinguished by the addition of mind (*manas*), power (*bala*), and vitality (*prāṇa*).
Regarding those indicated by the word "etc. (*ādi*) whose number was not previously determined, one must establish their exact quantity; therefore, he says:
The five faculties (*pañcendriyāṇi*). The meaning of the word "faculty" (*indriya*) has already been explained.
The mention of "five" is for the sake of restriction, meaning there are exactly five and no more.
Should the organs of action, such as speech and so forth, be included here? They should not be included; because this is a section concerning utility (*upayoga*).
What is included here are the instruments of utility, not the instruments of action; furthermore, because that would lead to an infinite regress.

Since all things that serve as means for action— including those designated by the names of major and minor limbs and those produced by karma— possess the status of being means for action, there are not merely five organs of action.
To demonstrate their internal subdivisions, he says:
"Of two kinds": the word *vidha* denotes a type or variety.
Those which possess two modes are "twofold," meaning they are of two types.
What, then, are those two types? They are the material faculty (*dravyendriya*) and the functional faculty (*bhāvendriya*).

In that regard, for the purpose of explaining the nature of the substantial sense organ (*dravyendriya*), he says: "The substantial sense organ consists of the organic formation (*nirvṛtti*) and the accessory (*upakaraṇa*).
(Sūtra 294)
That which is brought to completion is called *nirvṛtti*. By what is it brought to completion? By action (*karman*).
It is of two kinds, due to the distinction between external and internal.

The internal formation (*nirvṛtti*) is the existence of pure soul-particles (*ātmapradeśa*), measured by an incalculable fraction of a finger-breadth (*utsedhāṅgula*), which abide in the specific configuration of the sense organs such as the eye.

The external formation is the accumulation of matter (*pudgalapracaya*) in those very soul-particles—which receive the designation of "sense organ"—that possesses a specific configuration and a particular state produced by the manifestation of name-karma (*nāmakarman*).
The instrument (*upakaraṇa*) is that by which benefit is rendered to the formation.
As before, that too is twofold.
Therein, the internal consists of the black and white circles, while the external consists of the two eyelids, eyelashes, and so forth.
This should be understood to apply likewise to the remaining sense faculties as well.
The functional sense-organ (bhāvendriya) is defined as follows: the functional sense-organ consists of both acquisition (labdhi) and utilization (upayoga).
§ 296. Attainment (*lambhana*) is acquisition (*labdhi*).
What, then, is this? It is a specific state of the subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣayopaśama*) of the karma that obscures knowledge (*jñānāvaraṇa*).
That through whose proximity the self (ātman) exerts itself toward the manifestation of the material sense-organ (dravyendriya), that modification (pariṇāma) of the self is "function" (upayoga).
Both of these constitute the "ontological sense-organ" (bhāvendriya).
Function is the fruit of the sense-organ; how, then, can it possess the status of a sense-organ? Because the property of the cause is observed in the effect.
Just as consciousness transformed into the form of a jar is called a "jar," so too, because its own primary meaning (svārtha) is predominant therein.

Regarding the term *indriya* as "the mark (*liṅga*) of Indra," that which constitutes its own primary meaning is predominant in the sense of "functioning" (*upayoga*), according to the statement: "The soul (*jīva*) is characterized by functioning."
Therefore, it is logical that the faculty consists of the act of application.
To demonstrate the sequence of names for the faculties already mentioned, he says:
In the world, one observes an intention to express the dependence of the sense faculties— namely, touch, taste, smell, sight, and hearing.
"By this eye I see clearly; by this ear I hear well.
Thus, because of their dependence [on other factors], touch and the other senses function as instruments (*karaṇa*).

Due to the support provided by the destruction-cum-subsidence (*kṣayopaśama*) of the *vīryāntarāya* and *mati-jñānāvaraṇa* karmas, and by the acquisition of the purity of the limbs and sub-limbs (*aṅgopāṅga-nāma*), that by which the self touches is called "touch" (*sparśana*).
That by which one tastes is the gustatory faculty (*rasana*). That by which one smells is the olfactory faculty (*ghrāṇa*).
Since the root *cakṣ* has multiple meanings, when the sense of "seeing" is intended, it is called the eye (*cakṣus*) because one sees objects by means of it.
"Ear" (*śrotra*) is so called because one hears by means of it;
yet, we also observe the intention to express independence [of the sense organ], as in:
"This eye of mine sees very well."
This ear of mine hears well;
from that, there is the accomplishment [of the sense] in the agent of touching and so forth.
It touches, therefore it is "touching" (sparśana).
It tastes, thus it is the sense of taste (rasana). It smells, thus it is the sense of smell (ghrāṇa). It sees, thus it is the eye (cakṣus).
It is called "ear" (*śrotra*) because it hears.
This sequence of their explanation is for the purpose of indicating the progressive increase of each one.
To demonstrate the objects of those sense faculties, he says:
"Touch, taste, smell, color-form, and sound are their respective objects.

When there is an intention to emphasize the substance (dravya) and its modes (paryāya), it should be understood that words such as "touch" (sparśa) function as both objective (karman) and abstract (bhāva) nouns. When there is an intention to emphasize the substance, they are designated as objective nouns; for instance, "that which is touched is touch" (spṛśyata iti sparśaḥ).
It is called *rasa* because it is tasted;
*gandha* because it is smelled;
*varṇa* because it is colored.
That which is sounded is "sound" (*śabda*).
When there is an intention to emphasize the action, it is expressed as a verbal noun (*bhāva*).
Touching is "touch" (*sparśa*).
Tasting is taste; smelling is odor; seeing is color.
"Sounding is sound.
The sequence of these has been explained according to the sequence of the sense faculties.
Here it is asked: as for the rejection of the claim that the mind (*manas*) is not a sense-faculty (*indriya*) because it lacks stability—is that [rejection] helpful to its function or not?
It is indeed helpful;
for without it, the sense-faculties lack the activity toward their respective objects that serves their own purpose.
Furthermore, is the purpose of this [scriptural authority] merely its acting as a cooperative cause for these [other means of knowledge], or is there something else as well? To this he says:
"Scripture [is the authority] for that which is beyond the senses.

The object that is the domain of scriptural knowledge (*śrutajñāna*) is "scripture" (*śruta*). That object belongs to the non-sensory faculty (*anindriya*); for in the case of a self that has attained the destruction-cum-subsidence (*kṣayopaśama*) of the obscuration of scriptural knowledge, there occurs the operation of knowledge based on the non-sensory faculty regarding the object of scripture. Alternatively, "scripture" is scriptural knowledge itself; thus it means that this [knowledge] is the object—that is, the purpose—of the non-sensory faculty.
This purpose is to be accomplished through independence for that which is not a sense-faculty.

Regarding the designation of ownership for the aforementioned sense-faculties, each of which has its own specific object, he first takes up the tactile faculty (*sparśana*) and speaks as follows in order to determine its ownership:
"Of those ending with the forest trees, one" (§304); "one" means the first.
What is that? It is touch. Of what things is it to be understood? It should be known as belonging to those beginning with earth and ending with plants.

Its cause of origination is stated: when there is the subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣayopaśama*) of the obstruction to energy (*vīryāntarāya*) and the obstruction to the sense of touch (*sparśanendriyāvaraṇa*), and when there is the manifestation of all-destructive (*sarvaghāti*) passion-throws (*spardhaka*) for the remaining senses; and when there is the support of the acquisition of the body-name-karma (*śarīranāman*) and the subservience to the manifestation of the one-sensed genus-name-karma (*ekendriyajātināman*), the single sense of touch manifests.
To demonstrate the sovereignty of the other faculties, he says:
[the faculties] increase one by one in worms, ants, bees, humans, and so forth.
‘Ekaikam’ (each one) expresses repetition (*vīpsā*), hence the dual number.
Those increased by each one are “increased by each one” (*ekaikavṛddhāni*).
Starting with worms (*kṛmi*) as the first, and starting with the sense of touch (*sparśana*) because it is the governing factor, the connection is made that [the senses] increase one by one.
The word "first" (*ādi*) is completed with each term. The explanation of the connection according to the respective order is as follows:

for worms and so forth, there is the sense of touch plus the sense of taste; for ants and so forth, the senses of touch and taste plus the sense of smell; for bees and so forth, the senses of touch, taste, and smell plus the sense of sight; and for humans and so forth, those same [senses] plus the sense of hearing. Thus the connection has been explained.
Their completion is explained by the arising of *sparśana* through the successive emergence of all-destructive (*sarvaghāti*) *spardhakas*.

Thus, among these transmigrating beings who are divided into two types and further into five kinds according to their faculties, he speaks in order to demonstrate the division of those with five faculties, which has not yet been mentioned: § 307. Evam eteṣu saṃsāriṣu dvibhedeṣu indriyabhedāt pañcavidheṣu ye pañcendriyās tadbhedasyānuktasya pratipādanārtham āha —
Those possessing perception possess the mind.
The mind has already been explained.
Those who exist together with that [mind] are "possessing mind" (samanaska);
they are called "sentient" (saṃjñin).
By process of elimination, it is established that the other transmigrating beings are "non-sentient" (asaṃjñin).
But is it not the case that the qualification "possessing mind" (*samanaskā*) is redundant, since its meaning is already conveyed by the term "possessing perception" (*saṃjñina*) alone?

For the activity of the mind consists in the examination of what is beneficial and harmful, as well as in the attainment of the former and the avoidance of the latter; and perception (*saṃjñā*) is precisely that very same [activity].
This is not tenable, because there is a deviation between the term "name" (saṃjñā) and its referent.
"Name" is said to be the designation (nāman).
If [the opponent claims] that those which possess it are the "named" (saṃjñin), then this would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) for all things.
If it is argued that perception (*saṃjñā*) is knowledge (*jñāna*), then there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), because all living beings consist of knowledge.
If it is argued that perception is the desire for objects such as food, then the same [objection] applies.
Therefore, they are said to "possess mind" (*samanaska*).

And by establishing this, even in states such as being in the womb, born from an egg, fainting, or deep sleep— where there is an absence of the examination of what is beneficial or harmful— the status of being "possessed of perception" (*saṃjñin*) is logically established due to the presence of the mind.

If the movement of living beings toward objects such as the beneficial or the harmful is preceded by the application of the mind, then one might ask: from where does that karma arise for one who is about to take up a new body, whose previous body has disintegrated, and who is currently without a mind? To this it is said: "The conjunction with karma exists during the transition of the body."
*Vigraha* means body (*deha*).
Movement for the sake of the body is "movement of the body" (*vigrahagati*).
Alternatively, *vigraha* means an adverse planet, a conflict, or an obstruction.
The meaning is that even when there is the undertaking of karma (*karmādāna*), there is no cessation of the taking up of the non-karmic *pudgalas*.
"Obstructed motion" (*vigrahagati*) is motion characterized by such an obstruction.
The *kārmaṇa* body, which serves as the seed for the growth of all bodies, is called "karma.
"Yoga" is the vibration of the soul's spatial units (*ātmapradeśa*) caused by the groups of matter (*vargaṇā*) associated with speech, mind, and body.
The meaning is that "karmic yoga" (*karmayoga*) is the yoga produced by karma, which occurs during the transition between physical bodies (*vigrahagati*).
By that, there occurs the undertaking of karma and the transition to another location.

It is asked: as the living beings (jīva) and material particles (pudgala) traverse their course, does their transition to another location occur by means of a sequential progression through points of space (ākāśapradeśa), or without such distinction? To this, he says:
§312. Sequential movement (*anuśreṇigati*):
Beginning from the center of the world, a row (*śreṇi*) is said to be a line of spatial points (*ākāśapradeśa*) arranged in succession upwards, downwards, and across.

The word *anu* functions in the sense of "successively. The meaning is that the movement of living beings (*jīva*) and matter (*pudgala*) occurs along a line, successively, as in "along the line" (*anuśreṇi*). If it is asked how matter not under discussion is included [in this definition], it is because of the mention of "movement" (*gati*).

If only the movement of souls (jīvas) were intended, the mention of "movement" (gati) would be redundant, as that is already established by the context. Furthermore, because the term "souls" (jīva) is used later on, it is understood here to refer to matter-particles (pudgalas).

[Objection: But surely, at the time of the circumambulation of Meru by the luminaries such as the moon, the movement of beings like the Vidyādharas is also seen to be non-linear (viśreṇi); why then is it said that "movement is along the line" (anuśreṇi)?
In this context, the restriction of time and place is to be understood.

Regarding the restriction of time: first, at the moment of death for living beings when transitioning to another existence, and at the moment of ascending for those who are liberated, movement occurs only along the serial line (*anuśreṇi*).

Regarding the restriction of place as well: movement from the upper world downward, from the lower world upward, or from the intermediate world either downward or upward, occurs there only along the serial line.
And for individuals, that [attainment] which reaches the end of the world is necessarily only along the sequence; other destinies are subject to variation. § 313.
Furthermore, for the sake of understanding the specific nature of movement, he says:
"The soul is without a body.
"Vigraha" means obstruction or crookedness;
that movement in which this does not exist is "avigrahā" (unobstructed).
Of what? Of the soul (jīva).
Of what kind [of being]? Of one who is liberated (mukta).

How is it understood that it refers to one who is liberated? Because the term "one in saṃsāra" (saṃsārin) is used in the subsequent sūtra, it is understood here that it refers to one who is liberated.
But is it not the case that by the very statement "movement along the line" (anuśreṇi gatiḥ), the absence of transition to another line has already been explained?
This is not for the sake of [establishing] a meaning.
This statement is intended to indicate that even movement outside the regular sequence (*viśreṇi*) exists in some cases, as stated in the preceding sūtra.
[Objection: But was not the restriction of place and time already stated in that very [sūtra]?
No; for that [movement] is established from this [very fact].

If it is asserted that the movement of the unattached self reaches the end of light without obstruction for a determined duration, then one must ask: is the movement of the embodied self obstructed, or is it like that of the liberated self? To this, he says:
And for those in saṃsāra, [the body] possesses form prior to the four [nutriments].
The phrase "prior to the four" is stated for the purpose of defining the temporal limit.
The word “prior” (*prāk*) is used in the sense of a limit; that is, the embodied state of existence (*vigrahavatī gati*) occurs prior to the fourth moment, but not in the fourth.

If one asks why, it is because a living being (*prāṇin*) who intends to be born in the *niṣkuṭa* garden—the field that is the cause for the most excellent embodiment—initiates a three-embodied movement (*trivigrahā gati*) aimed at reaching the *niṣkuṭa* field, provided there is no absence of the sequence and the straight line (*anuśreṇi*) leading to that *niṣkuṭa* field; it does not initiate an upward movement, because there is no such place of rebirth (*upapādakṣetra*) above.
The word “and” (*ca*) has the sense of conjunction.
[There is] that which possesses form and that which is formless.
Regarding the movement that possesses form, its duration has been determined.
It is said: how long is the duration of the non-obstructed [movement]?
It lasts for a single moment (*ekasamaya*).
That which has a single moment is "single-moment" (*ekasamayā*).
That which has no obstruction is "unobstructed" (*avigrahā*).
For the movement of living beings (*jīva*) and matter (*pudgala*), who possess motion, is single-momentary without obstruction even as far as the end of light.

In the continuum of the bondage of karma from beginningless time, one who, under the influence of conditions such as false view, takes up karmas and is intensely attached to the state of embodiment (*vigraha-gati*) while taking food, is [thereby] bound. Therefore, for the sake of restriction, this is stated: "For one, two, or three [moments], he does not take food."
The connection with the conventional term [‘time’] is due to its specific application (*adhikāra*).
The word ‘or’ (*vā*) has the sense of an alternative (*vikalpa*).
And "option" (*vikalpa*) means acting according to one's wish.
The meaning is that one may remain without food for one, two, or three watches (*samaya*).

Food (*āhāra*) consists of the grasping of suitable matter (*pudgala*) for the three bodies and the six modes of completion (*paryāpti*); because of the absence of that, one is "without food" (*anāhāraka*).
For there is continuous intake of matter as long as the *kārmaṇa* body exists.
In the case of a straight course toward the place of rebirth, there is intake of matter;
in the other three moments, there is no intake of matter.
Thus, in order to demonstrate the manner in which a new physical form is produced for one who is passing away, he says: "Birth is [of three kinds: by coagulation, from the womb, and by apparition."
*Saṃmūrcchana* is the coagulation of the body all around—in the three worlds, above, below, and across—and the formation of its constituent parts.
*Garbha* is the swelling together and mixing of semen and blood within the womb of a woman.
Or, the embryo (*garbha*) arises from consuming the food consumed by the mother.
"Upapāda" means that which falls (*padyate*) into it after having approached (*upetya*);
it is a designation for the specific places of birth for gods and hell-beings.
These three modes of birth for transmigrating living beings are produced by the ripening of various karmas caused by auspicious and inauspicious transformations.
Now, since the various conceptualizations regarding the birth of the subject under discussion— one who is intent upon the locus of experiencing the objects of saṃsāra— must be stated, he says:
Those [beings] are classified as having their own minds, being restrained by cold, the opposite, mixed, and single; they have that as their source.
Mind (*citta*) is the transformation of the specific consciousness of the self.
That which exists together with the mind is "with mind" (*sacitta*).

"Cold" is a specific kind of tactile sensation (*sparśaviśeṣa*); because it functions as a term for both [the quality and the substance], just like "white" and other such terms, it also denotes the substance endowed with that quality.
One who is properly restrained is "restrained" (*saṃvṛta*).
"Concealed" (*saṃvṛta*) refers to a place that is difficult to perceive.
"Together with others" (*setara*) means they exist along with others; the meaning is "possessing counterparts" (*sapratipakṣa*).
What, then, are the others? Those that are without mind (*acitta*), not hot (*anuṣṇa*), and uncovered (*vivṛta*).
That which possesses both natures is mixed (*miśra*);
it is with mind (*sacitta*) and without mind (*acitta*), cold (*śīta*) and hot (*uṣṇa*), and covered (*saṃvṛta*) and uncovered (*vivṛta*).
The word "ca" (and) has the sense of conjunction, [indicating] that there are also mixed modes of birth (*miśrā yonayaḥ*).
Otherwise, it would be a qualification of only those previously mentioned.
The term "ekaśaḥ" (each one) has the sense of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*).
Its inclusion is for the purpose of indicating a mixed practice;
so that it may be understood as "with mind and without mind," "cold and hot," and "concealed and revealed.
It should not be understood as "with mind and cold," and so forth.
The mention of "those" (*tadgrahaṇa*) is for the purpose of referring back to the modes of birth;
that is, these are the "birth-places" (*yoni*) for those births, such as spontaneous generation (*saṃmūrcchana*) and so forth.
These nine birth-places are to be understood as follows.
If it is argued that there is no distinction between the womb and birth, we say no; for there is a distinction between them due to the difference between the container and the contained.
These wombs, such as the sentient and so forth, are the containers (*ādhāra*).
The various modes of birth are the things contained (*ādheya*).

Because, in the case of birth from a womb involving consciousness (*sacitta-yoni*) and so forth, the self (*ātman*) takes up, through birth by coagulation (*saṃmūrcchana*) and other modes, those *pudgala*s suitable for the body, food, sense-faculties, and so on.
Devas and hell-beings have a birth-source without consciousness (*acitta-yoni*);
for their birth-source is a mass of *pudgala*s at the place of rebirth that is devoid of consciousness.

Those born from a womb have mixed origins (*miśrayoni*). For in the mother’s womb, the semen and blood are without mind; because they are mixed with that which possesses a mind—the self—they have a mixed origin. Those born by spontaneous generation (*saṃmūrcchanaja*) have three types of origins (*trivikalpayoni*).
Some have a mind as their source of birth; others have no mind as their source of birth; and still others have a mixed source of birth.
Those with a mental origin have a common body. Why? Because they depend upon one another. Others, however, have a non-mental origin and a mixed origin.
Devas and hell-beings have cold and hot origins;
for some of their birthplaces are cold and some are hot.
Those with a fiery origin are the fire-bodied beings.
The others have three types of origins:
some have a cold origin,
some have a hot origin, and others have a mixed origin.
Devas, hell-beings, and those with a single sense-faculty have concealed birth-sources (saṃvṛtayoni).
Those with incomplete sense-faculties have uncovered birth-sources (vivṛtayoni).
Those born from a womb have mixed birth-sources (miśrayoni).

The subdivisions of these [meditations] should be understood from scripture as numbering eighty-four hundred thousand. And it is said: "Seven from the immobile and one-sensed beings, ten from those with two to four senses, six from the five-sensed, four from gods, hell-beings, and animals, and fourteen hundred thousand among humans."
Seven [types of beings] possess no sense-faculties; ten possess one sense-faculty;
six possess two up to five sense-faculties; four possess all five sense-faculties among gods, hell-beings, and animals; and fourteen hundred thousand exist among humans.

Thus, since birth from all three types of wombs—which are crowded with nine varieties of origins—occurs without restriction for all living beings, he says the following in order to determine their specific categories:
"The womb-born, the egg-born, and the sweat-born [are those] whose [birth is] from a womb.
That which is spread out like a net, enveloping the living being with flesh and blood, is the *jarāyu*.
That which resembles nails or skin, having acquired hardness, enveloping the semen and blood, and being circular, is the *aṇḍa* (egg).
A *pota* is one whose limbs are fully developed without such an external covering, and who, immediately upon emerging from the womb, is endowed with the capacity for movement and other functions.
Those born from a womb are "womb-born" (*jarāyuja*).
Those born from an egg are "egg-born" (*aṇḍaja*).
Womb-born, egg-born, and those born as sprouts are "womb-born, egg-born, and sprout-born," which constitute the womb-births (*garbhayoni*).
If the embryo of these beings born from a womb, born from an egg, or born from moisture is not retained, then for whom does "spontaneous birth" (upapāda) occur? To this he says:
the spontaneous birth belongs to gods and hell-beings.
The birth of gods and hell-beings is to be understood as *upapāda*.
Now, as to what the birth of others is, he says:
The remaining [beings] undergo spontaneous generation (*saṃmūrcchana*).
Those other than those born from a womb (*garbhaja*) and those born by apparition (*aupapāduka*) are the "remaining" ones.
"Conception is birth.
These three [terms] are also for the purpose of restriction;
and a mutual restriction is to be understood.
The womb belongs only to those born from a womb, those born from an egg, and those born from moisture;
and the womb belongs only to those born from a womb, those born from an egg, and those born from moisture.
Apparitional birth belongs only to gods and denizens of hell.
Furthermore, gods and hell-beings are born by apparitional birth (*upapāda*) alone;
the rest are born by spontaneous generation (*saṃmūrcchana*).
And the rest are born by spontaneous generation alone.

Furthermore, regarding those transmigrating beings who possess three types of birth and many varieties of new distinctions of origin, what are the bodies that serve as the substrata for experiencing the fruits of bondage, produced by the ripening of auspicious and inauspicious *nāmakarma*? To this he says:
the bodies are the gross (*audārika*), the transformable (*vaikriyika*), the assimilative (*āhāraka*), the fiery (*taijasa*), and the karmic (*kārmaṇa*).
Bodies (*śarīra*) are so called because they "perish" (*śīryante*), their functions being brought about by the arising of specific *nāmakarma*.
The [bodies] such as the gross (*audārika*) are so called because their functions are attained through the arising of specific primary dispositions (*prakṛti*) such as the gross.
*Udāra* means coarse (*sthūla*). That which exists in what is coarse, or that which has a coarse purpose, is *audārika*.

Because of its connection with the eightfold supernatural powers (*guṇaiśvarya*), it performs the formation of bodies that are singular or manifold, minute or large; this transformation is its purpose, hence it is called *vaikriyika*.

The *āhāraka* [body] is that which is brought forth or produced by one who is restrained yet heedless (*pramatta-saṃyata*), either for the sake of discerning subtle objects or out of a desire to avoid non-restraint.
That which has fire as its cause or exists within fire is the *taijasa*.
The *kārmaṇa* is the effect of karmas.
Although all [phenomena] have karma as their cause, it should be understood that they function with respect to specific objects by virtue of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*).
As for the question, "If the coarse [object] is perceived by the sense faculties, why is this not the case for the others?", he says:
"Higher and higher, more subtle.
Although the word *para* has multiple meanings, its specific referent is determined by the speaker's intention.
A sequential indication by way of repetition is made regarding the subtle qualities of the distinct bodies:

the gross is the *audārika* (physical); subtler than that is the *vaikriyika* (transformative); subtler than that is the *āhāraka* (projective); subtler than that is the *taijasa* (flame-bodied); and subtler than the *taijasa* is the *kārmaṇa* (karmic body).
If "successively more subtle" were understood as "successively inferior" even in terms of spatial extent (*pradeśataḥ*), then, in order to prevent such a misconception, it is said:
"Successively [increasing] by incalculable multiples (*asaṃkhyeyaguṇa*) in terms of spatial extent, up to the *taijasa* [body].
"Directions" (*pradeśa*) are so called because they are pointed out; they are atoms (*paramāṇu*).
That which has transcended number is "incalculable" (*asaṃkhyeya*).
This [space] possesses an incalculable quality; thus, it is "of incalculable qualities" (*asaṃkhyeyaguṇa*).
Why? Because [it applies] by way of spatial location (*pradeśataḥ*), not by way of pervasion (*avagāhataḥ*).

Since the term "successively" (*paramparam*) is understood from the preceding context, there would be the undesirable consequence that this would apply even up to the *kārmaṇa* body; therefore, to exclude that, he says "prior to the *taijasa*."

The transformation body (*vaikriyika*) has an incalculable number of constituent parts (*pradeśa*) compared to the gross [body]; the assimilative body (*āhāraka*) has an incalculable number of constituent parts compared to the transformation body. What is this multiplier?
It is an incalculable fraction of a *palyopama*.

If this is so, does it not follow that there would be a mutually inconsistent magnitude? Not so; due to the specific nature of their binding, there is no difference in magnitude, just as in the case of a heap of cotton and a lump of iron.
Now, as to whether the two higher [realms] possess equal spatial extent or if there is some distinction between them, he says:
"The higher [realm] has infinitefold qualities. (337)

The term "by way of space-points" (*pradeśataḥ*) carries over; thus, the connection is made as follows: the *taijasa* body has infinitely more space-points than the *āhāraka* body, and the *kārmaṇa* body has infinitely more space-points than the *taijasa* body.
What is the multiplier? It is infinitely more than that of the incapable (*abhavya*) souls, and an infinite fraction of that of the perfected (*siddha*) souls.

In this regard, it might be argued that because the transmigrating soul (*jīva*) is composed of a material substance like a thorn, there would follow the consequence of its intended movement being obstructed. That is not so; for what reason?
Because both of these are non-obstructive.
*Pratighāta* (resistance) is the obstruction of one corporeal entity by another corporeal entity.

Since this does not exist for these two, they are called "non-resistant" (*apratighāte*). Due to their subtle transformation, there is no obstruction for the fiery (*taijasa*) and karmic (*kārmaṇa*) bodies even within diamond slabs and the like, just as fire penetrates a mass of iron.
But is it not the case that there is also no resistance for the *vaikriyika* and *āhāraka* [bodies]? It is "non-resistance everywhere" that is intended here.
Just as there is no resistance anywhere up to the end of the world for the *taijasa* and *kārmaṇa* [bodies], such is not the case for the *vaikriyika* and *āhāraka* [bodies].
He asks: "Is this the only distinction, or is there some other as well? He replies: "And [there is] the beginningless connection.
The word “and” (*ca*) has the sense of an alternative. It refers to both a beginningless connection and a connection with a beginning.

[This applies] to a beginningless connection by way of the continuity of the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), and to a connection with a beginning in view of specific instances, as in the case of a seed and a tree.
Just as the gross, transformational, and assimilative bodies are sometimes present for a living being and sometimes not, so it is not with the luminous and karmic bodies;
for those two are eternally connected [to the soul] until the destruction of *saṃsāra*.
Are these two—the taijasa and the kārmaṇa bodies—possessed by some individuals only, or without distinction? To this he says:
"Of everyone. (343)
The word "all" (sarva) signifies without exception. It is fitting [to say] that both of these bodies belong to every single transmigrating soul (jīva).

Since it would follow that all transmigrating beings are simultaneously connected with those [categories] such as the gross body because they are mentioned without distinction, the following is stated in order to demonstrate the possible bodies:
"Those beginning with that [the gross body] are to be distributed; [they may occur] simultaneously, up to four for one [being].
The word "tad" (that) serves to refer back to the previously mentioned *taijasa* and *kārmaṇa* [bodies].
Those for which the *taijasa* and *kārmaṇa* are the first are "those beginning with that" (*tadādini*).
They are "to be distributed" (*bhājyāni*), meaning they are to be optionally combined.
From how many? From four.
Simultaneously for a single soul:
for some, two—the taijasa and the kārmaṇa.
For another, there are three: the gross, the fiery, and the karmic; or the transformational, the fiery, and the karmic.
For yet another, there are four: the gross, the assimilative, the fiery, and the karmic—such is the classification made.
Furthermore, in order to explain their specific distinctions, he says:
"The last is without enjoyment. (347)
That which exists at the end is the final [body].
What is that? It is the *kārmaṇa* body.
Enjoyment (*upabhoga*) is the perception of sound and other objects through the channels of the sense organs.
Due to the absence of those [organs], it is devoid of experience.

Even when there is a physical body and the attainment of the sense organs (*indriya*), because of the absence of the manifestation of the material sense organs (*dravyendriya*), there is an absence of the experience of sound and other objects. Now, one might object: "The luminous (*taijasa*) body is also devoid of experience; why then is it said that the 'last' [body] is devoid of experience? The luminous body, even though it is caused by yoga, does not serve as a basis for experience; therefore, it has no standing in the investigation of experience.
Thus, regarding the births characterized as described therein, do these bodies that come into manifestation arise without distinction, or is there some specific difference? To this he says:
"The first is born from coagulation in the womb."
With respect to the sequence of the sūtras, "initial" (ādya) means that which occurs at the beginning;
the meaning is "gross" (audārika).
Whatever is born from a womb and whatever is born by spontaneous generation— all that should be understood as coarse.
Regarding what was indicated immediately after that— namely, in which birth [it occurs]— he says:
Born by apparition and transformational.
That which exists at birth is "born by apparition" (*aupapādika*); all of that should be understood as transformational (*vaikriyika*).

If the transformation-body (*vaikriyika*) belongs only to those who are spontaneously born (*aupapādika*), then there would be an absence of the transformation-body for those who are not spontaneously born; therefore, he says:
"and [it is] conditioned by attainment (*labdhipratyaya*)."
By the word "ca" (and), the *vaikriyika* [body] is connected.
Attainment (*labdhi*) is the acquisition of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) resulting from a specific austerity (*tapas*).
*Labdhipratyaya* means that its condition (*pratyaya*) is attainment (*labdhi*).
It is connected [to the previous statement] thus: "The transformational body (*vaikriyika*) is both [produced by] karma and has attainment as its condition.
Is this alone dependent on attainment, or is there something else as well? To this he says:
"The taijasa [body] also."§ 355.
By the word "also" (api), the condition of attainment (labdhi-pratyaya) is connected;
that is, the fiery [body] is also [produced] by the condition of attainment.

In order to determine the nature and to specify the possessor of that which was taught immediately after the *vaikriyika* [body], he says: "The *āhāraka* [body] is auspicious, pure, non-obstructive, and belongs only to one who is restrained with negligence (*pramatta-saṃyata*). (357)
It is designated as "wholesome" because it is the cause of what is wholesome;
that is, because it is the cause of the bodily application (*kāyayoga*) that brings about wholesome karma, it is called "wholesome," just as food is designated as "life-force" (*prāṇa*).
It is designated as "pure" because it is the effect of purity.
It is called "pure" because it is produced by pure meritorious karma that is unblemished and faultless, just as threads are designated as "cotton.
It is "unobstructed" because there is no mutual interference;
for the *āhāraka-śarīra* does not obstruct anything else.
Nor [is it produced] by anyone other than the one who possesses the *āhāraka* body.

The word "and" (*ca*) is used here to signify a collection of purposes for that [body]. Namely: sometimes for the purpose of making known the existence of a particular attainment (*labdhi*), sometimes for the purpose of determining subtle objects, and sometimes for the purpose of maintaining self-restraint (*saṃyama*).
The term "āhāraka" is a restatement of what was previously mentioned.
When one begins to produce an *āhāraka* body, one becomes negligent (*pramatta*); therefore, it is said to belong to a "negligent self-restrained person" (*pramattasaṃyata*).

The inclusion of the word "only" (*eva*) is for the sake of restriction according to what is intended, so that it may be understood that the *āhāraka* [body] belongs only to the negligent self-restrained person and not to anyone else.
Let it not be understood that for the careless restrained (pramatta-saṃyata) there is only the assimilative body (āhāraka);
let there not be the cessation of the gross [body] and so forth.

Since transmigrating beings who bear such divided bodies may, at each rebirth, possess all three genders or perhaps have some restriction regarding gender, he says: hell-beings and those born by spontaneous generation (*saṃmūrchana*) are not neuter.
The hells will now be described.

Those who exist in the hells are "hell-beings" (nāraka). "Conception by coagulation" (saṃmūrccha) refers to the process of coagulation; those who possess this are "conceived by coagulation" (saṃmūrcchin).
The hell-beings and those born by spontaneous generation (saṃmūrcchita) are "hell-born-spontaneously-generated" (nāraka-saṃmūrcchin).

Due to the activation of the male-female-ness (napuṃsaka-veda) from the sub-classification of conduct-deluding (cāritra-moha) non-passionate (no-kaṣāya) delusion, as well as the inauspicious name-karma (aśubha-nāman), they are neither women nor men; thus they are neuter (napuṃsaka).
It is a fixed rule that those born in hell through spontaneous generation are exclusively neuter.
For in that [state], there is not even the slightest measure of pleasure caused by contact with agreeable sounds, smells, forms, tastes, and tangibles pertaining to the objects of women and men.

If it is thus determined, it follows by implication that those transmigrating beings other than those mentioned possess the three genders; therefore, in order to demonstrate where the neuter gender is absolutely absent, he says:
As for the gods:
since they experience that unsurpassed pleasure— whether feminine or masculine— which depends upon the arising of the name of a fortunate rebirth, there are no neuter beings among them.
Now, as to what the genders of the others are, he says:
"The remaining ones belong to the three Vedas."
Those who possess the three Vedas are called "trivedas.
What, then, are those Vedas? They are femininity, masculinity, and neuter-ness.
How is their establishment [proven]? That which is known is "veda" (the Veda);
the meaning is "linga" (the mark).
That is twofold: the material mark (*dravyaliṅga*) and the existential mark (*bhāvaliṅga*).
The material mark (*dravyaliṅga*) consists of the female organ, the male organ, and so forth, produced by the emergence of name-karma (*nāmakarma*).
The functional mark (*bhāvaliṅga*) is that whose activity is brought about by the emergence of the secondary passions (*nokaṣāya*).
A woman is so called because the embryo develops within her due to the emergence of female gender (*strīveda*).
One is called a "male" because, through the arising of male-vedanīya karma, he produces or begets offspring;
one is a "neuter" because, through the arising of neuter-vedanīya karma, one is devoid of the capacity for both [procreation].
These are conventional (rūḍhi) terms.
Furthermore, action [is mentioned] in conventional designations for the sake of etymological derivation,
as in "a cow (go) is so called because it goes.

Otherwise, if the primary emphasis were on actions such as conceiving a fetus and so forth, then the designation of "femininity" and so on would not apply to infants, the elderly, animals, humans, or gods, nor to those abiding in the *kārmaṇakāya-yoga*, since such actions are absent in them.
These three Vedas pertain to the remaining beings born from a womb.

Regarding those living beings who are designated by specific distinctions based on their birth, origin, body, and gender—such as gods and others who, under the influence of various merits and demerits, assume bodies within the four states of existence—one might ask: do they, having exhausted their lifespan at the proper time, migrate into other forms, or even prematurely? To this, he says:
Those born by spontaneous generation (*aupapāduka*), those in their final and supreme body, and those with an incalculable lifespan have an irreversible lifespan.
Regarding those born by spontaneous generation, it has been explained that they are gods and hell-beings.
The word *carama* means "final.
*Uttama* means "supreme" or "excellent.
Those for whom the body is final and supreme are called *caramottamadeha*.
"Having limited saṃsāra" means they are worthy of attaining nirvāṇa in that very birth.

"Those with an incalculable lifespan" refers to animals and humans born in places such as Uttarakuru, whose life-span is an *asaṃkhyeya*—that is, a number beyond calculation—comprehensible only through measures of comparison such as the *palya* and so forth.

"Spontaneously born (*aupapāduka*), those in their final and supreme bodies, and those with an incalculable lifespan" is a compound meaning: those who are spontaneously born, those in their final and supreme bodies, and those with an incalculable lifespan.
When external causes of injury, such as poison or weapons, are present, [the lifespan] becomes short; thus it is "reducible" (*apavartya*).
Those whose lifespan is reducible are "those of reducible lifespan" (*apavartyāyuṣaḥ*). Those who are not of reducible lifespan are "those of non-reducible lifespan" (*anapavartyāyuṣaḥ*).
For the lifespan of these beings, such as those born by apparitional birth (*aupapāduka*), is not shortened by the power of external causes; this is the rule. For others, there is no such fixed rule.
The term "supreme" (*uttama*) is employed to demonstrate the excellence of the final body; it does not signify any other distinct category.
Or the reading is “caramadehāḥ.
Thus ends the second chapter in the *Tattvārthavṛtti* titled *Sarvārthasiddhi*.
Now begins the third chapter.
Regarding such statements as "the avadhi-perception of gods and hell-beings has existence as its cause," since hell-beings are mentioned therein, one asks: "Who are these hell-beings?
To explain that, the description of their locus is provided:

The grounds characterized by the radiance of jewels, gravel, sand, mud, smoke, darkness, and great darkness are supported respectively by layers of clouds, water, wind, and space, each situated one below the other.
"Jewel, gravel, sand, mud, smoke, darkness, and great darkness" refers to these: jewels, gravel, sand, mud, smoke, darkness, and great darkness.
The word *prabhā* (light) is completed with each [term].
The designation is applied by virtue of association (*sāhacarya*).

The earth associated with the light of gems such as the *citra* is *ratnaprabhā*; the earth associated with the light of gravel (*śarkarā*) is *śarkarāprabhā*; the earth associated with the light of sand (*vālukā*) is *vālukāprabhā*; the earth associated with the light of mud (*paṅka*) is *paṅkaprabhā*; the earth associated with the light of smoke (*dhūma*) is *dhūmaprabhā*; the earth associated with the light of darkness (*tamas*) is *tamaḥprabhā*; and the earth associated with the light of great darkness (*mahātamas*) is *mahātamaḥprabhā*.
These designations are explained by this means.
The mention of "ground" (*bhūmi*) is for the purpose of indicating a specific locus;
for the dwellings of hell-beings are not situated without depending upon a ground in the same way that the layers of heaven are.
What then?
[They are said to be] "dependent on the levels" (bhūmi).
In order to ascertain the objective supports (ālambana) of these levels, the mention of dense clouds, water, wind, and so forth is made.
"Clouds, water, wind, and space" refers to clouds, water, wind, and space.
Those for which these are the foundation or support are "those supported by clouds, water, wind, and space. All these earths are supported by the ring of the ocean of dense water.
The circle of dense water rests upon the circle of dense wind;
the circle of dense wind rests upon the circle of subtle wind;
the circle of subtle wind rests upon space.
Space is established upon itself, because it is both the support and the supported.
Each of these three enclosures is twenty thousand yojanas in thickness.
The mention of "seven" is for the purpose of excluding any other number.
There are seven levels, neither eight nor nine.
The expression "lower and lower" is intended to exclude horizontal accumulation.
To determine whether those levels of the hells are dwellings everywhere or only in certain places, he says:

"In them, there are, respectively, three million, two million five hundred thousand, one million five hundred thousand, one million, five hundred thousand, one hundred fifty thousand, and fifty-five thousand hells. (369)
In those levels, beginning with Ratnaprabhā, the hells are enumerated in this sequence:

in Ratnaprabhā there are three million hells; in Śarkarāprabhā, twenty-five million hells; in Vālukāprabhā, fifteen million hells; in Paṅkaprabhā, ten million hells; in Dhūmaprabhā, three million hells; in Tamaḥprabhā, ninety-nine thousand nine hundred and fifty hells; and in Mahātamaḥprabhā, five hells.
In the Ratnaprabhā [earth], there are thirteen layers of hells.
Below that, down to the seventh earth, there are two layers of hells each that are inferior.
The other distinctions are to be understood from the Lokānuyoga.
Now, as to what the specific distinction among the hell-beings in those various levels is, he says:
"The hell-beings possess transformations of constant, increasingly more inauspicious *leśyās*, bodies, sensations, and activities."
The *leśyās* and so forth have already been explained.

The term "more inauspicious" (*aśubhatara*) is an indication of intensity; it should be understood as being in reference to the inauspicious *leśyās* and so forth pertaining to the animal realm, and also in reference to the progressively lower [realms] within one's own destiny.
The word *nitya* signifies "constantly.

Those for whom the transformations of their bodies, sensations, and mental fluctuations—such as their *leśyās* (aura-colors) and so forth—are constantly more inauspicious, are the hell-beings (*nāraka*).

In the first and second [hells], the *leśyā* is *kāpotī* (dove-colored). In the third, it is *kāpotī* above and *nīlā* (blue) below. In the fourth, it is *nīlā*. In the fifth, it is *nīlā* above and *kṛṣṇā* (black) below. In the sixth, it is *kṛṣṇā*. In the seventh, it is the most extreme black.
The material *leśyās* have been described as determined by the measure of one's own lifespan. Among the *bhāva-leśyās*, which change every *antarmuhūrta*,
the transformations of touch, taste, smell, color, and sound become extremely inauspicious and causes of great suffering due to the influence of specific locations.
And their bodies, due to the emergence of extremely inauspicious *nāma-karma*, are exceedingly foul, deformed in shape, misshapen, and hideous to behold.
Their height in the first [hell] is seven bows, three cubits, and six finger-breadths.
Below that, the height doubles successively for each successive hell.
When internal non-pleasant-feeling-producing karma arises, the hell-beings experience extremely intense pains produced by external causes such as cold and heat, which are innate and beginningless.
In the first, second, third, and fourth hells, there are only hot sensations.
Above the fifth hell, there are two hundred thousand hells characterized by hot sensation.
Below, there is one hundred thousand [leagues] of cold sensation.
In the sixth and seventh [levels], there are only sensations of cold.
Thinking, "We shall transform what is beautiful," they transform it into something even more unattractive; thinking, "We shall produce causes of happiness," they produce only causes of suffering.
These states should be understood as becoming progressively more rapid as one goes lower and lower.
Regarding whether the suffering of these hell-beings is produced solely by cold and heat or otherwise, he says:
They experience suffering brought about by one another.

How is it that they inflict intense suffering upon one another? The hell-beings, by means of their limited range determined by the condition of their rebirth (*bhava-pratyaya*), perceive the causes of suffering from afar due to the arising of false views (*mithyā-darśana*) characterized as distorted vision (*vibhaṅga*). Having thus experienced suffering, and because they see one another when in close proximity, the fire of their anger blazes up. Furthermore, by recollecting their previous lives, they harbor extremely intense and persistent enmity; like dogs and jackals, they engage in attacking one another. Using weapons such as swords, scimitars, axes, *bhiṇḍipālas*, spears, *tomaras*, and *kuntas* produced by their own transformations, as well as hammers and other implements, and using their own hands, feet, and teeth for cutting, piercing, hacking, and biting, they inflict extreme suffering upon each other.
§ 374. Is this the only category of causes for the arising of suffering, or is there some other as well? To this he says:
"And [they experience] the sufferings produced by the afflicted Asuras, prior to the fourth [stage]."

Because of the arising of the karma that brings about the state of an *asura*—which is a specific classification of the karma belonging to the destiny of the gods—they hurl others [down], and thus they are called *asuras*.

Due to the arising of the evil karma acquired through the extremely intense transformation of affliction cultivated in a previous birth, they are constantly afflicted, thoroughly afflicted, and utterly afflicted; thus they are the *asuras*, the utterly afflicted *asuras*.
Because of the qualification "defiled" (*saṃkliṣṭā*), not all *asuras* cause suffering for the hell-beings.
What then? Only certain ones, such as Ambāvarīṣa and others.
The qualification "prior to the fourth [case-ending]" (*prāk caturthyāḥ*) is for the purpose of indicating the limit.
This is for the purpose of demonstrating that the defiled *asuras* in the three upper earths (*pṛthvī*) are the causes of affliction, and there are none beyond these.
The word "and" (*ca*) serves to aggregate the previously mentioned causes of suffering.

They produce suffering for the denizens of hell (*nāraka*) through such means as drinking molten copper and iron, embracing heated iron pillars, climbing up and descending from the *Kūṭaśālmalī* tree, being struck by iron hammers, being carved with adzes and knives, being drenched with caustic salt and boiling oil, being cooked in iron cauldrons (*kumbhī*), being roasted on iron griddles (*ambarīṣa*), being immersed in the *Vaitaraṇī* river, and being crushed in machines.
Thus, even for those whose bodies have been torn to pieces by cutting, splitting, and so forth, death does not occur prematurely.
Why? Because their lifespan is non-declinable (*anapavartyāyuṣka*).
If this is so, then let that very measure of the lifespan of the hell-beings be stated; therefore, he says:
"In those [hells], the maximum duration for beings is one, three, seven, ten, seventeen, twenty-two, and thirty-three *sāgaropamas*.
The phrase "in due order" (yathākramam) is understood [to carry over].
In those hells, according to the sequence of their levels, the lifespans of one and so forth are connected respectively.
In the Ratnaprabhā hell, the maximum lifespan is one *sāgaropama*.
In Śarkarāprabhā, it is three sāgaropamas;
in Vālukāprabhā, seven sāgaropamas; in Paṅkaprabhā, ten sāgaropamas.
In Dhūmaprabhā, it is seventeen sāgaropamas;
in Tamaḥprabhā, twenty-two sāgaropamas;
and in Mahātamaḥprabhā, thirty-three sāgaropamas.
"Supreme" (parā) means "excellent" (utkṛṣṭā).
The mention of "of beings" (sattvānām) is for the purpose of excluding the [spiritual] stages (bhūmi);
that is, this state belongs to beings within the stages, not to the stages themselves.
The lower world, extending across seven levels, has been described.
Now the horizontal world (tiryagloka) must be discussed.

How, then, is the horizontal world (tiryagloka) defined? It is so called because the continents and oceans, extending from [Mount] Meru up to the Svayaṃbhūramaṇa ocean, are situated in a specific horizontal arrangement; therefore, it is the "horizontal world. But what, then, are those things situated horizontally? To this he says:
The continents and oceans, such as Jambūdvīpa and the Salt Ocean (Lavaṇoda), have auspicious names.
The continents begin with Jambūdvīpa.
The oceans beginning with the Lavaṇoda;
whatever auspicious names exist in the world, those are their names.
For example: Jambūdvīpa is a continent.
The salt-water ocean;
the continent of Dhātakīkhaṇḍa;
the Kāloda ocean.
The continent Puṣkaravara; the ocean Puṣkaravara;
the continent Vāruṇīvara.
The ocean is Vāruṇīvara;
the continent is Kṣīravara;
the ocean is Kṣīravara.
The continent of Ghṛtavara;
the ocean of Ghṛtavara;
the continent of Ikṣuvāra.
The excellent sea of sugarcane.
The excellent island of Nandīśvara.
The excellent sea of Nandīśvara.
There is the continent Aruṇavara and the ocean Aruṇavara; in this manner, it should be understood that there are incalculable continents and oceans extending as far as the Svayambhūramaṇa.
In order to explain the specific dimensions, locations, and shapes of these [mountains], it is said:
"The diameters are doubled at each successive stage, and they are ring-shaped, encircling each preceding one."

The expression "twice, twice" (*dvir dvir*) is a term denoting repetition (*vīpsā*) intended to convey the state of being double the diameter (*viṣkambha*). Whatever is the diameter of the first continent, the salt ocean has a diameter double that; the second continent has a diameter double that [of the salt ocean].
"The second ocean has a diameter twice that [of the first].
Those whose diameters are doubled [at each stage] are "those with doubled diameters.
The expression "encircling each preceding one" is used so that it might not be understood as being situated like villages, cities, and so forth.
The description of its shape as being like a circle is for the purpose of excluding other configurations, such as being square and so forth.
Here it is asked: "The dimensions of the regional configurations of Jambūdvīpa must be stated, because the knowledge of the dimensions of the others depends upon them. To this it is said:
In the midst of those [continents], Jambūdvīpa is circular, with Meru as its navel, and has a diameter of one hundred thousand yojanas.
"In the midst of those" means in the center of them.
Of what? Of the previously mentioned continents and oceans.
Like a navel is a "nābhi.
That which has Meru as its navel is "merunābhi."
Its circumference is comparable to the orb of the sun.
A hundred times a thousand is a hundred-thousand (śatasahasra). A hundred-thousand of yojanas is a hundred-thousand-yojana (yojana-śatasahasra).
That which has a diameter of one hundred thousand yojanas is "one hundred thousand yojanas in diameter.
What is it? It is Jambūdvīpa.
Why is it called Jambūdvīpa? Because it is characterized by the Jambu tree.

In the center of the Uttarakurus stands the Jambu tree, which is without beginning or end, a transformation of the earth, uncreated, and accompanied by its surroundings; this continent is designated by it.
In that Jambudvīpa, there are seven regions divided by six mountain ranges. As to what those are, he says:
The regions (varṣas) are Bharata, Haimavata, Harivarṣa, Videha, Ramyaka, Hairaṇyavata, and Airāvata.

The designations "Bharata" and so forth are beginningless and without any [external] cause. Among them, where is the region of Bharata situated? In the southern quarter, between the three oceans and south of the Himavat mountain, the region of Bharata is shaped like a drawn bow.
Divided by Vijayārdha and by the Gaṅgā and Sindhu rivers, it consists of six regions.
To the north of the Lesser Himavat and to the south of the Great Himavat, between the eastern and western oceans, lies the region of Haimavata.
To the south of Niṣadha and to the north of Mahāhimavat, within the interval between the eastern and western oceans, lies Harivarṣa.
The location of Videha is to be seen to the north of Niṣadha, to the south of Nīla, and between the eastern and western oceans.
To the north of Nīla, to the south of Rukmin, and between the eastern and western oceans lies the region of Ramyaka.
To the north of Rukmin, to the south of Śikhari, and between the eastern and western oceans lies the location of the region of Hairaṇyavata.
To the north of Śikhariṇ, in the midst of three oceans, lies the region of Airāvata. Divided by Vijayārdha and by the rivers Raktā and Araktodā, it consists of six sectors.
It has been stated that there are six mountain ranges; who are they, and how are they situated? To this he says:
