"Dividing those [continents], extending from east to west, are the mountain ranges that support the regions (varṣadhara-parvata): Himavat, Mahāhimavat, Niṣadha, Nīla, Rukmin, and Śikhari.
"Dividing those fields"—those whose nature is such are "dividers thereof.
"Extending from east to west" means they touch the salt ocean at both their eastern and western limits.

The Himavat and other mountains, which have existed since beginningless time and possess no [specific] causal signs, are called "range-bearing mountains" (*varṣadhara-parvata*) because they serve as the cause for the division of the regions (*varṣa*).
In that regard, where is Himavān? It is situated on the boundary between Bharata and Haimavata.
Kṣudra-Himavān is one hundred yojanas in height.
Mahā-Himavān, which forms the division between Haimavata and Harivarṣa, is two hundred yojanas in height.
To the south of Videha and to the north of Harivarṣa is the mountain named Niṣadha, four hundred yojanas in height.
All three mountains to the north, which likewise divide their respective varṣas, have been explained;
their heights should be understood as one hundred, two hundred, and one hundred yojanas respectively.
The depth of all these mountains is one-fourth of their height.
To explain the distinction of their colors, he says:
These mountains,
beginning with Himavat, are to be understood as consisting respectively of gold, silver, tapanīya gold, lapis lazuli, silver, and gold.
Himavat is made of gold and has the color of fine Chinese silk;
Mahāhimavat is made of silver and is white in color;
Niṣadha is made of refined gold and has the color of the rising sun.
The blue one is made of beryl and has the luster of a peacock's neck;
the silver one is golden and white;
the peak made of gold has the color of Chinese silk.
Furthermore, in order to specify that [characteristic], he says:
"Their sides are variegated with jewels, and they are equal in width at the top and at the base."
Those whose sides are variegated with jewels endowed with qualities such as various colors and radiance are called "maṇivicitrapārśva" (those with sides variegated by jewels).
The mention of "above" and so forth is made for the purpose of excluding undesirable shapes.
The word “and” (*ca*) has the sense of a conjunction of the middle;
that which is their width at the base is equal [to it] at the top and in the middle.
Among them, those that have found their place are called lakes— the lakes Padma, Mahāpadma, Tigiñcha, Kesari, Mahāpuṇḍarīka, and Puṇḍarīka are situated above them.
Padma, Mahāpadma, Tigiñcha, Kesarī, Mahāpuṇḍarīka, and Puṇḍarīka— these lakes are to be understood as being situated respectively above those [mountains] beginning with Himavat.
Regarding the first of these, he speaks in order to explain its specific configuration:
The first lake,

named Padma, is one thousand *yojanas* in length from east to west and half that [five hundred] in width; it extends five hundred *yojanas* toward the north, has a floor made of diamond, and its banks are variegated with various jewels and gold.
To explain its depth, this is said:
it has a depth of ten yojanas.
*Avagāha* means downward entry or depth.
"Ten *yojanas* of *avagāha*" means its depth is ten *yojanas*.
What is within that? Within that is the lotus (*puṣkara*) measuring one *yojana*.
It is one *yojana* in measure; because its petals extend for two *krośas* in length and its pericarp is two *krośas* in width, it is one *yojana* in both length and width.
One should understand that the lotus flower has a stalk rising two *krośas* from the surface of the water, up to the dense mass of its many petals.
To determine the dimensions and other characteristics of the remaining lakes and lotus ponds, he says: "The lakes and lotus ponds are each double the size of the preceding."

That [length], and that [width], and those two; twice as much as those two, twice as much again, and twice as much as that twice-as-much—this doubling is for the purpose of making known the pervasion (*vyāpti*).
By what are they doubled? By length and so forth.
The Mahāpadma lake has twice the length, width, and depth of the Padma lake. The Tigiñcha lake has twice the length, width, and depth of that.
And there are also the Puṣkara lakes.
What [is it]? It is connected with the phrase "twofold, twofold.
To provide the names, lifespans, and retinues of the goddesses dwelling there, he says:
The goddesses dwelling there—Śrī, Hrī, Dhṛti, Kīrti, Buddhi, and Lakṣmī—have a lifespan of one *palyopama* and are accompanied by their retinues of *sāmānika* gods.

In those lotuses, situated in the center of the pericarps, are palaces that captivate with the luster of the stainless full moon of autumn; they are one *krośa* in length, half a *krośa* in width, and slightly less than a *krośa* in height.

Those who dwell in them and possess such a nature are the "dwellers therein"; these goddesses—known by the names Śrī, Hrī, Dhṛti, Kīrti, Buddhi, and Lakṣmī—are to be understood as residing respectively in those lotuses and other [seats].
By the phrase “having a lifespan of one palyopama,” the measure of their life span is stated.
Those who exist in the same place are the *sāmānikas* (attendant deities).

The *sāmānikas* and the assemblies (*pariṣads*) are "the *sāmānika*-assemblies. Those who exist together with the *sāmānika*-assemblies are "those accompanied by their *sāmānika*-assemblies" (*sasāmānikapariṣatkāḥ*).
Upon the palaces atop the surrounding lotuses of that central lotus, the *sāmānikas* and the assemblies dwell.
Those rivers by which those fields are divided are as follows:
the Gaṅgā, Sindhu, Rohit, Rohitāsyā, Harit, Harikāntā, Sītā, Sītōdā, Nārī, Narakāntā, Suvarṇakūlā, Rūpyakūlā, Raktā, and Raktōdā; these are the rivers flowing through their midst.
Are the rivers and ponds [located] within or near them? He says: "In the midst of them" (*tanmadhyagāḥ*); "in the midst of those fields" (*teṣāṃ kṣetrāṇām madhyam*) is "their midst" (*tanmadhyam*).

They go through the middle of that, or by the middle of that, thus they are "those going in the middle" (*tanmadhyagāḥ*). To prevent the [erroneous] application of this term to all [of them] in one place, and for the purpose of indicating a specific direction, he says: "Of each pair, those in the east are 'eastward-going' (*pūrvagāḥ*)."
Because of the connection with the elliptical phrase “one field is the domain for each pair of rivers,” the possibility that all [rivers] belong to a single [field] is excluded.
The statement “the eastern ones flow eastward” is for the purpose of indicating a specific direction.
In that regard, those rivers which are in the east are "eastward-flowing.
They are called "eastward-flowing" because they go to the eastern ocean.
With respect to what is their "easternness"? It is with respect to the description in the Sūtra.
If this is so, does it not follow that the seven rivers, such as the Gaṅgā and Sindhu, flow eastward? This is not a fault, because of the connection "of each pair.
It should be understood that for each pair, the first [river] flows eastward.
To facilitate the understanding of the other directional divisions, he says: "The remaining [rivers], however, flow toward the west."
Those which remain from each pair of rivers are to be understood as the "outward-flowing" (aparaga).
They are called outward-flowing because they go toward the western ocean.
Among them, the Gaṅgā originates from the Lotus Lake and exits through the eastern gate-tower.
The Sindhu issues forth from the western gate-tower;
the Rohitāsyā issues forth from the northern gate-tower;
and the Rohit, originating from the Mahāpadma lake, issues forth from the southern gate-tower.
The Harikāntā flows out from the northern gate of the archway;
the Harit originates from Lake Tigiñcha and flows out from the southern gate of the archway;
and the Sītodā flows out from the northern gate of the archway.
Sītā originates from the Kesari lake and exits through the western gate-tower; Narakāntā originates from the same lake and exits through the northern gate-tower;
and Nārī originates from the Mahāpuṇḍarīka lake and exits through the southern gate-tower.
The Rūpyakūlā flows out through the northern gate-tower;
the Suvarṇakūlā originates from the Puṇḍarīka lake and flows out through the southern gate-tower;
the Raktā flows out through the eastern gate-tower.
The Raktodā river issues forth from the western gate-tower.
To demonstrate their retinue, he says:
The rivers such as the Gaṅgā and Sindhu, surrounded by fourteen thousand tributaries—
why is the mention of "the Gaṅgā, Sindhu, and so forth" made? It is for the purpose of including all rivers.

Are those [rivers] mentioned in the context being referred to here? One should not think so; for according to the principle that "a rule or a prohibition applies to what is immediately preceding," only the rivers flowing westward would be understood.
If it is argued that the mention of the Gaṅgā and others exists [in the present sūtra], then only the rivers flowing eastward would be understood.
Therefore, the term "Gaṅgā-Sindhu, etc. is employed in order to include both sets of rivers.
The mention of "river" is for the purpose of connecting [the statement] "twice as many, twice as many"; that is, the Gaṅgā is surrounded by fourteen thousand rivers, and so too is the Sindhu.
In this way, each subsequent river in every field becomes twice as many as the preceding one, up to the end of Videha.
Thereafter, each successive [continent] is reduced by half of its preceding one.
To provide an understanding of the diameters of the aforementioned fields, he says:
Bharata is five hundred and twenty-six yojanas and six nineteenth parts of a yojana in extent;
"twenty-six" means twenty plus six.
Those in which there are twenty-six added [units] are "twenty-six-fold" (*ṣaḍviṃśāni*).
Bharata has a width of five hundred *yojanas* that are twenty-six-fold, thus he is "five hundred and twenty-six-fold in width.
Is it only this much? No; therefore it is said: "and six parts of a *yojana* out of nineteen" is connected as his width.
To explain the specific dimensions of the others, he says:
"The mountain ranges and the regions, extending as far as Videha, are each double the width of the preceding."
Therefore, those whose extent is double, double [that] of Bharata are "those with a double-doubled extent. Which are these mountain ranges and regions?
Are all [of them]? No; thus he says, "ending with Videha. Now, as to how it is for those who follow, he says:
The northern [continents] are equal to the southern.
The northern [continents], beginning with Airāvata and ending with Nīla, should be understood as being equal to the southern ones, beginning with Bharata.
This distinction should be understood to apply to all that has passed.
By means of this, the similarity [of the mind] to lotuses in a lake and so forth is to be applied.

Regarding this, it is asked: among the human beings in the aforementioned fields such as Bharata and the others, is their experience and so forth equal, or is there some distinction? To this it is replied:
in Bharata and Airāvata, there is increase and decrease by means of the six time-periods of the *utsarpiṇī* and *avasarpiṇī* cycles.
"Increase and decrease" means increase and decrease.
By what two? By the two six-period cycles of the ascending (utsarpiṇī) and descending (avasarpiṇī) aeons.
Of which two? Of Bharata and Airāvata.
There is no increase or decrease in those two fields, because such is impossible.
However, there is increase and decrease for the humans residing therein.
Alternatively, this is a locative indication of the locus.
Regarding Bharata and Airāvata, there is an increase and decrease among human beings.
By what are this increase and decrease caused? They are caused by experience, the measure of lifespan, and so forth.

Experience refers to enjoyment; lifespan refers to the duration of life; and measure refers to the height of the body—it is through these and other such factors that the increase and decrease of human beings occur.
What, then, are their causes? They have time as their cause. That time is twofold: the ascending cycle (*utsarpiṇī*) and the descending cycle (*avasarpiṇī*).
Each of these has six subdivisions.
These two names are also etymologically significant:
that which has the nature of rising up through experience and the other factors is called *utsarpiṇī*; that which has the nature of subsiding through those very same factors is called *avasarpiṇī*.
In that regard, the *avasarpiṇī* (descending cycle) is of six kinds: *suṣamasuṣamā*, *suṣamā*, *suṣamaduṣṣamā*, *duṣṣamasuṣamā*, *duṣṣamā*, and *atiduṣṣamā*.
The *utsarpiṇī* (ascending cycle) likewise consists of exactly six kinds, beginning with *atiduṣṣamā* and ending with *suṣamasuṣamā*.
The duration of the *avasarpiṇī* is ten *koṭīkoṭīs* of *sāgaropamas*.
The *utsarpiṇī* [aeon] is likewise of the same duration. Both together are designated as a *kalpa*. Within that, the *suṣamasuṣamā* period lasts for four *koṭīkoṭīs* of *sāgaropamas*.
At the beginning of that period, humans were equal to the humans of Uttarakuru.
Then, as there was a gradual decline, the Suṣama period occurred, lasting for three koṭīkoṭīs of sāgaropamas.
At the beginning of that period, humans were equal to the humans of Harivarṣa.
Then, as the [period] gradually declines, the *Suṣamaduṣṣamā* (the "Good-Bad" eon) occurs, lasting for two *koṭīkoṭīs* of *sāgaropamas*.
At its beginning, humans are equal to the inhabitants of the Haimavata continent.
Then, as it gradually declines, the *Duṣṣamasuṣamā* (the "Bad-Good" eon) occurs, lasting for one *koṭīkoṭī* of *sāgaropamas*, minus forty-two thousand years.
At the beginning, humans become equal to the people of Videha.
Then, as there is a gradual decline, the Duṣṣama period occurs for twenty-one thousand years. Then, as there is further gradual decline, the Atiduṣṣama period occurs for twenty-one thousand years.
In this way, the *utsarpiṇī* [aeon] should also be understood as having the reverse order.
Now, as to what the state is in the other stages, he says:
Other lands are situated beyond those two.
Beyond those two, namely Bharata and Airāvata, other lands are situated.
For in those [realms], there are no periods of increase (utsarpiṇī) or decrease (avasarpiṇī).
Regarding whether humans on those stages have equal lifespans or if there is some distinction, he says:
The inhabitants of Haimavata, Hārivarṣa, and Devakuru have lifespans equal to one, two, and three *pala*s respectively.
Since they are born in Haimavata, they are called "Haimavatakas"; thus, by the application of the suffix *-vuñ*, the understanding of them as humans arises.
The same applies to the two [continents] to the north as well.
There are three, beginning with the Haimavata;
and three, beginning with the Eka.
In this regard, the connection is made according to the respective order:
those of the Himavat region have a lifespan of one *palyopama*;
those of the Hārivarṣa region have a lifespan of two *palyopamas*.
The inhabitants of Devakuru have a lifespan of three *palyopamas*.
There, among the five regions of Haimavata, the period of "Great-Equilibrium-with-Slight-Disturbance" (*suṣamaduṣṣamā*) is constantly present.
There, the humans have a lifespan of one *palyopama*, are two thousand *dhanus* in height, take food every fourth mealtime, and have the color of a blue lotus.
In the five Harivarṣas, the age of perfect happiness (suṣamā) is ever-present.
There, humans have a lifespan of two *palyas*, a height of one thousand *arpas*, eat every sixth mealtime, and are conch-white in color.
In the five Devakurus, the age of perfect-perfect happiness (suṣamasuṣamā) is ever-present.
There, the humans have a lifespan of three *palyas*, a height of six thousand *dhanus*, eat every eighth meal, and are golden in color.
Now, as to what their condition is in the northern regions, he says:
Likewise for the northern [directions]: just as the southern ones have been explained, so too should the northern ones be understood.
The Hairanyavatakas are equal to the Haimavatakas;
the Ramyakas are equal to the Harivarṣakas;
and the Auttarakuruvakas are declared to be equal to the Daivakuruvakas.
Now, as for what the state is when [beings] reside in the Videha continents, it is said in this regard:
in the Videhas, the duration is a countable period of time (*saṃkhyeyakāla*).
In all the Videhas, human beings have a calculable lifespan.
Therein, the duration of time is always constant, resembling the period between the ages of perfect excellence and decline.
And the humans there are five hundred bows in height;
they take food daily;
and their lifespan lasts for a maximum of one *pūrvakoti*.
At the minimum, their lifespan is an antarmuhūrta.
Regarding this, they recite a verse: "The measure of a *pūrva* should be known as sixty-five thousand and six hundred and fifty million billion years."
Furthermore, the measure of the Pūrvā is exactly sixty-five thousand crores, and fifty-six thousand crores of years; this is how it should be understood.
The measurement of Bharata has been stated.
Now, in order to explain that again by another method, he says:
"The measurement of Bharata is one-ninth-hundredth part of Jambūdvīpa."
When the diameter of Jambūdvīpa, which is one hundred thousand yojanas, is divided into nine hundred parts, one part is the diameter of Bharata.
That is exactly as previously described.
It has been stated that the railing stands encircling Jambūdvīpa; beyond that is the salt-water ocean, with a circumference of two hundred thousand yojanas.
Beyond that is the continent of Dhātakīkhaṇḍa, with a circumference of four hundred thousand yojanas.
In that regard, for the purpose of understanding the rules concerning the number and so forth of the years and other units, he says:
"Twice in Dhātakīkhaṇḍa" (§430).
In this context, the repetition (*abhyāvṛtti*) of substances such as *bhara* and so forth is intended.
How, then, is the suffix *suc* applied here? The suffix *suc* serves to indicate the repetition of an action that is being supplied by ellipsis (*adhyāhriyamāṇa*).
For example: "This palace is measured twice as large."

In this manner, Bharata and the other regions are measured twice over in Dhātakīkhaṇḍa. To explain: Dhātakīkhaṇḍa is divided into eastern and western halves by two bow-shaped mountains (*iṣvākāra-parvata*) that extend from south to north, their peaks touching the salt-water and the waterless (*āloda*) boundary-walls (*vedikā*). In the center of both the eastern and western halves, there are two Mount Mandaras.
On both sides of those two are the regions beginning with Bharata and the mountain ranges that serve as boundaries between the regions beginning with Himavat.
Thus, the enumeration should be understood as doubled: there are two Bharatas, two Himavats, and so forth.
Whatever the width of the boundary mountains such as Himavat in Jambūdvīpa, the width of the boundary mountains such as Himavat in Dhātakīkhaṇḍa is twice that.
The mountain ranges stand like the spokes of a wheel.
The fields are situated in the intervals between the spokes.
In Jambūdvīpa, where the Jambū tree stands, there is likewise a Dhātakī tree with its retinue in Dhātakīkhaṇḍa.
Because of its connection with that [tree], the name of the continent is known as Dhātakīkhaṇḍa.

Encompassing it is the Kāloda ocean, whose shores are cut like a chisel, and which has a circumference of eight hundred thousand yojanas. Encompassing the Kāloda ocean is Puṣkaradvīpa, which has a circumference of sixteen hundred thousand yojanas.

In this regard, following the principle that the circumference is twice the diameter of the continents and oceans, and given the consequence of a doubling of size for the region of Dhātakīkhaṇḍa and so forth, he says— specifically to determine the distinction—
"and in Puṣkarārddha" (§ 432).
What [is the referent]?
The word "twice" (dvis) is understood from the previous context.
With reference to what is there this twofold repetition? It is precisely with reference to Jambūdvīpa, Bharata, Himavat, and so forth. Why? Because of the explanation.
Just as the width of the Himavān and other mountains in Dhātakīkhaṇḍa is such, so it is explained that the width of the Himavān and other mountains in Puṣkarārdha is double that amount.
Their names are the same; the two bow-shaped mountains and the Mandara mountains are as before.
Where the Jambū tree is located, there is the Puṣkara tree along with its retinue.
From that very [lotus] the name of that continent became established as Puṣkaradvīpa.
Now, how is the designation "Puṣkarārdha" (Half of Puṣkara) derived?
Because it is divided into two halves by the Mānuṣottara mountain, it is designated as Puṣkarārdha.

Here it is asked: For what reason is the enumeration of Jambūdvīpa, Himavat, and so forth stated as being doubled in the half of Puṣkaradvīpa, rather than for the entire Puṣkaradvīpa? To this it is replied:
§ 434. To the east of Mount Mānuṣottara dwell human beings.
In the central region of Puṣkaradvīpa, there is a mountain named Mānuṣottara, which is circular in shape like a ring.
Therefore, humans do not go outside [of this world] even before that. Consequently, there is no division of the aforementioned fields outside [this realm].
Beyond this, humans never go, even if they have attained supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) as *vidyādharas*, except by means of rebirth (*upapāda*) or the destruction of the body (*samudghāta*).
Therefore, its name is etymologically appropriate.
In this way, humans are to be understood as existing in two and a half continents—namely Jambūdvīpa and the others—and in two oceans.
They are of two kinds:
The noble ones (*ārya*) and the barbarians (*mleccha*):
they are called "noble" because they are honored (*aryante*) for their virtues or for being possessed of virtues.

They are of two kinds: noble ones who have attained supernatural powers (*ṛddhiprāpta*) and noble ones who have not attained supernatural powers (*anṛddhiprāpta*). Noble ones who have not attained supernatural powers are of five types: field-noble ones (*kṣetrārya*), birth-noble ones (*jātyārya*), action-noble ones (*karmārya*), conduct-noble ones (*cāritrārya*), and vision-noble ones (*darśanārya*).

Noble ones who have attained supernatural powers are of seven types, distinguished by: transformation through intelligence (*buddhi-vikriyā*), austerity (*tapas*), power (*bala*), medicinal herbs (*oṣadha*), elixirs (*rasa*), and the inexhaustible (*akṣīṇa*).
The Mlecchas are of two kinds: those born in the intermediate islands (antaradvīpa) and those born in the lands of action (karmabhūmi).
Among them, there are eight intermediate islands on the eight sides within the salt ocean, and another eight in the spaces between them.
And at the ends of both Himavacchikhariṇas and both Vijayārddhas, there are eight [islands].
Among them, the islands in the cardinal directions are located after entering five hundred yojanas horizontally from the terrace (vedikā).
The islands in the intermediate directions and the corners are located after traveling five hundred and fifty yojanas.
Beyond the mountain ranges, at intervals of six hundred yojanas, there are islands.
In the cardinal directions, the islands are one hundred yojanas in extent;
in the intermediate directions and the intervening spaces, the islands have half that width.
On the edges of the mountains, they are twenty-five yojanas in width.
There, in the eastern direction, are the Ekorukas;
in the western direction, the Lāṅgūlins.
In the northern direction are those without speech;
in the southern direction are those with horns;
and in the intermediate directions are those with ears like rabbits, ears like shells, ears like hoods, and long-hanging ears.
Those with the faces of horses, lions, dogs, buffaloes, boars, tigers, crows, and monkeys are in the intermediate spaces.
Those with the faces of clouds and lightning are on the peaks at both ends.
Those with the faces of fish and the faces of Time (Kāla) are at both ends of the Himavat mountain.
The Hastimukhas and Ādarśamukhas dwell at both ends of the northern Vijayārdha;
the Gomukhas and Meṣamukhas dwell at both ends of the southern Vijayārdha.
The Ekorukas subsist on clay and live in caves.
The remaining ones subsist on flowers and fruits and dwell in trees;
they all have a lifespan of one *palyopama*.
All those twenty-four islands rise one *yojana* above the surface of the water.
In the same way, twenty-four islands are to be understood on the outer side of the salt ocean; likewise, they are to be known in the Kāloda ocean as well.
These are the Mlecchas born of the intermediate islands.
And those born in the lands of action include the Śakas, Yavanas, Śabaras, Pulindas, and so forth.
What, then, are the lands of action? To this he says:
Bharata, Airāvata, and Videha are the lands of action, with the exception of Devakuru and Uttarakuru.
Bharata, Airāvata, and Videha— these five, five [sets]— are designated as the lands of action (*karmabhūmi*).
In that context, since the mention of "Videha" might imply the inclusion of Devakuru and Uttarakuru, he says—"except for Devakuru and Uttarakuru"—in order to exclude them.
The word "anyatra" (except) has the sense of exclusion.
Devakuru, Uttarakuru, Haimavata, Harivarṣa, Ramyaka, Hairanyavata, and the intermediate islands (*antardvīpa*) are designated as lands of enjoyment (*bhogabhūmi*).
Now, what constitutes being a "land of action" (*karmabhūmi*)? It is because it serves as the locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*) for action characterized by the auspicious and the inauspicious.
But is not the entirety of the three worlds indeed a locus for action?
Therefore, its status as such will be understood through the sense of excellence—that is, that which is a locus for action in a preeminent degree.

In this regard, it should be understood that the designation "land of action" (*karmabhūmi*) applies specifically to Bharata and the other regions, because it is there alone that unwholesome karma leading to rebirth in the seventh hell is acquired, and it is there alone that wholesome karma leading to specific states such as Sarvārthasiddhi is accumulated; furthermore, it is there alone that the six kinds of worldly activities, such as agriculture, are undertaken when accompanied by the giving of gifts to worthy recipients.

The other regions, however, are designated as "lands of enjoyment" (*bhogabhūmi*), because they are the spheres for experiencing the enjoyments produced by the ten kinds of wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpavṛkṣa*).

Regarding the aforementioned realms, he speaks for the purpose of defining the duration of human existence: "The higher and lower human lifespans are three *palyopamas* and an *antarmuhūrta*, respectively.
That which has three *palyopamas* is "three-palyopama" (*tripalyopamā*).
That which has an *antarmuhūrta* within it is "intermediate-muhūrta" (*antarmuhūrtā*).
The connection is according to their respective order.
The supreme or highest lifespan of humans is three *palyopamas*;
the lowest or minimum is an *antarmuhūrta*;
and in between, there are many various possibilities.
In this context, there are three kinds of *palya*: the conventional *palya* (*vyavahāra-palya*), the subtractive *palya* (*uddhāra-palya*), and the temporal *palya* (*addhā-palya*).
These names correspond to their respective meanings.
The first is called the conventional *palya*, because it serves as the seed for the usage of the latter two types of *palya*.
"There is nothing whatsoever to be measured by this"—
this is the second *uddhāra-palya*.
By means of the hair-clippings extracted from that [first *uddhāra-palya*], the continents and oceans are enumerated.
The third is the *addhā-palya*. "Addhā" means duration or the state of time. Among these, the measure of the first is stated for the purpose of defining it.
For example—three *palyas*, meaning granaries, each having a width, length, and depth measured by *yojanas* of standard finger-breadths (*pramāṇāṅgula*).

These are filled with hair-tips grown over a period ranging from one to seven days; they are cut so many times that they do not reach a second cutting by the scissors. A *vyavahārapalya* (conventional palya) is said to be a mass compacted and filled with such hair-cuttings. Then, by the method of removing one hair-tip every hundred years, the time required for it to become empty is called a *vyavahārapalyopama* (conventional palya-division).
With those very hair-tips, each cut at intervals of an incalculable number of millions of years (*asaṃkhyeya-varṣakoṭī-samaya*), that *uddhāra-palya* is filled.
Then, as each single hair-tip is removed one by one at every moment (*samaya*), the duration of time required for it to become empty is called an *uddhāra-palyopama*.
Ten million times ten million (*daśakoṭīkoṭi*) of these *uddhāra-palyas* constitute one *uddhāra-sāgaropama*.
As many hair-tips as there are in two and a half *uddhāra-sāgaropamas*, so many are the continents and oceans.
Furthermore, an *addhā-palya* is filled with hair-tips from an *uddhāra-palya* that have been cut at intervals of every hundred years.
Then, by removing one hair-tip at each passing moment until it is completely emptied, the duration of time required is called an *addhā-palyopama*.
Ten times ten million *addhāpalyas* make one *addhāsāgaropama*.
Ten times ten million *addhāsāgaropamas* make one *avasarpiṇī*.
An *utsarpiṇī* is of exactly the same duration.

By means of this true analogy, one should discern the stability of karma, the stability of existence, the stability of lifespan, and the stability of the body for those born in the hells, the animal realm, and among gods and humans.
And the summary verse has been spoken:
Just as these superior and inferior states exist for humans, so too do they exist for those born of animal wombs.
The womb of animals is the animal womb (*tiryagyoni*).
The meaning is: a birth produced by the arising of the karma named "animal destiny" (*tiryaggati-nāmakarma*).
Those born in the animal womb are "born from the animal womb" (*tiryagyonijāḥ*).
For those born in the animal realm, the maximum duration of existence is three *palyopamas*;
the minimum is an *antarmuhūrta*;
and in between, there are many varieties.
Thus ends the third chapter in the *Tattvārthavṛtti*, titled *Sarvārthasiddhi*.
Now begins the fourth chapter.

In such passages as “the avadhi-knowledge of gods and hell-beings has existence as its condition,” the word "gods" (deva) is mentioned repeatedly; however, it is not known therein who the gods are or how many kinds there are. To determine this, he says:
"The gods consist of four classes. (443)

When the karma named "divine destiny" (devagatināmakarma) arises as the internal cause, they sport and play at will according to their specific excellences in external manifestations across regions such as continents, mountains, and oceans; thus they are called "gods" (devas).

In this context, the use of the singular number—as in “the gods consist of four classes” (devāś caturṇikāyāḥ)—is appropriate, for it expresses many individuals by means of a designation for the genus.
The mention of plurality is for the purpose of indicating the various subdivisions contained therein.
There are many subdivisions, such as those of the Sāmānika Indras and others, as well as those produced by differences in duration and so forth; the purpose [of the term] is to suggest these.

They are called *nikāyas* (groups) because they are gathered together through the power of the manifestation of the *devagati-nāmakarma* (the karma that determines birth as a deity), which produces subdivisions according to the specific nature of their own karma; thus, the meaning is "assemblies."
Those who belong to four classes are the "fourfold classes.
Who, then, are they? They are the Bhavanavāsins, the Vyantaras, the Jyotiṣkas, and the Vaimānikas.
To determine their respective *leśyās*, it is said:
from the beginning, those in the first three [stages] possess *leśyās* ending with yellow (*pīta*).
It is said "from the beginning" (*āditaḥ*) so that it may not be understood as being grasped at the end, in the middle, or elsewhere.
The word "beginning" (*ādau*) becomes *āditaḥ*.
The term "three" (*tri*) is employed in order to exclude the possibility of [referring to] two or one.
Why, then, is it not for the purpose of excluding the four [lower ones]? Because of the statement "from the beginning.
Six *leśyās* have been mentioned;
among them, the term "ending with yellow" (*pītānta*) is employed for the sake of including the four [upper] *leśyās*.
"Yellow radiance" (pītaṃ tejaḥ) is the meaning.
Those whose ends are yellow are "yellow-ended" (pītāntāḥ).
Those whose leśyās (psychic tints) are yellow-ended are "those with yellow-ended leśyās" (pītāntaleśyāḥ).
This is what is meant: from the beginning, among the three classes of gods known as the Bhavanavāsins, Vyantaras, and Jyotiṣkas, there are four *leśyās*—black, blue, pigeon-grey, and yellow.
To demonstrate the internal subdivisions of those classes, he says:
The ten, eight, five, and twelve divisions, extending up to the Kalpopapanna [gods],
should be understood as being connected respectively with the four classes of gods by means of the numerical terms beginning with "ten."
The Bhavanavāsins consist of ten classes;
the Vyantaras, eight classes;
and the Jyotiṣkas, five classes.

"Twelvefold are the gods of the celestial palaces (*vaimānika*). Since it might follow that all gods of the celestial palaces are included within these twelve categories, the qualification "up to those born in the [heavenly] kalpas" (*kalpopapannaparyantāḥ*) is employed in order to exclude the *graiveyaka* gods and others.
Now, how is the designation "kalpa" [derived]? These ten types, beginning with Indra and so forth, are conceptualized (*kalpyante*) within them; thus they are called *kalpas*.
Although that conceptualization is possible among the *bhavanavāsins*, the word "kalpa" (eon) is used here specifically for the *vaimānikas* by virtue of conventional usage.

Those born in the kalpas are "born-in-a-kalpa" (*kalpopapanna*). Those for whom the "born-in-a-kalpa" beings constitute the limit are "those whose limit is the born-in-a-kalpa" (*kalpopapannaparyanta*).
Furthermore, in order to explain their specific distinctions, he says:
"The Sāmānika, Trāyastriṃśa, Pāriṣadya, Ātmarakṣa, Lokapāla, Anīka, Prakīrṇaka, Abhiyogya, and Kilbiṣika [retinues] of Indra, each one by one.
The *indrās* are those who rule (*indanti*) by virtue of possessing unique qualities such as *aṇimā* and the rest.

That which is common—namely, [status] excluding the sovereignty of command, as well as station, lifespan, vigor, retinue, enjoyment, and secondary enjoyments—is shared; those who exist within that commonality are the *sāmānikas*, the great ones who are equal to fathers, gurus, and preceptors.
Those who occupy the positions of ministers and domestic priests are the *trāyastriṃśās*.
The Trāyastriṃśas are indeed thirty-three [in number].
Those who are present in the assembly, similar to companions or court jesters, are the Pariṣads.
The Ātmarakṣas are comparable to bodyguards.
The world-protectors (lokapāla) are like guardians who move about for the sake of [protecting] wealth.
They are called "world-protectors" because they protect the world.
The seven military divisions, beginning with the infantry, stand in the place of the staff of punishment.
The miscellaneous [officers] are those who follow the customs of the city-dwellers and country-folk.
The laborers (*ābhiyogya*) are like slaves, engaged in tasks such as driving vehicles and the like.
The *kilbiṣika*s occupy the position of apprentices.
Those who possess *kilbiṣa*, meaning sin, are called *kilbiṣikas*.

For each individual class (*nikāya*), these ten alternatives beginning with Indra are generally applicable across the four classes; therefore, he speaks [as follows] for the purpose of providing an exception (*apavāda*).
Excluding the Trāyastriṃśa gods and the World-protectors, there are the Vyantara and Jyotiṣka gods.
Among the Vyantaras and Jyotiṣkas, excluding the Trāyastriṃśas and the World-protectors, the other eight categories are to be understood.
Now, regarding those classes [of gods], is there one Indra for each, or is there some other fixed rule? To this he says:
"In the first two, there are two Indras."
Regarding the two preceding classes, namely the Bhavanavāsin and the Vyantara classes:
how is the second one designated as "preceding"? Its status as preceding is stated metaphorically on account of its proximity.
The term “dvindrāḥ” contains an internal distributive sense (*vīpsā*).
Those who have two Indras each are called “dvīndrāḥ,” just as [one speaks of] a *saptaparṇa* (seven-leaved) tree or an *aṣṭāpada* (eight-footed) creature.
It is as follows: among those dwelling in the celestial abodes (bhavanavāsin), first, the asura-kumāras have two lords, Camara and Vairocana;
the nāga-kumāras have Dharaṇa and Bhūtānanda;
and the vidyut-kumāras have Harisiṃha and Harikānta.
Among the Suparṇakumāras are Veṇudeva and Veṇudhārī;
among the Agnikumāras are Agniśikha and Agnimāṇava;
and among the Vātakumāras are Vailamba and Prabhañjana.
Among the Stanitakumāras, there are Sughoṣa and Mahāghoṣa; among the Udadhikumāras, Jalakānta and Jalaprabha;
and among the Dvīpakumāras, Pūrṇa and Vasiṣṭha.
Among the Dikkumāras, there are two lords: Amitagati and Amitavāhana.
Among the Vyantaras as well, there are two lords of the Kinnaras: Kinnara and Kiṃpuruṣa.
Among the Kiṃpuruṣas, there are two: Satpuruṣa and Mahāpuruṣa.
Of the mahoragas, Matikāya and Mahākāya; of the gandharvas, Gītarati and Gītayaśas;
of the yakṣas, Pūrṇabhadra and Maṇibhadra;
and of the rākṣasas, Bhīma and Mahābhīma.
Among the *bhūtas*, there are Pratirūpa and Apratirūpa;
among the *piśācas*, there are Kāla and Mahākāla.

Now, when it is asked what kind of happiness these gods possess, he says—in order to make that happiness understood: "From [the Heaven of the Four Great Kings] up to Īśāna, they have physical contact as their pleasure.
*Pravīcāra* means the practice of sexual intercourse.
Those for whom there is *pravīcāra* by means of the body are called "those who have bodily *pravīcāra*" (*kāyapravīcārāḥ*).
The prefix *ā-* has the sense of inclusion (*abhividhi*).
The teaching is presented without euphonic combination (*asaṃhitā*) for the sake of avoiding ambiguity.
The meaning is that these beings, from those dwelling in the *bhavana* heavens up to the realm of Īśāna, because their karma is defiled, experience sexual pleasure with women just like humans.
Because the others have not yet been determined in their division according to pleasure, he says—in order to explain them—the following:
"The remaining [beings] have sexual intercourse through touch, form, sound, and mind.
The term "remainder" (*śeṣa*) is used for the purpose of including those not previously mentioned.
Who, then, are those remaining from what was already stated? They are the inhabitants of the *kalpas*.

"Contact, form, sound, and mind"—that is, contact, form, sound, and mind; those who have sexual enjoyment (*pravīcāra*) with respect to these are called "those whose sexual enjoyment consists of contact, form, sound, and mind."
How is the connection [to be understood]? It is by way of not contradicting the teachings of the sages (ārṣa).
But why is the term "sexual enjoyment" (pravīcāra) included? It is for the sake of conveying what is intended.

What, then, is the intended connection? That which does not contradict the teachings of the sages: the gods of the Sānatkumāra and Māhendra realms experience supreme delight from the mere touch of the bodies of the celestial maidens, and the goddesses do likewise.

In the Brahma, Brahmostara, Lāntava, and Kāpiṣṭha heavens, the gods obtain supreme bliss merely by beholding the divine women’s charming attire and forms, which are so skillful in their amorous gestures and playful grace.

In the Śukra, Mahāśukra, Śatāra, and Sahasrāra heavens, the gods attain the highest delight merely by hearing the sweet music, gentle laughter, elegant speech, and the tinkling of the ornaments of the celestial damsels.
In the Ānata, Prāṇata, Āraṇa, and Acyuta kalpas, the gods obtain supreme happiness merely through the mental intention of their own consorts.
Now, when it is asked what kind of happiness belongs to those in the higher realms, he says— in order to determine that— “In the higher [realms], there is no sexual intercourse.”
The mention of "supreme" (*para*) is for the purpose of including all others without exception;
the mention of "without sexual intercourse" (*apravīcāra*) is for the purpose of understanding the highest bliss.
For sexual intercourse is the remedy for sensation;
in its absence, they experience supreme and uninterrupted bliss.
Regarding those gods of the first category who were said to be of ten types, this is stated for the purpose of making known their general and specific designations:
the Bhavanavāsins consist of the Asura-kumāras, Naga-kumāras, Vidyut-kumāras, Suparṇa-kumāras, Agni-kumāras, Vāta-kumāras, Stanita-kumāras, Udadhi-kumāras, Dvīpa-kumāras, and Dik-kumāras.
Those whose nature is to dwell in palaces (*bhavana*) are called "Palace-Dwellers" (*bhavanavāsin*).
This is the general designation for this primary class.

The specific designations such as "Asuras" and so forth refer to those whose activities are brought about by the arising of particular names and karma. Although all gods possess a fixed age and nature, because their dress, ornaments, weapons, vehicles, mounts, and play appear like those of youths, the term "Kumāras" (Youths) has become conventionally established for the Palace-Dwellers.
Each of these categories is completed [by its respective group], beginning with the *asura-kumāras*.
If one asks, "Where are their abodes?
it is said: the abodes of the *asura-kumāras* are in the portion of the *Ratnaprabhā* hell that consists largely of mud.
Excluding one thousand yojanas each from the top and bottom of the hard earth portion, the remaining space is the abode of the nine Kumāras.
To determine the general and specific designations of the second group, he says:
The *vyantara*s— namely, the *kiṃnara*s, *kiṃpuruṣa*s, *mahoraga*s, *gandharva*s, *yakṣa*s, *rākṣasa*s, *bhūta*s, and *piśāca*s—
are so called because they dwell in various different regions; this is a general designation for all eight classes that is etymologically appropriate.
It should be understood that there are eight classes of these *vyantara* beings, beginning with the *kiṃnara*s, which are produced by specific manifestations of the karma of name.
If one asks where their dwellings are located, it is said:
beyond innumerable continents and oceans from this Jambūdvīpa, in the upper portion of the hard earth, lie the dwellings of the seven types of *vyantara*s.
In the portion of the Rākṣasas abounding in mud.
To proclaim the general and specific designations of the third category, he says:
The luminaries consist of the sun and moon, the planets, the constellations, and the scattered stars.
Because these five possess the nature of light (*jyotis*), the general designation "luminaries" (*jyotiṣka*) is etymologically appropriate for all of them.
The sun and so forth are specific designations [for bodies] conditioned by the arising of name-karma (*nāmakarma*).
The separate mention of "the sun and the moon" is for the purpose of indicating their preeminence. What constitutes this preeminence? It is produced by their power and other such qualities.
Where, then, are their dwellings? To this it is said: rising upward from this level ground by seven hundred and ninety *yojanas*, the stars move, stationed below all the luminaries.
Rising ten *yojanas* from there, the sun moves.
Rising eighty *yojanas* from there, the moons revolve.
Then, rising four yojanas, are the lunar mansions (nakṣatras). Then, rising four yojanas, are Mercury (budha).
Then, rising three yojanas, are Venus (śukra).
Then, having ascended three yojanas, are the planets of Bṛhaspati;
then, having ascended three yojanas, are the Aṅgārakas;
then, having ascended three yojanas, the Śanaiścara planets move.

This very realm of light, the sphere of the celestial bodies, is the space of the sky; it is one hundred and ten yojanas in thickness, and its horizontal extent is equal to the measure of the continents and oceans, reaching as far as the Ghanodadhi ocean.
And it has been said:
"Nine hundred and seventy, ten, eight, four, two, four, and four."
The stars, the sun, the moon, and the constellations; Budha, Bhārgava, Guru, Aṅgiras, Rāhu, and Śanaiścara;
nine hundred and twenty-eight; ten, zero, four, two, three, and four; the stars, the sun, the moon, and the constellations; Budha, Bhārgava, Guru, Aṅgiras, Rāhu, and Śanaiścara.
To explain the specific manner of movement of the luminous bodies (jyotiṣka), he says: "In the world of men, they possess constant motion while circumambulating Meru."

*Meroḥ pradakṣiṇā* means circumambulating Meru. The expression “circumambulating Meru” is intended to clarify the specific manner of movement, so that it might not be understood as a movement in the opposite direction.
The qualification "always moving" (*nityagatayaḥ*) is for the purpose of demonstrating that their activity is uninterrupted.
The mention of "the world of men" (*nṛloka*) is for the purpose of specifying the scope;
the luminous bodies (*jyotiṣkāḥ*) move constantly within two and a half continents and in two oceans, and not elsewhere.
If it is argued that because there is no cause for motion, the celestial palaces (*vimāna*) of the Jyotiṣkas do not move, we say:
no, because this is unproven. Their movement occurs through the transformation of motion induced by gods who are intent on such activity, due to the diversity of the ripening of karma.
For their karma indeed ripens precisely by way of motion.
At a distance of one hundred and twenty-one yojanas from Meru, the luminous bodies (jyotiṣka) revolve around it clockwise.
Regarding the connection with the moving luminaries for the purpose of determining conventional time, he says:
The division of time is produced by that.
The inclusion of the word "that" (tat) is for the purpose of referring back to the luminaries possessing motion.
Time is not delimited by motion alone, nor even by celestial luminaries alone, because [the latter] are imperceptible and subject to revolution.
Time is of two kinds: conventional (*vyāvahārika*) and primary (*mukhya*).

Conventional time is the division of time and its subdivisions—such as *samaya*, *avalikā*, and so forth—which are determined by specific actions; it serves as the means of delimiting that which is otherwise undelimited.
The primary [fire] is the other one, whose characteristics will be explained.
In order to demonstrate the location of the luminaries elsewhere, he says:
Those situated outside are called "external."
From where is it "outside"? From the world of humans (nṛloka).
How is this understood? A change of grammatical case occurs by virtue of the sense of the meaning.
But surely, since the term "constant motion" (nityagati) is used for the world of humans, the stationary nature of the luminaries elsewhere is established.
Therefore, the statement "they are situated outside" is meaningless.
That is not so; for what reason? Because the existence and the location of the luminaries elsewhere than in the world of men are not established.
Therefore, in order to establish both of these, it is said that they are "situated outside."
The Sūtra has been commenced for the purpose of turning back from a perverted course and for the purpose of turning back from an occasional course.
To proclaim the general designation of the fourth group, he says:
Regarding the term *vaimānika*:
the inclusion of the word “vaimānika” is for the purpose of indicating the scope of the subject matter.
From this point forward, an introductory heading is established so that there may be a clear understanding of those who will be described as "residing in celestial palaces" (*vaimānika*).
They are called *vimānas* because they honor those of good deeds who dwell within them in a distinguished manner. Those who exist in these *vimānas* are the *vaimānikas*.

Those celestial palaces (*vimāna*) are of three kinds, distinguished as the central (*indraka*), the linear (*śreṇī*), and the scattered (*puṣpaprakīrṇaka*). Among them, the central celestial palaces are situated in the middle like Indra himself. Because they are situated in the four directions like rows of points in space, they are called linear celestial palaces (*śreṇivimāna*).
Because they are situated like flowers scattered in the intermediate directions, they are called "scattered flowers" (*puṣpaprakīrṇaka*).
To explain the distinctions among those celestial beings (*vaimānika*), he says:
Those born in the aeons and those beyond the aeons.
"Born in the aeons" means born within the aeons; "beyond the aeons" means those who have transcended the aeons. Thus, the gods of the celestial palaces (vaimānika) are of two kinds.
In order to ascertain the specific distinctions of their states, he says:
"higher and higher."
For what purpose is this stated?
It is stated for the purpose of negating a horizontal state of existence.
They are not situated horizontally like the Jyotiṣkas,
nor are they irregularly situated like the Vyantaras; rather,
they are said to be "one above the other."
Which ones? The eons (*kalpa*). If this is so, in how many celestial palaces (*vimāna*) of the eons do those gods reside? To this he says:

In the [heavens] of Saudharma, Aiśāna, Sānatkumāra, Māhendra, Brahma, Brahmapurohita (Brahmottara), Lāntava, Kāpiṣṭha, Śukra, Mahāśukra, Śatāra, Sahasrāra, Ānata and Prāṇata, Āraṇa and Acyuta, in the nine Graiveyakas, in Vijaya, Vaijayanta, Jayanta, Aparājita, and Sarvārthasiddhi—

how is it that these terms beginning with "Saudharma" denote the *kalpas*? They denote the *kalpa* either by means of the secondary suffix *-aṇ* in the sense of "belonging to" (*cāturarthika*), or by their own inherent nature (*svabhāvataḥ*).
Now, how is the designation "Indra" [applied]? Is it by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) or by way of association (*sāhacarya*)?
If one asks how that is so, it is said: there is a hall named Sudharmā; because that exists in this [heaven], it is the Saudharma Kalpa.
Because that [name] exists in this, the suffix *aṇ* is applied.
By association with that eon (*kalpa*), Indra is also called Saudharma.
There is an Indra named Īśāna by nature;
the eon that is the dwelling place of Īśāna is the Aiśāna [eonic period].
The suffix *aṇ* is applied because he is his abode;
by association with him, Indra also is called Aiśāna.
There is an Indra named Sanatkumāra who is so by nature.
The suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "his residence," resulting in *sāṃnakumāraḥ*, meaning the *kalpa*.
By association with that [kalpa], Indra is also called *sāṃnakumāraḥ*.
Mahendra is Indra by nature;
his abode is the realm called Māhendra,
and because of this association, Indra is also called Māhendra.
The same should be applied to what follows as well.

Since the systematic arrangement is established with reference to the scriptures (*āgama*), one should understand that by the phrase "higher and higher" (*upary upari*), there is a connection between each pair [of heavens].

First are the *Saudharma* and *Īśāna* kalpas; above those two are the *Sānatkumāra* and *Māhendra*; above those two are the *Brahmaloka* and *Brahmottara*; above those two are the *Lāntava* and *Kāpiṣṭha*; above those two are the *Śukra* and *Mahāśukra*; above those two are the *Śatāra* and *Sahasrāra*; above those two are the *Ānata* and *Prāṇata*; and above those two are the *Āraṇa* and *Acyuta*.
Below and above, the connection with Indra should be understood to apply individually;
however, in the middle, it applies to each pair.
There are four Indras for the four [heavens] of Saudharma, Aiśāna, Sānatkumāra, and Māhendra.

In the Brahma-world and the Brahmottara realm, there is one [deity] named Brahmā. In the Lāntava and Kāpiṣṭha realms, there is one known as Lāntava. In the Śukra and Mahāśukra realms, there is one designated as Śukra.
Of the two [heavens], Śatāra and Sahasrāra, there is one named Śatāra.
Of the four—heavenly realms of Ānata, Prāṇata, Āraṇa, and Acyuta—there are four [Indras].
Thus, there are twelve Indras among those who dwell in the Kalpas.
In Jambūdvīpa, Mount Mahāmandara has a depth of one thousand yojanas and a height of ninety-nine thousand yojanas.
Below it lies the lower world (adholoka).
The transverse world (tiryagloka) extends horizontally with a thickness equal to that [of the mountain].
Above that is the upper world.
The crest of Mount Meru is forty *yojanas* in height.
Atop it, at a distance of no more than the length of a hair, stands the straight celestial palace (*ṛjuvimāna*), the central hall of the Saudharma [heaven].
Everything else is to be understood from the corresponding sections on the worlds (*loka*).

As for the separate mention of the word "nine" in the phrase "in the nine *graiveyaka*s," what is its purpose? It is for the sake of making known that there are also other nine palaces designated as the *anudiśas*. Therefore, it should be understood that this includes the *anudiśas* as well.
To explain the distinctions among these aforementioned inhabitants of the celestial palaces (vaimānika) relative to one another, it is said:
they are superior in terms of lifespan, power, pleasure, radiance, purity of complexion (leśyā), the faculties (indriya), and the range of their clairvoyant perception (avadhi).
*Sthiti* (duration) is the continued existence of the body together with that [particular] birth due to the arising of the life-span one has acquired.
*Prabhāva* (power) is the capacity for cursing and bestowing grace.
Happiness (*sukha*) is the experience of the objects of the senses.
Splendor (*dyuti*) is the radiance of the body, clothing, ornaments, and so forth;
this is what is called *leśyā*.

"Purity of the *leśyās* (lesyāviśuddhiḥ)" means the purification of the *leśyās*. "The range of the senses and of limited clairvoyance" (*indriyāvadhiviṣayaḥ*) refers to the objects of the senses and of limited clairvoyance.
The suffix *-tasi* is used in the sense of "superior to those" or "by means of those."
The meaning is that, higher and higher, in each successive eon and each successive tier, the gods of the celestial palaces (*vaimānika*) are superior in terms of their lifespan and other qualities.

To prevent the over-extension [of this principle]— namely, that just as they are superior higher and higher in terms of lifespan and so forth, they must likewise be superior in terms of their destiny (*gati*) and other factors— he says:
They are devoid of movement, body, grasping, and conceit.
Movement is the cause for reaching one place from another.
The transformational body has been described.
Attachment to sense objects arising from the emergence of the passion of greed is possession (*parigraha*).
Arrogance (*abhimāna*) is the egoism produced from the passion of pride.
By these [factors] such as movement and so forth, they are progressively inferior.
Because they lack the excellence of traveling to other regions, sporting, and sensual delight, their movement becomes increasingly inferior.
The body of the gods of the Saudharma and Aiśāna realms measures seven *aratnis* in height.
In the realms of Sānatkumāra and Māhendra, the measure is six cubits.
In the realms of Brahmaloka, Brahmottara, Lāntava, and Kāpiṣṭha, the measure is five cubits. In the realms of Śukra, Mahāśukra, Śatāra, and Sahasrāra, the measure is four cubits.
In Ānata and Prāṇata, the measure is three and a half cubits;
in Āraṇa and Acyuta, it is three cubits;
and in the lower Graiveyakas, it is two and a half cubits.
In the middle *graiveyaka* heavens, the measure is two *aratnis*;
in the upper *graiveyaka* heavens and in the *anudiśa* palaces, the measure is one and a half *aratnis*;
and in the *anuttara* heavens, the measure is one *aratni*.
Furthermore, their possessions, such as celestial palaces and furnishings, become progressively inferior;
and their pride becomes progressively diminished due to the attenuation of their afflictions.

Previously, the rule regarding the *leśyās* (psychic colors) of the gods in the three classes was stated. Now, in order to establish the rule for the *leśyās* among the inhabitants of the celestial palaces (*vaimānika*), he says:
"The yellow, pink, and white *leśyās* belong to those in the second, third, and remaining [classes]."
Yellow, lotus-colored, and white— these are "yellow-lotus-white.
Those whose *leśyās* (affective dispositions) are yellow, lotus-colored, and white are "those with yellow-lotus-white *leśyās*."
How is there shortness?
It belongs to the latter member of the compound.
For example, regarding the rule for the addition of *t* (taparakaraṇa) in the case of a rapid [utterance], there is an extension of the rule to include the medium and slow [utterances].
Alternatively, "yellow," "lotus-colored" (pink), and "white" refer to objects possessing those colors.
Those whose *leśyās* are like those [objects] are called yellow-lotus-white-*leśya*s.
In that regard, which [being] has which *leśyā*?
To this it is replied: In the Saudharma and Aiśāna [heavens], there is yellow leśyā.
In the Sānatkumāra and Māhendra [heavens], there is yellow-pale yellow leśyā.
In the Brahma-loka, Brahmanottara, Lāntava, and Kāpiṣṭha [heavens], there is pale yellow leśyā.
In Śukra, Mahāśukra, Śatāra, and Sahasrāra, there is white radiance (padma-śukla-leśyā).
In Ānata and the other [heavens], there is white radiance (śukla-leśyā).
Even there, in the higher Anudiśas, there is supreme white radiance (parama-śukla-leśyā).
How is it that there is a mention of "mixed" when it is not explicitly stated in the Sūtra? It is by virtue of association (*sāhacarya*), as in common worldly usage.
For example, in the expression "the umbrella-bearers are going," the term "umbrella-bearer" is applied even to those who do not possess umbrellas.
Likewise here, there is the mention of one of two things that are mixed together.
If it is asked how this meaning is understood from the Sūtra, it is said:

the connection is made as follows: in the two pairs of kalpas [starting from Saudharma], there is yellow-leśyā (pītaleśyā); this is because lotus-leśyā (padmaleśyā) is not intended to be mentioned in the case of Sānatkumāra and Māhendra.
In the three pairs of kalpas beginning with Brahma-loka, there is lotus-leśyā; this is because white-leśyā (śuklaleśyā) is not intended to be mentioned in the case of Śukra and Mahāśukra.
In the remaining cases, such as those with one hundred spokes and so forth, there is white leśyā; since pink leśyā is not intended to be mentioned here, there is no fault. § 486.
It was said that they are "born in the aeons" (*kalpa*); however, it is not known there what those aeons are. To this it is replied:
the aeons [extend] prior to the *Āraṇeyaka* heavens.
It is not known from what point these "aeons" (kalpa) begin; therefore, the mention of "Saudharma and so forth" continues [from the previous context].
By this, the following meaning is obtained: those beginning with Saudharma and ending before the Graiveyakas are "aeons" (kalpa);
by process of elimination, the others are "beyond the aeons" (kalpātīta).
Where are the *laukāntika* gods, who belong to the celestial palaces (*vaimānika*), included? They are included among those born in the [heavenly] eons (*kalpa*).
If it is asked how so, it is said:
The *laukāntikas* have the Brahma-world as their abode (*ālaya*).
An "abode" (*ālaya*) is a dwelling (*āvāsa*), so called because they come to it and dissolve (*līyante*) therein.
Those for whom the Brahma-world is their abode are to be understood as the *laukāntika* gods, whose abode is the Brahma-world.
If this were so, it would follow that all gods whose abode is the Brahma-world are *laukāntika*.
There is no fault here, because the name is taken according to its literal meaning (*anvarthasaṃjñā*).
The world of Brahmā is *loka*; its end is *lokānta*. Those who exist therein are the *Lokāntikas*; thus, not all [deities] are included.
For their celestial palaces (*vimāna*) are situated at the boundaries of the Brahmā-world.
Alternatively, the world is *saṃsāra*, which is strewn with birth, old age, and death; its end is *lokānta*.
Those who exist at the edge of the world are the *laukāntikas*.
They have all reached the limit of saṃsāra; having passed away from there, they will attain parinirvāṇa after undergoing only one more birth in a womb.
To show the distinctions among those who have been taught in general, he says:
"The Sārasvatas, Ādityas, Vahnis, Aruṇas, Gardatoyas, Tuṣitas, Avyābādhās, and Ariṣṭas.

Where are these [deities] such as Sārasvata and the others? These groups of deities, beginning with Sārasvata, are to be known as residing respectively in all eight directions, starting from the northeast and proceeding clockwise.

Namely: the celestial palace of Sārasvata is in the northeast; the celestial palace of Āditya is in the eastern direction; the celestial palace of Vahni is in the southeast; the celestial palace of Aruṇa is in the southern direction; the celestial palace of Gardatoya is in the southwest; the celestial palace of Tuṣita is in the western direction; the celestial palace of Avyābādha is in the northwest; and the celestial palace of Ariṣṭa is in the northern direction.
By the word "and" (*ca*), two groups of gods are included among them. Namely: between Sārasvata and Āditya are Agnyābha and Sūryābha;
and between Āditya and Vahni are Candrābha and Satyābha.

Between Vahni and Aruṇa dwell those who bring about welfare and security; between Aruṇa and Gardatoya dwell those who move at will like bulls and bricks. Between Gardatoya and Tuṣita dwell those protected by Nirmāṇaraja and the guardians of the intermediate directions.
Between Tuṣita and Avyābādha dwell those protected by themselves and those protected by all.
Between Avyābādha and Ariṣṭa dwell the Maruts and Vasus;
between Ariṣṭa and Sārasvata dwell the Aśvis and Viśvadevas.

All these are independent, as they lack deficiency or excess; being devoid of attachment to sense-objects, they are divine sages (devarṣis), worthy of worship by other gods, and should be understood as possessing the fourteen *pūrvas* and being intent on awakening the Tīrthaṅkaras at their renunciation.
He said: It has been stated that those who are *laukāntika* gods, having passed away from there and entered into one womb-dwelling (*garbhavāsa*), will attain parinirvāṇa.
Is such a division regarding the time of attaining nirvāṇa found for others as well?
Therefore, he says:
"In [the cases of] Vijayā and the others, they are the two penultimate [syllables].

The word "ādi" (and so forth) functions in the sense of "type" or "kind"; by this, the inclusion of the desired celestial palaces (*vimāna*)—namely Vijaya, Vaijayanta, Jayanta, Aparājita, Anudiśa, and Vimāna—is established.
What, then, is the common type here?
It is the state of being an *ahamindra* (self-sovereign) accompanied by birth with right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*).

If it is argued that this would entail the attainment of all goals [for all beings], we say no; for they are supremely distinguished, and their status as "last" is established by the literal meaning of their designation.
This "lastness" of the body is in relation to the human existence.

Those who have two final bodies are called *dvicarama*. Having fallen from the [heavens] such as Vijaya while their right view (*samyaktva*) remains unimpaired, they are born among humans, practice self-restraint (*saṃyama*), and are then born again in the Vijaya heavens and so forth. Falling from there, they attain human existence once more and achieve liberation; thus they possess the state of having two final bodies. § 494.

He asks: regarding the soul's (*jīva*) states arising from the operation of karma (*audayika*), it was stated that "the state of birth as an animal (*tiryagyonigati*) is one arising from the operation of karma," and furthermore, in the section on duration (*sthiti*), it says "and of those born as animals.
In this regard, it is not known what constitutes "animal births" (*tiryagyonayaḥ*). To this, it is said:
Excluding humans who are born spontaneously, the remaining [beings] belong to the animal realm.
Those who are born spontaneously have already been mentioned: namely, gods and hell-beings.
And humans have been specified [in the rule]: "Humans are those prior to the Mānuṣottara mountain.
Other transmigrating souls besides these are to be understood as the remaining animal births (*tiryag-yoni*).
Should the spatial division of those animals not be specified again, as it was for the gods and others? No spatial division has been stated for them because they pervade the entire world.
He said: "The duration of life for hell-beings, humans, and animals has been stated; that of the gods has not been stated."
Regarding that which is to be explained, in order to establish the lifespan of those first mentioned who dwell in the palaces, he says:
"The lifespan of the Asuras, Nāgas, Suparṇas, Dvīpas, and the rest is measured by one *sāgara*, three *palyopamas*, and half a *palyopama* less [one].
The connection here should be understood respectively with the ocean, heat, and so forth for the asuras and the others.
This duration is the maximum; the minimum will also be explained later.
For example, the lifespan of the asuras is one *sāgaropama*.
The lifespan of the nāgas is three *palyopamas*; that of the *suparṇas* is two and a half;
and that of the island-dwellers is two.
The remaining six [classes] have a lifespan of one and a half *palyopamas*.

Immediately after the description of the lifespans of the first class of gods, it would have been the turn to state the lifespans of the *vyantara* and *jyotiṣka* gods; however, bypassing that, the lifespan of the *vaimānika* gods is now stated.
Why? Because their duration will be stated later by means of a concise method.
And in order to establish the duration for those two kalpas mentioned at the beginning, he says:
"In the realms of Saudharma and Aiśāna, [the lifespan] is one *sāgaropama* and more."
Because of the dual-number indication in the term ‘sāgaropame’, there is a dual state [of the subject]. The word ‘adhike’ (in the case of an excess) serves as a governing heading.
From where [does this extend]? Up to the Sahasrāra heaven. But how is this known? From the inclusion of the word "but" (tu) later on.
Therefore, one should understand that for the gods of the Saudharma and Aiśāna heavens, the lifespan is two sāgaropamas plus a little more.
To explain the specific stability and attainment of the two higher [heavens], he says:
there are seven [kalpas] for Sānatkumāra and Māhendra.
In these two kalpas, the maximum lifespan of the gods is slightly more than seven *sāgara* units.
In order to explain the specific distinctions in the states of existence from the Brahma-worlds up to the Unshakable (acyuta) realm, he says:
"But [the lifespans] are increased by three, seven, nine, eleven, thirteen, and fifteen [kalpas].
The term "seven" is the subject under discussion. It should be understood that this [number] is here connected with the numbers three and so forth,
such as "seven increased by three," "seven increased by seven," and so on.
The connection should be understood as being between each pair [of items].
The word "but" (*tu*) serves to specify.

What does it specify? It specifies that the word "additional" (*adhika*), which is carried over [from the previous context], is connected with the first four [items] and not with the latter two; this is the meaning specified.

Therefore, this is the meaning: in the Brahmakāyika and Brahmapurohita heavens, the lifespans are ten *sāgaropamas* plus a fraction more. In the Lāntava and Kāpiṣṭha heavens, they are fourteen *sāgaropamas* plus a fraction more.
In the Śukra and Mahāśukra heavens, they are sixteen *sāgaropamas* plus a fraction more.
For the Śatāra and Sahasrāra heavens, the lifespan is slightly more than eighteen sāgaropamas.
For the Ānata and Prāṇata heavens, it is twenty sāgaropamas.
For the Āraṇa and Acyuta heavens, it is twenty-two sāgaropamas.

Thereafter, for the purpose of explaining the distinctions in their duration of stay, he says: "Above Āraṇācyuta, by means of each [successive stage], one reaches the nine *graiveyaka* heavens, beginning with Vijaya, and finally Sarvārthasiddha."
The term "additional" (*adhika*) is understood to carry over.
Therefore, it should be understood as being connected here [with the following].
"Each one is greater by one.
For what purpose is the mention of "nine"? It is for the sake of making known that each [level] is greater by one individually;
otherwise, there would be only one additional [unit] in the neck-ornaments (graiveyaka).
In the phrase "in Vijayā and the others," because the word "ādi" (and so forth) has the sense of "type," the Anudiśas are also included.
However, the separate mention of Sarvārthasiddhi is for the purpose of demonstrating the absence of anything lower than it.
Therefore, the meaning is as follows: in the first of the lower Graiveyakas there are twenty-three [yojanas], in the second twenty-four, and in the third twenty-five.
In the middle *graiveyaka* heavens, there are twenty-six in the first, twenty-seven in the second, and twenty-eight in the third.
In the upper *graiveyaka* heavens, there are twenty-nine in the first, thirty in the second, and thirty-one in the third.
In the *anudiśa* palaces, there are thirty-two.
In the [heavens] beginning with Vijaya, the maximum lifespan is thirty-three *sāgaropamas*.
In Sarvārthasiddha, it is likewise exactly thirty-three.
In order to establish the minimum lifespan among the gods whose maximum lifespans have been specified, he says:
"The other is more than a *palyopama*.
(Section 507)
The *palyopama* has been explained. The other, the minimum duration, is slightly more than a *palyopama*.
Of whom? Of those belonging to the Saudharma and Aiśāna [heavens].
How is this known? Because it will be stated later on that "each subsequent [level is twice as high] than the preceding one.
Thereafter, for the purpose of establishing the minimum duration [of existence], he says:
"From each subsequent [level], the preceding one is immediately adjacent.
"In another place" means "beyond. There is reduplication due to distributive repetition (*vīpsā*),
which applies to the word "prior" (*pūrva*) as well.
The term “additional” (*adhika*) is carried over [from the previous context].

By means of that, the connection is made as follows: two *sāgaropamas* plus an addition are stated for the Saudharma and Aiśāna heavens; those same additions constitute the minimum lifespan in the Sānatkumāra and Māhendra heavens.

The maximum lifespan in the Sānatkumāra and Māhendra heavens is seven *sāgaropamas* plus an addition; those same additions constitute the minimum lifespan in the Brahma and Brahmapurohita heavens, and so forth.
The maximum lifespan of the hell-beings has been stated.
Desiring to demonstrate the minimum lifespan—which was not mentioned in the Sūtra and is not the current subject—by means of a concise method, he says:
Regarding the phrase "and for those in the hells" in the second [verse] and so forth:
what is the purpose of the word "and" (*ca*)? It serves to include the subject under discussion.
Furthermore, what is the subject under discussion? It is that "each subsequent state of existence is respectively shorter than the preceding one.
From this, the following meaning is obtained: the maximum lifespan of the hell-beings in Ratnaprabhā is one sāgaropama;
that same duration is the minimum in Śarkarāprabhā.
In Śarkarāprabhā, the maximum duration is three sāgaropamas; in Vālukāprabhā, that same duration is the minimum, and so forth. § 512.
Thus, the minimum duration has been stated for the second [heaven] and those following.
To demonstrate what the minimum is for the first [heaven], he says:
"Ten thousand years in the first."
"The minimum life span" continues [to apply here]. In the Ratnaprabhā hell, the minimum life span should be known to be ten thousand years.
Now, as to what the minimum lifespan is for those dwelling in the celestial palaces (bhavana), he says: "And in the palaces..."
What is the purpose of the word “and” (*ca*)? It serves to include what has been previously mentioned.
By it, the other lifespan of the inhabitants of the *bhavana* realms—ten thousand years—is connected [to the context].
What, then, is the minimum lifespan for the *vyantara* gods? To this he says:
"And for the *vyantaras*..."
The word "ca" (and) has the sense of a conjunction with the subject under discussion;
by it, it is understood that the other lifespan of the Vyantara deities is ten thousand years.
Now, as to what their maximum duration is, it is said here:
the maximum is more than a *palyopama*.
The supreme, highest duration of the Vyantara beings is one *palyopama* plus more.
Now, the maximum lifespan of the celestial beings (jyotiṣka) must be stated; therefore, he says: "And of the celestial beings...
The word "ca" (and) has the sense of a conjunction with the subject under discussion.
By it, the connection is as follows:
the maximum lifespan of the Jyotiṣkas is one *palyopama* plus [an additional unit].
Now, as to how much the other [light] is, he says:
"The other is one-eighth of that."
One-eighth of that *palyopama* is the other [lesser] lifespan of the celestial beings of light (*jyotiṣka*); such is the meaning.
Now, although the specific [deities] among the Laukāntikas have been mentioned, their specific duration of stay has not been stated.
To the question of how long that is, it is said here:
for all the Laukāntikas, it is eight sāgaropamas.
They are all alike, possessing white *leśyā* and bodies five cubits in height.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the *Tattvārthavṛtti*, known as the *Sarvārthasiddhi*. 4.
Now begins the fifth chapter.
Now, among the categories beginning with the soul (jīva), which were introduced as the objects of right vision (samyagdarśana), the category of the soul has been explained.

Now, this is stated for the purpose of enumerating the different designations of the category of non-living entities (ajīva) that have been introduced for investigation: "The non-living bodies are dharma, adharma, space, and matter.
The word *kāya* is etymologically derived in the sense of "body. Here, it is applied through metaphorical extension (*upacāra*).

Why is there this metaphorical extension? Just as the body consists of an accumulation of the substance of the person (*pudgala-dravya*), so too, with respect to the accumulation of spatial parts (*pradeśa-pracaya*), the [atoms] within the *dharmas* and other categories are called "bodies" (*kāya*) because they are like bodies.
"Non-sentient" (*ajīva*) and "bodies" (*kāya*) constitute "non-sentient bodies" (*ajīvakāya*); this is a compound formed by a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) with the qualified (*viśeṣya*).

Now, one might object: while the relationship between qualifier and qualified occurs in cases such as "blue lotus," where there is a possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), here too there is a connection involving deviation.
The term *ajīva* (non-soul) also applies to *akāya* (non-body) and *kāla* (time), while *kāya* (body) also applies to *jīva* (soul).
For what purpose is the word *kāya* used? It is for the purpose of making known the multiplicity of spatial points (*pradeśa*).
That is to say, the spatial points of *dharma* and the other [categories] are numerous.

But is it not the case that the multiplicity of space-points (*pradeśa*) is already indicated by the statement, "The space-points of *dharma*, *adharma*, and each individual soul (*jīva*) are innumerable" (*asaṃkhyeyāḥ pradeśā dharmādharmaikajīvānām*)?
True, this is so;
however, under this rule, that specific determination is understood: that the space-points are innumerable—neither numerable (*saṃkhyeya*) nor infinite (*ananta*).
Furthermore, the term "body" (*kāya*) is used here in order to make known that time lacks an accumulation of spatial parts (*pradeśapracaya*).
Time will be discussed later;
the term "body" is used here for the purpose of negating its possession of spatial parts.

Just as an atom (*aṇu*) is "without parts" (*apradeśa*) because, having only a single spatial dimension, it possesses no second or subsequent parts, so too the atom of time (*kālaparamāṇu*) is without parts because it consists of a single part.

For those [substances] such as *dharma* and the rest, the general designation "non-living" (*ajīva*) is applied by way of the absence of the characteristics of a living being (*jīva*). The specific designations—“*dharma*, *adharma*, *ākāśa*, and *pudgala*”—are conventional (*sāmayikyaḥ*).

Here it is asked: "In such passages as 'of the absolute [knowledge] regarding all substances and modes' (*sarvadravyaparyāyeṣu kevalasya*), substances have been mentioned; what are they? It is said: [they are] the substances (*dravyāṇi*).
They are called *dravyas* because they are themselves described (*drūyante*) or they flow (*dravanti*) by means of their respective synonyms.
If it is argued that something is a *dravya* because of its connection with the universal *dravyatva* (substanceness), [we reply:]...
No; because both [premises] are unestablished.
Just as there is a conjunction between a staff and a staff-bearer who are established separately, substance and substantiality are not established separately in that manner.

If conjunction were to occur even between things that are not established separately, then there would be a conjunction between a sky-flower and a person under discussion, or between a person and a second head.
Now, if separate establishment (*pṛthaksiddhi*) is admitted, the postulation of "substantiality" (*dravyatva*) is purposeless.

If it is argued that a substance (*dravya*) is a collection of qualities (*guṇasamudāya*), even in that case, since there is no distinction between the qualities and the collection, that designation [of "substance"] is not tenable.
And if a distinction is admitted, the very same fault as previously stated arises.

If it is objected that even in the analysis of the compound as "those which flow toward the qualities" (*guṇān dravanti*) or "those by which one is carried away through the qualities" (*guṇair vā drūyante*), the same fault remains, we say no. For since difference and non-difference can be established in some sense, the designation [of them as such] is proven.
There is non-difference because they are not perceived apart [from the substance], and there is difference because of the distinction in name, characteristic, purpose, and so forth.
Since the factors under discussion, such as the *dharma*s and others, are many, they are designated in the plural due to their grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with that [term].

It might be argued that, just as the number [of the preceding term] persists, the masculine gender would also persist. This is not a fault; for words whose gender is inherent (*āviṣṭaliṅga*) never deviate from their gender.
Therefore, *dharma* and the others are substances (*dravya*).
