Because there is no interval [between them], and since it would follow that only four [of these] could be designated as substantial entities (*dravya*), this is stated for the purpose of superimposition:
"And the living beings (*jīva*)."
The term ‘jīva’ has its meaning already explained.
The indication of plurality is for the purpose of understanding the various distinctions that have been explained.
The word “and” (ca) serves to draw in the designation of “substance,” meaning that souls are also substances.
Thus, these become six substances when taken together with the time that is about to be described.
Now, it will be stated that the definition of substance is: “A substance possesses qualities and modifications.”

Is it not the case that because they possess the characteristics of "tallness" (tallakṣaṇa), dharma and the others receive the designation of "substance" (dravya), and there is no need for an enumeration? [Response: The enumeration is for the purpose of restriction.
By means of it, the exclusion of earth and so forth as postulated by other proponents is accomplished.
How so? Earth, water, fire, air, and mind are included within the substance of the person (pudgaladravya); because they possess color, taste, odor, and tangibility.

If it is argued that there is an absence of the connection with color and so forth in air and mind, we say no: air, for its part, possesses color and so forth, because it possesses touch, like a jar and the like.

If it is argued that there is an absence of color and so forth because [air] is not graspable by the sense organs such as the eye, we say no: this would lead to the over-extension [of the argument] to atoms and the like.
Water possesses odor, because it possesses touch, like earth.
Fire also possesses taste and smell, because it possesses color, just like those [other elements].
The mind (*manas*) is also a twofold substance: the substantial mind (*dravyamana*) and the mental state (*bhāvamanas*).
Among these, the mental state is cognition; since it is a quality of the living being (*jīva*), it is included within the self (*ātman*).
And the mind (*manas*) is a substance because it is associated with form (*rūpa*) and other qualities; it is a modification of the substance *pudgala*.
The mind is like form and so forth; and because it is the instrument for the application of cognition (*jñānopayoga*), it is like the visual faculty (*cakṣurindriya*).

If it is argued that the reason is inconclusive (*vyabhicārī*) because even sound (*śabda*), though formless (*amūrta*), is seen to be an instrument for the application of cognition, we say no; for sound is composed of *pudgala* matter, and thus its possession of form is logically established.

If it is argued that, just as atoms possess color and other qualities because their effects are seen to possess color and other qualities, such an effect of color and so forth is not observed in the case of wind and the mind—[we reply: no, for that [possession of color] is possible even for them.
This is because it is accepted that all atoms are capable of being joined with the production of every effect possessing color and other qualities.
Furthermore, there are no atoms that are restricted to specific classes such as "earthy" and so forth, since we observe the commencement of production through the intermixture of classes.

The directions (*diś*) are also included within space (*ākāśa*), because the conventional usage of "this is here" and "that is there" is established with respect to rows of spatial points (*ākāśapradeśapaṅkti*) based on the rising of the sun and so forth.
Having stated [the categories], he says the following for the purpose of understanding the specific characteristics of the substances (*dravya*) mentioned:
The formless [realms] are eternally abiding;
"eternal" means constant and stable.
Because it has been established by the statement, “That which is eternal is [the substance]” (*ner dhruve tyaḥ*).

Substances such as *dharma* and the rest are eternal because they never perish, whether from the perspective of the substantial standpoint characterized by specific attributes—such as being the cause of motion—and from the perspective of the substantial standpoint characterized by general attributes—such as existence (*astitva*).
For it will be stated later: “Eternal is that which does not deviate from its own nature” (*tadbhāvāvyayaṃ nityam*).
They are established because their number is invariable.
Even all six substances, beginning with *dharma*, never exceed the number six;
therefore, they are said to be "established."
They are called "formless" (arūpa) because form does not exist in them; when form is negated, its concomitants—taste and so forth—are also negated.
Therefore, the meaning is that they are formless, that is, immaterial.
Just as the common characteristic "permanently abiding" applies to all substances, so too would formlessness apply to persons (*pudgala*); therefore, in order to refute that [misconception], he says:
"Persons possess form.
"Form" (rūpa) means "materiality" (mūrti).
What is materiality? Materiality is the transformation consisting of the configuration of form and so forth.
Those which possess this form are called "possessors of form" (rūpin).

The meaning is that they possess form. Alternatively, "form" (*rūpa*) is a term denoting a specific quality (*guṇaviśeṣa*); since these [elements] possess that, they are called "possessing form" (*rūpin*).

If it is argued that taste and so forth are not included [in the aggregates], we say no; they are included within them because they are inseparable from them. The plural number in the term “pudgalāḥ” (persons) is for the purpose of indicating their diversity.
For persons are indeed diverse, due to the distinction between the aggregates and the atoms.
The analysis of that [position] will be explained below.
If it were intended that [the cause] is formless and unitary like the *pradhāna*, there would be a contradiction with the observation of effects possessing manifold forms.
He asked: "Are phenomena (*dharma*) and so forth also distinct substances (*dravya*) for each one, just like the person (*pudgala*)? To this it is replied:
"Up to space (*ākāśa*), they are single substances."

The prefix *āṅ* here has the sense of inclusion (*abhividhi*). This was stated by following the sequence [of elements] given in the Sūtra; therefore, *dharma*, *adharma*, and space (*ākāśa*) are included.
The word "one" (*eka*) expresses number. By it, the substance is qualified: "one substance" is *ekadravya*.
If this is so, is the plural form not improper? The establishment of plurality occurs in relation to [other] factors such as qualities (*dharma*).

[Objection: Since a single [substance] possesses the capacity to convey multiple meanings, let it be called "each one" (*ekaika*) for the sake of brevity; thus, the mention of "substance" (*dravya*) would be redundant. [Response: True; nevertheless, the mention of "substance" is for the purpose of clarifying its unity in relation to substance itself. This is because, in view of field (*kṣetra*), state (*bhāva*), and so forth, the alternatives of being innumerable (*asaṃkhyeya*) or infinite (*ananta*) are accepted; therefore, unlike souls (*jīva*) and matter (*pudgala*), these do not possess plurality. This is what is clarified by this [mention of "substance"].
This is stated for the purpose of understanding the specific distinctions among those very substances that have already been introduced:
"and they are devoid of activity."
An occurrence (*paryāya*) arising through the power of both causes is action (*kriyā*), which is the cause for a substance’s reaching another location.
Those [occurrences] that have departed from it are "devoid of action" (*niṣkriyā*).
Here an objection is raised: if substances such as *dharma* and the rest are devoid of action (*niṣkriya*), then their production would not occur.
For the production of things such as a jar is observed to be preceded by action;
and in the absence of production, there is also an absence of destruction.
Therefore, [it might be argued that] there is a contradiction in postulating the triad of arising and so forth for all substances.
That is not so; why? Because it is possible otherwise.
Even in the absence of arising caused by action (*kriyā*), another kind of arising is postulated for these factors (*dharma*) and so on.
That is to say—origination is twofold: that which has its own cause (*svanimitta*) and that which depends on external conditions (*parapratyaya*).

First, regarding that which has its own cause: since the infinite qualities of heaviness and lightness (*agurulaghuguṇa*) are accepted on the authority of scripture as functioning through increase and decrease occurring in sixfold stages, their origination and destruction proceed from their own nature.

As for that which depends on external conditions: because they are the causes of movement, stability, and immersion for horses and other things, they differ at every moment; thus, since the causality itself is different, origination and destruction are conventionally designated in dependence upon external conditions.

Now, if it is argued that if *dharma* and the other [substances] are inactive (*niṣkriya*), their status as causes for the movement and so forth of souls (*jīva*) and matter (*pudgala*) would not be tenable—since water and the like, which possess activity, are observed to be the causes for the movement of fish and other creatures—this is not a fault. For they serve as causes by providing power (*balādhāna*), just like the eye.
Just as the eye is the cause for the perception of form, yet this does not occur even for one whose mind is distracted.
Since it is accepted that the [three] subjects under discussion—dharma, adharma, and space—are inactive, it follows by implication that living beings (*jīva*) and matter (*pudgala*) possess activity.
If it is argued that time (*kāla*) also possesses activity, we say no; because it is not included among the subjects under discussion.
For this very reason, it is not treated together with these others.

Regarding the phrase "the bodies of non-living entities" (*ajīvakāyā*), by the mention of "body" (*kāya*), only the existence of spatial divisions (*pradeśa*) is established, but the specific number of those divisions is not determined. Therefore, in order to determine that, it is said:
"The spatial divisions of *dharma*, *adharma*, and each individual soul (*jīva*) are innumerable (*asaṃkhyeya*)."
Those that have passed beyond calculation are the incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*).
The incalculable is of three kinds: the inferior, the superior, and the neither-inferior-nor-superior.
In this context, the "innumerable" (asaṃkhyeya) that is neither minimal nor maximal is intended.
"Directions" (pradeśa) means those which are pointed out.
An atom (paramāṇu), whose characteristics will be described below, occupies a certain amount of space; that [space] is conventionally designated as a "direction" (pradeśa).
Dharma, adharma, and the soul (jīva) are uniform in having an innumerable number of spatial units (pradeśa).
Among these, dharma and adharma are inactive and remain pervading the entire space of the world (lokākāśa).

As for the soul, although it consists of an innumerable number of spatial units, because its nature is to contract and expand, it occupies as much space as the body—whether minute or large—that is produced by karma, remaining therein while pervading it.
But when there is a filling of the world, then eight central points of the soul (jīva) remain within the middle of the variegated vajra-layer beneath Mount Mandara;
the other points extend upwards, downwards, and across, pervading the entire space of the world (lokākāśa).
Now, as to how many spatial points (pradeśa) space has, he says:
"The spatial points of space are infinite.
Those for whom no end exists are "infinite" (ananta). What are they? They are the spatial points (pradeśa).
Of what? Of space (ākāśa).
As before, the conceptualization of spatial divisions for this [unmanifest karma] is also to be understood.
The measurement of the spatial divisions of formless entities has been explained.
Now, the measurement of the spatial units (*pradeśa*) of material *pudgala*s must be determined; therefore, he says:
"The *pudgala*s are both numerable and innumerable. (Section 545)
By the word "and" (*ca*), the term "infinite" (*ananta*) is drawn forward [from the previous rule].

For some substance (*pudgala-dravya*), such as a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth, there are numerable (*saṃkhyeya*) spatial units (*pradeśa*); for others, they are innumerable (*asaṃkhyeya*) or infinite (*ananta*).
If it is asked whether the addition of "infinitely infinite" (*anantānanta*) should also be included: [the answer is that it is not necessary].
No; because of the commonality of "the infinite.
It has been stated that there are three kinds of infinite magnitude: the limited-infinite (*parītānanta*), the joined-infinite (*yuktānanta*), and the infinite-of-the-infinite (*anantānanta*).
All of these are grasped through the commonality of being infinite.

It might be argued that there is a contradiction because the world consists of a non-countable number of spatial units (*pradeśa*), yet it serves as the locus for aggregates (*skandha*) composed of infinite and even infinitely-infinite units; therefore, there can be no infinity [of units]. This is not a fault, because of the possession of the power of subtle transformation and capacity for accommodation (*avagāhana*).

For atoms and other entities, having been transformed into a subtle state, abide—even within each single spatial unit of space—in infinitely infinite numbers. Furthermore, their power of accommodation remains unimpeded.
Therefore, the coexistence of infinitely infinite entities within even a single spatial unit is not contradictory.

Since the statement "of persons" (*pudgalānām*) is made without qualification, it would follow that even an atom (*paramāṇu*) possesses spatial parts; therefore, in order to refute that, he says: "not of an atom" (*nāṇoḥ*).

Regarding the atom (*aṇu*), the supplementary statement is: "it has no spatial divisions (*pradeśa*). If one asks why they do not exist, it is because it consists of nothing but spatial division itself.

Just as a single point of space (*ākāśapradeśa*) lacks internal distinctions of spatial division and is therefore without parts (*apradeśa*), so too the atom, being nothing more than a mere spatial division, lacks any distinction of spatial division.
Furthermore, because there is no [entity] of smaller dimension than that;
for there is nothing else smaller than an atom (*aṇu*) from which its parts could be distinguished.
In order to establish the substratum for these [entities] such as *dharma* and so forth, whose locations have been determined, this is stated:
"Their immersion is in the space of the world (*lokākāśa*).
The meaning is that the substances previously mentioned, such as *dharma* and the rest, have their subsistence (*avagāha*) within the world-space (*lokākāśa*) and not outside of it.
If *dharma* and the others have the world-space as their support, what is the support of space? Space has no other support;
space is self-sustained (*svapratiṣṭha*).
If space is self-supported, then the dharmas and so forth must likewise be self-supported.
If, on the other hand, another support is postulated for the dharmas and so forth, then another support must also be postulated for space.

If it is argued that this leads to the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), we reply: this is not a fault; for there exists no substance larger in dimension than space upon which space could be said to rest.
For that [space] is indeed infinite in every direction.
Furthermore, space is called the substratum of dharma and the other categories by virtue of the conventional method (*vyavahāra-naya*).
However, with respect to the mode of being as it is (*evambhūta-naya*), all substances are established only within themselves.
And so it has been said: "Where do you reside? "In the self.
The result to be accomplished here by the conceptualization of support and supported is simply this: that phenomena and the like do not exist outside of the world-space (*lokākāśa*).

But is it not the case that in the world the relationship of container and contained is observed between things existing at earlier and later times, as for example jujube fruits and so forth in a bowl? It is not so in the case where space is prior and phenomena and so forth exist at a later time; therefore, even from the perspective of the conventional method (*vyavahāranaya*), the conceptualization of container and contained is untenable. This is not a fault, for the relationship of container and contained is also observed among things that arise simultaneously, such as color and other qualities in a jar, or the hands and other limbs in a body.
It is called "the world" (*loka*).
What is the world? That in which substances such as merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) are perceived is the world.
The suffix *-ghañ* is used here in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa-sādhana*).

Space is divided into two kinds: the space of the world (lokākāśa) and the space beyond the world (alokākāśa). That which has been described as the "world" (loka) is where that [space] exists; that is the space of the world.
Beyond that, on all sides, is the infinite non-worldly space (*alokākāśa*).

The distinction between world and non-world is to be understood from the existence or non-existence of the substance of merit (*dharma-astikāya*) and demerit (*adharma-astikāya*). For if that substance of merit did not exist, there would be no distinction [between the two], because there would be no cause for the restriction of the movement of souls (*jīva*) and persons (*pudgala*).

Furthermore, if the category of non-existence (adharmāstikāya) did not exist, there would be an absence of stability due to the lack of a cause for the basis of stability, or else there would be no distinction between the inhabited world (loka) and the non-inhabited space (aloka).
Therefore, the establishment of the distinction between the inhabited world and the non-inhabited space depends upon the existence or non-existence of both.
In that regard, because there is the possibility of a distinction in the location of those [qualities] being delimited, he says— [for the sake of understanding their specific nature]—
"in the entire [space] of dharma and adharma" (sūtra §5.1).
The term "entire" (*kṛtsna*) is used for the purpose of demonstrating complete pervasion.
Just as one says "a jar is not situated in a house," so too there is no immersion (*avagāha*) of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) in the world-space (*lokākāśa*).
What then? It is like oil in sesame seeds; they occupy the entire [space].
The absence of obstruction due to the mutual entry of spatial points (pradeśa) is to be understood as resulting from the possession of the capacity for penetration (avagāhana-śakti).

Therefore, in order to demonstrate the specific distinctions in the penetration of material (mūrtimat) *pudgala*s—which possess spatial points that are non-spatial, numerable, innumerable, or infinite—he says:
The distribution of *pudgala*s across one space-point (*pradeśa*) and so forth is to be analyzed.
One space-point is called "one space-point" (*ekapradeśa*).
Those things of which a single spatial unit (*ekapradeśa*) is the first are "those beginning with a single spatial unit" (*ekapradeśādayaḥ*).
Within these, the subsistence (*avagāha*) of persons (*pudgala*) is to be analyzed—that is, it is to be considered as a possibility.
Since the analysis of the compound is by its constituent parts, the collective sense of the compound includes even a single spatial unit.

For example: the occupation of a single point of space by one atom; by two atoms, both when they are bound together and when they are not; and by three atoms, both when they are bound together and when they are not, occupying one, two, or three points respectively.

In this manner, the existence of aggregates (*skandha*) consisting of numerable, innumerable, and infinite space-points (*pradeśa*) within the space-points of a single numerable or innumerable portion of the world-space (*lokākāśa*) is to be understood.

Now, while it may indeed be logical for the formless *dharma* and *adharma* to coexist in one place without contradiction, how can this be so for material (*mūrtimat*) *pudgala*s? To this it is replied: because their nature is that of accommodation (*avagāhana*) and due to their subtle transformation (*sūkṣma-pariṇāma*), the accommodation of even material things is not contradictory, just as the light of many lamps can exist within a single room.
And it must be determined as such on the basis of the authority of scripture.
As it has been said:
Now, as to how the immersion of souls occurs, it is said here:
[it occurs] in the innumerable parts and so forth of the souls.
The term “in the world-space” (lokākāśe) is understood to carry over [from the previous context].
When that [world-space] is divided into innumerable parts, one such part is called an "innumerable part" (asaṃkhyeyabhāga).
Those for which this is the first are the "innumerable parts and so forth" (asaṃkhyeyabhāgādayaḥ).
The immersion of living beings (*jīva*) within them should be understood as follows: one living being resides in one *asaṃkhyeya* part [of space].
In this same manner, the immersion should be recognized as extending from two, three, four, and so forth, through *asaṃkhyeya* parts, up to the entire world.
As for various living beings (*jīva*), however, this applies to the entire world.

If one living being occupies one *asaṃkhyeya* part [of space], how can the infinite-infinite mass of living beings exist with their bodies within the space of the world (*lokākāśa*) in terms of the measure of substance? Their existence should be understood through the distinction between the subtle (*sūkṣma*) and the gross (*bādara*). First, the gross ones possess bodies that are subject to resistance (*sapratighāta*).

The subtle beings, however, even while possessing bodies, dwell in infinite-infinite numbers within a single spatial point occupied by one nigoda-jīva, precisely because of their subtle state; they possess common bodies.
They are not obstructed by one another nor by gross beings, and thus there is no contradiction regarding their occupation of space.

Here it is asked: It has been stated that a single soul possesses as many spatial points (*pradeśa*) as there are in the world-space (*lokākāśa*); how then can its existence be restricted to an innumerable part (*asaṃkhyeyabhāga*) or other portions of that world?
Surely it ought to pervade the entire world. To this it is replied:
By means of the contraction and expansion of its spatial points, like a lamp.

Since the self (*ātman*), whose nature is formless, has been bound as a single entity since beginningless time and thus possesses, in some sense, corporeality, it occupies a body—whether large or minute—under the influence of the *kārmaṇa* body. Because its nature consists in the contraction and expansion of its spatial points (*pradeśa*) due to that [body], its existence within an innumerable part (*asaṃkhyeyabhāga*) and so forth is logically established when it possesses that specific dimension, just like a lamp.

For example, although a lamp has an unmeasured extent of light in an unobstructed space, its light assumes the dimensions of a vessel, a jar, a room, or other such obstructions due to their influence.

Here it may be asked: since the dharmas and so forth interpenetrate one another's locations, does this not lead to a confusion of entities such that they attain oneness? This is not so; for even when there is extreme mutual contact, they do not abandon their own intrinsic natures.
And it has been said:
If this is so, let the distinction between the intrinsic natures of *dharma* and the other [categories] be stated; therefore, he says:
"The assistance provided by *dharma* and *adharma* consists in the grasping of motion and stability.
Motion (*gati*) is the cause for reaching another location;
its opposite is stability (*sthiti*).
It is called "appropriation" (*upagraha*) because it is grasped (*upagṛhyate*).
Movement and rest constitute "movement-and-rest.
Movement-and-rest themselves are the "auxiliaries" (upagraha), hence "the auxiliaries of movement-and-rest.
The phrase "of merit and demerit" is an indication of the agent.
That which is assisted is called "assistance" (*upakāra*). What, then, is this? It is the assistance of motion and the assistance of stability.
If this is so, would it not follow that there should be a dual designation?
This is not a fault; a word that has been established in its general sense does not abandon the number previously assigned to it even when it enters into a relationship with another word.
For example: "The duty of a virtuous person is austerity and sacred learning" (*sādhoḥ kāryaṃ tapaḥśrute*).

What is meant by this is as follows: when the assistance for movement must be provided to living beings (*jīva*) and matter (*pudgala*) which are subject to the transformation of motion, the category of *dharmāstikāya* serves as a common support, just as water is for the movement of a fish.

Likewise, when the support of stability must be provided for souls (*jīva*) and matter (*pudgala*) which are subject to transformation while remaining stationary, the category of non-dharma (*adharmāstikāya*) serves as their common substratum, just as the earth element is the basis for the stability of horses and other such beings.
Now, one might object that the term "support" (*upagraha*) is redundant, since the meaning is already established by the word "assistance" (*upakāra*), as it is stated:
"Motion and stability are the assistance provided by dharma and adharma."
This is not a fault; the term "assistance" (*upagraha*) is stated for the purpose of preventing a correspondence based on numerical order (*yathāsaṃkhya*).

For [otherwise], a correspondence would occur between merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*) on one hand and motion and stability (*gati-sthiti*) on the other, such that the assistance of merit would result in the motion of souls (*jīva*) and the assistance of demerit would result in the stability of matter-particles (*pudgala*).
To prevent this, the term "assistance" is employed.

If it is argued that the assistance provided by *dharma* and *adharma* is logically applicable to space because of its omnipresence (*sarvagatatva*), that is incorrect; for there exists another benefit for it.
The purpose of all substances, such as *dharma* and the rest, is to provide accommodation (*avagāhana*).
If one were to postulate multiple purposes for a single entity, there would be no distinction between the inhabited world (*loka*) and the non-inhabited world (*aloka*).

If it is argued that the earth, water, and so forth alone are capable of fulfilling that purpose, and there is no need for merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), we say: no; because it has been specifically stated that [the body] has a common substratum (*sādhāraṇāśraya*).
Furthermore, a single effect is produced by multiple causes.
If it is argued that movement and stability are obstructed by those two [merit and demerit] because they possess equal force, we say: no; because they are not impellers (*aprerakatva*).

If it is argued that those two do not exist because they are unperceived, like the horn of a donkey, we say no; for there is no disagreement among any proponents [of philosophical systems]. Indeed, all proponents desire objects, whether perceptible or imperceptible. Furthermore, the reason [you offer] is unestablished with respect to us.
By means of the eye of unsurpassed direct perception, the Omniscient One perceives all things, such as the Dharma and so forth;
and through his instruction, those possessing knowledge derived from hearing also perceive them.

Here he says: if the existence of the two supersensible factors, merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*), is determined through a relationship of assistance (*upakāra*), then what is the assistance in the apprehension of space (*nabhas*), which was mentioned immediately thereafter and is likewise supersensible?
It is said: the accommodation (*avagāha*) of space.
The term "benefit" (upakāra) is understood to carry over.

It should be understood that providing space for those things that possess extension, such as living beings (jīva) and matter (pudgala), is the benefit of space (ākāśa) consisting of their accommodation (avagāha). [An objector] says: It is logical that space provides accommodation for living beings and matter, which possess activity and extension.

If it is asked: "But since the *dharmāstikāya* and the other [substances] are inactive (*niṣkriya*) and eternally connected, how can there be 'pervasion' (*avagāha*) for them?"—it is not so; for that is established through metaphorical designation (*upacāra*).

Just as it is said that "space is all-pervading" even though there is no act of going, because it exists everywhere, so too *dharma* and *adharma*, although lacking the activity of pervasion, are metaphorically designated as "pervasive" because they are seen to extend everywhere. Objection: If giving space is its inherent nature (*svabhāva*), then obstruction by diamonds and the like for clods of earth, or by walls and the like for cows and the like, would not occur.
Furthermore, a contradiction is observed.
Therefore, its capacity to provide space is lost.

This is not a fault; for while there is mutual obstruction among gross objects such as diamonds and clods of earth, their capacity to provide space is not lost, because the obstruction occurs only among those things that occupy space within it.
Furthermore, because objects such as vajras are coarse, they provide mutual space for one another; thus, this is not a fault of space.
Indeed, those individuals (*pudgala*) which are subtle provide mutual space for one another.

If this were so, one might object: "This is not the unique characteristic (*asādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa*) of space, since it exists in other things as well? That is not the case; its unique characteristic is being the cause of the common capacity for penetration (*avagāhana*) for all entities. Thus, there is no fault.
If it is argued that [space] is non-existent in the non-luminous space (*alokākāśa*) because of its absence there, we say no; for it does not abandon its own nature (*svabhāva*).
The service rendered by space has thus been explained.
Now, as to what benefit there is for the persons (pudgala) mentioned immediately following that, it is said here:
"The body, speech, mind, and the out-breath and in-breath [belong] to the persons.
This is incorrect.

What is incorrect here? [The objection: When the question is asked, "What benefit do the *pudgalas* provide?", the definition of *pudgalas* is stated: that the body and so forth consist of *pudgalas*. This is not incorrect; the definition of *pudgalas* will be explained later.

However, this [statement] is made in the section on benefits precisely for the purpose of demonstrating the benefits that *pudgalas* provide to living beings (*jīvas*). Thus, it is stated in the context of benefits.
The bodies have been described.
Those beginning with the gross (audārika) are imperceptible due to their subtlety.
However, certain bodies of accumulation, whose functions are brought about by the arising of those [subtle bodies], are perceptible while others are imperceptible.
The karmas that serve as the causes for these [bodies] are also included by the term "taking on a body.

Since these are considered to belong to the *pudgala*, the *pudgalas* function for the benefit of the souls (*jīvas*). It might be thought that the *kārmaṇa* [body] is not composed of *pudgala*; because it lacks form.

Is it not the case that for those things possessing form (*ākāravat*), it is logical that coarseness and so forth belong to the person (*pudgala*)? That is not so; even that belongs to the person alone, because its maturation (*vipāka*) is caused by a connection with material objects (*mūrtimat*).
For it is observed that rice and other grains, having reached maturity through contact with substances such as water, possess the quality of belonging to the person.
Likewise, it should be understood that karmic matter (*kārmaṇa*) also belongs to the person, since it matures when there is the encounter with material substances such as sugar or thorns.
Speech is of two kinds: substantial speech (*dravyavāk*) and dispositional speech (*bhāvavāk*).

Of these, dispositional speech is composed of matter (*paudgalikī*), because it is caused by the subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣayopaśama*) of the *vīryāntarāya*, *mati-śruta-jñānāvaraṇa*, and *aṅgopāṅga-nāman* karmas;
for in the absence of those [karmic causes], its manifestation would not occur.

Impelled by a soul endowed with that capacity and possessed of activity, *pudgalas* undergo transformation into the state of speech (*vāk*); thus, substantial speech (*dravyavāk*) is also composed of *pudgalas*, because it is an object of the sense of hearing.
Why is it not an object of the other senses?
Because it is unfit to be grasped by them.
Just as fragrance, which is perceptible by the nose, is not perceived as taste and so forth [by other senses].
If it is argued that speech is formless (*amūrta*), we say no; for its possession of form (*mūrtimat*) is established through the observation of its being grasped, obstructed, pierced, and overcome.
The mind (*manas*) is of two kinds: substantial mind (*dravyamana*) and mental state (*bhāvamanas*).
The *bhāvamanaḥ* (psychic activity) is characterized by the acquisition (*labdhi*) and the application (*upayoga*); because it has the *pudgala* (matter) as its object, it is *paudgalika* (material).

As for the *dravyamanaḥ* (the material mind), it is *paudgalika* because the *pudgalas*—which serve as the conditions for the attainment of the *aṅga* and *upāṅga* [karmans] resulting from the subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣayopaśama*) of the *jñānāvaraṇa* and *vīryāntarāya* [karmans]—are the benefactors of the self that is oriented toward the contemplation of virtues and defects, recollection, and so forth, having transformed into the mind.

Someone might say: "The mind is a distinct substance, devoid of transformations such as color and form, and is merely atomic in size; therefore, its being *paudgalika* is illogical. That is incorrect.
How so? It is said: that [object] must be either connected with the sense-faculty and the self, or unconnected.
If it were unconnected, it could not be of service to the self, nor would it provide assistance to the sense-faculty.
If, on the other hand, it were connected, being connected in one location, as an atom it would not provide service in other locations.
If it is argued that its rotation like a whirling firebrand occurs by the power of the unseen (adṛṣṭa), we say no; because it lacks that capacity.
The unseen is a quality of the formless and inactive self; being itself inactive, it is not capable of initiating action elsewhere.

For a specific substance of air is observed to possess activity, to possess touch, and to be the cause of vibration in trees when it reaches them; however, this [breath] has characteristics contrary to that, and thus lacks the quality of being a cause of activity.

The abdominal air, characterized as exhalation (*ucchvāsa*), which is impelled by the self depending upon the subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣayopaśama*) of the veils of energy (*vīrya-antarāya*) and knowledge (*jñānāvaraṇa*), and upon the manifestation (*udaya*) of the primary and secondary limbs (*aṅga-upāṅga-nāman*), is called *prāṇa*.
By that same self, the external air being drawn inward, characterized as inhalation (*niḥśvāsa*), is designated as *apāna*.
Thus, these two [the mind and the vital breaths] are also benefactors of the self, because they are the cause of life.
It should be understood that those—mind, prāṇa, and apāna—are corporeal.
Why? Because resistance and other such qualities are observed in things that possess form.
Obstruction of the mind is observed through terrifying causes such as the falling of thunderbolts,
as well as by the overpowering influence of gods and others.
Furthermore, obstruction of the inhaled and exhaled breaths (*prāṇa* and *apāna*) is perceived through the closing of the mouth by the palms of the hands, cloths, and so forth.
And there is also subjugation by phlegm.
Furthermore, for that which is formless, there could be no such things as physical impact from things possessing form.
For this very reason, the existence of the self is established.

Just as the movement of a mechanical statue indicates the existence of an operator, so too the activity of inhalation, exhalation, and so forth establishes the existence of a self that possesses action.
Is the benefit produced by the person (pudgala) limited to this alone, or is there another as well? To this, he says:
Regarding the acquisition of pleasure, pain, life, and death:

when there exists an internal cause in the form of the arising of karma to be experienced as either existent or non-existent, the transformation that arises— taking the form of joy or distress due to the influence of external conditions such as the ripening of material substances— is designated as "pleasure" and "pain."

Life (*jīvita*) is defined as the non-interruption of the aforementioned specific activities of inhalation and exhalation in a living being who maintains its existence through the manifestation of the karma known as *āyuḥ* (life-span), which is the cause for sustaining existence.
The cessation of that [life] is death (*maraṇa*).
These qualities, such as pleasure and so forth, constitute the benefit to the soul (*jīva*) produced by material entities (*pudgala*); for they arise when there is the presence of material causes.

Is the mention of "assistance" (*upagraha*) redundant because of the context of "benefit" (*upakāra*)? It is not redundant; this is for the purpose of demonstrating one's own assistance, namely, that the benefit for persons (*pudgala*) is produced by persons.

For example: an assistance is rendered to bell-metal and the like by means of ashes and so forth; to water and the like by means of *kataka* nuts and so forth; and to iron and the like by means of water and so forth.
What is the purpose of the word “and” (*ca*)? It serves the purpose of conjunction (*samuccaya*).
It conjoins the fact that there is also another assistance performed by a person (*pudgala*).
Just as it is with bodies, so it is also with the sense faculties, such as the eye.
Having thus demonstrated the primary assistance not produced by a living being (*ajīva*), he speaks in order to demonstrate the assistance produced by a living being (*jīva*):
"There is mutual assistance among living beings.
The word "paraspara" is used in the sense of reciprocal action.
The exchange of actions is the exchange of activities. Mutual assistance is reciprocal support; it is the benefit rendered to living beings.
What, then, is this? It is mutual assistance through such relationships as master and servant, or teacher and disciple.
To begin with, the master serves the servants by means of the distribution of wealth and so forth;
and the servants serve him by providing what is beneficial and preventing what is harmful.
The teacher is engaged in benefiting his disciples by demonstrating the teachings that bestow the fruits of both worlds and by causing them to perform the actions prescribed by those teachings.
The disciples likewise benefit the teachers through conduct favorable to them.

Furthermore, for what purpose is the word "benefit" (*upagraha*) used again in the section on the "obligation to assist"? The word "benefit" is stated once more in order to demonstrate the fourfold [fruits] previously mentioned, beginning with happiness.
Pleasure and so forth are also benefits to living beings produced by the *jīva*. [The opponent] says:
"If it must necessarily be that there is a benefit, and time is accepted as being existent, then what benefit does it provide? To this, it is said:
Duration, transformation, action, priority, and posteriority are the functions of time.
From the root *vṛt* with the suffix *ṇic*, followed by the suffix *yuṭ* in the sense of the object (*karman*) or the abstract state (*bhāva*), the feminine form *vartanā* is derived.
*Vartanā* means "to proceed" (*vartyate*) or "mere proceeding.

Since substances such as *dharma* and so forth—which exist by their own nature with respect to the cessation of their own modifications—lack that activity in the absence of external assistance, time is defined as that which is characterized by the impelling of those [substances]. Thus, *vartanā* is the service rendered by time. What is the meaning of the root *vṛt*? The substance and its modification proceed; time is their cause of proceeding (*vartayitā*).

If this were so, it would follow that time possesses action, just as one says, "the student studies" and "the teacher teaches. This is not a fault; for we observe the designation of a cause as an agent even when it is merely an instrumental condition (*nimitta*). For example, one says, "the fire of dried cow-dung teaches."
Thus, time possesses the status of being a causal agent.

How is that [time] determined to be "time"? Even though there exists the conventional usage of specific names—such as "the time [of cooking]" for particular actions like cooking, or "cooking" for the results produced by those actions—the application of the designation "time" when one says "the time [of the meal]" or "the time [of the rice-cooking]" is superimposed upon them. This superimposition indicates the existence of time, which is the primary cause for such designations.
Why? Because a secondary (gauna) usage depends upon a primary (mukhya) one.
The modification (*paryāya*) of a substance is a transformation (*pariṇāma*) consisting in the cessation of one attribute and the arising of another attribute, which is non-kinetic in nature.
For the soul (*jīva*), it is anger and so forth; for matter (*pudgala*), it is color and so forth;
for the media of motion (*dharma*), rest (*adharma*), and space (*ākāśa*), it is caused by the increase or decrease of the quality of heaviness-lightness (*agurulaghutva*).
Action consists of the nature of motion.

It is of two kinds, distinguished as that which is produced through effort (*prāyogika*) and that which is spontaneous (*vaisrasika*). Among these, that produced through effort belongs to things such as carts, while the spontaneous belongs to things such as clouds.
Remoteness and proximity exist as produced by space and as produced by time.
In this context, because the section concerns the assistance provided by time, those produced by time are understood.
These aforementioned assistances—subsistence and so forth—demonstrate the existence of time.

Now, one might object: let there be the mention of *vartanā* alone; since *pariṇāma* and the others are its subdivisions, their separate mention is purposeless. It is not purposeless, because it serves to indicate two types of time, for the detailed exposition [of the categories] has that aim.
Time is indeed twofold: ultimate time (*paramārthakāla*) and conventional time (*vyavahārakāla*).
Ultimate time is characterized by *vartanā*.
The conventional time, characterized by transformation and so forth, is designated as "time" when it is a specific action delimited by one thing that serves as the cause for delimiting another.
It is established as threefold: past, present, and future.
In that regard, at the time of ultimate reality (paramārtha), the designation "time" is primary,
while the designations "past" and so forth are secondary.
At the time of conventional usage (vyavahāra), the designations "past" and so forth are primary.
The designation of "time" is figurative, because it depends upon substances possessing activity and because it is produced by [the movement of] time.
Here it is said: the benefits (upakāra) of dharma, adharma, space, matter, souls, and time have been stated.
And their defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa) has also been stated, beginning with "consciousness (upayoga) is the defining characteristic," and so forth.
The general characteristic of these categories has indeed been stated as "the non-living bodies" (ajīvakāya);
however, their specific characteristics have not been stated.
Why is that? To this, it is said:
§ 570. *Pudgalas* possess touch, taste, smell, and color.
Touch (*sparśa*) is that which is touched, or it is merely the act of touching.
It is of eight kinds, distinguished by being soft, hard, heavy, light, cold, hot, oily, and dry.
Taste (*rasa*) is that which is tasted, or merely the act of tasting.
It is of five kinds, distinguished by being bitter, sour, pungent, sweet, and astringent.
Odor is that which is smelled, or the mere act of smelling;
it is twofold: fragrant and foul-smelling.
Color is that which is seen, or the mere act of seeing.
It is of five kinds, distinguished as black, green, yellow, white, and red.
These primary types each have further subdivisions that are numerable, innumerable, and infinite.
"Touch, taste, smell, and color"—these are touch, taste, smell, and color; because they possess these, they are said to be "possessing touch, taste, smell, and color."
The suffix *mat* is used here to denote a constant connection (*nityayoga*), as in the expression "the *nyagrodha* trees are full of sap" (*kṣīriṇo nyagrodhāḥ*).

[Objection: But was it not already stated in the passage “material persons” (*rūpiṇaḥ pudgalāḥ*) that persons possess form, and that taste and the other [sensory objects] were included therein precisely because they are inseparable from it? Therefore, since the fact that persons possess form and so forth is established by that very [statement], this sūtra is redundant. [Reply: This is not a fault. In the passage “the immaterial [elements] remain eternally” (*nityāvasthitāny arūpāṇi*), the nature of the [unconditioned] factors such as *dharma* and so forth was defined as eternal and so on; consequently, there arose the implication that persons are likewise immaterial. It was for the purpose of refuting that [implication] that this was stated.
But this is stated for the purpose of understanding the specific nature of those [elements].
This is stated for the purpose of understanding the remaining transformations of the person (pudgala):
They possess sound, binding, subtlety, grossness, configuration, division, darkness, shadow, light, and radiance.
Sound is of two kinds: characterized by speech and its opposite.
The characteristic of speech is twofold: with syllables (*sākṣara*) and without syllables (*anakṣara*).
That which has been rendered into syllables manifests the treatises; through its division into *saṃskṛta* and its opposite, it is the cause for the linguistic usage of both Āryans and Mlecchas.
That which consists of non-syllables is the cause for establishing the nature of extraordinary knowledge in those such as the two-sensed beings.
All of this is produced through application (*prāyogika*).
That which is non-verbal in nature is of two kinds: produced through application and produced spontaneously (*vaisrasika*). The spontaneous kind arises from clouds and similar sources.
The *prāyogika* (produced by effort) is fourfold, distinguished as struck (*tata*), stretched (*vitata*), solid (*ghana*), and hollow (*sauṣira*).
Among these, that which arises from the striking of leather, such as from drums, kettledrums, and frogs, is the *tata*.
That which originates from stringed instruments such as the *vīṇā* and *sughoṣā* is the *vitata*.
The *ghana* [sound] is produced by striking objects such as cymbals or bells;
the *sauṣira* [sound] has its cause in hollow instruments such as flutes or conchs.
*Bandha* (bondage) is of two kinds: *vaisrasika* (natural) and *prāyogika* (artificial).
That which is independent of human effort is spontaneous (*vaisrasika*).
For example, it has as its objects lightning, meteors, rain-showers, fire, Indra’s bow (the rainbow), and so forth, being caused by the qualities of smoothness (*snigdha*) and roughness (*rūkṣa*).

That which is caused by human effort is produced (*prāyogika*); it is divided into two types: that which has non-living beings (*ajīva*) as its object, and that which has both living and non-living beings (*jīvājīva*) as its object.
Among these, the subject of non-living matter (ajīva) is characterized by such things as lacquer and wood;
the subject of both living and non-living matter is the bondage of karma and quasi-karma (nokarma).
Subtlety (saukṣmya) is of two kinds: ultimate (antya) and relative (āpekṣika).
Among these, the latter [type of minuteness] belongs to atoms;
the relative [type] belongs to things such as the bilva, the āmalaka, and the badara fruits.
Grossness, too, is twofold: ultimate and relative.
Among these, the last [type of configuration] exists in the great aggregate (*mahāskandha*) that pervades the world;
the relative [configuration] exists in things such as the jujube, the *āmalaka*, the *vilva*, and the *tāla* tree.
Configuration (*saṃsthāna*) is shape (*ākṛti*).
That [shape] is of two kinds: *itthaṃlakṣaṇa* (definite shape) and *anitthaṃlakṣaṇa* (indefinite shape).
*Itthaṃlakṣaṇa* refers to circular, triangular, square, oblong, spherical, and so forth.
Other than these, the various shapes of clouds and the like are *anitthaṃlakṣaṇa*, because they lack a specific determination such as "this is this."

There are six types of disintegration (*bhedāḥ*): through the distinctions of splitting (*utkara*), powdering (*cūrṇa*), fragmenting (*khaṇḍa*), pulverizing (*cūrṇikā*), flattening (*pratara*), and atomizing (*aṇu*).
Among these, *utkara* is the splitting of wood and the like by means of saws and such instruments. *Cūrṇa* refers to the flour, small particles, and so forth, of barley, wheat, and the like.
A fragment is [the breaking] of jars and the like into shards, gravel, and so forth; powder is [the grinding] of mung beans, green gram, and the like;
a layer is [the splitting] of clouds, cloth, and the like.
*Anucaṭana* is the emission of sparks when objects such as heated iron balls are struck by hammers and the like.
*Tamas* is the cause of obstruction to vision and is opposed to light. *Chāyā* (shadow) is caused by the obstruction of light.
It is twofold: that which is transformed through changes in color and so forth, and that which consists merely of a reflected image.
Heat (*ātapa*) is characterized by warmth and light, caused by the sun and similar sources.
Radiance (*udyota*) is light originating from the moon, gems, fireflies, and so forth.
These—sound and the rest—are modifications of the substance *pudgala*.
Because they possess these [qualities], they are said to "possess sound, bondage, subtlety, grossness, shape, division, darkness, shadow, light, and radiance";
thus they are designated as *pudgalas*.
By the word "and" (ca), those transformations of the person (pudgala) such as impulsion and impact, which are well-known in the scriptures, are included.
To demonstrate the distinctions among the persons already mentioned, he says:
Atoms (*aṇavaḥ*) and aggregates (*skandhāḥ*):

they are called "atoms" because they are measured (*aṇyante*) or designated (*śabdyante*) by virtue of their capacity to produce derivative states (*paryāya*) such as touch, which exist only within a single spatial point (*pradeśamātra*).
Due to its subtlety, the self and so forth have the self as their beginning, the self as their middle, and the self as their end.

And it has been said: "That substance which has the self as its beginning, the self as its middle, and the self as its end, and which cannot be grasped by the senses because it is indivisible—that you should know to be the atom (paramāṇu)."
They are designated as "aggregates" (*skandha*) because they consist of a mass of activities such as grasping, depositing, and so forth, by virtue of their gross nature.

In the case of conventional usage, an existing activity is sometimes relied upon merely as a defining characteristic; thus, the designation "aggregate" applies even to dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and the like, which are incapable of activities such as grasping.

Furthermore, although *pudgala*s are of infinite variety, they are all included by being subsumed under the two categories of atoms (*aṇu*) and aggregates (*skandha*). Therefore, the plural number is employed to indicate the infinite variety of the substrata belonging to those respective categories.
The designation of the two categories as "atoms" (*aṇu*) and "aggregates" (*skandha*) is for the purpose of connecting with the distinctions mentioned in the two preceding sūtras.
Atoms possess touch, taste, smell, and color.
Aggregates, moreover, possess sound, cohesion, subtlety, grossness, shape, division, darkness, shadow, glare, and light, as well as touch and the other [sensory qualities].
Know that substance which has no beginning, middle, or end, and which cannot be grasped by the senses— that indivisible entity is the atom (paramāṇu).
He asked: "Is the transformation of these persons, characterized as atoms and aggregates, beginningless, or is it said to have a beginning?
Since it possesses the quality of being produced, it is indeed asserted to have a beginning.
If this is so, then let it be stated: from what cause do they arise?"
In that regard, first, for the purpose of demonstrating the cause of the arising of the aggregates (*skandha*), it is said:
"They arise from differentiation and aggregation.
(Section 576)
Disintegration (*bheda*) is the splitting apart of aggregates (*saṃghāta*) due to the power of two causes.
An aggregate (*saṃghāta*) is the attainment of oneness by things that were previously separate.
Now, one might object: since there are two [causes], there ought to be a dual ending.
The use of the plural number is for the purpose of including the triad [of causes]:
they arise from division, from aggregation, and from both division and aggregation.
For example: from the aggregation of two atoms, a dyad (dvipradeśa) aggregate arises.
From the aggregation of two or three atoms (aṇu) belonging to a two-partite [substance], there arises a three-partite [substance].
From the aggregation of two two-partite substances and one three-partite atom, or from four atoms, there arises a four-partite [substance].
In this manner, through the aggregation of countable, incalculable, infinite, and even infinitely infinite [atoms], there arise [substances] with a corresponding number of parts.
From the disintegration of these very [atoms], aggregates (*skandha*) consisting of up to two spatial units (*pradeśa*) arise.
Thus, through simultaneous disintegration and aggregation, aggregates of two spatial units and so forth arise;
that is, by the disintegration of one [atom] and the aggregation of another.
Thus, the cause for the arising of the aggregates has been explained.
To demonstrate the cause for the arising of the atom, he says:
Because of the distinction, [the atom] is minute.
When a rule is commenced once [a fact] is established, it serves as a restrictive rule (niyama).
The arising of an atom occurs only from division, neither from aggregation nor from both division and aggregation.

[Objection: Since it is established that the aggregates (skandhas) acquire their self-nature through aggregation alone, the mention of "division and aggregation" is redundant. To demonstrate the purpose of including those terms, this is said:
Regarding visibility through division and aggregation:
although it is produced by the collection of infinite and infinite atoms, some things are visible and some are invisible.
If it is asked, "How does that which is not visible become visible there?", it is said: it becomes visible through both differentiation (*bheda*) and aggregation (*saṃghāta*).
It is not [visible] through differentiation alone.

If one asks what the reasoning for this is, we reply: when a subtle transformation (*sūkṣmapariṇāma*) undergoes differentiation as a constituent aggregate (*skandha*), because it does not abandon its subtlety, it remains indeed invisible.

Furthermore, another [substance] transformed into subtlety becomes visible when, despite that difference [of state], through conjunction with another aggregate, the transformation into subtlety ceases and grossness arises.
[The opponent] says: The specific characteristics of the substances such as *dharma* have been stated, but their general characteristic has not been stated; that must now be explained.
It is said:
"Existence is the defining characteristic of a substance.
The meaning is that whatever exists is a substance (*dravya*).
If this is so, then first it must be stated: what is existence (*sat*)?
Therefore, he says:
"That which is endowed with origination, destruction, and persistence is existent. (TS 584)

The production (*utpāda*) of a substance— whether conscious or unconscious— which does not abandon its own nature, is the attainment of another state (*bhāvāntara*) due to the power of both causes, such as the transformation of a lump of clay into the state of a jar.
Likewise, *vyaya* is the disappearance of the previous state, as when the form of the lump vanishes upon the arising of the jar.

Because there is no disappearance or arising due to its beginningless, transformative intrinsic nature (*anādipāriṇāmikasvabhāva*), it remains constant (*dhruvati*) and becomes stable; thus, it is "constant" (*dhruva*).
The state or activity of that which is constant is "constancy" (*dhrauvya*).
This is like the persistence of clay and so forth through various states such as a lump of clay or a jar.

"Endowed with those [three]—arising, passing away, and persistence—is what is meant by 'endowed with arising, passing away, and persistence,' which is the existent (*sat*). He asks: "The word 'endowed' (*yukta*) is observed when there is a distinction, as in 'Devadatta is endowed with a staff.

If that were the case, would it not follow that there is a non-existence of those three and of the substance endowed with them? This is not a fault; for even in the absence of distinction, the word 'endowed' is observed from the perspective of a certain kind of distinction (*bhedanaya*).

Just as [one says] "a pillar provided with timber," so too, since they are inseparable, the designation "existent" (sat) is appropriate for them; or else, the word "yukta" (provided/endowed) may be understood in the sense of "concentration" (samādhi).
"Endowed" (yukta) means "concentrated" (samāhita), that is to say, having that as its nature.
"Existent" (sat) is that which is endowed with arising, passing away, and persistence; that is to say, it has arising, passing away, and persistence as its nature.
This is what is meant: arising and the other [characteristics] are the defining marks (lakṣaṇa) of a substance (dravya).
Substance is the object of definition.
In that regard, from the perspective of the mode-orientated standpoint (paryāyārthika-naya), there is a state of being a different entity both mutually among modes and from substance.
From the perspective of the substance-orientated standpoint (dravyārthika-naya), because it is not perceived as distinct [from the modes], there is no state of being a different entity.
Thus is established the relationship between the characterized and the characteristic.
It is said: "The non-forms (arūpa) are eternally abiding. In that regard, it is not known what is eternal; therefore, he says:
That which is the non-decline of that state is called "eternal" (*nitya*). By this, "that state" (*tadbhāva*) is expressed.
What is that state? It is being the cause of recognition. Recognition is the memory [expressed as] "this is that very same thing.
Since that does not occur without a cause, its cause is that state.
*Bhāvanā* is the act of bringing into being (*bhāva*).
The state of that [act] is *tadbhāva*.
Because an object previously perceived by means of a certain nature is brought back into being by that very same nature once again, it is recognized as "this is that very same thing."
If there were absolute cessation, or if there were merely the manifestation of something entirely new, then recollection would be impossible.
The worldly conventions dependent upon that [recollection] would be contradicted.
Therefore, by the absence of such [cessation], it is determined to be imperishable; because its nature is imperishable, it is eternal.
That, however, must be understood in some sense;
for if there were absolute permanence, because there would be no possibility of change, there would be a contradiction regarding the process of the causes for both saṃsāra and its cessation.
Is it not a contradiction to say that "that very same thing is both eternal and non-eternal"?

If it is eternal, then because there is no passing away or arising, its non-eternality is contradicted; if it is indeed non-eternal, then because there is no persistence, its eternality is contradicted. This is not a contradiction.
Why?
Because of the establishment of what is assigned and what is not assigned.

Of an entity that possesses a manifold nature (*anekāntātmaka*), whatever attribute is intended to be expressed for a particular purpose attains predominance; that is to say, it is "conferred" (*arpita*), "imposed," or "brought forward.
Its opposite is "not conferred" (*anarpita*).
Because there is no purpose [to express it], even though it exists, there is no intention to express it; thus, having become subordinate, it is called "not conferred."

There is no contradiction between the "dedicated" (*arpita*) and the "not dedicated" (*anarpita*), nor between the "dedicated-and-not-dedicated" and the "not-dedicated-and-not-not-dedicated," because there is no contradiction in the establishment [of reality] through those two—namely, the establishment of what is dedicated and not dedicated.

For example: for a single Devadatta, the relationships of father, son, brother, nephew, and so forth—which are based on causes such as being a progenitor or being born from him—are not contradictory, because there is no difference in the act of dedication (*arpaṇā*).
A father is [defined] in relation to his son, and a son in relation to his father, and so forth.

Likewise, even a substance is eternal when considered in terms of its universal aspect (*sāmānyārpaṇā*) and non-eternal when considered in terms of its particular aspect (*viśeṣārpaṇā*); thus, there is no contradiction.
Furthermore, those two—the universal and the particular—serve as the basis for conventional usage through their being in some sense both distinct and non-distinct.

Here it is objected: Since existent things depend upon various methods of conventional expression, it is logical that existents arise from the aggregation of distinct entities as the nature of the aggregates (*skandha*).

However, this remains doubtful: does the aggregate characterized by dyads and so forth arise solely from conjunction (*saṃyoga*), or is some specific distinction determined? It is replied: "When conjunction exists, through binding—which consists of the transformation into unity—the aggregate is produced."

If this is so, then let this be explained: since the individual soul (pudgala) does not abandon its generic nature and yet enters into conjunction, why is it that for some there is bondage while for others there is not? It is said: because, although there is no difference in the essence of those individual souls, bondage occurs through the power imparted by their infinite modalities (*paryāya*), which arise from mutually distinct transformations—namely, through the qualities of smoothness (*snigdha*) and roughness (*rūkṣa*). § 590.
One is called "unctuous" (*snigdha*) because it has become unctuous through the manifestation of the state of unctuousness due to external and internal causes.
Likewise, one is "dry" (*rūkṣa*) because of being dried out.
"Unctuous and dry" refers to both the unctuous and the dry.
The state of these two is "smoothness and roughness" (*snigdharūkṣatva*).
Smoothness is a synonym characterized by the quality of slickness (*cikkaṇa*);
its opposite transformation is roughness.
‘Because of oiliness and roughness’ is the statement of the reason.
Bondage produced by that is the transformation into dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth.
When there is bondage characterized by mutual adhesion between two atoms—one oily and one rough—a dyad aggregate (*dvyaṇuka-skandha*) comes into being.
In this way, a constituent (skandha) consisting of numerable, innumerable, or infinite atoms (pradeśa) should be applied.
In that regard, the quality of moisture (sneha-guṇa) has the distinctions of being one, two, three, four, numerable, innumerable, or infinite;
the same applies to the quality of dryness (rūkṣa-guṇa).
Atoms possess those qualities.
For example, the quality of viscidity (sneha) manifests with varying degrees of intensity in the milk and clarified butter of cows, goats, buffaloes, camels, and female camels;
likewise, the quality of dryness (rūkṣa) is observed in particles of dust, gravel, and the like.
Likewise, even in the case of atoms, the operation of the qualities of smoothness (*snigdha*) and roughness (*rūkṣa*) is inferred through their intensity and lack of intensity.
Since bondage would result without distinction whenever the qualities of smoothness and roughness are present, he says the following in order to exclude undesirable qualities:
"Not of inferior qualities": inferior means base.
A *guṇa* is a constituent part.
Those whose *guṇas* are inferior are called "inferior-*guṇa*" beings.
For those of inferior *guṇas*, there is no bondage.

For example: there is no bondage between that which has a single degree of smoothness (*snigdha*) and that which has a single degree of smoothness, nor with that which has two or more degrees—whether numerable, innumerable, or infinite—of smoothness.

Likewise, there is no bondage between that same thing having a single degree of smoothness and that which has a single degree of roughness (*rūkṣa*), nor with that which has two or more degrees—whether numerable, innumerable, or infinite—of roughness.
The same principle should be applied to that which has a single degree of roughness as well.

Having excluded these two—the inferior qualities of *snigdha* (unctuous) and *rūkṣa* (dry)—there arises the contingency that the binding of other *snigdha* and *rūkṣa* substances occurs with one another without distinction; therefore, in order to clarify the scope of the prohibition even in that case, he says:
"When there is equality of qualities among similar [substances]."
The mention of "similar" (*sadṛśa*) is for the purpose of conveying similarity of kind;
the mention of "equality of qualities" (*guṇasāmya*) is for the purpose of conveying equality of degree.

This is what is meant: there is no binding between those that are twice as smooth with those that are twice as rough; nor between those that are thrice as smooth with those that are twice as rough; nor between those that are twice as smooth with those that are twice as smooth; nor between those that are twice as rough with those that are twice as rough—and so forth. If this is so, for what purpose is the term “similar” (sadṛśa) included? The term “similar” is included in order to establish that binding occurs even among similar substances when there is a disparity in their qualities. § 595.

Therefore, since there would follow the contingency of binding between substances of unequal qualities—whether of the same or different classes—in an unrestricted manner, this is stated for the purpose of establishing the intended meaning:
"But [binding occurs] between those possessing two or more additional qualities," etc.
"Exceeding by two qualities" means having two more.
What, then, is this? It is that which possesses four qualities.
The word "ādi" (and so forth) has the sense of "type" or "kind."
What, then, is this specific mode? It is the state of being exceeded by two.
By this, there is no cognition of [qualities] such as fivefold and so forth.
Therefore, bondage is stated to occur between qualities exceeding [the minimum] by two or more, whether they be of the same or different classes, but not for others.

For example: there is no binding of a particle possessing two units of viscidity with one possessing one unit of viscidity, nor with one possessing two units, nor with one possessing three units of viscidity.
However, there is binding with one possessing four units of viscidity.

Furthermore, for that same particle possessing two units of viscidity, there is no binding with one possessing five units of viscidity, nor with one possessing six, seven, eight, numerable, or infinite units of viscidity.
Thus, for that which is threefold-unctuous (*triguṇasnigdha*), there is binding with that which is fivefold-unctuous (*pañcaguṇasnigdha*).
With the remaining [qualities], there is no binding with those preceding or following it. For that which is fourfold-unctuous, there is binding with that which is sixfold-unctuous.
There is no bondage with the remaining [karmas] of the preceding or succeeding types.
This should be applied similarly to the remaining cases as well.
Likewise, for one possessing two units of roughness (*rūkṣa*), there is no bondage with those possessing one, two, or three units of roughness.
However, there is binding when that which is twice as dry binds with that which is four times as dry.
There is no binding when that same [substance] which is twice as dry binds with one that is five times as dry or more.
In this manner, the binding of those that are three times as dry and so forth should be applied by means of those exceeding them by two degrees.
This should be applied even to those of different classes.

And it has been said: "There is no binding of the viscous with the viscous, nor of the dry with the dry, when both are ill-disposed; rather, binding occurs between the viscous and the dry, whether they be dissimilar or similar, provided the inferior [quality] is excluded."
The word “tu” (but) serves as a qualification; it sets aside the [previous] prohibition and qualifies the state of bondage. [It means:
"The moist with the moist is not [bound] by that which is ill-disposed, nor the dry with the dry by that which is ill-disposed."
The binding of the smooth occurs with the rough, excluding the minimum, whether the qualities are unequal or equal.
(597) For what reason is binding explained as having superior qualities as its object, and not as having equal qualities? To this he says:
In the section on bondage, the two additional [karmas] are transformative;
by virtue of the context, the word "quality" (guṇa) is connected [to them].
"Those with superior qualities are superior.
Transformation (*pāriṇāmikatva*) consists in bringing about a change of state, like moistened molasses.
Just as moistened molasses possesses an intensified sweet taste because it brings about its own qualities in the surrounding particles of dust and so forth, it is thus transformative.

Likewise, another [substance] possessing superior qualities, by virtue of being transformative (*pāriṇāmika*) even when fewer in number, becomes the transformative basis for that which has twice as many or more *snigdha* (cohesive) or *rūkṣa* (dry) qualities;
thus, having first undergone the departure from its prior state, a third distinct state manifests, whereby their unity is established.
Otherwise, like white and black threads, even though there is contact, because they would not be transformative, everything would remain in its distinct form alone.

When bondage occurs again according to the stated rule, the duration of thirty *koṭī-koṭīs* of *sāgaropamas* and so forth for the karmas such as knowledge-obscuring (*jñānāvaraṇa*) becomes established.

Having stated that "existence (*sat*) is characterized by origination, destruction, and persistence," he speaks again in another manner in order to demonstrate the characteristic of substance (*dravya*):
Substance possesses qualities and modifications;
qualities and modifications together are called "qualities-and-modifications."
"Substance possesses qualities because it has them" (*te ’sya santi*).
Regarding the derivation of the suffix *-mat* here, the solution has already been stated: it is because a certain degree of distinction [between substance and its attributes] is logically possible.
What, then, are qualities (*guṇa*) and what are modes (*paryāya*)? Qualities are those that persist through change; modes are those that are distinct from one another.

"Substance is endowed with both. And it has been said: "Quality is the classification of substance; indeed, modification is called a mode (paryāya). Substance, which is not deficient of these [qualities and modes], is established as eternal."
This is what is meant: that by which one substance is distinguished from another substance is a quality (*guṇa*).
For by that [quality] the substance is defined;
if it were absent, there would be the undesirable consequence of a confusion of substances.
For example—the soul (jīva) is distinguished from matter (pudgala) and the rest by qualities such as knowledge, while matter and the rest are distinguished by form and the like.
Consequently, if there were no distinction, there would be confusion.

Therefore, with respect to their commonality, knowledge and the other qualities belong to the soul as its inherent attributes (anvayin), while form and the other qualities belong to matter and the rest.
Their modifications, being differentiated by way of their specific natures, are the synonyms [of substance]:
such as the cognition of a jar, the cognition of a cloth, anger, pride, odor, color, intense, mild, and so forth.
A collection that attains a state of some kind of difference from these is designated as a "substance" (*dravya*).
For if the aggregate were in every respect not something distinct from its parts, there would be a total non-existence [of the aggregate].

For example: when there is an aggregate of mutually distinct things, because the aggregate does not exist as something distinct from any one part, there is a total non-existence [of the aggregate], since [the parts] are distinct from one another.
If this is form, then taste and the other [sensory objects] are distinct from it.
Therefore, the collection is not a separate entity [from its constituents].
And how could that collection, which is not a separate entity from form—which itself is a separate entity from taste and so forth—not also be a separate entity from taste and so forth?
Consequently, it follows that the collection would be nothing more than form alone.
Furthermore, a single form cannot constitute a collection;
therefore, there is an absence of a collection.
And because of the absence of a collection, there is also an absence of the constituents that do not exist as something other than that collection; thus, there is a total non-existence.
The same should be applied to taste and the other qualities as well.
Therefore, by one who desires [the existence of] a collection, some form of being a distinct entity must be admitted.
A quality is a designation for a substance; for a modification of a substance is called a mode (*paryāya*).
"By those [categories], substance is established as non-deficient and eternal.

(601) Since the definition of the aforementioned substances has been stated, and since the determination of "substance" might consequently apply only to those specific objects, he says the following in order to indicate the existence of substances not yet mentioned:
And what is time? “Substance” is the remainder of the explanation.
Why is it so called? Because it possesses those defining characteristics.

Two types of defining characteristics have been stated: “Existence (sat) is that which is endowed with origination, destruction, and persistence,” and “Substance (dravya) is that which possesses qualities (guṇas) and modes (paryāyas).
Both of these defining characteristics are found in time (kāla).
For example: permanence (*dhrauvya*) of time is self-dependent (*svapratyaya*) because it is established by its own nature;

its destruction (*vyaya*) and emergence (*udaya*) are other-dependent (*parapratyaya*), yet they are also self-dependent in relation to the increase and decrease of the qualities of heaviness and lightness (*agurulaghuguṇa*).
Likewise, the qualities of time also exist in both common (*sādhāraṇa*) and uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) forms.

In this regard, its specific characteristic is being the cause of continuity (*vartanāhetutva*), while its general characteristics include insentience (*acetanatva*), formlessness (*amūrtatva*), subtlety (*sūkṣmatva*), and the qualities of being neither heavy nor light (*agurulaghutva*), among others.
Furthermore, its modalities (*paryāya*) are to be understood as characterized by the production of substances (*dravyotpāda*).
Therefore, because it possesses these two types of characteristics, the substantiality (*dravyatva*) of time is established, just like space and other such entities.
The evidence for its existence has been explained as being like that of *dharma* and the other categories: "Time is characterized by the function of persistence (*vartanā*).
Now, for what purpose is this time mentioned separately?
It should have been mentioned in the very same place where *dharma* and the others were stated, namely: "The non-living bodies are *dharma*, *adharma*, space, time, and matter (*pudgala*)."
This should not be suspected; for if there were such a designation [of "body"] there, it would follow that this [dharma] possesses corporeality (*kāyatva*).
And this is not accepted, because there is no conceptualization of a collection of primary or metaphorical spatial points (*pradeśa*).
First, a collection of primary spatial points has been stated for *dharmas* and so forth by such expressions as "innumerable spatial points" (*asaṃkhyeyāḥ pradeśāḥ*).

Even for an atom (*aṇu*), which consists of a single spatial point (*pradeśa*), a "collection of points" (*pradeśapracaya*) is spoken of by means of metaphorical conceptualization (*upacārakalpanā*), in consideration of the method (*naya*) for designating its prior and posterior states.
However, for time (*kāla*), there is no such conceptualization of a collection of points in either way; thus, it lacks corporeality (*akāyatva*).

Furthermore, in that textual reading where it says "and they are inactive" (*niṣkriyāṇi ca*), once the inactivity of the [categories] beginning with *dharma* and ending with space (*ākāśa*) has been established, it would follow—just as activity is attributed to the others, namely souls (*jīva*) and matter (*pudgala*)—that time (*kāla*) too must possess activity.

Now, if time were intended to be mentioned before space, that would not be correct; for [according to the rule] "up to space, [substances] consist of a single substance," time would possess the property of being a single-substance entity.
Therefore, time is mentioned here separately.
If it consists of multiple substances, what is its proof?
