There are as many atoms of time (kālāṇu) as there are spatial points (pradeśa) of the world-ether (lokākāśa); they are devoid of motion and are situated pervading the world by residing one by one in each individual point of space.
And it has been said: "Those which reside in each individual space-point of the world-space, like heaps of jewels, are to be known as atoms of time (kālāṇu);
they are formless because they are devoid of qualities such as color and so forth."
Those which reside in each individual space-point of the world, like heaps of jewels, are to be known as the atoms of time (kālāṇu).
The measure of primary time, characterized by *vartanā*, has been stated.
Now, what is the measure of conventional time (*vyavahārakāla*), which is understood through transformation (*pariṇāma*) and so forth? To this, it is said:
"That consists of infinite moments (*samaya*)."
Although the present consists of only a single moment, because past and future moments are infinite, it is called "of infinite moments.
Alternatively, this is stated for the purpose of determining the measure of time itself as the primary entity.

Because it is the cause for the turning of infinite modes, even a single atom of time (*kāla-aṇu*) is metaphorically designated as "infinite. Furthermore, a *samaya* is an extremely subtle fraction of time; one should understand that a specific accumulation of these [fractions] constitutes the *āvalikā* and so forth.
It was stated that a substance possesses qualities and modifications; therein, as to what the qualities are, it is said here:
qualities are those which reside in a substance and are themselves devoid of qualities.
Those whose substratum is substance are "substance-dependent" (dravyāśraya).
Those that have emerged from qualities are "quality-less" (nirguṇa).
Thus, qualities are endowed with both characteristics.
The qualifier “devoid of qualities” (*nirguṇāḥ*) is for the purpose of excluding dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and the like.
For even those [dyads] reside in substances that serve as their causes—the atoms—and they themselves possess qualities; therefore, by the qualifier “devoid of qualities,” they are excluded.
[Objection: But even modes (*paryāya*), such as the shape of a jar and so forth, reside in a substance and are devoid of qualities; would it not follow, then, that these too are qualities?

Because of the statement “they have substance as their substratum” (*dravyāśrayāḥ*), and because of the specific definition that “those which exist always depending on a substance are qualities” (*guṇāḥ*), modifications (*paryāyāḥ*) are excluded;
for they are occasional.
The word "transformation" (pariṇāma) has been mentioned more than once.
In response to the question "What is its meaning?", he says:
"Transformation is the state of becoming that [other thing]."
Alternatively, there is the view of some that qualities (*guṇa*) are entities distinct from substance (*dravya*); is that what you accept?

No; so he says: although they may in some sense be different from substance with respect to causes such as the distinction in designations and so forth, nevertheless, because they are not separate from it and because they are its transformations, they are not [ultimately] other.
If this is so, let it be explained what transformation (*pariṇāma*) is.
To determine that, this is said: the state of being (*tadbhāva*), the reality (*tattva*), or the nature by which substances such as *dharma* and the rest exist, is designated as "transformation.
It is of two kinds: beginningless (*anādi*) and having a beginning (*ādimān*).
In that regard, the beginninglessness of the movement, support, and so forth of the *dharmas* and other [substances] is from the perspective of their general nature (*sāmānya*).
Yet, that very same thing becomes "having a beginning" from the perspective of their specific distinctions (*viśeṣa*).
Now begins the sixth chapter.
It is said: The category of non-living entities (*ajīva*) has been explained.
Now, the category of "influx" (*āsrava*), which was indicated immediately following that, must be explained; therefore, for the sake of establishing it, this is said:
"Action of body, speech, and mind is *yoga*. (610)
The terms "body" and so forth have already been explained.
"Karma" and "action" (kriyā) are synonymous.
The action of body, speech, and mind is designated as "bodily, vocal, and mental karma-yoga."
Yoga is the vibration of the spatial units of the self (*ātmapradeśa*).
It is divided into three types according to the difference in its causes:
body-yoga (*kāyayoga*), speech-yoga (*vāgyoga*), and mind-yoga (*manoyoga*).

For example: bodily yoga (*kāyayoga*) is the vibration of the soul’s spatial units (*ātmapradeśa*) contingent upon any one of the seven types of body-matter aggregates (*vargaṇā*), such as the gross body, provided there exists the subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣayopaśama*) of the energy-obstructing karma (*vīryāntarāya*).

Vocal yoga (*vāgyoga*) is the vibration of the soul’s spatial units directed toward the transformation of speech, occurring when there is the presence of the internal acquisition of speech (*abhyantaravāglabdhi*) brought about by the subsidence-cum-destruction of the energy-obstructing karma and the obstructions to speech and letters, contingent upon the matter-aggregates of speech produced by the rising of the name-karma of the body (*śarīranāmakarma*).

Mental yoga (*manoyoga*) is the vibration of the soul's spatial units (*ātmapradeśa*) directed toward mental transformation, occurring when there is the presence of the attainment of mind—which consists of the subsidence and destruction of the internal obstructions to vigor and the veils over the non-sensory faculties—and when external causes in the form of mental material groups (*manovargaṇā*) serve as objects.

Even in the case of destruction (*kṣaya*), the vibration of the soul's spatial units belonging to the *sayogakevalin* (the omniscient one with residual karma) should be understood as yoga, depending upon the three types of material groups.
He said: "We accept that yoga is the activity characterized by the threefold [karmic influx].
Now, let the subject at hand be explained: what is the definition of *āsrava*?
It is that which is denoted by the term *yoga* for the transmigrating person.
That is an influx (*āsrava*).

Just as the water-outlet of a lake is designated as an "influx" because it is the cause of the inflow [of water], so too, since karma flows into the self by means of the channel of the *yoga*, the *yoga* deserves the designation "influx."
He said: "Karma is twofold, namely merit and demerit.
Is its connection with the cause of the influx (āsrava) without distinction, or is there some specific distinction? To this it is replied:
The auspicious is the result of merit, and the inauspicious is the result of evil.
What is an auspicious application, or what is an inauspicious one?
Unwholesome bodily activity consists of killing, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, and so forth.
Unwholesome vocal activity consists of speaking falsehoods, harsh words, and indecent speech, and so forth.
Unwholesome mental activity consists of thoughts of killing, envy, and malice, and so forth.
The opposite of that is auspicious.
How is there auspiciousness or inauspiciousness of yoga? Yoga produced by an auspicious transformation is auspicious.
And it is "impure" because it is produced by an impure transformation,
and not because it has pure and impure karma as its cause.

If this were the case, there would be no connection with the pure at all, since it is admitted that even the connection with the pure is a cause for bondage such as the obscuration of knowledge (*jñānāvaraṇa*).

It is *puṇya* because it purifies oneself, or because one is purified by it; this refers to [karma] such as that to be experienced as pleasure (*sadvedya*). It is *pāpa* because it protects or guards oneself from the auspicious.
That [is] the non-meritorious [karma], etc.
It is asked: Is this influx (āsrava) the cause for the commencement of equal results for all transmigrating beings, or is there some specific distinction? To this it is replied:

Due to the difference in their owners, there is a difference in the influx (āsrava) for those with passions and those without passions, and for that which leads to future rebirth and that which pertains to the path of conduct.
There are two types of possessors [of karma]: those with *kaṣāya* and those without *kaṣāya*. *Kaṣāya* refers to anger and so forth.
It is called *kaṣāya* because it is like a stain (*kaṣāya*).

What is the meaning of the term *upamā* (comparison)? Just as a decoction (*kaṣāya*) derived from the *nyagrodha* tree and so forth is a cause for adhesion, so too anger and the like are called "decoctions" (*kaṣāya*) because they are causes for the adhesion of karma to the self, being like a decoction. That which exists together with a decoction is "with-decoction" (*sakaṣāya*).

One who has no *kaṣāya* (passion) is "without *kaṣāya*" (*akaṣāya*). Those with *kaṣāya* and those without *kaṣāya* are "those with and without *kaṣāya*" (*sakaṣāyākaṣāyau*); [the compound] refers to these two.
*Saṃparāya* is cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*); action whose purpose is that [existence] is "pertaining to future states" (*sāmparāyika*).
*Īraṇa* means movement; *īryā* means application, which is to say, motion. Action performed through that [movement] is *īryāpatha*.

That which pertains to the future life (*sāṃparāyika*) and that which pertains to movement (*īryāpatha*) together constitute "that which pertains to the future life and movement" (*sāmparāyikeryāpathe*).

Regarding those two—the *sāṃparāyika* (pertaining to future lives) and the *airyāpathika* (pertaining to bodily postures)—the connection is according to their respective order: for a self possessed of *kaṣāya* (passions), such as one with false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and so forth, there is the influx (*āsrava*) of *sāṃparāyika* karma;
for one devoid of *kaṣāya*, such as one whose passions are stilled (*upaśāntakaṣāya*) and so forth, there is the influx of *airyāpathika* karma.

In order to demonstrate the divisions of the influx (āsrava) previously mentioned, he says: the senses, passions, non-vows, and activities—numbering five, four, five, and twenty-five respectively—are the subdivisions of the former.
Here, it should be understood that the faculties (*indriya*) and the following are to be connected with the numbers five and so forth respectively: the faculties are five;
the passions (*kaṣāya*) are four.
There are five vows and twenty-five actions.
Among these, the five faculties, such as the faculty of touch and so forth, have already been explained.
The four passions (*kaṣāya*) are anger and the others.
The five vows of non-restraint (*avratas*), such as the taking of life and so forth, will be explained later.

Twenty-five types of action (*kriyā*) are stated: the action that increases right view (*samyaktva*), characterized by the worship of shrines (*caitya*), teachers (*guru*), and the scriptures (*pravacana*), is called the action of right view (*samyaktva-kriyā*).
Mithyātva-kriyā (action of falsehood) is activity caused by falsehood, consisting of such things as the praise of other deities.
Prayoga-kriyā (action of application) is the engagement in going, coming, and so forth, by means of the body and other faculties.
Samādāna-kriyā (action of undertaking) is the orientation toward non-restraint while being a self-controlled person.
The action of deportment is characterized by the signs of deportment.
These are the five types of action.
The action arising from malice is due to the onset of anger.
The exertion of one who is already corrupt is physical action (*kāyikī kriyā*).

The action pertaining to the taking up of instruments for violence is the action pertaining to the basis (*adhikaraṇikī kriyā*). Because it is dependent on the production of suffering, it is the action of causing affliction (*pāritāpikī kriyā*).
The action of taking life consists in causing the separation of the vital faculties, strength, inhalation, exhalation, and the life-force.
These are the five actions.
The action of seeing is the intention to look at a beautiful form by one who is heedless because of being moistened by passion.
The action of touching is the continuous volition regarding the tangible under the influence of negligence.
The consequential action arises from the production of a new locus [of karmic matter].
The action of total contamination is the discharge of internal waste in a place frequented by women, men, or animals.
On the stage where [the mind] has not yet been wiped clean or seen, the laying down of the body and so forth is effortless action (*anābhoga-kriyā*).
These are the five actions.
That action which one performs oneself, which would otherwise have to be accomplished by another, is "action with one's own hand" (*svahasta-kriyā*).
The act of natural commission (*nisargakriyā*) is the authorization of specific activities such as the taking up of evil.
The act of disclosure (*vidāraṇakriyā*) is the publicizing of faults and so forth committed by another.

The act of violating the command (*ājñāvyāpādikī kriyā*) occurs when one, being unable to carry out the prescribed injunctions—such as those regarding the *āvaśyaka* duties—due to the arising of delusion regarding conduct (*cāritramoha*), misrepresents them.
Due to deceit and laziness, there is a lack of regard for performing the duties prescribed by the teachings; this is "action without aspiration.
These are the five types of action.
Furthermore, being intent on actions such as cutting, piercing, and slaughtering, or feeling joy when another person undertakes such an enterprise, is "action of undertaking."
The *pārigrāhikī* activity is that which has the purpose of not losing what has been acquired.
The *māyā* activity is deceit or fraud regarding knowledge, vision, and so forth.

The *mithyādarśana* activity is when one strengthens another—who is already possessed by the performance and instigation of the activity of false view—through praise and other means, saying, for example, "You are doing well. This is the *mithyādarśana* activity.
Non-restraint is the activity of non-renunciation resulting from the rise of obstructive karmas that hinder self-control.
These are the five activities;
when combined, they constitute twenty-five activities.
These [faculties] such as the senses, undergoing differentiation through the distinction between cause and effect, become the doors of influx (*āsrava*) for future karma (*sāṃparāyika-karman*).

Here it is objected: since the three types of activity (*yoga*) have all things as their object, they are common to all transmigrating beings; therefore, there would be no distinction regarding the experience of the fruits of bondage. To this it is replied: this is not so.

Since, even though they arise within each individual, a distinction among them is admitted in relation to the infinite varieties of the transformations of the life-monad (jīva); if one asks how this is so, it is said:
their distinction [arises] from the distinctions of intensity, mildness, known or unknown state, locus, and energy (vīrya).
Transformation that is intensified by the force of external or internal causes is "intense" (*tīvra*). Its opposite is "weak" (*manda*).
Engagement [in action] after having known, "This living being must be killed by me," is called "known" (*jñāta*).
Engaging in action through intoxication or negligence without understanding is "acting unknowingly.
That in which objects are contained is called an "adhikaraṇa" (locus); the meaning is "substance" (*dravya*).
The specific capacity inherent in a substance is "vigor" (*vīrya*).
The word *bhāva* (state/intensity) applies to each [of the three roots] individually—such as "intense state," "weak state," and so forth.
From these, a distinction arises for that influx (*āsrava*).
For, from a difference in cause, there is a difference in effect.
Here it is said: "The locus (*adhikaraṇa*) has been mentioned, but its essential nature (*svarūpa*) is not yet known; therefore, let that be explained.
To this end, for the purpose of ascertaining the essential nature of the locus by means of demonstrating its divisions, he says:
The subject matter consists of living beings and non-living beings.
Living beings and non-living beings have been defined as previously stated.
If they already possess the characteristics previously stated, for what purpose is there a repetition? The repetition is for the purpose of making known a specific category (*adhikaraṇa*).
It is intended to make known this specific distinction: that living beings (*jīva*) and non-living things (*ajīva*) constitute the category.
What, then, is this [distinction]? It is their state of being instruments (*upakaraṇa*) for violence and so forth.
It might be argued that because there are two fundamental categories, the dual number "living and non-living" (*jīvājīvau*) is logically required.
That is not so, because it is the *paryāyas* (modal states) that constitute the substrata.
Since a substance qualified by any particular *paryāya* constitutes the substratum—and not the general category itself—the plural number has been employed.
To whom do living beings, non-living beings, and the instruments of action belong? To influx (āsrava).
The connection is established by the force of the context.
In this regard, in order to establish the distinction between the soul and its substratum, he says:

"The first [set of activities] is threefold each by way of exertion (*saṃrambha*), preparation (*samārambha*), and commencement (*ārambha*); it is thirtyfold by way of performance, causing to be performed, and approval; and it is fourfold by way of the specific passions (*kaṣāya*). (624)
*Saṃrambha* is the application of effort by one who is negligent regarding the taking of life and other such acts.
*Samārambha* is the preparation, the undertaking, or the commencement [of the means].
The meaning of the word *yoga* has already been explained.
The term "done" (*kṛta*) is for the purpose of establishing independence;
the expression "caused to be done" (*kārita*) depends upon the instigation by another;
and the word "consented to" (*anumata*) is for the purpose of demonstrating the mental transformation of the instigator.
The passions (*kaṣāya*) such as anger and so forth are defined by their specific characteristics.

A "distinction" (*viśeṣa*) is that which differentiates an object from other objects; this term is applied to each [subsequent item], such as "the distinction of impetuousness" (*saṃrambhaviśeṣa*), "the distinction of undertaking" (*samārambhaviśeṣa*), and so on.
The first section concerning the soul (*jīvādhikaraṇa*) is "divided" by these specific distinctions; this is the completion of the sentence.

These four words ending in the suffix *su*—namely, the words beginning with *tri* (three)—are connected respectively: the three [types of] exertion (*saṃrambha*, *samārambha*, and *ārambha*), the three [types of] yoga, the three [types of action]—done, caused to be done, and approved—and the four passions (*kaṣāya*).
The repetition in counting these is indicated by the suffix *su*.
"Each one" (*ekaśas*) is an indication of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*).
The meaning is that one should lead each individual [element] through three or more divisions.

For example—bodily agitation caused by anger, bodily agitation caused by pride, bodily agitation caused by deceit, bodily agitation caused by greed; bodily agitation instigated by anger, bodily agitation instigated by pride, bodily agitation instigated by deceit, bodily agitation instigated by greed; and bodily agitation consented to by anger, bodily agitation consented to by pride, bodily agitation consented to by deceit, and bodily agitation consented to by greed—thus there are twelve types of bodily agitation. Likewise, there are twelve types of agitation regarding vocal activity and mental activity.
These, when totaled, are thirty-six; likewise, the *samārambhas* are also thirty-six, and the *ārambhas* are also thirty-six.
When these varieties of *jīva-adhikaraṇa-āsrava* are combined, they amount to one hundred and eight in number.
The word "and" (*ca*) is intended to include the internal subdivisions created by the distinctions between the *anantānubandhin*, *apratyākhyāna*, *pratyākhyāna*, and *saṃjvalana* passions.
To explain the distinctions for the sake of understanding the subdivisions of the external basis of non-living things (ajīvādhikaraṇa), he says:
"Production, depositing, conjunction, and emission have two, four, two, and three subdivisions respectively, in relation to the external."
It is called "completion" (*nirvartanā*) because it is brought to completion;
it is called "deposition" (*nikṣepa*) because it is deposited, that is, established.
"Conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) means being joined together, that is, being mixed.
"Emission" (*nisarga*) means being released, that is, setting forth.

These are connected respectively with the groups of two and so on: accomplishment (*nirvartanā*) is of two kinds, depositing (*nikṣepa*) is of four kinds, conjunction is of two kinds, and emission is of three kinds.
These are to be understood as the divisions of the non-living substratum (*ajīvādhikaraṇa*). [Objection:

The subsequent statement is purposeless, because since the first [category] was already mentioned in the preceding sūtra, this [subsequent one] would merely be for the sake of what remains. [Response:
It is not purposeless.
The word *para* has a different meaning [here].

Actions such as *nirvartanā* (production) are distinct from *saṃrambha* (agitation) and the others. For otherwise, since *nirvartanā* and the rest involve the transformation of one's own self (*ātmapariṇāma*), they would be understood merely as varieties of the *jīvādhikaraṇa* (karmic activity pertaining to the soul).
The *nirvartanādhikaraṇa* is twofold: the *nirvartanādhikaraṇa* of the primary qualities (*mūlaguṇa*) and the *nirvartanādhikaraṇa* of the secondary qualities (*uttaraguṇa*).
In that regard, the accomplishment of the fundamental virtues (*mūlaguṇa*) is fivefold: [restraint of] body, speech, mind, inhalation, and exhalation.
The accomplishment of the secondary virtues (*uttaraguṇa*) includes woodwork, basketry, painting, and so forth.

Deposits (*nikṣepa*) are fourfold: the basis of depositing without inspection, the basis of depositing after improper wiping, the basis of impulsive depositing, and the basis of depositing without careful consideration.
Natural outflow is threefold: the basis for the natural outflow of the body, the basis for the natural outflow of speech, and the basis for the natural outflow of the mind.
Thus has the general classification of the influx of karma been stated.
Now, the distinction of the influx (*āsrava*) of specific types of karma must be stated.

Regarding that which is to be stated, in order to understand the distinction of the influx of the first two—namely, knowledge-obscuring (*jñānāvaraṇa*) and perception-obscuring (*darśanāvaraṇa*) karma—he says:
"Malice toward them, concealment, envy, obstruction, deprival, and injury [are the causes] of knowledge- and perception-obscuring karma."
When the knowledge of reality, which is the means to liberation, has been proclaimed, *pradoṣa* (malice) is the internal transformation of malice toward someone who remains silent.
*Nihnava* (concealment) is the denial of knowledge, such as saying "it does not exist" or "I do not know," due to some cause.
Miserliness (*mātsarya*) is that because of which consciousness, though cultivated for some reason and though worthy of being given as a gift, is not given.
An obstacle (*antarāya*) is the creation of a partition regarding knowledge.
It is the withholding or disparaging of knowledge that is to be revealed to others through body or speech.
"Affliction" (*upaghāta*) is the disparagement of praiseworthy knowledge.
If it is argued that this is simply "insulting" (*āsādana*), [we reply: insulting is the practice of proclaiming the virtues of existing knowledge, such as its discipline and so forth;
whereas affliction is the intention to destroy knowledge by treating knowledge itself as ignorance.
Thus, this is the distinction between these two.
By the word "that" (tat), there is a reference back to knowledge and vision.
But how can there be a reference by means of the word "that" to two things that have not been introduced and have not been mentioned? It is possible by virtue of the question.

When the question is asked, "What is the influx (āsrava) for knowledge-obscuring (jñānāvaraṇa) and perception-obscuring (darśanāvaraṇa) [karmas]?", the pronoun *tat* refers back to knowledge and perception in relation to that question.
By this, malice and the like are to be applied to those possessing knowledge and perception, as well as to their means, because they are the causes thereof.
These are the causes of influx for knowledge-obscuring and perception-obscuring [karmas].

Since multiple effects are observed to be produced by a single cause, the influx (*āsrava*) of both knowledge-obscuring (*jñānāvaraṇa*) and perception-obscuring (*darśanāvaraṇa*) karma is established even when the defilements (*pradoṣa*) and other factors are identical. Alternatively, there is a distinction between the influxes due to the distinction between their objects: the defilements directed toward objects of knowledge constitute the influx of knowledge-obscuring karma, while the defilements directed toward objects of perception constitute the influx of perception-obscuring karma.

§ 629. Just as there are these distinctions among the influxes (*āsrava*) of these two types of karma, so too are suffering, grief, torment, lamentation, killing, and wailing— whether residing in oneself, in another, or in both— the [fruits] of unwholesome feeling (*asadvedya*).
Suffering is transformation characterized by affliction.
Grief is a particular state of despondency resulting from the severance of a relationship with that which is beneficial.
Suffering (*tāpa*) is the intense latent affliction (*anuśaya*) of one whose internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) has become turbid due to the causes of slander and the like.
Lamentation (*ākrandana*) is the act of crying out clearly, characterized by the shedding of tears born of intense distress and abundant wailing.
Killing (*vadha*) is that which effects the separation from life-span (*āyus*), faculties (*indriya*), strength (*bala*), and vital breath (*prāṇa*).

Lamentation (*paridevana*) is weeping characterized by an abundance of compassion, directed toward objects that involve the transformation and defilement [of the aggregates], preceded by the recollection and proclamation of virtues, and having as its object the desire to benefit oneself and others.

Now, since grief (*śoka*) and the rest are specific types of suffering, should one not simply include them under the term "suffering" (*duḥkha*)? This is true; nevertheless, by specifying certain particular instances, their conformity to the general category of suffering is established.

Just as when the word "cow" is uttered, because its specific characteristics are not yet known, particulars such as "hornless," "tailed," "black," or "white" are employed to convey those specifics; so too, when "suffering" is mentioned, since the specific instances are not yet known due to the possibility of innumerable varieties of worlds that are objects of suffering, the understanding of those specific instances is achieved by pointing out a few particular cases.
These aforementioned [instances], beginning with suffering, exist within oneself, within others, or in both, arising from the possession of anger and other passions.
All of these should be understood as causes for the influx (*āsrava*) of unwholesome karma (*asat-vedya*).

Here an objection is raised: if suffering and the other [passions] residing in oneself, others, or both are caused by the influx (*āsrava*) of unwholesome karma (*asadvedya*), for what purpose do the Arhats practice such causes of suffering as plucking out the hair, fasting, and standing in the heat, and why are they taught to others? This is not a fault, because it was specified that suffering and the rest are causes of the influx of unwholesome karma only when preceded by the internal obsession with anger and the like.

Just as when a physician who is supremely compassionate, free from malice, and self-restrained makes an incision upon a boil, there is no bond of sin even though it is a cause of suffering— this being due solely to the external circumstance—

so too for a monk who is weary of the great suffering of the objects of cyclic existence and whose mind is concentrated on the means for its cessation, there is no bond of sin even though [his actions] are causes of suffering, because there is an absence of the transformation into affliction (*saṃkleśa*) as he engages in action prescribed by the scriptures.
And it has been said:
The causes for the influx of non-pleasant-feeling karma have been explained.
Now, as to what the causes for pleasant-feeling karma are, it is said here:

Compassion for living beings, kindness toward those observing vows, giving, self-restraint while still possessing passion, and the like, as well as forbearance and purity, constitute the experience of pleasant karma (*sadvedya*).
"Living beings" (*bhūta*) means sentient creatures (*prāṇin*), so called because they come into existence in various states of rebirth through the power of the arising of karma.
The vows, beginning with non-violence, will be explained; those who possess them are the "vow-observers" (vratins).
They are of two kinds:
those whose eagerness for the household has ceased.

"Self-restrained" refers to householders who are self-controlled; "both self-restrained and unrestrained" refers to those whose minds are moistened with compassion for others, acting as if the suffering of others were their own. Compassion (*anukampā*) is the state of feeling pity.
Compassion toward living beings and toward those observing vows is "compassion toward living beings and observers of vows."
Giving (*dāna*) is the relinquishing of one's own possessions with the intention of benefiting others.
One who is intent upon the cessation of the causes of *saṃsāra*, yet whose resolve (*āśaya*) is not yet exhausted and who still possesses passion (*sarāga*), is so described.
Restraint (*saṃyama*) is the desisting from unwholesome engagement regarding the sense-faculties of living beings.

The compound *sarāga-saṃyama* means restraint (*saṃyama*) belonging to one who possesses passion (*sarāga*), or restraint that is itself characterized by passion. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is an inclusion of partial restraint (*saṃyamāsaṃyama*), non-willing destruction of karma (*akāmanirjarā*), and the penance of the ignorant (*bālatapaḥ*). Yoga means concentration (*samādhi*), which is to say, right application (*samyak-praṇidhāna*).

The compound *bhūta-vratyanukampā-dāna-sarāga-saṃyamādi-yoga* refers to the yoga consisting of compassion for living beings and those observing vows, giving, and the aforementioned restraint with passion, and so forth.
Patience is the cessation of anger and so forth.
Purity is the relinquishing of the various forms of greed.
The word "iti" has the sense of "in this manner" (or "and so on").
What, then, are those types?
They are: devotion to performing worship of Arhats, service to children, the elderly, and ascetics, and so forth.
Although the term "beings" (*bhūta*) would have sufficed, the inclusion of the term "vow-holders" (*vrati*) is for the purpose of making known that compassion toward them is the primary focus.
These should be known as the influxes (*āsrava*) of pleasant-feeling karma (*sadvedya*).

Now, since the causes of influx for delusion (*moha*), which occupies the intermediate position, must be stated, the following is said in order to demonstrate the cause of influx for its specific variety, namely, the delusion of vision (*darśanamoha*):
Speaking ill of the Kevalins, the Śruta, the Saṅgha, the Dharma, and the Devas is [the cause] of the delusion of vision (darśanamoha).
The Kevalins possess unobscured knowledge.
That which was taught by him and recorded in written form by the Gaṇadharas, who were endowed with supreme intelligence and supernatural powers, is the Śruta (Scripture).
The Saṃgha is the community of ascetics possessed of the Three Jewels.
The Dharma is characterized by non-violence and is taught in that scripture.
The gods are said to consist of four classes.
To proclaim faults that do not exist in great beings who possess virtues is slander.
Slander directed toward these [beings] is a cause for the influx of delusion regarding the views (*darśanamoha*).

Statements such as "the Kevalins subsist on mouthfuls of food" and so forth constitute disparagement of the Kevalins. To describe the consumption of meat and other such things as blameless constitutes disparagement of the Śruti. To manifest [accusations of] Śūdra status, impurity, and so forth constitutes disparagement of the Saṅgha.
To speak such things as, "The Dharma taught by the Jina is devoid of qualities; those who practice it will become asuras," and so forth, is disparagement of the Dharma.
To proclaim such things as the consumption of liquor and meat is disparagement of the gods.

In order to demonstrate the classification of the second type of delusion (*moha*), namely the flow (*āsrava*) of conduct-delusion (*cāritramoha*), he says: "From the arising of the passions (*kaṣāya*), there is an intense transformation (*tīvrapariṇāma*) of conduct-delusion.
The passions (kaṣāya) have been explained.
"Arising" (udaya) means fruition (vipāka).
From the arising of the passions, the influx (āsrava) of conduct-deluding karma (cāritramoha), which consists of intense transformation, is to be understood.

In this regard, the influx (*āsrava*) of *kaṣāyavedanīya* karma consists of provoking passions in oneself and others, defiling the conduct of ascetics, and wearing signs or observing vows that are spiritually defiled.
The influx of *hāsyavedanīya* karma consists of mocking the true Dharma, excessive laughter, lewd joking, much idle chatter, and a habit of derisive laughter.
The influx of *rativedanīya* karma consists of devotion to various forms of play, lack of interest in vows and moral conduct, and so forth.

The manifestation of aversion toward others, the destruction of one's own delight, association with those of evil character, and so forth, are the causes for karma to be experienced as aversion (*arativedanīya*). The production of grief within oneself, the exultation over the immersion of others in grief, and so forth, are the causes for karma to be experienced as grief (*śokavedanīya*).
The transformation of one’s own fear and the production of fear in others, and so forth, are the causes for karma to be experienced as fear (*bhayavedanīya*).
The causes for experiencing the female gender are: a disposition toward loathing and disparaging virtuous conduct, and so forth;
speaking falsehoods, being intent on deceiving others, looking for the vulnerabilities of others, and having increased passion and other such traits.
The causes for experiencing the male gender are: having little anger, lacking eagerness for sensual pleasure, contentment with one’s own wife, and so forth.
Excessive passion, the destruction of the secret organ, and the assault upon another's wife are the causes for the experience of the neuter gender (*napuṃsakavedanīya*).
Thus has the classification of the influx of deluding karma (*mohanīya*) been explained.

Now, since the cause for the outflow (*āsrava*) of the lifespan (*āyus*) mentioned immediately prior must be stated, this is said in order to demonstrate the cause of the first type of lifespan, which ripens after a fixed period:
"The state of having many undertakings and possessions is the cause of hellish lifespan.

*Ārambha* is activity that causes injury to living beings. *Parigraha* is the sense of "this is mine," characterized by the notion of ownership. *Ārambha-parigrahāḥ* refers to both such activities and such possessions.
One who possesses many undertakings and possessions is called "one with many undertakings and possessions" (*bahvārambhaparigraha*).
The state of being such is "the condition of having many undertakings and possessions" (*bahvārambhaparigrahatva*).

This—characterized by the constant engagement in cruel deeds such as violence, greed for the property of others, and the arising of raudra-dhyāna (fierce meditation) born from the black *leśyā*—becomes the influx (*āsrava*) for the life-span of a hell-being.
He said: "The influx of the lifespan of hell-beings has been explained. Now that of animals must be discussed. To this it is replied:

Deceit (*māyā*) is the crooked state of the self manifested through the arising of a specific type of conduct-deluding karma (*cāritramoha-karman*); it is guile (*nikṛti*), and it should be understood as the influx (*āsrava*) for animal life (*tairyagyonika-āyus*).

Its elaboration consists of teaching doctrines endowed with falsity, lack of moral discipline, a fondness for deception, the blue and grey-leśyās, painful meditation, and the time of death, and so forth. He said:
"The influx of the life-span of animals has been explained."
Now, as to what the cause of human lifespan is, it is said here:
the state of having few undertakings and possessions is the cause of human [lifespan].

The influx of hellish lifespan has been explained. Its opposite is the influx of human lifespan; this is the summary. The detailed explanation is as follows: a disciplined nature, natural goodness, upright conduct, thinness of the passions (*kaṣāya*), lack of affliction at the time of death, and so forth.
Is the outflow of human life merely this much? To this it is said:
there is also natural gentleness.
The state of being mild is mildness (*mārdava*). Mildness by its very nature is natural mildness (*svabhāvamārdava*).
The meaning is "independent of instruction.
This too is an influx (*āsrava*) of human lifespan.
For what purpose is a separate formulation made? It is for the sake of what follows, so that this may also be an influx of divine lifespan.
§ 645. Is this alone the second human influx (āsrava)? No; it is said:
and for all [beings], there is the state of being devoid of moral discipline and vows (niśśīlavratatva).

The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of a cumulative conjunction with what precedes: namely, having few undertakings and possessions, and being devoid of [false] moral precepts and observances (*śīla-vrata*).
Moral precepts and observances are "precept-observances" (*śīla-vrata*); these will be explained below.

One who has departed from moral precepts and vows is "one devoid of precepts and vows" (*niḥśīlavrata*). The state of being such is "the condition of being devoid of precepts and vows" (*niḥśīlavratatva*).
The inclusion of the term "of all" (*sarveṣām*) is for the purpose of indicating that this applies to every single lifespan and every influx (*āsrava*).
Does this also apply to the lifespan of the gods? Truly, it does, with reference to those born in the realms of enjoyment.
Now, as to what the influx (*āsrava*) of the fourth lifespan is, it is said here:
Passion-with-restraint, restraint-with-non-restraint, involuntary shedding of karma, and the penance of the ignorant constitute the divine [cause].
Passion-with-restraint and restraint-with-non-restraint have already been explained.

Unwilling effacement (*akāmanirjarā*) is the involuntary [suffering] experienced by those bound in prisons, confinement, or fetters, such as the suppression of hunger and thirst, the practice of celibacy, sleeping on the ground, wearing dirty clothes, and exposure to heat and so forth. Unwilling effacement is effacement occurring without desire.

Foolish austerity (*bālatapaḥ*) is that which is accompanied by false view (*mithyādarśana*), characterized by excessive physical mortification through improper means, and the observance of vows with much hypocrisy.
These should be understood as the causes for the influx of divine lifespan.
Is the influx of divine lifespan limited to these alone?
"No," he says—
"and there is rightness.
What [is meant]? It follows that this refers to the influx (*āsrava*) of divine lifespan (*daivam āyuḥ*).
Although no specific distinction is explicitly stated, the particularity of the Saudharma heaven and so forth is understood.
Why? Because of their separate enumeration.

If this is so, then the rule regarding the influx (*āsrava*) stated in the preceding sūtra applies without distinction; consequently, it would follow that both passion-possessing restraint (*sāra-gasaṃyama*) and partial restraint-non-restraint (*saṃyamāsaṃyama*) are also influxes of the life-span of the celestial beings of the *bhavana* and other realms.
This is not a fault; for since those designations do not apply in the absence of right view (*samyaktva*), both of these are included here [within the category of non-influx].§ 651.

Since the outflow (*āsrava*) of *nāman* was taught immediately after *āyus*, and its method must now be explained, he says the following regarding the realization of the outflow of the inauspicious (*aśubha*) *nāman*:
"Crookedness of application (*yogavakratā*) and deception are the outflow of the inauspicious *nāman*.
Yoga has been explained as being of three kinds.
Its crookedness is its deviousness;
it is the act of deceiving or proceeding in a contrary manner.
But is there not a difference in meaning?

Is it not simply that "crookedness of application" (*yogavakratā*) is the act of proceeding otherwise? True, this is so; however, what is called "crookedness of application" here is internal (*svagata*), whereas [the other] is deception directed toward others (*paragata*).

One who engages in activities for the sake of right worldly prosperity and the highest good deceives another—who is acting in the opposite manner—by means of contrary body, speech, and mind, saying, "Do not do this; do it thus.
Both of these should be understood as causes for the influx of karma named *aśubha*.
By the word "and" (*ca*), false views, backbiting, instability of mind, the use of false weights and measures, reviling others, praising oneself, and so forth, are included.
Now, as to what the influx (*āsrava*) of wholesome karma (*śubha-nāma-karman*) is, it is said here:
for the wholesome, it is the opposite of that [unwholesome influx].
Rectitude and non-deceptiveness of body, speech, and mind are the opposites of their contraries.
By the word "and" (*ca*), the opposite of that which is conjoined [with them] is also to be understood.
This includes reverence for the vision of the Dharma, the cultivation of its true existence, fear of cyclic existence, and the avoidance of negligence;
this should be understood as the cause for the influx of karma characterized by auspicious names.

He asked: "Is the method for the influx (*āsrava*) of that which is called 'auspicious' (*śubha*) limited to this alone, or is there some specific distinction? To this it is said: regarding this *tīrthaṃkara-nāma-karma*—which possesses infinite and incomparable power, is the cause of inconceivable and extraordinary majesty, and effects victory over the three worlds—there exists a specific method for its influx.
If this is so, let it be told: what is its influx?
Therefore, this [section] is commenced.

Purity of vision (*darśanaviśuddhi*), perfection in discipline (*vinayasampannatā*), non-transgression regarding vows and observances (*śīlavrateṣv anatīcāraḥ*), frequent application of knowledge and spiritual agitation (*abhīkṣṇajñānopayoga-saṃvegau*), renunciation and austerity according to one’s capacity (*śaktitas tyāga-tapasī*), right concentration (*sādhusamādhiḥ*), service (*vaiyāvṛttyakaraṇam*), devotion toward the Arhats, the Teachers, the learned, and the Scripture (*arhad-ācārya-bahuśruta-pravacanabhaktiḥ*), non-neglect of the obligatory duties (*āvaśyakāparihāṇiḥ*), glorification of the Path (*mārgaprabhāvanā*), and affection for the Teaching (*pravacanavatsalatvam*)—these constitute the state of being a Tīrthaṅkara.

Purity of vision is the inclination toward the path to liberation characterized by the marks of a Nirgrantha as taught by the Blessed Jina, the Supreme Arhat; it possesses the characteristics previously described.
It has eight limbs: freedom from fear, freedom from doubt, absence of hesitation, unclouded vision, nourishment, stabilization, affection, and manifestation.

"Perfection in discipline" (*vinayasaṃpannatā*) is the state of being endowed with respect and reverence toward right knowledge and the other paths to liberation, as well as toward the teachers and others who facilitate them, through conduct appropriate to oneself.

"Non-transgression regarding conduct and vows" (*śīlavratānatīcāra*) is faultless behavior regarding the vows such as non-violence and the ethical rules such as the avoidance of anger, which serve to maintain those vows.

Constant application to right knowledge regarding the true nature of categories such as the living being (jīva) is the frequent employment of cognition. A state of constant fear of the sufferings of saṃsāra is spiritual urgency (saṃvega).
Renunciation is giving.
That [generosity] is threefold: the gift of food, the gift of fearlessness, and the gift of knowledge.

When these are practiced according to one's capacity and in accordance with the rules, they are called "renunciation" (*tyāga*). Austerity (*tapas*) is bodily exertion that does not conceal one's vigor and is not contrary to the Path.

Just as when a fire breaks out in a storehouse, its suppression is carried out because it is of great benefit, so too, when some obstacle arises to the austerity of a sage who is enriched by many vows and moral precepts, the maintenance of that austerity is *samādhi*. When suffering befalls one endowed with virtues, the removal of that [suffering] by means of a blameless method is *vaiyāvṛtya*. Devotion (*bhakti*) is an affection characterized by purity of intention toward the Arhats, the teachers, those of great learning, and the teaching.
The non-neglect of the necessary duties is the timely performance of the six essential rites (*ṣaḍ-āvaśyaka*).
The illumination of the Path is the proclamation of the Dharma according to the rules for knowledge, austerity, charity, and the worship of the Jinas.
Affection toward one who possesses the nature of a calf toward its mother is "fondness for the teaching" (*pravacanavatsalatva*).
These sixteen causes, when properly cultivated either individually or collectively, are to be understood as the causes for the *nāmakarma* of a Tīrthaṅkara.

Now, since the influx of lineage (*gotrāsrava*) must be explained immediately after the explanation of the influx of name (*nāmāsrava*), he says this in order to establish the influx of the lowly lineage (*nīcairgotra*).
§ 658. Self-deprecation and self-praise, as well as the concealing and manifesting of one's own good and bad qualities, constitute the low family [disposition].
Blame is the desire to manifest a fault, whether it be real or unreal.
Praise is the intention to manifest virtues.
The connection is according to their respective order: namely, disparaging others and praising oneself.
Suppression is the non-manifestation, that is, the state of having unmanifested activity when an obstructing cause is present.
The manifestation of qualities through the removal of obstacles is "exaltation.
Here too, the connection is to be understood according to the sequence: the concealment of true virtues and the manifestation of false virtues.
These are to be known as the causes for the influx [of karma] into one of low lineage.
Now, the method regarding the outflows (*āsrava*) for one of high lineage is stated here:
its opposite [is the case] for one of low [lineage], and for the latter, there is lack of arrogance in conduct.
By the word "that" (*tat*), through proximity, the outflow (*āsrava*) of the low lineage (*nīcairgotra*) is indicated.
Occurrence in another manner is its opposite (*viparyaya*).
The opposite of that is its reverse.
What, then, is this reverse? It is self-reproach, praising others, proclaiming good qualities, and concealing bad qualities.
Toward those superior in virtue, it is humility through modesty and a lowly manner of conduct.
Even though one is superior by virtue of consciousness and so forth, the absence of intoxication produced by those [qualities] is non-conceit (*anahaṃkāratā*) and lack of arrogance (*anutseka*).
These are the causes for the influx of the higher lineage (*uccairgotra*).

Now, regarding the obstacle (*antarāya*) mentioned immediately after the spiritual lineage (*gotra*), it is stated: what is the outflow (*āsrava*) of the obstacle? It is the act of creating an impediment.
Generosity and the other [perfections] were mentioned in the passage: "generosity, gain, enjoyment, utilization, and vigor.

The obstruction of these is "hindrance" (vighna). The act of creating such hindrance is "the creation of hindrance" (vighnakaraṇa); this should be understood as the method of influx (āsrava) for obstacles (antarāya).

Here an objection is raised: malice toward them (*tatpradoṣa*), concealment (*nihnava*), and so forth, have been described as the specific causes of influx (*āsrava*) for knowledge-obscuring (*jñānāvaraṇa*), perception-obscuring (*darśanāvaraṇa*), and other karmas. Are these exclusively the specific causes of influx for knowledge-obscuring karma and the rest, or are they [causes] without distinction? If they are exclusively the specific causes of influx for knowledge-obscuring karma and the rest, it would entail a contradiction with the scripture (*āgama*). For in the scripture it is stated that, with the exception of life-span (*āyus*), the seven karmas flow into the soul simultaneously at every moment.
That would constitute a contradiction.

Now, if it is argued that since the causes of the influx (*āsrava*) are stated without distinction, a specific designation [of their subdivisions] is not appropriate, it is replied as follows: although there is no fixed rule regarding the bondage of space-points (*pradeśabandha*) for all types of karma (*karmaprakṛti*), such as knowledge-obscuring (*jñānāvaraṇa*) and the rest, due to malice toward them (*tatpradoṣa*) and so forth, nevertheless, malice toward them, concealment (*nihnava*), and the like are categorized as the causes for the fixed rule of intensity (*anubhāga*).
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the *Tattvārthavṛtti* known as the *Sarvārthasiddhi*. 6.13–20.
Now begins the seventh chapter.
The category of the outflows (*āsrava*) has been explained.
At the very beginning of that [work], it was stated that "the auspicious [leads] to merit"; this was stated in general terms.
To understand its specific nature, when the question "What, then, is the auspicious? is asked, this is said:
abstention from violence, falsehood, theft, unchastity, and possessiveness is the vow (*vrata*).
By means of such aphorisms as "Harm is the depriving of life through negligent application," harm and the other [vices] will be defined.
Abstention from these is called *virati*, which is to say, a vow (*vrata*).
A *niyama* is a restriction undertaken with a specific intention (*abhisandhi*), such as "this must be done" or "this must not be done.

Now, one might ask: since violence and the like are particular modifications of thought (*pariṇāma-viśeṣa*) and are therefore unstable, how can they be said to function as the point of departure (*apādāna*)? This is possible because, when the modification of the intellect (*buddhi*) ceases, there is a legitimate desire to express their stability [at that moment]. For example, in the expression "he desists from dharma," a person whose intellect is still clouded perceives: "Dharma is difficult to practice, and its fruit is accessible only through faith. Having reached this conclusion through his intellect, he turns away.

Likewise here too, that person who acts with foresight perceives: "These transformations such as violence and so forth are causes of sin. Kings punish people in this very world when they engage in sinful actions, and they experience suffering in the next world. Having understood this through his intellect, he desists.
Therefore, since the intention to express constancy (*dhruvatva*) is established by means of the intellect, it is logical for [the object] to have the status of an *apādāna* (ablative).
The word *virati* (abstinence) is completed with each [term], as in "abstinence from violence," "abstinence from falsehood," and so forth.
Among these, the vow of non-violence (*ahiṃsā-vrata*) is undertaken first because of its preeminence;
for truthfulness and the other vows serve to protect it, just as a fence surrounds a crop.
With respect to the *sāmāyika* characterized by the cessation of all blameworthy actions, there is one vow; that same [vow] is said here to be fivefold with respect to *chedopasthāpanā*.
But is it not the case that the status of this vow as a cause of influx (*āsrava*) is untenable, since it is included among the causes of restraint (*saṃvara*)?
The causes of restraint will be explained as the restraints (*gupti*), the codes of conduct (*samiti*), and so forth.

In that regard, is the inclusion of the vows (*vrata*) within the tenfold *dharma* or *saṃyama* not a flaw? This is not a flaw; for in that context, *saṃvara* will be described as having the characteristic of cessation (*nivṛtti*).

Here, however, activity (*pravṛtti*) is observed; because in the renunciation of injury, falsehood, taking what is not given, and so forth, there is the perception of the performance of non-injury, truthful speech, giving, and so on, and because [the vows] serve as the preparatory purification (*parikarma*) for the restraints (*saṃvara*) such as the three types of protection (*gupti*), a virtuous person who has performed this purification easily achieves *saṃvara*. Therefore, they are taught separately.
But is it not the case that there is a sixth minor vow, the abstention from eating at night, which should be included here? No; because it is included within the meditations (*bhāvanās*).
For the meditations on the vow of non-violence will be explained below.
Among those, the meditation on "eating and drinking only what has been inspected" is to be practiced.
To explain the breach of that fivefold vow, he says: "Partial and complete, small and great."
"A region" (deśa) is a partial area;
"the whole" (sarva) is the entirety.
*Deśa* means partial and *sarva* means whole; from those two, [the compound] *deśasarvataḥ*.
The term “abstinence” (*virati*) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule].
*Aṇu* means small and *mahat* means large; [the compound] *aṇumahatī*.
The neuter gender is used because of its connection with the word *vrata* (vow).

It is connected according to their respective order: "abstinence from [harm] in a limited sense is a minor vow (*aṇuvrata*), while abstinence in every respect is a major vow (*mahāvrata*). Thus, each vow is divided into two types.

These vows, when cultivated, become causes for the cessation of suffering for one who exerts effort, like an excellent medicine. Regarding the purpose and the manner of their cultivation, it is said here:
For the sake of stabilizing those [vows], there are five meditative cultivations for each.
To ensure the firmness of those vows, it should be understood that there are five meditative cultivations for each individual vow.
If this is so, what are the meditations (*bhāvanā*) for the first vow, non-violence (*ahiṃsā*)? To this it is said:
there are five—guarding of speech and mind, care in taking up and putting down [objects], and drinking and eating after inspection.

Guarding speech, guarding the mind, carefulness in walking, carefulness in taking up and setting down objects, and eating and drinking after inspection— these are the five meditations for the vow of non-violence.
Now, as to what constitutes the second vow, it is said here:
The renunciation of anger, greed, fearfulness, and frivolous laughter, as well as speech that is consistent with reality— these five,

namely, the renunciation of anger, the renunciation of greed, the renunciation of fearfulness, the renunciation of frivolous laughter, and speech that is not inconsistent with reality, are to be known as the five meditations of the vow of truth.
"Speaking in accordance with [the truth]" means speaking blamelessly.
Now, regarding what the cultivation of the third vow is, he says:
There are five [qualities] identical to the purity of alms-seeking: dwelling in empty houses, not causing obstruction to others, and non-deception regarding the true Dharma.
Dwelling in empty houses refers to residing in mountain caves, hollows of trees, and so forth.
One should dwell in lodgings belonging to others that have been made available;
one should not cause obstruction to others;
and one should maintain purity in alms-seeking according to the path of the treatises on proper conduct.
"Not to dispute with those who share the same Dharma regarding 'this is mine' or 'this is yours'":
these are the five meditations on the vow of abstaining from taking what is not given.
Now, the cultivation of the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya-vrata*) must be explained; regarding this, he says:

the abandonment of listening to talk about women, gazing at their charming limbs, recollecting former sexual pleasures, using aphrodisiacs or desirable flavors, and grooming one's own body—these are the five [abstinences].
The word "renunciation" (tyāga) applies to each [item] individually.

The five meditations (*bhāvanā*) of the fourth vow are to be understood as follows: renunciation of listening to stories about passion for women; renunciation of gazing at their captivating limbs; renunciation of recollecting former sexual pleasures; renunciation of aphrodisiacs and desirable flavors; and renunciation of grooming one's own body.
Now, what is the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of the fifth vow? To this it is said:
the five [cultivations] consist in the avoidance of attachment and aversion toward agreeable and disagreeable objects of the senses.

When desirable or undesirable objects have presented themselves to the five sense-faculties, such as touch and the rest, the abandonment of attachment toward those touches and so forth should be understood as the five meditations (*bhāvanā*) for the vow of non-possession (*ākiṃcanya*).
Furthermore, just as these meditations are prescribed by the wise for the sake of strengthening these vows, so too [should they be practiced] regarding things that oppose them; thus he says:
§ 679. Regarding violence and other such acts, one should perceive their misfortune and fault both in this world and the next.
"Misfortune" (*apāya*) refers to an application that destroys actions intended for higher rebirth (*abhyudaya*) and the ultimate good (*niḥśreyasa*).

*Avadya* means blameworthy. *Apāya* (misfortune) and *avadya* (blame) together constitute *apāyāvadye*; one should cultivate the vision of these two, *apāyāvadyadarśana*. Where? Both in this world and in the next.
In what [actions]? In killing and so forth.

If it is asked "How so?", it is said: first, regarding killing—a killer is constantly to be feared and is perpetually bound by enmity; he receives execution, imprisonment, and afflictions in this world, and after death, an inauspicious rebirth, and he becomes despised. Thus, desisting from killing is better.

Likewise, a speaker of falsehood becomes untrustworthy; even in this world, he suffers such punishments as the cutting off of his tongue, and from those who are tormented by his false accusations and harbor enmity toward him, he encounters many calamities. After death, he goes to an inauspicious rebirth and becomes despised. Therefore, it is better to abstain from speaking untruth. Similarly, a thief, being addicted to seizing the property of others, becomes a source of terror to everyone.

In this very life, one encounters beating, killing, imprisonment, and the amputation of hands, feet, ears, nose, or upper lips, as well as piercing, the seizure of all one's property, and so forth; and after death, one goes to an inauspicious rebirth and becomes despised. Therefore, abstaining from theft is superior.

Likewise, one who practices unchastity—with a mind wandering in the delusions of intoxication—is like a wild elephant deceived by the scent of a female; rendered helpless, he undergoes the afflictions of execution, imprisonment, and torture. Because he is overwhelmed by delusion, he is ignorant of what ought and ought not to be done and performs no wholesome deed. Finding pleasure in the embrace and contact with another’s wife, he incurs enmity even in this life and encounters calamities such as mutilation, execution, imprisonment, and the confiscation of all his property. After death, he experiences an inauspicious rebirth and becomes an object of reproach; therefore, abstention from it is for one's own welfare.

Likewise, one who possesses possessions is like a bird that has seized a piece of meat; even in this very life, he becomes subject to being overcome by other birds seeking that same prey, as well as by thieves and others. He incurs many faults arising from the acquisition, preservation, and loss of those things, and yet he finds no satisfaction, just as fire is never satiated with fuel. Because he is overwhelmed by greed, he disregards what ought and ought not to be done, and after death he falls into an inauspicious rebirth. Furthermore, he is despised, being reviled as "this greedy man. Therefore, abstaining from such attachment is better.
In this way, one should cultivate the perception of the misfortune and the fault inherent in violence and other such acts.
To demonstrate another method of cultivation regarding violence and so forth, he says:
Or rather, one should cultivate the reflection that violence and the like are indeed suffering, for they are nothing but suffering.
How are violence and the like suffering? Because they are causes of suffering, just as it is said, "Food is indeed the life-breaths.
Or else, because they are the cause of the cause.
Just as it is said that "life is wealth," meaning that life has food and drink as its cause,
so too violence and the like are the causes of karma to be experienced as unpleasant (*asātavedya*).

Furthermore, since karma that is experienced as unpleasant (*asadvedya*) is a cause of suffering, the term "suffering" is applied metaphorically to that which is a cause of suffering, or to the cause of the cause of suffering.
Thus, one should understand that these [forms of karma] are indeed suffering, a realization to be witnessed by oneself and others.

Now, one might object: "But is not all of that necessarily suffering? For there exists the pleasure of delight in sense objects. This is not true pleasure, because it is merely a remedy for pain, like scratching an itch.
Furthermore, he speaks of another stage of cultivation:
"Loving-kindness, sympathetic joy, compassion, and equanimity toward beings who possess virtues, those who are superior, those who are afflicted, and those who are to be trained."
Loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is the aspiration that others may not experience suffering. Joy (*pramoda*) is the internal absence of passion manifested through such signs as a brightened countenance.
Compassion is the disposition of favoring the distressed.
Impartiality is the absence of partiality preceded by attachment or aversion.
Sentient beings (*sattvas*) are living creatures (*jīvas*) who sink into various wombs due to the ripening of their evil karma.
Those who are superior by virtue of right knowledge and other qualities are "those with superior qualities.
Those afflicted by the suffering brought about by the arising of non-meritorious karma are "those being afflicted.
Those who have not acquired qualities through hearing and grasping the true meaning [of the teachings] are "those who are not to be trained."
Toward these beings and others, one should cultivate loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables] in their respective order:
loving-kindness toward all beings, sympathetic joy toward those possessing virtues and the like, compassion toward those who are suffering, and equanimity toward those who are undisciplined.
For one who cultivates in this way, the vows of non-violence and the rest become perfected.
Furthermore, he speaks of another meditation:
"Alternatively, [one meditates on] the world and the body as having the nature [of suffering], for the sake of spiritual urgency and dispassion."
The nature of the world is thus without beginning and without end, resembling a cane seat, a *jhallarī* drum, or a *mṛdaṅga* drum.
Within this, sentient beings wander through endless time in various states of existence within beginningless saṃsāra, repeatedly experiencing suffering.
And herein nothing whatsoever is permanent: life is like a bubble on water, and the abundance of enjoyments is as fickle as the shifting forms of lightning and clouds.
Through such reflection upon the nature of the world, a sense of spiritual urgency regarding cyclic existence arises.

The intrinsic nature of the body consists of impermanence, being the cause of suffering, insubstantiality, and impurity. Through such contemplation on the intrinsic nature of the body, detachment arises from the cessation of passion for sense objects. Thus, the world and the intrinsic nature of the body should be meditated upon. § 686.
Here he says: You have stated that there is a vow consisting of abstention from violence and so forth; however, we do not know what those specific actions such as violence are. To this it is replied:
because it is impossible to state their definitions all at once, they will be explained in the order of their occurrence. First, that which was mentioned at the outset is now stated:
*Violence (hiṃsā) is the depriving of life through the activity of a careless person (pramatta-yoga)*.
Negligence (*pramāda*) is the state of being possessed of passions (*kaṣāya*); one who possesses that [state] is a negligent self-transformation (*ātmapariṇāma*).

The activity (*yoga*) of a negligent person is "negligent activity" (*pramattayoga*). From that negligent activity, the ten vitalities (*prāṇa*), beginning with the sense organs, are [derived]; the deprivation or causing the separation of these, as far as possible, is designated as "violence" (*hiṃsā*).
That [killing] is a cause of unrighteousness because it is a cause of suffering for living beings.
The qualification "through negligent application" is for the purpose of making known that the mere taking of life is not necessarily unrighteousness.
And it has been said: "He separates [the being from its life] but is not joined with impurities through the act of killing."

And it has been said: "If a kulīṅga insect should die in a hole or a crevice at the place of exit when the foot of one who is restrained in conduct (īryā-samita) is lifted, he would incur a fault for that occasion."

For indeed, not even the slightest bondage caused by that [act] is taught in the doctrine; rather, it is declared according to the authority of the inner self (*adhyātma*) that there is delusion and possessiveness.
And is it not the case that even in the absence of the actual taking of life, injury (*hiṃsā*) is held to occur merely through the connection with negligence (*pramatta-yoga*)?

And it has been said: "Whether the living being dies or lives, for one who acts without self-restraint there is certainly violence; but for one who is disciplined and restrained, there is no bondage through the mere act of violence.
This is not a fault.
In this case as well, there is the taking of life characterized by a state of being.
Thus it has been said: "The self, being negligent, first destroys itself by itself; the killing of other living beings may or may not follow afterwards."
If a kuliṅga insect should die upon being stepped on by the foot of one practicing restraint in movement (īryā-samiti) while exiting his dwelling or entering a village,
that person does not incur even the slightest bondage caused by that act; so it is taught in the sacred doctrine (samyag-vākya).
Regarding "possession through delusion," it is said according to the standard of one's own inner state:
whether the soul dies or lives, for one of uncontrolled conduct there is certainly violence; however, for one who is restrained and diligent, there is no bondage through the mere act of violence.
The self, being heedless, first destroys itself by its own means; the killing of other living beings may or may not follow afterwards. § 688.
He said: "Violence has indeed been defined.
What is the definition of falsehood, which was mentioned immediately after that? To this it is replied: Falsehood is the utterance of what is untrue."
*Sacchandaḥ* is a word expressing praise;
that is to say, it refers to what is good or excellent, as opposed to what is bad or unpraiseworthy.
The expression of a non-existent object is a false expression; it is untruth (*anṛta*).
Truth (*ṛta*) is reality; that which is not truth is untruth.
What, then, is reprehensible? That which causes harm to living beings is reprehensible, whether its object is an existing thing or a non-existing thing.
And it has already been stated that the other vows exist for the sake of maintaining the vow of non-violence (*ahiṃsā*).
Therefore, it must be concluded that speech which causes harm is untruth (*anṛta*).
Now, regarding theft (*steya*), which was mentioned immediately after falsehood (*anṛta*), he states what its definition is:
"Theft is the taking of what has not been given" (§ 691).
Taking—that is, seizing—what has not been given is called "taking what is not given" (*adattādāna*), which is theft (*steya*).

If this were the case, then even the taking of *karma* and *nokarma* would result in theft, since they have not been given by another. This is not a fault, for the conventional designation of theft applies only where giving and taking are possible.
Why?
[This is] because of the force of the term "taking what is not given.

Even so, does it not follow that when a monk wanders through villages, cities, and the like, there would be the offense of taking what is not given due to entering streets, gates, and so forth? This is not a fault, because [the rule] is stated in general terms.
For instance, this monk does not enter places where the doors are closed and so on, because he has not been granted permission.
Alternatively, the phrase "through careless application" (*apramattayogāt*) is understood to carry over [from the preceding rule].
That which is taking what is not given through careless application is called theft (*steya*).
And for one who is merely entering a street or similar place, there is no careless application.
Therefore, this is what is meant: wherever there is activity through the transformation of defilement, there theft occurs, whether in the grasping or the non-grasping of an external object.
Now, as for the fourth [unvirtuous action], unchastity (*abrahmacarya*), what is its characteristic? To this it is said:
Sexual intercourse (*maithuna*) is non-celibacy (*abrahma*).
When the deluding karma of conduct (*cāritramoha*) arises, the desire for mutual touch between a man and a woman who are possessed by a transformation of passion is sexual intercourse.
The activity of a couple is called "sexual intercourse" (maithuna), not every kind of activity.
Why? Because it is so well-established in common worldly usage and in the scriptures.
In the world, first of all, from cowherds upward, the activity of men and women resulting from the transformation of passion is known as sexual intercourse (*maithuna*).
In the scriptures as well, in such passages as "when there is a desire for sexual intercourse between a horse and a bull," that very same thing is understood.

Furthermore, the phrase "from careless application" (*pramattayogāt*) carries over [from the preceding rule]; therefore, sexual intercourse is understood here as that activity directed toward the union of a man and a woman which is afflicted by the pleasure of passion, and not every kind of activity.
That in which virtues such as non-violence flourish and attain growth when it is protected is *brahman*. That which is not *brahman* is *abrahman*.
What is that? It is sexual intercourse.
For therein the defects such as violence and the like flourish;

because one who is intent upon indulging in sexual intercourse harms stationary and moving living beings, utters false speech, takes what is not given, and seizes both insentient and other sentient property as possession.
Now, as to what the characteristic of the fifth appropriation is, he says: "Fainting is appropriation.
It is called *mūrchā*.

What is *mūrchā*? *Mūrchā* is the non-abandonment (*avyāvṛtti*) characterized by the guarding, acquisition, and embellishment of external things—such as cattle, buffaloes, gems, and pearls—which are both sentient and insentient, as well as internal acquisitions (*upadhi*) such as passion and the like.

[Objection: But in the world, it is well known that a specific disturbance of wind and the other humors is called *mūrchā*; why is that not included here? [Response: This is true; however, this root *mūrch* functions in the general sense of delusion (*moha*).
When it is said that "general injunctions apply to specific instances," that which is established in a specific instance is what is understood, because of the context of inclusion.

Even so, one might argue that the external does not attain the status of being included, since only the internal is comprised [in the list]. This is true; however, because of its primacy, only the internal is included.

Even in the absence of an external object, one who possesses the mental resolve "this is mine" is indeed possessed of possession (*saparigraha*). Now, if external possession does not exist at all, [one might ask: since the resolve "this is mine" is the cause of infatuation (*mūrchā*), is that resolve itself possession? If so, would even cognition (*saṃjñā*) and so forth also result in possession, for they too are resolved upon as "this is mine," like the transformation consisting of passion and the rest? This is not a fault; the phrase "due to the application of negligence" (*pramattayogāt*) is understood to carry over [from the preceding rule]. Therefore, for one who possesses knowledge, vision, and conduct, and is thus non-negligent (*apramatta*), there is no infatuation because of the absence of delusion (*moha*); hence, the state of being without possession (*niṣparigrahatva*) is established.
Furthermore, because those qualities such as knowledge (jñāna) are not to be abandoned, they constitute the very nature of the self and thus are not objects of grasping.
On the other hand, passion and the like are dependent upon the arising of karma; therefore, because they do not constitute the nature of the self, they are to be abandoned.
Consequently, it is logical that the conceptualization of them constitutes grasping.
All faults have their root in that.
For when the conceptualization "this is mine" exists, guarding and other such actions arise;
and therein, violence is necessarily present.
For that purpose, he speaks untruth,
practices theft,
or exerts himself in the act of sexual intercourse.
The various forms of suffering in the hells and other realms arise from those [actions].

Thus, one who perceives the faults of violence and so forth in the manner described, whose mind is directed toward the virtues of non-violence and so forth, and who possesses the vows of non-violence and the rest through supreme effort— he is [the practitioner].
The one who is free from the thorn is the observer of vows. A "thorn" (śalya) is so called because it pierces or injures.

A "thorn" (*śalya*) is so called because it is like a weapon such as an arrow that penetrates the body; just as such a thing causes pain to a living being, so too the transformation resulting from the rise of *karma* is metaphorically designated as a "thorn," since it is the cause of physical and mental affliction.
It is threefold: the thorn of deceit (*māyā-śalya*), the thorn of worldly longing (*nidāna-śalya*), and the thorn of false view (*mithyādarśana-śalya*).
Deceit (*māyā*) is dishonesty or trickery.
The cause is the longing for the enjoyment of sense objects.
False view is faith in what is not reality.
One who has emerged from these three kinds of thorns is called a "thornless" ascetic (*vratī*).

To this it is objected: because of the absence of thorns he is "thornless" (*niḥśalya*), and because of his connection with a vow he is a "vow-keeper" (*vratin*); one cannot be a vow-keeper simply by virtue of being thornless.
For Devadatta does not become a "parasol-bearer" merely through his connection with a staff.
To this it is replied: because [the term] is intended to be qualified by both attributes.

One does not become a practitioner of vows (*vratī*) merely through the connection with vows such as abstaining from violence, provided there is no absence of the "dart" (*śalya*). When the dart has been removed, one is intended to be called a practitioner of vows by virtue of the connection with those vows; just as one is designated as "possessing cows" (*gomān*) because of having much milk and ghee. Just as one is not "possessing cows" despite the presence of cows due to the absence of much milk and ghee, so too, because of the presence of the dart, one is not a practitioner of vows despite the presence of the vows.
But he who is free from the arrow is the one who observes the vow.
To explain the distinction regarding him, it is said:
One who has a house (*agārin*) and one who is without a house (*anagāra*). Since it is sought by those seeking shelter, a "house" (*agāra*) is a dwelling; he is one who is without such a house.
"One who has no house (agāra) is a homeless one (anagāra).

The practitioner of vows is of two kinds: the householder and the homeless one. But does it not follow here that the opposite would also occur—that a sage dwelling in an empty house, a temple, or the like, would be a householder, and that one who, though having not ceased craving for sense objects, leaves home for the forest for some reason, would become a homeless one? This is not a fault, because what is intended here is the house of existence (bhāvāgāra)."
When there is the arising of delusion regarding conduct (*cāritramoha*), a mental disposition that has not turned away from attachment to the household is called the "house of being" (*bhāvāgāra*).
One who possesses this is a "householder" (*agārī*) even while living in the forest;
conversely, even while living in a house, one is "homeless" (*anagāra*) due to the absence of that [delusion].

But surely, does not the state of being a practitioner (*vratin*) fail to apply to a householder (*agārin*), because he possesses only partial vows? This is not a fault. With respect to the *naigama* and other standpoints (*naya*), the status of a practitioner is established even for a householder, just like the case of residing in a city.
