Just as one might be called a resident of a city even while living in a house or a room, so too one who possesses only partial vows is designated a "practitioner" with respect to the *naigama*, *saṃgraha*, and *vyavahāra* standpoints.
Here it is asked: Is one who has desisted from any one of [the transgressions] such as violence, indeed a householder-vow-holder (*agārī-vratī*)? It is not so.
What then? It is said that he is intended [as such] even through the deficiency of the fivefold abstention—that is, a householder is one who possesses the minor vows (*aṇuvrata*).
The word *aṇu* signifies "small. One whose vows are small is called a householder with minor vows (*aṇuvrata*).

How is this the minor vow (*aṇuvrata*) among his vows? Because it is impossible for him to abstain from all blameworthy actions. From what, then, has he abstained? He has abstained from taking the life of a trembling living being; this is the first minor vow for the householder. Having abstained from false speech intended to cause the destruction of a house or the destruction of a village due to the influence of attachment, delusion, and so forth, the householder [observes] the second minor vow.

The third minor vow (*aṇuvrata*) is that of the lay follower (*śrāvaka*) who, having desisted from what was not given—even if it must necessarily be relinquished due to fear of the king or other such constraints—provided it causes harm to others.
The fourth minor vow is that of the householder whose delight has turned away from sexual union with another’s wife, whether she is married or unmarried.
The fifth minor vow is that of the householder who, by his own will, has established a limit regarding wealth, grain, fields, and so forth.
He asked: "For one who has not yet abandoned the household life, is this alone the distinction, or is there some other as well? To this he replied:

"And [he is] perfected in the vows of refraining from purposeless injury to directions and places (*digdeśānarthadaṇḍavirati*), periodic abstinence (*sāmāyika*), the fast on the sacred days (*proṣadhopavāsa*), moderation in the use of enjoyments and necessities (*upabhogaparibhogaparimāṇa*), and the distribution of alms to guests (*atithisaṃvibhāga*).
The word ‘virati’ (abstinence) is completed with each [term].

These three—abstinence from [harming] directions, abstinence from [harming] regions, and abstinence from purposeless violence—are the *guṇavratas* (qualitative vows), because the word ‘vratam’ (vow) is connected with each one.
Likewise, the *sāmāyikavrata*, the *proṣadhopavāsavrata*, the *upabhogaparibhogaparimāṇavrata*, and the *atithisaṃvibhāgavrata*—these four are the *śikṣāvratas* (disciplinary vows).
A householder endowed with these vows is called one who is both abstinent and non-abstinent.

For example: the eastern direction and so forth; having established a limit therein by means of well-known landmarks, the restriction [of movement] is the vow of *digvirati* (restraint regarding directions).
Beyond that, the status of a *mahāvratam* (great vow) is to be understood as the cessation from harming mobile and immobile beings.
In that regard, even when gain occurs, because of the cessation of transformation, the abandonment of greed is accomplished.

A "region" (*deśa*) is a portion of space with a determined extent, such as a village and so forth. The vow of regional abstinence (*deśavirati-vrata*) consists of desisting from activity beyond that [region].
As before, the state of the Great Vow (mahāvratatva) is to be established externally.
When there is no benefit [to others], the cause for undertaking evil is harmful activity (anarthadaṇḍa). Abstinence from that is the abstinence from harmful activity (anarthadaṇḍavirati).

Meaningless violence (*anarthadaṇḍa*) is fivefold: malicious thought (*apadhyāna*), instruction in evil (*pāpopadeśa*), negligent conduct (*pramādācarita*), providing instruments of harm (*hiṃsāpradāna*), and listening to impure teachings (*aśubhaśruti*).
Among these, *apadhyāna* is the mental contemplation of how one might bring about victory or defeat, killing, imprisonment, mutilation of limbs, or the seizure of another’s property for others.
*Pāpopadeśa* is speech associated with evil, such as [teaching] the trade in animals, the slaughter of living beings, or the initiation of violent enterprises.
The destruction of living beings without a purpose—such as cutting down trees, digging the earth, or pouring water—is the practice of negligence (*pramādācarita*).
Providing instruments of violence, such as poison, thorns, weapons, fire, ropes, whips, or sticks, is the act of providing means for violence (*hiṃsāpradāna*).
Engaging in listening to or teaching wicked stories that increase passion for violence and the like constitutes impure hearing (*aśubhaśruti*).

It exists in a state of oneness (*samekībhāva*). For example, when ghee is congealed or oil is congealed, one says "it has become one," which is understood as having attained unity. *Samaya* is the going or proceeding toward oneness; *sāmāyika* is that which is itself the *samaya*, or it is derived by analyzing it as "that for which *samaya* is the purpose. Thus, it is called *sāmāyika*.

When the scope is determined as "in such a place" and "for such a time," the status of the Great Vows (mahāvratatva) for one who remains within that conventional limit (sāmāyika) should be understood as before.
Why? Because of the cessation of violence and so forth, whether subtle or gross.
If it is argued that this entails [the presence of] restraint (saṃyama), we say no; because of the existence of the arising of those karmas that destroy that [restraint].

If it is argued that there is an absence of the status of a "great vow" (*mahāvrata*), that is not so; for it is used figuratively (*upacāra*), just as one might refer to Caitra as being "everywhere" when he is actually in the royal palace.
The word *proṣadha* is a synonym for a sacred festival day (*parvan*).
It is called a fast (*upavāsa*) because the five sense faculties, having turned away from their eagerness toward the apprehension of sound and other objects, approach and abide in that [day].
The meaning is the renunciation of the four kinds of nutriment.
*Proṣadhopavāsa* is the fast on the *proṣadha* day.

Devoid of bathing, perfumes, garlands, ornaments, and other such causes for the adornment of one's own body, and with his internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) directed toward hearing, reciting, and reflecting upon the Dharma, the lay follower (*śrāvaka*), remaining free from worldly activity (*nirārambha*), should observe the fast in a clean place, in a dwelling of the virtuous, in a shrine temple (*caityālaya*), or in his own fasting hall (*proṣadhopavāsagṛha*).
Enjoyment (*upabhoga*) consists of food, drink, perfumes, garlands, and so forth;
utilization (*paribhoga*) consists of clothing, upper garments, ornaments, beds, seats, houses, vehicles, mounts, and so forth. The measure of these two is the "measure of enjoyment and utilization.
Honey, meat, and intoxicants should always be avoided by one whose mind has turned away from the slaughter of living beings.

Flowers such as the *ketakī* and *arjuna*, roots such as *śṛṅgavera* and *mūlaka*, and other things that are the abodes of many living beings and are designated as "infinite-bodied" (*anantakāya*), must be avoided because they involve much harm and yield little fruit.

Regarding vehicles, carriages, ornaments, and so forth, only this much is desired; everything else is undesired. Therefore, one must desist from what is undesired, either for a fixed period of time or for as long as life lasts, according to one's ability.
One who moves about without destroying self-restraint (*saṃyama*) is an *atithi*.
Alternatively, one who has no fixed date [for arrival] is an *atithi*; the meaning is that he arrives at an indefinite time.
The distribution of gifts for such a guest is *atithisaṃvibhāga*. That is fourfold, distinguished by alms-food (*bhikṣā*), requisites (*upakaraṇa*), medicine (*auṣadha*), and shelter (*pratiśraya*).
Alms that are free from fault should be given with a pure mind to a guest who is striving for liberation, devoted to self-restraint, and pure.
Furthermore, articles for the practice of Dharma that nourish right vision and other virtues should be given;
even medicine should be administered when appropriate.
"And a shelter should be provided with supreme faith in the Dharma.
The word "and" (*ca*) serves to include the householders' duties that are about to be described.
Who, then, is this one?
It is he who has devoted himself to the sallekhanā at the end of life.
Death is the exhaustion of the life-span, the sense-faculties, and the powers that have been acquired through one's own transformation, due to the force of their causes.
The inclusion of the term "end" (anta) is for the purpose of indicating death within that very existence.
Death is the end; thus, it is "death-end" (maraṇānta).
That which has this as its purpose is *māraṇāntikī*. *Sallekhanā* is the thorough scraping away of the impurities of the body.
*Sallekhanā* is the correct scraping away of both the external body and the internal impurities by means of gradually abandoning their causes.
That *sallekhanā* which ends in death is to be understood as "delighted in," "practiced," and "adopted.
Now, one might ask: should it not have been stated simply as "practiced" (*sevitā*) for the sake of clarity? No; because a specific meaning is intended here.
In this context, mere practice (*sevana*) alone is not what is being grasped.
What then? It is also for the sake of pleasure.
For if there is no pleasure, the scraping is not performed by force;
rather, when there is pleasure, one does it of one's own accord.

It might be thought that he incurs the sin of self-destruction, because of the cessation of his own life-span and so forth resulting from his prior intention; this is not a fault, because he is free from negligence (*apramatta*).
For it has been stated: "Harm is the taking of life through the conjunction with negligence.
And for him, there is no conjunction with negligence.
Why?
Because of the absence of passion and the other [afflictions].
For it is when one is possessed by passion, hatred, and delusion that self-destruction occurs, as when one kills oneself through the application of instruments such as poison or weapons.
For one who has undertaken sallekhanā, passion and the like do not exist; therefore, there is no fault of self-killing.
And it is said: "The non-arising of passion and the like is taught in the scripture as non-violence (*ahiṃsā*);
indeed, the arising of those [passions] is designated by the Jinas as violence."
Furthermore, because death is undesirable, just as it is undesirable for a merchant— who is intent on the accumulation of various goods through their exchange— to have his own house destroyed,
so too, when some cause of its destruction arises from anywhere, he avoids it to the best of his ability;
and if it cannot be avoided, he exerts himself so that there may be no loss of his merchandise.

In the same way, even a householder engaged in the accumulation of the "merchandise" of vows and moral conduct does not desire the downfall of that which is their basis. When a cause for its impairment arises, he avoids it by opposing his own faults; and when avoidance is difficult, he exerts himself so that there may be no destruction of his own virtues. How, then, could this be self-destruction?
Here it is said: "The observer of vows is one who is free from thorns," and therein the third thorn is false view (*mithyādarśana*).
Therefore, it has been stated that the observer of vows must be one who possesses right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) and is free from thorns.
Is that right view (samyagdarśana) subject to exceptions (sāpavāda) or free from exceptions (nirapavāda)?

It is said: for some, due to a particular state of deluding karma (mohanīya), these exceptions may occasionally arise—namely, doubt, curiosity, hesitation, praising other views, and associating with them—which are transgressions (aticāra) against right view.
The qualities beginning with freedom from doubt have been explained under the heading "purity of vision" (*darśanaviśuddhi*).
It should be understood that doubt and its like are their opposites.

Now, what is the distinction between *praśaṃsā* (praise) and *saṃstava* (flattery)? *Praśaṃsā* is the manifestation of the qualities of knowledge and conduct based on a perception of them as real through the mind; *saṃstava* is speech that manifests qualities, whether they are real or unreal. This is the difference between the two.
[Objection: But right view (*samyagdarśana*) has been said to have eight limbs; therefore, it must also have eight transgressions (*aticāras*).

[Response: This is not a fault. Since the teacher intends to state later that there are five transgressions for each of the vows and the minor precepts (*śīlas*), he mentions only five transgressions here by not including *praśaṃsā* and *saṃstava* within the other transgressions.
[The opponent] asks: "The transgressions of right view have been explained.
Do similar [transgressions] also exist for the vows and moral precepts? Having replied, "Yes," [the author] speaks in order to indicate the enumeration of those transgressions.

Regarding "vows and moral conducts" (*vrataśīleṣu*): vows and moral conducts are *vrataśīla*; [the phrase refers to] in those vows and moral conducts. There are five and five [qualities] respectively.

Is the mention of *śīla* (virtuous conduct) redundant, since it is already established by the mention of *vrata* (vows)? It is not redundant; it is for the purpose of indicating a distinction and for the purpose of protecting the vows. Here, by the term *śīla*, the directional abstinences (*digvirati*) and so forth are included.

Since the section concerns householders, the five transgressions (*aticāra*) for each of the vows and conducts of householders, which will be explained below, are to be understood in their respective order.
It is as follows—first, regarding the vow of non-violence (*ahiṃsā*):
binding, killing, mutilation, loading with excessive burdens, and the withholding of food and drink.
Bondage is the cause of obstruction to movement toward a desired location.

Killing (*vadha*) is the striking of living beings with sticks, whips, canes, and so forth; it is not the taking away of life, because that [taking of life] has already been excluded [by the preceding definition].
Mutilation (*cheda*) is the removal of limbs such as the ears, nose, and so on.
Transporting more than the proper load is the imposition of excessive weight.
Causing cattle and other animals suffering from hunger and thirst is the withholding of food and drink.
These five are the transgressions of the minor vow of non-violence (*ahiṃsāṇuvrata*).

§ 712. False instruction, secret slander, the composition of forged documents, the misappropriation of deposits, and the disclosure of secrets through gestures constitute [falsehood]. Regarding specific rites for the sake of worldly prosperity or the supreme good, false instruction is the inducing of another to act otherwise than intended, or causing them to be deceived.

The disclosure of a specific act performed in private by a man and a woman should be understood as "revealing a secret. Writing for the purpose of deception—such as writing that someone has said or done something which was not actually said or done by them, but occurred solely through the influence of another's instigation—is "forgery.
Appropriating gold or other property from a depositor who has forgotten its quantity or has miscounted it, while assenting with words such as "it is so," is "embezzlement of a deposit."

Having discerned the intentions of others through means such as gestures, context, changes in physical appearance, or the movement of the eyebrows, to disclose those thoughts for the sake of envy or other motives is called "disclosure of a secret with signs" (*sākāra-mantra-bheda*).
These are to be understood as the five transgressions (*aticāra*) of the minor vow of truthfulness (*satyāṇuvrata*):
employing thieves, receiving what has been stolen by them, violating the laws of the state, using deficient or excessive measures and weights, and dealing in counterfeit goods.
Whether one steals by oneself, causes another to steal, or approves of what has been stolen—this is the instigation of a thief (*stenaprayoga*).
The taking of what has been brought by a thief who was neither instigated nor approved [of the act] is "taking what has been brought" (*āhṛtādāna*).

Transgression (*atikrama*) is the giving or receiving [of goods] by means other than the established rule. A hostile kingdom is a *viruddharājya*; transgression within a hostile kingdom is *viruddharājyātikrama*.
For in such a place, there is an effort [to acquire] highly valuable goods that can be obtained for a small price.
*Prastha* and the like are measures of volume (*māna*), while *tulā* and the like are measures of weight (*unmāna*).

Using these [instruments] with less than the standard when giving to another, or more than the standard when taking for oneself—such fraudulent applications as these constitute "deficient or excessive measures and weights" (*hīnādhikamānonmāna*).
Conducting transactions preceded by deception through counterfeit gold and other materials constitutes "transactions involving counterfeits" (*pratirūpakavyavahāra*).

These are the five transgressions of the minor vow against taking what is not given: arranging marriages for others, sexual intercourse with a temporary wife, with one who is married, or with one who is unmarried, sexual play with non-genital parts, and intense obsession with sensual desire.
The giving away of a maiden is marriage (*vivāha*).
Marriage performed for another is "marriage for another" (*paravivāha*).
The act of performing such marriage for another is "the performance of marriage for another" (*paravivāhakaraṇa*).
One who goes to or approaches other men is thus characterized by such a habit; she is an *itvarī*.
One who is a contemptible *itvarī*—the suffix *ka* being used in the sense of contempt—is called an *itvarikā*. She who has a single man as her husband is one who is "taken" (*parigṛhītā*).

One who, by virtue of being a courtesan or a wanton woman, has the habit of going to other men and is without an owner is "unappropriated" (*aparigṛhītā*). Both the appropriated (*parigṛhītā*) and the unappropriated (*aparigṛhītā*) constitute "the appropriated and the unappropriated" (*parigṛhītāparigṛhīte*). These two—the appropriated and the unappropriated—are temporary; thus they are "temporary, appropriated, and unappropriated" (*itvarikāparigṛhītāparigṛhīte*). Sexual intercourse with those two constitutes "intercourse with the temporary, appropriated, and unappropriated" (*itvarikāparigṛhītāparigṛhītāgamane*).
The limbs are the genitals and the female organ; sexual play other than in those places is "play outside the limbs" (*anaṅgakrīḍā*).
An intensified transformation of desire is "intense attachment to desire" (*kāmatīvrābhiniveśa*).
These five are the transgressions of the vow of contentment with one's own wife.
Exceeding the prescribed limits regarding fields, dwellings, silver, gold, wealth, grain, female slaves, male slaves, and base metals:
*kṣetra* is the site for crops.
*Vāstu* is a dwelling. *Hiraṇya* is the basis for the transaction of silver and so forth.
*Suvarṇa* is well known [as gold].
Wealth consists of cattle and the like;
grain consists of rice and the like;
and male and female slaves consist of the class of servants, both men and women.
Base metals (*kupya*) include linen, cotton, silk, sandalwood, and so forth.

Fields and buildings are "fields-and-buildings" (*kṣetravāstu*); gold and bullion are "gold-and-precious-metal" (*hiraṇyasuvarṇa*); wealth and grain are "wealth-and-grain" (*dhanadhānya*); female and male slaves are "female-and-male-slaves" (*dāsīdāsa*).

Fields and buildings, gold and precious metal, wealth and grain, female and male slaves, and base metals together constitute "fields, buildings, gold, precious metal, wealth, grain, slaves, and base metals" (*kṣetravāstuhiraṇyasuvarṇadhanadhānyadāsīdāsakupyāni*).

Thinking, "Only this much is my possession, nothing else," one has delimited the size of one's acquisitions to a minute measure regarding objects such as fields and dwellings. However, due to the force of excessive greed, any excess beyond that limit constitutes a transgression of the prescribed measure;
these are the transgressions of the vow of limiting possessions (*parigrahaparimāṇavrata*).
The transgressions of the vows have been stated; the transgressions of the ethical disciplines (śīla) will now be explained. They are as follows:
transgressing in the upward, downward, or horizontal directions; increasing the area of the restriction; and the failure of mindfulness (smṛti).
Transgression (*atikrama*) is the overstepping of a limited spatial boundary.
Briefly stated, it is threefold: transgression upward, transgression downward, and transgression horizontally.
In that regard, ascending mountains and the like constitutes transcendence of the upward direction;
descending into wells and the like constitutes transcendence of the downward direction;
and entering caves and the like constitutes transcendence of the horizontal direction.
The intention to increase a direction already acquired out of a surge of greed is "field-increase" (*kṣetravṛddhi*).
It should be understood that this transgression arises from negligence, delusion, or attachment.
Non-recollection is the failure to maintain mindfulness.

These are the transgressions of the vow of directional restraint (*digviramaṇa*): employing messengers to bring things from beyond the limit, employing servants for that purpose, making sounds or gestures to attract attention, and throwing objects to draw someone across the boundary.
"Bringing" (*ānayana*) is the command "bring whatever [is needed]" issued to one who is stationed in a place designated by oneself for that purpose, on account of some requirement.
"Employment of a servant" (*preṣyaprayoga*) is the injunction "do it thus.
"Following through sound" (*śabdānupāta*) is the making of sounds such as clapping or coughing toward men engaged in work. "Following through form" (*rūpānupāta*) is the showing of one's own body.

The throwing of clods of earth and the like constitutes the casting of objects at a person. These are the five transgressions of the vow of partial abstinence (*deśaviramaṇa*): frivolous talk, contortion of the body, idle chatter, undertaking activities without due reflection, and the useless consumption of goods and enjoyments.

*Kandarpa* is the employment of improper speech mixed with laughter arising from an excess of passion. That same [laughter] and [speech], when applied toward another through corrupt physical action, is *kautkucya*.
Excessive talkativeness (*maukharya*) is the state of being prone to audacity and whatever is useless chatter.

Acting with excess without having considered the purpose is "unconsidered over-action" (*asamīkṣyādhikaraṇa*). That amount of wealth which suffices for enjoyment and use is "wealth" (*artha*); anything beyond that is "uselessness" (*ānarthakya*).

These are the transgressions regarding the abstention from the fivefold useless violence (*anarthadaṇḍa*): improper application of the body, speech, and mind; lack of respect; and non-presence of mindfulness.
Yoga has been explained as being threefold.
Its improper application is *yogaduṣpraṇidhāna*—namely, improper application of body, improper application of speech, and improper application of mind.
Lack of respect is lack of enthusiasm.
Lack of one-pointedness is the non-presence of mindfulness. These are the five transgressions of the *sāmāyika* vow:
discarding, taking up, spreading out, and undertaking [actions] without inspection or cleaning; and lack of respect and the non-presence of mindfulness.
To examine whether living beings are present or not is the function of the eye.
That which is performed with a soft implement for a specific purpose is called "wiping."

Both of these, qualified by the negation [of inspection and cleaning], are connected with the three [actions] beginning with "disposal" (*utsarga*), such as: "disposal without having inspected or cleaned.
In this context, "disposal without having inspected or cleaned" refers to the disposal of urine and feces on ground that has not been inspected or cleaned.

"Taking up without having inspected or cleaned" refers to taking up objects for the worship of Arhats and teachers—such as perfumes, garlands, and incense—or items for one's own use, such as clothing, without having inspected or cleaned them.
"Commencing the use of a bedding or covering such as a robe without having inspected and cleansed it is 'commencing the use of bedding without inspection and cleansing.
Due to being oppressed by hunger, there is a lack of regard for necessary duties, which is 'lack of enthusiasm.
'Non-presence of mindfulness' has already been explained."
These are the five transgressions of the *poṣadha* fast: food that is associated with living beings, mixed with them, prepared by fermentation, undercooked, or overcooked.

That which exists together with the mind (*citta*) is "with-mind" (*sacitta*), meaning a substance possessing volition (*cetana*). It is "adhered to" by that [mind], "intermingled" with it, and "mixed" with it.
But how does this [intoxication] proceed in those with minds and so forth? Through negligence and delusion.
*Drava* refers to a distillation that is either stimulating or aphrodisiac.
*Duṣpakva* means improperly cooked.

By these, food is distinguished as: food with living beings (*sacittāhāra*), related food (*saṃbandhāhāra*), mixed food (*saṃmiśrāhāra*), pressed food (*abhiṣavāhāra*), and undercooked food (*duṣpakvāhāra*).

These five constitute transgressions of the vow of limiting enjoyments and luxuries (*bhogopabhogaparisaṃkhyāna*). [The other transgressions are: depositing [food] with living beings, covering [it] with living beings, designating it for another, stinginess, and passing over the [proper] time.
"Placing on something with life" (sacittanikṣepa) means depositing [something] upon a lotus leaf or similar object that possesses life.
"Covering" (apidhāna) means an obstruction.
It is connected with the mind itself, as in the expression "a covering with a cloth.
"Designation by another" refers to the act of offering the gift to someone other than the actual giver.
Stinginess (*mātsarya*) is the absence of respect when giving, or the inability to tolerate the virtues of another donor.
Eating at the wrong time is the transgression of the rule regarding the passing of the proper time.
These are the five transgressions of the precept of sharing with guests.
Their causes are the longing for life, the longing for death, attachment to friends, and the pursuit of pleasure.
*Āśaṃsanam* means wishing or desiring.
*Jīvitamaraṇam* is life and death; *jīvitamaraṇāśaṃse* refers to the two wishes for life and death.
Attachment to friends consists in the recollection of former friendships, such as playing together in the dust;
the continuous mental application of remembering specific past experiences of joy constitutes the connection with pleasure;
and the cause is that the mind is invariably directed toward that [object] due to the desire for enjoyment, or because it is given over to that [object].
These are the five transgressions of sallekhanā.

Here it is asked: You have stated in the exposition on the influx of karma that causes the state of being a *tīrthakara*, "renunciation and austerity according to one's ability," and yet you have further stated in the section on the rules of conduct, "distribution [of food] to guests."
Since the characteristic of that gift has not been understood, let it be stated; therefore, he says:
"Giving is the relinquishing of one's own [possessions] for the sake of favoring [others].
Benefit for oneself and others is "favor" (*anugraha*).
Benefit for oneself is the accumulation of merit (*puṇya*); benefit for others is the increase of right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) and so forth.
The word "self" (*sva*) is a synonym for "wealth."
Generosity (*dāna*) should be understood as the relinquishment of one's own possessions for the sake of benefiting others.
Here, it is asked: "Generosity has been described; does it have an undifferentiated fruit, or is there some specific distinction? To this, he says:
The distinction [in the fruit] arises from the distinction in the ritual, the substance, the donor, and the recipient.
The "ritual" refers to the sequence beginning with the act of acceptance.
The distinction is produced by the qualities [of the act].

It is applied individually to each: namely, the distinction of the rite (*vidhi*), the distinction of the substance (*dravya*), the distinction of the giver (*dātṛ*), and the distinction of the recipient (*pātra*).
Among these, the distinction of the rite is the difference caused by respect or lack of respect in the acceptance and so forth.
A specific material object is that which serves as a cause for the increase of austerity, Vedic study, and so forth;
a specific donor is one characterized by freedom from envy, lack of despondency, and so forth;
and a specific recipient is one endowed with the qualities that are causes for liberation.
And therefore, there is a distinction in the fruit of merit resulting from a distinction in the soil and other factors, just as there is a distinction in the fruit of a seed.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the *Tattvārthavṛtti* titled *Sarvārthasiddhi*.
Now begins the eighth chapter.
The category of the outflows (*āsrava*) has been explained.
Immediately following that, the category of bondage (*bandha*), which was next in the enumeration, must now be explained.
Since that [bondage] is to be explained, the presentation of the causes of bondage is made first; for bondage is preceded by those—
namely, false view, non-abstinence, negligence, passions, and activity are the causes of bondage.
False view and the others have been mentioned.

Where? False view was first mentioned in the definition of right view, “Right view is faith in the true principles,” as its opposite; and it was explained under the section on the influx (*āsrava*) among the activities as "the activity of false view. Abstention has also been mentioned.
Non-restraint (*avirati*) should be understood as the opposite of that [restraint].
The act of violating what has been taught (*ājñāvyāpādana*) and the act of lack of desire [for the Dharma] (*anākaṅkṣākriyā*): non-heedfulness (*pramāda*) is included within these two.
And that non-heedfulness is a lack of respect for wholesome qualities (*kuśala*).
The passions (*kaṣāya*)—namely anger and the rest—are said to be divided into the categories of *anantānubandhin*, *apratyākhyāna*, *pratyākhyāna*, and *saṃjvalana*.
Where? Precisely in the passage "the senses and passions" (*indriyakaṣāyā*).
The activities (*yoga*) are said to be the divisions of body and so forth.
Where? In the passage: "Yoga is the activity of body, speech, and mind.
False view (*mithyādarśana*) is of two kinds: innate and that preceded by the instruction of another.

Among these, that which arises without the instruction of another, due to the influence of the rising of *mithyātva* karma, characterized by a lack of faith in the true principles (*tattvārtha*), is the innate (*naisargika*) [false view].

That which is caused by the instruction of another is fourfold, based on the distinctions of the proponents of action (*kriyāvādin*), non-action (*akriyāvādin*), agnosticism (*ajñānika*), and discipline (*vainayika*).

Alternatively, false view (*mithyādarśana*) is fivefold: absolute false view (*ekānta-mithyādarśana*), perverted false view (*viparīta-mithyādarśana*), doubtful false view (*saṃśaya-mithyādarśana*), false view of discipline (*vainayika-mithyādarśana*), and false view of agnosticism (*ajñānika-mithyādarśana*).
In this context, "one-sidedness" (*ekānta*) is the dogmatic insistence that "this is exactly thus," regarding both the subject (*dharmin*) and its properties (*dharma*).
For example: "All this is indeed the Self (*puruṣa*)," or "it is necessarily eternal," or "it is necessarily non-eternal";
or such views as "the one with fetters is free from fetters," "the omniscient one consumes solid food," or "a woman attains liberation," and so forth—these constitute "error" (*viparyaya*).
Doubt (*saṃśaya*) is the failure to adopt either side of the alternative as to whether right view, knowledge, and conduct constitute the path to liberation or not.
The state of being a follower of discipline (*vainayika*) is the impartial regard for all deities and all doctrines.
Ignorance (*ajñānikatva*) is the absence of examination regarding what is beneficial and what is harmful.
And it is said:
non-restraint is of twelve kinds, due to the distinction between the six bodies, the six organs of action, and the objects [of the senses].
There are sixteen *kaṣāyas* and nine *nokaṣāyas*; since their distinction is slight and not a fundamental difference, they constitute twenty-five *kaṣāyas*.
There are four types of mental activity (*manoyoga*), four types of vocal activity (*vāgyoga*), and five types of bodily activity (*kāyayoga*), making thirteen varieties of *yoga*.
However, because the *āhāraka-kāyayoga* and *āhāraka-miśra-kāyayoga* can occur in one who is restrained with negligence (*pramatta-saṃyata*), there are also fifteen varieties.
Negligence (*pramāda*) is of many kinds, due to the distinction of its objects, such as the eight purities (*śuddhi-aṣṭaka*) and supreme forbearance (*uttama-kṣamā*).
These five causes of bondage (*bandha-hetu*) exist both collectively and individually.
For example, for one with false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), all five together constitute the causes of bondage.

For those with right view accompanied by means of accomplishment, those with right-cum-wrong view, and those with right view who are unrestrained, there are four [types of karma]: non-restraint and so forth.
For one who is both restrained and unrestrained, there is non-restraint mixed with restraint, as well as negligence, passions, and activity.
For one who is restrained but negligent, there are negligence, passions, and activity.
For the four [stages] beginning with the "careful" (apramatta), there are both yoga and kaṣāya.
For those who have pacified kaṣāya, those whose kaṣāya is destroyed, and those who are kevalins with yoga, there is only yoga. For the kevalin without yoga, it is not a cause of bondage.
The causes of bondage have been explained. Now, since bondage must be discussed, he says:

Because it possesses passion (kaṣāya), the soul (jīva) takes up matter-particles (pudgala) suitable for karma; that is bondage (bandha). It is "possessing passion" because it exists together with passion.
The state of having passions is "passion-possessing-ness" (*sakaṣāyatvam*).

[The phrase] "from that passion-possessing-ness" is a further statement of the reason, intended to demonstrate the specific attainment of the experience and duration [of karma] in accordance with the disposition of intense, mild, or medium passions, just as there is the taking up of food in accordance with the disposition of the digestive fire in the stomach.
Being questioned—“How can the formless, handless self take up karma?”—he replied, “It is the *jīva*.

It is called *jīva* because of its living (*jīvana*), that is, because it sustains the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) through its connection with life-force (*āyus*), and not due to the absence of life-force. Although the meaning would have been established by the concise expression “suitable for karma” (*karmayogyān*), the separate utterance of the distinct case-ending in “suitable for action” (*karmaṇo yogyān*) is intended to indicate a different syntactical sentence.
What, then, is that other statement? "The soul becomes possessed of passions (kaṣāya) because of karma"—this is one statement.

This is what is meant: the phrase "because of karma" is an indication of the cause; by reason of karma, the soul becomes possessed of passions, for there is no staining by passion for that which is without karma.
Consequently, it is stated that there is a beginningless connection between the soul and karma.
Thus, the objection—“How can the formless soul be bound by material karma?”—is refuted.
Otherwise, if bondage had a beginning, it would follow that for one who possesses absolute purity, as in the case of a perfected being (*siddha*), there could be no bondage at all.
The second statement is: “It takes up those *pudgala* particles which are suitable for karma.”

By the force of the sense, there is a transformation of the case-ending: having abandoned the connection with the previous cause, it adopts a genitive connection, as in "of the action [it is] suitable.
The mention of "person" (pudgala) is for the purpose of declaring the identity of the action [with the person].
By this, the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) as a quality of the self is refuted; for it is untenable that such a thing could be the cause of saṃsāra.
The term “takes up” (*ādatte*) is used for the purpose of indicating the relationship between cause and effect.

Therefore, due to the penetration of false views and so forth, the soul becomes moistened; then, through specific conjunctions on all sides with those *pudgala* particles—which possess infinitely infinite space-points, occupy a single subtle space-point, and are capable of becoming karma—their inseparable adhesion is designated as "bondage" (*bandha*).

Just as various seeds, juices, flowers, and fruits cast into a particular vessel undergo transformation into the state of wine, so too should it be understood that the *pudgalas* residing within the self undergo transformation into the state of karma through the power of yoga and the passions (*kaṣāya*).
The word "that" (*saḥ*) is used for the purpose of excluding anything else;
[it means] this very thing is bondage, and there is no other.
By that, the bondage consisting of qualities and the possessor of qualities is brought to cessation.
The word "bondage" (bandha) should be explained as having "karma" and so forth as its grammatical basis.

He asks: Is this bondage of a single uniform nature, or does it also possess various types? To this, it is said: "The modes of that [bondage] are the duration of the primary matter (prakṛti), the experience (anubhava), and the spatial units (pradeśa).
Nature is intrinsic character.
What is the nature of the nimba tree? Bitterness. What is the nature of molasses? Sweetness.

Likewise, what is the nature (*prakṛti*) of knowledge-obscuring karma (*jñānāvaraṇa*)? It is the non-comprehension of objects. What is the nature of perception-obscuring karma (*darśanāvaraṇa*)? It is the failure to perceive objects. What is the nature of the karma characterized by pleasure and pain (*vedya*)? It is the experience of pleasure and pain.
The nature of delusion of vision (*darśana-moha*) is lack of faith in the true principles;
that of delusion of conduct (*cāritra-moha*) is non-restraint;
and that of lifespan (*āyus*) is the maintenance of existence.
The function of *nāman* is the assigning of names such as "hell-being" (*nāraka*) and so forth. The function of *gotra* is the designation of high or low status.
The function of *anantarāya* is the creation of obstacles to giving and other such acts.
Thus, the characteristic is established: it is called *prakṛti* (nature) because it originates from this. *Sthiti* (stability) is the non-deviation from that intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
For example—just as the milk of goats, cows, buffaloes, and so forth does not deviate from its intrinsic nature of sweetness, that is stability.
Likewise, *sthiti* (duration) is the non-deviation from the essential nature of knowledge-obscuring karma (*jñānāvaraṇa*) and the others, such as their capacity for the comprehension of objects.

*Anubhava* (intensity) is a specific quality of its essence (*rasa*), just as there is a specific difference in the taste of the milk of goats, cows, buffaloes, and so forth, according to whether it is strong, mild, or otherwise.
Similarly, *anubhava* is a specific inherent capacity belonging to the matter-particles (*pudgala*) of karma.
*Pradeśa* (region/part) is the determination of a specific limit (*iyattāvadhāraṇa*).
It is the determination, by means of the delimitation of atoms (*paramāṇu*), of the aggregates (*skandha*) of *pudgala* matter that have been transformed into the state of being karma.
The word "method" (*vidhi*) denotes a mode or manner (*prakāra*).
These four—beginning with *prakṛti*—are the types of that bondage.
Among them, *prakṛti* and *pradeśa* have yoga as their cause;
*sthiti* and *anubhava* have *kaṣāya* as their cause.
Due to the distinction between the excellence and non-excellence of that [karma], there is the manifold nature of its bondage.
And so it has been said:
In that regard, in order to demonstrate the divisions of the first, the natural bondage (*prakṛti-bandha*), he says:

"The first consists of knowledge-obscuring (*jñānāvaraṇa*), perception-obscuring (*darśanāvaraṇa*), feeling-producing (*vedanīya*), deluding (*mohanīya*), life-span (*āyuṣ*), name (*nāma*), status (*gotra*), and obstructive (*antarāya*) [karmas]. (738)
The first is the bond of nature (*prakṛti-bandha*), which should be understood as having eight varieties, beginning with knowledge-obscuration (*jñānāvaraṇa*).
It is called *āvaraṇa* because it obscures or that by which one is obscured.
This term is connected to each [variety] individually—namely, knowledge-obscuration (*jñānāvaraṇa*) and perception-obscuration (*darśanāvaraṇa*).
It is "to be experienced" (*vedanīya*) because it causes one to experience or because it is itself experienced.
It is "deluding" (*mohanīya*) because it causes delusion or because one is deluded by it.
It is "life-span" (*āyuṣ*) because by means of it one goes toward existence as a hell-being and so forth.
It is called *nāma* because it bends (*namayati*) the self, or because one is bent by it. It is called *gotra* because it is praised or sounded (*gūyate*) as high or low.
It is called *antarāya* because it goes between (*antaram eti*) the donor, the gift, and so forth.

Individual souls, being affected by a single transformation of their own nature, undergo numerous divisions such as the obscuration of knowledge (*jñānāvaraṇa*) and so forth, just like food consumed at once undergoes transformations such as chyle, blood, and the rest.
[An opponent] says: The eightfold primary bondage (*mūlaprakṛtibandha*) has been explained.
Now, the bondage of the sub-classes (uttaraprakṛtibandha) must be explained; therefore, he says:
"The divisions are five, nine, two, twenty-eight, four, forty-two, two, and five, respectively.
(Section 740)

Should the word "second" be included here [in the rule], such that the option applies only to the second, namely the bondage of the secondary types (*uttaraprakṛti*)? It need not be included, because it is established by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*).
The first, which is the bondage of the primary types (*mūlaprakṛti*), has been stated to have eight varieties.
Therefore, by the principle of elimination, this rule regarding the varieties of the secondary types follows.

The word "division" (*bheda*) is connected respectively with the numbers five and so forth: knowledge-obscuring karma has five divisions; perception-obscuring karma has nine divisions; feeling-producing karma has two divisions; deluding karma has twenty-eight divisions; life-span karma has four divisions; name karma has forty-two divisions; status-determining karma has two divisions; and obstructive karma has five divisions.
(741) If knowledge-obscuring karma has five divisions, let its exposition be stated; therefore, he says:
Regarding mati, śruta, avadhi, manaḥparyaya, and kevala:
the types of knowledge beginning with mati have been explained.
Because there is a breaking of the veil due to the obscuration of these [karmas], five additional types of karma are to be understood.
Here it is objected: Does the capacity for *manaḥparyaya* knowledge and the capacity for *kevalajñāna* exist in an incapable person (*abhavya*) or not?
If they did exist, he would lack the state of being incapable.
If it is argued that, in that case, the postulation of two obstructions is useless, it is replied: there is no fault, because of the statement regarding the two perspectives (*ādeśa*).
From the perspective of substance (*dravyārthādeśa*), there is the possibility of the power of mind-reading knowledge (*manaḥparyaya*) and omniscience (*kevalajñāna*);
from the perspective of modes (*paryāyārthādeśa*), there is the absence of that power.

If this were so, the distinction between the "capable" (bhavya) and the "incapable" (abhavya) would not be tenable, since that potential exists in both cases. It is not said that the distinction between the capable and the incapable depends on the presence or absence of the potential itself.
From what, then? It depends on the presence or absence of its manifestation.
One for whom manifestation through right vision (*samyagdarśana*) and so forth will occur is "capable."
But he for whom it will not arise is incapable [of attainment],
like a stone other than kanaka-stone.
He said: The classification of the sub-types of knowledge-obscuring karma (*jñānāvaraṇa*) has been explained.
Now, that of the perception-obscuring karma (*darśanāvaraṇa*) must be stated; therefore, he says:

[The sub-types of *darśanāvaraṇa* are] those of the eye, non-eye, clairvoyance (*avadhi*), and omniscience (*kevala*), as well as sleep (*nidrā*), drowsiness (*nidrā-nidrā*), torpor (*pracalā*), restlessness (*pracalā-pracalā*), and lethargy (*styāna-gṛddhi*).

Regarding the phrase "of the eye, non-eye, limited, and total [perceptions]," this is a specification of distinctions with respect to the obscuration of vision (*darśanāvaraṇa*): namely, the obscuration of visual perception (*cakṣurdarśanāvaraṇa*), the obscuration of non-visual perception (*acakṣurdarśanāvaraṇa*), the obscuration of limited perception (*avadhidarśanāvaraṇa*), and the obscuration of total perception (*kevaladarśanāvaraṇa*).
Sleep (*nidrā*) is for the purpose of dispelling intoxication, exhaustion, and fatigue.
The occurrence of that [drowsiness] repeatedly is *nidrā-nidrā*.
That which agitates the self is *pracalā*, arising from grief, fatigue, intoxication, and so forth; it indicates distortions of the eyes and limbs even in one who is sitting.
That same state, when recurring again and again, is *pracalā-pracalā*.

Just as there is the manifestation of a particular intensity (*vīrya-viśeṣa*) in a dream, so too is *styānagṛddhi*. Since the root *styai* has multiple meanings, "dream" (*svapna*) is understood here as its sense; likewise, from the root *gṛdh*, "intensity" (*dīpti*) is taken.
That which, upon its arising, causes the self to become intensely attached to or inflamed by a dream—thereby performing fierce and manifold actions—is *styānagṛddhi*.

In this context, "sleep" (*nidrā*) and the others are connected with "obscuration of vision" (*darśanāvaraṇa*) through grammatical coordination— namely, "sleep-obscuration of vision," "deep sleep-obscuration of vision," and so forth.
To explain the secondary subdivisions (*uttaraprakṛti*) of the third primary category (*prakṛti*), he says:
Regarding pleasant and unpleasant feeling (*sadasadvedya*):
that which, upon its arising, results in the attainment of physical and mental pleasure within the destinies of gods and so forth, is pleasant feeling (*sadvedya*).

That which is praiseworthy is "wholesome experience" (*sadvedya*). That fruit which is manifold suffering is "unwholesome experience" (*asadvedya*); that which is not praiseworthy is "unwholesome experience."

To illustrate the classification of the subsequent sub-types of the fourth primary type [of karma], he says: those known as the deluding karmas of vision and conduct—consisting of three, two, nine, and sixteen varieties respectively—are: right belief, wrong belief, and their mixture; the non-kaṣāya and kaṣāya types; laughter, liking, disliking, sorrow, fear, disgust, the female, male, and neuter genders; and anger, pride, deceit, and greed, each divided into the four categories of infinite-binding, non-renouncing, renouncing, and flaming.
There are four [categories] beginning with *darśana* (vision), and there are also three and so forth.

In this regard, the connection is according to their respective order: deluding karma of vision (*darśana-mohanīya*) is of three types; deluding karma of conduct (*cāritra-mohanīya*) is of two types; non-passionate-feeling karma (*akaṣāya-vedanīya*) is of nine kinds; and passionate-feeling karma (*kaṣāya-vedanīya*) is of sixteen kinds.
Among these, the deluding karma of vision (*darśana-mohanīya*) is of three types: right view (*samyaktva*), wrong view (*mithyātva*), and the mixture of both (*tad-ubhaya*).
Having each become a separate bond, it is established as threefold with respect to its existence as actualized karma (*sat-karma*).

In this context, *mithyātva* (falsehood) is that [karmic state] through the arising of which one turns away from the path taught by the Omniscient One, becomes devoid of interest in faith in the true meaning of reality, is incapable of discerning between the beneficial and the harmful, and possesses false views.

That very same [karmic state], when its own flow has been suppressed by a wholesome transformation (*śubhapariṇāma*) and remains in a state of equanimity such that it does not obstruct the soul’s own faith—that being experienced, a person is designated as one of right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*).

That very same state of falsity (mithyātva), due to a specific degree of purification—like *kodrava* grain whose intoxicating power is partially diminished—is called "partially purified essence" (*sāmi-śuddha-svarasa*), which is to say "mixed-falsity" (*samyaṅ-mithyātva*).

Through the arising of this [karman], the transformation of the self becomes dual-natured, like the transformation produced by the consumption of *kodrava* rice where the intoxicating power is half-purified.

The deluding karma of conduct (*cāritramohanīya*) is twofold, due to the distinction between the non-passionate (*akaṣāya*) and the passionate (*kaṣāya*). Because the negative particle *nañ* is used here in the sense of "slight," "non-passionate" means "one with slight passion. The non-passionate [deluding karma] is of nine types.
Why?
Because of the distinction between laughter and the other [rasas]. That from whose arising laughter manifests is "laughter" (hāsya).
That which arises from which there is eagerness toward places and so forth is *rati* (attachment).
*Arati* (aversion) is the opposite of that.
That which results from which there is grieving is *śoka* (sorrow).

That which arises from which there is agitation is fear (*bhaya*). That which arises from which there is the concealment of one's own faults and the exposure of the faults of others is loathing (*jugupsā*).
That which arises from which one adopts feminine dispositions is the female inclination (*strīveda*).

That which, upon its arising, causes one to seize upon masculine states is male-vedana (puṃveda). That which, upon its arising, leads one to approach non-masculine states is neuter-vedana (napuṃsakaveda).
The karma to be experienced as passion (kaṣāyavedanīya) is of sixteen kinds.
Why?
Because of the distinctions such as the "endlessly binding" (anantānubandhi) and so forth.
They are as follows: the passions (*kaṣāya*) are anger, pride, deceit, and greed.

These have four states: those that bind one to endless [rebirth] (*anantānubandhin*), those that obscure partial renunciation (*apratyākhyānāvaraṇa*), those that obscure complete renunciation (*pratyākhyānāvaraṇa*), and those that are flickering (*saṃjvalana*).
Because it is the cause of endless saṃsāra, false view (*mithyādarśana*) is "endless."

The "infinite-bonding" (*anantānubandhin*) passions are anger, pride, deceit, and greed which follow upon that [delusion]. Due to the arising of these, one is unable to perform even a slight partial renunciation known as *saṃyamāsaṃyama*; obscuring partial renunciation (*deśapratyākhyāna*), they are the anger, pride, deceit, and greed called "obscuring non-renunciation" (*apratyākhyānāvaraṇa*). Due to the arising of these, one is unable to perform complete renunciation known as *saṃyama*; obscuring total renunciation (*kṛtsnapratyākhyāna*), they are the anger, pride, deceit, and greed called "obscuring renunciation" (*pratyākhyānāvaraṇa*).
They exist in a state of unification.

Because they abide together with *saṃyama*, they blaze having become one; or rather, *saṃyama* blazes when these are present. Thus, anger (*krodha*), pride (*māna*), deceit (*māyā*), and greed (*lobha*) are called "blazing" (*saṃjvalana*). When these are combined, there are sixteen *kaṣāyas*.
In order to determine the further sub-types of *āyus* (life-span), which follows immediately after *mohanīya* (deluding karma) in the enumeration, he says:
"those of hell-beings, animals, humans, and gods."
In the case of hell-beings and others, the designation of "life-span" (*āyus*) is made by way of connection with existence (*bhava*).

That which exists in the hells is "hellish" (*nāraka*) life; that which exists among animals is "animal" (*tairyagyonika*) life; that which exists among humans is "human" (*mānuṣa*) life; and that which exists among gods is "divine" (*daiva*) life.
That which is the cause for long life in the hells characterized by intense cold and heat is the hellish [karma].
The same applies to the remaining [realms] as well.
Life-span has been explained as being of four kinds.

Immediately following that, the *nāmakarma* (name-karma) which was mentioned is now stated for the purpose of determining its subsequent sub-types (*uttaraprakṛti*): Gait, genus, body, limbs and minor parts, formation, binding, cohesion, figure, bone-jointing, touch, taste, smell, color, succession, heaviness-lightness, self-obstruction, obstruction of others, heat, radiance, respiration, movement through space; individual body, mobile, beautiful, melodious voice, auspicious, subtle, fully developed, steady, impressive, fame and renown, and their opposites; and the state of being a Tīrthaṅkara.
That which, having the nature of arising, goes to another state of existence is a "destiny" (gati).
It is of four kinds: the destiny of hell-beings, the destiny of animals, the destiny of humans, and the destiny of gods.
That characteristic by which one becomes a hell-being is the "name of the hell-realm" (*narakagatināman*).
The same should be applied to the remaining [realms] as well.
Within those realms such as the hells, the essence of an entity (*arthātman*)—unified by a non-deviating similarity—is the "birth" (*jāti*).
The name "birth" (jāti-nāman) has that as its cause.

It is fivefold: the name of birth with one faculty, the name of birth with two faculties, the name of birth with three faculties, the name of birth with four faculties, and the name of birth with five faculties.
That from whose arising the self is designated by the term "one-facultied" is the name of birth with one faculty.
The same should be applied to the remaining [categories] as well.
That from whose arising the body of the self is produced is called "body-name" (*śarīranāman*).
It is fivefold: gross body-name, transformation body-name, assimilative body-name, fiery body-name, and karmic body-name.
Their distinction has been explained.
That from whose arising there is the differentiation of limbs and sub-limbs is called the *nāmakarma* of limbs and sub-limbs (*aṅgopāṅga-nāman*).

It is of three kinds: the *nāmakarma* of limbs and sub-limbs of the gross body (*audārika-śarīra*), the *nāmakarma* of limbs and sub-limbs of the transformational body (*vaikriyika-śarīra*), and the *nāmakarma* of limbs and sub-limbs of the assimilative body (*āhāraka-śarīra*).
That from which perfection arises is transformation (*nirmāṇa*).
It is of two kinds: transformation of place (*sthāna-nirmāṇa*) and transformation of dimension (*pramāṇa-nirmāṇa*).
Depending on the arising of the name of that particular class [of being], it brings about the place and the dimension of the eyes and so forth.
That by which something is created is "creation" (*nirmāṇa*).

That due to the arising of which there occurs the mutual joining of the spatial parts of embodied beings who possess appropriated [matter] because of the emergence of bodily karma is called "bonding" (*bandhana*).

That due to the arising of which there occurs the unification of coarse and other types of bodies through their mutual penetration of spatial parts without any intervening gaps is "cohesion" (*saṃghātana*).
That from whose arising the production of the form of the body—whether gross or otherwise—occurs is the name of shape (*saṃsthāna-nāman*).

It is divided into six types: the name of the symmetrical-quadrangular shape (*samacaturasra-saṃsthāna*), the name of the Banyan-tree-circumferential shape (*nyagrodha-parimaṇḍala-saṃsthāna*), the name of the Svāti-star shape (*svāti-saṃsthāna*), the name of the hunchbacked shape (*kubja-saṃsthāna*), the name of the dwarf shape (*vāmana-saṃsthāna*), and the name of the misproportioned shape (*huṇḍa-saṃsthāna*).
That from whose arising there occurs a particularity in the binding of the bones is the name of bone-jointing (*saṃhanana-nāman*).

That [bondage] is of six kinds: the name of adamantine *vajrarṣabhanārāca* bone-jointing, the name of *vajranārāca* bone-jointing, the name of *nārāca* bone-jointing, the name of *ardhanārāca* bone-jointing, the name of *kīlikā* (pin) bone-jointing, and the name of *asaṃprāptāsṛpāṭikā* (unjoined-separation) bone-jointing.
That which, through its arising, brings about the manifestation of touch is the name of touch (*sparśanāma*).

It is of eight kinds: the name of roughness, the name of softness, the name of heaviness, the name of lightness, the name of smoothness, the name of dryness, the name of coldness, and the name of heat.
That which is the cause for the discrimination of taste is called "taste" (*rasa*).
It is fivefold: the name "bitter," the name "pungent," the name "astringent," the name "sour," and the name "sweet.
That which has its origin in the arising of odor is called "odor" (*gandha*).

That is of two kinds: the name of pleasant odor and the name of unpleasant odor. That which is the cause for the differentiation of color is the name of color. That is fivefold: the name of black color, the name of blue color, the name of red color, the name of yellow color, and the name of white color.
That whose arising results in the non-destruction of the form of the previous body is the *ānupūrvya-nāman* (transmigratory karmic matter).

It is of four kinds: *ānupūrvya-nāman* suitable for the hellish state, *ānupūrvya-nāman* suitable for the animal state, *ānupūrvya-nāman* suitable for the human state, and *ānupūrvya-nāman* suitable for the celestial state.

That whose arising causes one neither to fall downward due to heaviness like a lump of iron, nor to rise upward due to lightness like cotton-wool from the sun, is the *gurulaghu-nāman* (heavy-light karmic matter).
That which, upon its arising, results in injury caused by such means as self-inflicted hanging or falling from a precipice, is called *upaghāta-nāma*.
That which is the cause of being struck down by the weapons of others and so forth is called *paraghāta-nāma*. That which, through its arising, brings about heat is *ātapa-nāma*.
That which exists in the sun is the cause of illumination; that is the name "illumination. That [name] exists in the moon, fireflies, and so forth.
That which is the cause of inhalation is called the name-aggregate of inhalation (*ucchvāsa-nāman*). Having left behind space,
that which effects movement therein is the name-aggregate of movement through space (*vihāyogati-nāman*).
That [body-making karma] is of two kinds, distinguished as auspicious and inauspicious.

That body-making karma (*śarīranāmakarma*) from whose arising a body is produced which serves as the instrument of experience for a single soul is called *pratyekaśarīranāma*. That body-making karma from whose arising a body is produced which is common to many souls by virtue of being the cause of their collective experience is called *sādhāraṇaśarīranāma*.
That which, through its arising, results in birth among those with two or more sense-faculties is the *trasa-nāma*.
That which, as its cause, results in manifestation among one-sensed beings is the *sthāvara-nāma*. That which, through its arising, results from the affection of others is the *subhaga-nāma*.
That which, upon its arising, causes displeasure even when endowed with qualities such as beauty of form is the *durbhaga-nāman* (name of ill-fortune).
That which is the cause for the production of a pleasant voice is the *susvara-nāman* (name of beautiful voice). Its opposite is the *duḥsvara-nāman* (name of harsh voice).
That from whose arising beauty results is the name "beautiful" (*śubha-nāman*).
Its opposite is the name "ugly" (*aśubha-nāman*).
That which brings about the subtle body is the name "subtle" (*sūkṣma-nāman*).
The name-karma called *bādara* is the cause of a body that does not obstruct others.
That which, through its arising, brings about the completion of the acquisitions (*paryāpti*) such as nutrition, is the *paryāpti-nāma*.

It is of six kinds: the acquisition of nutrition, the acquisition of the body, the acquisition of the sense organs, the acquisition of respiration, the acquisition of speech, and the acquisition of the mind.
The cause for the absence of the six kinds of completion is called "incompleteness" (aparyāpti-nāman).
That which brings about stability is called "stability" (sthira-nāman);
its opposite is called "instability" (asthira-nāman).
The name-field *ādeya* is the cause for having a body endowed with radiance.
The name-field *anādeya* is the cause for having a body devoid of radiance. The name-field *yaśaskīrti* is the cause for the manifestation of the qualities of merit.
The fruit opposed to that is the name "infamy" (ayaśaḥkīrti).
The cause of arhatship is the name "tīrthakaratva" (the state of being a ford-maker).

The classification of the secondary types (*uttaraprakṛti*) of the *nāmakarman* has been explained. Immediately following that, the classification of the secondary types of *gotra*, which is the subject of the next section, is now being explained: high and low.
Lineage is of two kinds: high lineage and low lineage.
That from the arising of which one is born into families honored by the world is high lineage.
That from whose arising there is birth in despised families is the *nīcairgotra* (low family status).
To explain the secondary subdivisions (*uttaraprakṛti*) of the eighth type of karma, he says:
A detailed classification is made with reference to the obstacles to giving, gain, enjoyment, utilization, and vigor— namely, "the obstacle to giving," "the obstacle to greed," and so forth.
It is designated as such because it is the cause of obstructing the transformation of giving and the other perfections.

Due to the arising of these [obstacles], one who wishes to give does not give; one who wishes to obtain does not obtain; one who desires to eat does not eat; one who longs to enjoy does not enjoy; and one who wishes to exert effort does not exert effort—these are the five types of obstacles.
The varieties of the bondage of nature (*prakṛti-bandha*) have been explained.
Now, the varieties of the bondage of duration (*sthiti-bandha*) must be discussed.
That duration is of two kinds: superior and inferior.
In this regard, for the sake of specifying those karma-natures whose maximum duration is equal, it is said:
the maximum duration for the first three [ghāti-karmas] and for obstructive karma (antarāya) is thirty *koṭīkoṭīs* of *sāgaropamas*.
The word "from the beginning" (*āditaḥ*) is stated so that there might not be a grasping of three [kalpas] in the middle or at the end.
The mention of "obstruction" (*antarāya*) is for the purpose of including those that are separated.
A *sāgaropama* has the measure already described.
*Koṭīṇāṃ koṭyaḥ* means *koṭīkoṭyaḥ*. "Para" means "supreme" or "highest.

This is what is being stated: the maximum duration (*sthiti*) of the karmas of knowledge-obscuration (*jñānāvaraṇa*), perception-obscuration (*darśanāvaraṇa*), feeling (*vedanīya*), and obstructive (*antarāya*) is thirty *koṭīkoṭya*s of *sāgaropama*s.
To whom does it belong? To one who possesses wrong view, who has perception, who possesses the five faculties, and who is fully developed.
Regarding others, conviction should be established based on scripture.
To explain the attainment of the maximum duration of deluding karma (mohanīya), it is said:
seventy [sāgaropamas] for deluding karma.
The phrase "the maximum duration is ten million times ten million *sāgaropamas*" continues [to apply here].
This maximum duration is also to be understood as applying to a five-facultied, fully developed being with perception who holds wrong view.
For others, the understanding should be made according to the scriptures.
In order to demonstrate the attainment of the maximum duration for both name and lineage, he says:
"The [duration] of name and lineage is twenty [kalpas]."
The phrase "the duration beyond is ten million times ten million sāgaropamas" continues [from the previous section].
This too is the maximum duration for a wrong-viewed being who is a fully developed five-facultied sentient being with perception.
The [lifespans] of others are to be understood according to their respective scriptures.
Now, the maximum duration of life is stated as follows:
The lifespan is thirty-three *sāgaropamas*.
Furthermore, the inclusion of the term "*sāgaropama*" is for the purpose of excluding [the calculation of] millions upon millions (*koṭīkoṭī*).
The phrase “the supreme state” (parā sthitiḥ) carries over [from the previous context].
This too belongs to what was previously mentioned;
the remainder is to be understood from scripture (āgama).
The superior duration has been explained.
Now, the inferior duration must be stated.

In this context, having set aside five types of karma whose minimum duration is equal [to that of the others], two sūtras are presented for the sake of brevity in order to establish the minimum duration of three [other] types:
the minimum duration of the *vedanīya* is twelve *muhūrta*s.
"Other" means inferior.
For the [karma] to be experienced [as feeling], there are twelve muhūrtas;
for name and lineage, eight.
The term ‘muhūrta’ is understood to carry over [from the previous context],
as is the phrase ‘another state.’
In order to demonstrate that the minimum duration established by nature is an *antarmuhūrta* for the remaining [karmas], he says: "For the others, it is an *antarmuhūrta*."
For the remaining five types of karma, the minimum duration is one antarmuhūrta.

The minimum duration for knowledge-obscuring (jñānāvaraṇa), perception-obscuring (darśanāvaraṇa), and obstructive (antarāya) karmas occurs at the stage of subtle-passion (sūkṣmasāṃparāya); for deluding (mohanīya) karma, it occurs at the stage of non-returning-gross-passion (anivṛttibādarasāṃparāya).
Regarding lifespan, it refers to animals and humans whose lifespans are calculable in years.
He said: "Both types of duration have been explained."
Now, as to what the characteristic of the experience (*anubhava*) of the [karmas] such as knowledge-obscuring (*jñānāvaraṇa*) is, he says:
"Experience is fruition (*vipāka*). (774)
Vipāka (ripening) is either distinguished or manifold.
It is "distinguished ripening" because it is distinguished by the specific influx (*āsrava*) of passions (*kaṣāya*), such as those previously mentioned as intense, mild, and so forth.

Alternatively, it is "manifold ripening" because it possesses a diverse nature produced by the differences in causes characterized by substance (*dravya*), field (*kṣetra*), time (*kāla*), birth-state (*bhava*), and mode (*bhāva*).
This is designated as "experience" (*anubhava*).
Due to the intensity of pure transformations, the experience of pure types of karma is intense, while that of impure types is weak.
Due to the intensity of impure transformations, the experience of impure types of karma is intense, while that of pure types is weak.
Thus, experience (anubhava) acquired through the power of conditions proceeds in two ways: by its own face and by the face of another.
For all root-natures (mūlaprakṛti), experience occurs only by their own face.
For the subsequent natures (uttaraprakṛti) of a similar class—excluding those of longevity, the delusion of vision, and the delusion of conduct—it also occurs by the face of another.
For the life-span of hell-beings does not ripen through the medium of the life-span of animals or humans;
nor does the delusion of views ripen through the medium of the delusion of conduct, nor does the delusion of conduct ripen through the medium of the delusion of views.
He said: "We admit that experience is the ripening of various kinds of karma accumulated previously.
However, we do not understand this: is this [experience] discerned (*prasaṃkhyāta*) or undiscerned (*aprasaṃkhyāta*)? To this it is replied: we say that it is experienced as something discerned.
Why? Because—"

Just as the absence of knowledge is the fruit of the obscuration of knowledge (*jñānāvaraṇa*), and the obstruction of the power of vision is the fruit of the obscuration of vision (*darśanāvaraṇa*), so too, through the designation of names that correspond to their actual meaning, a conviction based on experience arises regarding all the various types of karmic matter (*karmaprakṛti*).

He asks: "If it is asserted that experience is the fruition (*vipāka*), then once that karma has been experienced, does it remain like an ornament, or does it fall away with its essence extracted? To this it is replied:
"And from that, there is shedding (*nirjarā*)."

Nirjarā is the cessation of karma through the destruction of its prior state and the absence of its continued existence, occurring like the transformation of boiled rice and other foods after they have been consumed and provided for one's own benefit or harm.
It is of two kinds: that born of maturation (vipākajā) and the other (itarā).

In this regard, *vipākajā nirjarā* (decay born of fruition) is the cessation of that commenced fruit of auspicious and inauspicious karma which has entered the stream of the succession of experiences arising when its time for maturation has gradually arrived within the great ocean of *saṃsāra*, which is tossed by the various distinctions of many births across the four states of existence.

*Avipākajā nirjarā* (decay not born of fruition) is that [cessation] wherein karma—whose time for fruition has not yet arrived—is forcibly brought into the stream of rising experiences (*udayāvali*) through the power of specific intentional actions (*aupakramikakriyāviśeṣa*), even though it was not yet active (*anudīrṇa*), and is then experienced, like the ripening of mangoes, jackfruits, and the like.
The word *ca* (and) has the sense of collecting other causes.
Since it will be stated that "there is also shedding (*nirjarā*) through austerity (*tapas*)," the meaning of the aphorism is thus applied as "from another [cause] as well.
For what purpose is the mention of shedding made here? Should it not have been mentioned after *saṃvara*, following the order of the enumeration? It is mentioned here for the sake of brevity.
For in that reading, the statement "maturation is experience" would have to be restated again. He says:
"The bondage of experience has already been mentioned."
Now, the bondage of space-points (*pradeśabandha*) must be discussed.

Once that has been discussed, these points must be explained: what are its causes, when does it occur, from what does it arise, what is its nature, in what [karmic matter] does it reside, and what is its magnitude? To that end, this aphorism is formulated, which follows a sequence according to the distinctions of the questions raised:

"Conditioned by the name-karma (*nāmakarman*), due to specific types of yoga, [the karmic matter] remains with an infinitesimal penetration into a single space-point, occupying all the soul's space-points, and consisting of infinite-infinite space-points."
*Nāmapratyayāḥ* means “conditions of name. By the term “name,” all fundamental karmic substances (*karmaprakṛti*) are designated, according to the statement, “He [is reborn] according to his name.
By this, the state of being a cause is expressed.
In the phrase "sarveṣu bhaveṣu sarvataḥ," the suffix *tasi* is applied in the sense of "seen from another [perspective]" (*anyato ’pi*), resulting in *sarvataḥ*.
By this, the inclusion of time (*kāla*) is established.
For for each individual soul (*jīva*), there have been infinite past births, and there will be future ones—whether they be numerable, innumerable, or infinitely infinite.
Because individuals (*pudgala*) are taken up as karma due to specific conditions (*nimitta*) of yoga, this constitutes an explanation of the specific conditions.

The inclusion of the term "subtle" (*sūkṣma*) and so forth is for the purpose of following the nature of those individuals who are fit to be grasped as karma; that is, the individuals fit to be grasped are subtle, not gross.
The statement regarding "pervasion within a single space-unit" (*ekakṣetrāvagāha*) is for the purpose of excluding other spaces.
The word “sthitāḥ” (are situated) is intended to exclude other actions, meaning they are situated and not moving.
The phrase “in all parts of the self” is for the purpose of indicating the locus; it means that the particles of karma do not reside in only one part or similar [limited] areas.
Where, then? They remain pervading all parts of the self—above, below, and across.
The expression “infinitely infinite space-points” (*anantānantapradeśa*) is intended to exclude other measures; that is, they are neither numerable, nor innumerable, nor even merely infinite.

Indeed, those aggregates of matter (*pudgalaskandha*) possess infinitely many qualities that cannot be fully realized; they consist of space-points measured by an infinite fraction of the perfected souls (*siddha*); they occupy an innumerable fraction of the space of a cubic finger-breadth (*ghanāṅgula*); they have a duration of one, two, three, four, or a numerable number of time-units (*samaya*); they are characterized by five colors, five tastes, two smells, and four touches; and they are capable of becoming the eight types of karmic matter (*karmaprakṛti*), being assimilated by the self through the power of yoga.
Thus, the partial bondage (pradeśa-bandha) should be understood in brief.

[The opponent] says: "It was objected that merit (puṇya) and demerit (pāpa), which were mentioned as distinct categories from the category of bondage, are actually included within that [general] bondage; this objection has been refuted."
In this regard, it must be stated: what here is the bondage of merit (*puṇyabandha*) and what is the bondage of demerit (*pāpabandha*)?
To that end, for the purpose of enumerating the types of merit, this is commenced:
merit consists of [karmas] to be experienced as pleasant, as well as those of auspicious lifespan, name, and lineage (*gotra*).
"Wholesome" (śubha) means "praiseworthy.
This term is connected individually with each of the subsequent items: wholesome lifespan, wholesome name, and wholesome lineage.
The three types of auspicious lifespan are the lifespan of animals, the lifespan of humans, and the lifespan of gods.
Auspicious name has thirty-seven varieties.

Namely: human destiny, celestial destiny, five-sensed birth, the five bodies, the three limbs and minor limbs, symmetrical-quadrangular figure, adamantine-ox-like-joint, commendable color, taste, smell, and touch; the two types of progression (ānupūrvya) for human and celestial destinies; lightness, obstruction, respiration, heat, luster, commendable movement through space; the [eight sub-types]: mobile, gross, developed, individual body, stable, beautiful, fortunate, melodious voice, attractive, fame and renown; transformation; and the name of a Tīrthaṅkara.
There is one auspicious [karma], namely high status (uccairgotra), and pleasant-feeling [karma] (sadvedya).
These forty-two types of mental states are designated as "meritorious. Anything other than these is "evil."
Any action other than the collection of the fundamental natures of actions known as merit is called "evil.
That is of eighty-two kinds.

They are as follows: there are five types of knowledge-obscuring karma (*jñānāvaraṇa*), nine of perception-obscuring karma (*darśanāvaraṇa*), twenty-six of deluding karma (*mohanīya*), and five of obstructive karma (*antarāya*). There are thirty-four types of name-karma (*nāmakarma*): the two destinies of hell-beings and animals; the four classes of birth; the five bodily figures (*saṃsthāna*); the five bone-joints (*saṃhanana*); the unfavorable [qualities of] color, taste, smell, and touch; the two types of migratory flow (*ānupūrvī*) for hell-beings and animals; the [karmas of] harmfulness, unfavorable movement (*vihāyogati*), immobility (*sthāvara*), subtle (*sūkṣma*), incomplete (*aparyāpta*), common body (*sādhāraṇaśarīra*), unsteady (*asthira*), unpleasant (*aśubha*), unfortunate (*durbhaga*), harsh-voiced (*duḥsvara*), unattractive (*anādeya*), and ill-repute (*ayaśaḥkīrti*). Thus, there are thirty-four types of name-karma.
The non-existent [karmic matter] to be experienced consists of hellish lifespan and low status.
Thus has the category of bondage been explained in detail.
It is accessible through the direct perception of limited knowledge, mental perception, and omniscience, and is inferable from the scriptures taught by those [who possess such perception].
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Accomplishment of All Aims," in the *Tattvārthavṛtti*.
Now begins the ninth chapter.
The category of bondage has been explained.
Now, the occasion has arrived for the explanation of restraint (*saṃvara*), which follows immediately after it; therefore, he says this:
"Restraint is the cessation of the influxes (*āsrava*)."
The influx (*āsrava*) that is the cause for undertaking new karma has been explained.
Its cessation is called restraint (*saṃvara*).

It is twofold: restraint of existence (*bhāva-saṃvara*) and restraint of substance (*dravya-saṃvara*). Among these, the cessation of activity caused by cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) is the restraint of existence.
Upon that cessation, the severance of the appropriation of the person (*pudgala*) by means of prior karma is the restraint of substance.

This is now investigated: in which stage of spiritual development (*guṇasthāna*) does the restraint (*saṃvara*) of what occur? To this it is replied: the self (*ātman*), when brought under the sway of the rising of the karma of false view (*mithyādarśana*), is one of false vision (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
