In that state, whatever karma flows in (*āsravati*) primarily due to false vision, the restraint of that [karma] occurs in the remaining stages, beginning with the "right-vision-with-attachment" (*sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi*) and so forth, through its cessation.

What, then, is that [delusion]? It is characterized by sixteen types [of karmic matter]: false conviction (*mithyātva*); the neuter gender (*napuṃsaka-veda*); the life-span of hell-beings (*naraka-āyuḥ*); the hellish destiny (*naraka-gati*); the one-, two-, three-, and four-sensed births (*ekadvitricatur-indriya-jāti*); the irregular body-shape (*huṇḍa-saṃsthāna*); the unattained bone-joint (*asaṃprāpta-asṛpāṭika-saṃhanana*); the sequence suitable for the hellish destiny (*naraka-gati-prāyogya-anupūrvya*); heat (*ātapa*); immobility (*sthāvara*); subtlety (*sūkṣma*); the incomplete state (*aparyāptaka*); and the common body (*sādhāraṇa-śarīra*).

Non-restraint (*asaṃyama*) is of three kinds, according to the distinctions of the arising of the infinite-bonding (*anantānubandhi*), the non-renouncing (*apratyākhyāna*), and the renouncing (*pratyākhyāna*) [passions].
In the absence of that [object], restraint should be understood as pertaining to the action conditioned by it.

For example—of these twenty-five types of *prakṛtis*, namely: *nidrānidrā*, *pracalāpracalā*, *styānagṛddhi*, the four *anantānubandhi* [passions] of anger, pride, deceit, and greed, female gender (*strīveda*), animal lifespan (*tiryagāyuḥ*), the four types of animal gait (*tiryaggati*), the four types of physical configuration (*saṃsthāna*), the four types of bone-joint structure (*saṃhanana*), the animal-gait-proper (*tiryaggatiprāyogyānupūrvya*), luster (*udyota*), inauspicious movement (*apraśastavihāyogati*), misfortune (*durbhaga*), harsh voice (*duḥsvara*), untrustworthiness (*anādeya*), and low status (*nīcairgotra*)—the bonders (*bandhaka*) are those from the one-sensed beings up to the *sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi*, for these have as their primary influx (*āsrava*) the lack of self-restraint (*asaṃyama*) caused by the rise of the *anantānubandhi* passions.
In the absence of that [rise], there is the cessation (*saṃvara*) of these [bondages] hereafter.

The ten types of karmic matter—consisting of the non-renouncing (*apratyākhyāna*) passions of anger, pride, deceit, and greed; human lifespan; human destiny (*gati*); the gross body (*audārika-śarīra*) along with its limbs and minor parts (*aṅgopāṅga*); the adamantine *vajra-rṣabha-nārāca* bone-joint (*saṃhanana*); and the human-destiny-conducive transmigration-body (*anupūrvya*)—are bound by those ranging from the one-sensed beings up to the uncontrolled right-viewed (*asaṃyata-samyagdṛṣṭi*). These are caused by non-restraint (*asaṃyama*) produced by the rising of the non-renouncing passions. Above that level, due to the absence of these [passions], there is restraint (*saṃvara*) regarding them.
Furthermore, lifespan is not bound by the quality of mixed-right-and-wrong view (*samyag-mithyātva*).

The four types of karma—namely, the passions of anger, pride, deceit, and greed that obstruct partial renunciation (*pratyākhyānāvaraṇa*)—have as their causes for influx the lack of self-restraint (*asaṃyama*) resulting from the arousal of these partial-renunciation passions. Beings beginning with the one-sensed organisms and ending with those who are partially restrained (*saṃyatāsaṃyata*) are the binders of these karmas.
Due to the absence of those [passions], there is the cessation (*saṃvara*) of them in the higher stages.
In the absence of that [lack of restraint], there is the suppression of what has been brought about by negligence (*pramāda*).

The cessation of karma brought about by negligence should be understood as occurring from the stage of the "negligent self-restrained" (pramatta-saṃyata) upward, due to the absence of that negligence.
What, then, is that [karma]?
It consists of the variations of non-pleasurable experience (asadvedya), lack of delight (arati), sorrow (śoka), instability (asthira), inauspiciousness (aśubha), and ill-fame (ayaśaskīrti).
Negligence alone is the cause for the commencement of the bondage of celestial lifespan (*devāyurbandha*); non-negligence (*apramāda*) is also proximate to it.
Beyond that point, there is its restraint (*saṃvara*).

It should be understood that for whichever karma the influx (*āsrava*) consists solely of the passions (*kaṣāya*) and not negligence and so forth, there is no cessation [of that influx] when those [passions] are restrained.
And that kaṣāya, being devoid of negligence and the like, is established across three guṇasthānas according to its intense, medium, or mild state.
Therein, at the beginning of the apūrvakaraṇa stage, within a numerable fraction [of the duration], two karma-prakṛtis—namely, sleep (nidrā) and drowsiness (pracalā)—are bound.

Thereafter, within the remaining calculable portion, thirty *prakṛtis* are bound: the celestial state (*devagati*), the five-sensed birth (*pañcendriyajāti*), the *vaikriyika*, *āhāraka*, *taijasa*, and *kārmaṇa* bodies; the symmetrical (*samacaturasra*) figure; the limbs and sub-limbs of the *vaikriyika* and *āhāraka* bodies; color, smell, taste, and touch; the celestial-state-favorable transference (*devagatiprāyogyānupūrvya*); lightness (*agurulaghu*); self-obstruction (*upaghāta*); obstruction by others (*paraghāta*); respiration (*ucchvāsa*); favorable movement through space (*praśastavihāyogati*); mobile (*trasa*); gross (*bādara*); developed (*paryāpta*); individual body (*pratyekaśarīra*); stable (*sthira*); beautiful (*śubha*); fortunate (*subhaga*); melodious voice (*susvara*); lovable (*ādeya*); formation (*nirmāṇa*); and the Tīrthaṅkara quality (*tīrthakara*).
At the very last moment of that [stage], four natures—namely those designated as laughter, pleasure, fear, and disgust—undergo bondage.
These, being characterized by intense *kaṣāya* influxes, are closed off from the aforementioned portion due to their absence.
From the first moment of the *anivṛtti-bādara-sāmparāya* stage, the male gender and the passion of anger are bound for a number of calculable parts.
Thereafter, in the remaining numerable portions, the passion of pride (*māna-saṃjvalana*) and the passion of deceit (*māyā-saṃjvalana*) undergo bondage.
At the very last moment of that [state], the passion of greed (*lobha-saṃjvalana*) undergoes bondage.
These categories of karma are the influx of middling passions; in their absence, they attain cessation (*saṃvara*) beyond the aforementioned portion.

The subtle-passion (sūkṣmasāṃparāya) stage is the binder of the five types of knowledge-obscuring karma, the four types of perception-obscuring karma, fame and renown, high status, and the five types of obstructive karma; these are influxes of mild passion.
Due to the absence of those [passions], there is the cessation (saṃvara) of them thereafter.
Only through yoga alone does bondage occur for those with pleasant-feeling karma, as well as for those with subsided-passion, destroyed-passion, and those with residual yoga (sayoga).
Due to the absence of that [activity], there is restraint for the *ayogakevalin*.
Having thus described restraint, he speaks in order to demonstrate its cause:

He [attains liberation] through the vows of restraint (*gupti*), carefulness (*samiti*), the religious duties (*dharma*), the reflections (*anuprekṣā*), the conquest of the hardships (*pariṣaha*), and right conduct (*cāritra*).
Among these, *gupti* is that by which the self is protected from the causes of saṃsāra.
*Samiti* is the correct movement for the purpose of avoiding injury to living beings.
*Dharma* is that which places one in a desired state.
*Anuprekṣā* is the contemplation of the inherent nature of the body and other such things.
Parīṣaha is the endurance [of hardships] for the sake of the shedding of karma (karmanirjarā) when sensations such as hunger arise. The conquest of parīṣaha is "pariṣahajaya.
The word *cāritra* has its meaning explained in the opening sūtra.
Because these [factors] such as the protections (*gupti*) are the most effective means for the act of restraint (*saṃvaraṇa*), they are designated as the instrument (*karaṇa*).
Although restraint is the subject under discussion, it is referred to by the pronoun "that" (*sa*) in order to establish its direct connection with the protections and so forth.
What is the purpose? It is for the sake of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*).
This very restraint is achieved through guarding and so forth alone, and not by any other means.

By this, bathing at sacred fords (*tīrtha*), initiation (*dīkṣā*), tonsure, offerings (*upahāra*), propitiation of deities, and the like are excluded; for there is no other way to cease the karma acquired through passion, hatred, and delusion.
In order to demonstrate the specific causes for restraint and the shedding of karmic matter, he says:
"And by means of austerity, there is shedding. (791)

Although austerity (*tapas*) is included within the category of dharma, it is mentioned separately for the purpose of demonstrating that it is a means for achieving both [merit and liberation], and to establish its preeminence with respect to self-restraint (*saṃvara*).

Now, one might object: "Austerity is accepted as a factor for the attainment of prosperity (*abhudaya*), since it is admitted to be the cause for reaching such states as that of the Lord of the Gods (*devendra*); how then can it be a factor for the shedding of karma (*nirjarā*)? This is not a fault, because a single thing is observed to have multiple effects, like fire.

Just as fire, though being one, is found to serve purposes such as softening, burning to ashes, or acting as charcoal, so too there is no contradiction in austerity being the cause for both the attainment of prosperity and the destruction of karma.
In order to establish the essential nature of restraint (*gupti*), which was mentioned first among the causes of discipline (*saṃvara*), it is said: "Restraint is the correct control of activity."
Yoga has been explained in the passage: "Yoga is the action of body, speech, and mind. Its restraint consists in the voluntary cessation of its activity.

The qualification "rightly" (*samyak*) is for the purpose of prohibiting engagement in the pursuit of the objects of sensual pleasure. Therefore, when there is the cessation of the application of body and so forth—which is characterized by the qualification "rightly" and is directed toward the non-manifestation of afflictions—karma caused by that [application] does not flow in; thus, the establishment of restraint (*saṃvara*) is to be understood. That is threefold: restraint of the body, restraint of speech, and restraint of the mind.
In that regard, for the purpose of proclaiming the faultless conduct of a sage who is [otherwise] incapable [of full restraint], it is said:
"The samitis are [proper conduct] regarding movement, speech, seeking alms, receiving and placing down objects, and excretion."
The term "rightly" (samyak) is understood to carry over [from the previous context].
By this, the modes of conduct (*īryā*) and so forth are qualified.
Right movement, right speech, right seeking, right taking up and putting down, and right disposal—

these five carefulnesses (*samiti*) should be understood as the means for a sage who knows the rules regarding the stations of living beings (*jīvasthāna*) and so forth to avoid harming living creatures.
By proceeding in this manner, restraint (*saṃvara*) arises from the cessation of the influx of karma caused by the transformation of lack of self-restraint (*asaṃyama*).
In order to explain the divisions of the third cause of restraint, which is the Dharma, it is said:
"The Dharma consists of supreme forbearance, gentleness, straightforwardness, purity, truthfulness, self-restraint, austerity, renunciation, non-possessiveness, and celibacy."

For what purpose is this stated? The first [section] is for the sake of restraining [unwholesome] activity; the second is for the sake of showing the means of activity to those who are incapable [of restraint].
This, moreover, the exposition of the tenfold dharma, should be understood as being for the sake of avoiding negligence in one who is engaged in the assemblies.

For a monk who approaches the families of others in search of the means for maintaining his body, forbearance (*kṣamā*) is the absence of mental turbidity when confronted by the abuse, mockery, contempt, beating, or physical injury inflicted by wicked people. Gentleness (*mārdava*) is the removal of pride, which is the absence of arrogance arising from the intoxication of birth and other such factors.
Straightforwardness (*ārjava*) is the lack of crookedness in one's yoga.
Purity (*śauca*) is the cessation of greed that has reached its highest degree.
Truthful speech (*satya*) is said to be wholesome speech directed toward virtuous and praiseworthy persons.

Now, is this not already included within the restraint of speech (*bhāṣā-samiti*)? This is not a fault; for the meaning of the restraint of speech (*vāk-samiti*) is this: a sage engaged in the restraint of speech, when conducting verbal communication with both the virtuous and the non-virtuous, should speak what is beneficial and measured. Otherwise, through passion, there would be the fault of the "unjust infliction of punishment" (*anartha-daṇḍa*). Thus is the meaning.

Furthermore, in this context, it is permitted—even if there is much to be done—for virtuous renunciants or those devoted to them, regarding [the practice of] truth, knowledge, right conduct, training, and so forth, for the sake of augmenting the Dharma.
Restraint (*saṃyama*) is the avoidance of living beings and the sense objects by one who abides in the *samitis*.
Austerity (*tapas*) is that which is practiced for the purpose of the destruction of karma.
That which will be explained later as having twelve varieties is to be understood here.
Giving—namely, the bestowing of knowledge and so forth—is appropriate for one who is self-restrained.

Non-possessiveness (*ākiṃcanya*) is the cessation of the mental disposition "this is mine" even with respect to things already acquired, such as the body, for the sake of removing the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).
"One who has nothing" (*akiñcana*) is so called because he possesses nothing whatsoever; the state or activity of such a person is "nothingness" (*ākiñcanya*).

Through the avoidance of recollecting women experienced in the past, listening to stories about them, and using beds or seats associated with women, one's celibacy (*brahmacarya*) remains perfectly fulfilled. Alternatively, *brahmacarya* is dwelling in the teacher’s household for the purpose of attaining independent conduct.
The supreme qualification is for the purpose of abandoning visible motives.

When these very [factors] are cultivated in this way—being free from attachment toward the attainment of their own qualities, the designation of dharmas, and the presence of faults on the opposing side—they become causes for restraint.
He said: It has been stated that the non-arising of anger and so forth occurs through focusing on objects that are the opposites of the specific qualities such as forbearance.
In that regard, it is asked: why does he focus on forbearance and the like, rather than proceeding otherwise?
It is replied: because these must be practiced by one who desires his own welfare, transformed by forbearance and the other virtues, just like a red-hot iron ball.

The *anuprekṣās* (contemplations) consist of reflecting upon impermanence, the lack of refuge, the nature of *saṃsāra*, oneness, otherness, impurity, influx (*āsrava*), restraint (*saṃvara*), shedding (*nirjarā*), the world, the rarity of awakening, and the well-expounded nature of the Dharma. These things—the body, the senses, objects of enjoyment, and material substances—are of the nature of arising; they are unstable by their very essence like bubbles on water. Throughout the various stages beginning with the womb, they are observed to undergo conjunction and separation. Yet, out of delusion, the ignorant person imagines them to be permanent.
The reflection that nothing whatsoever in saṃsāra exists eternally arisen apart from the self’s nature of knowledge, vision, and experience is the contemplation of impermanence (*anityatānuprekṣā*).

For when this worthy person reflects in this way, because there is an absence of attachment toward those [objects], no downfall occurs even at the time of separation, just as with perfumes, garlands, and the like that have been enjoyed and then discarded.

Just as there is no refuge for a young deer overcome by a powerful, hungry tiger seeking meat in a secluded place, so too there is no refuge found for a living being wandering amidst the calamities of birth, old age, death, disease, and the like.
Even a well-nourished body serves as an aid only toward food, not when misfortune strikes.
And even wealth accumulated with great effort does not follow one into another existence.
Even friends who have shared in one's joys and sorrows do not protect one at the time of death;
nor do kinsmen gathered together preserve one when overwhelmed by disease.
If there exists well-practiced dharma, it becomes the means for crossing over the great ocean of calamity.
For one being led away by death, even those such as the Thousand-Eyed One (Indra) are no refuge.
Therefore, in the perilous straits of the calamities of existence, Dharma alone is the refuge;
even a friend’s purpose is not infallible, and there is no other refuge whatsoever—this contemplation is the reflection on the lack of refuge (*aśaraṇānuprekṣā*).
For one who thus reflects, constantly thinking "I am without refuge," and being deeply distressed by worldly phenomena, there arises a relinquishing of the sense of "mine" regarding saṃsāric states.
Effort is then directed solely toward the path taught by the Blessed One, the Arhat, the Omniscient One.
Saṃsāra is the attainment of another existence for the self by the power of the ripening of karma.
It has been explained previously in the form of fivefold transformations.

Wandering in that saṃsāra, which is crowded with many hundreds of thousands of millions of classes of births, the living being, impelled by the machine of karma, becomes a father, a brother, a son, and a grandson.
Having been a mother, one becomes a sister, a wife, and a daughter.
Having been a master, one becomes a servant;
having been a servant, one also becomes a master.

Like an actor on a stage— or rather, what need for more words?— the contemplation of the nature of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), such as how one becomes one's own son and so forth, is the reflection upon cyclic existence (*saṃsārānuprekṣā*).
For when one contemplates in this way, being distressed by the fear of the suffering of cyclic existence, detachment from it arises.
And being disillusioned, he strives to abandon cyclic existence.
Regarding the experience of the great suffering of the recurrence of birth, aging, and death, he thinks: "I am alone; no one exists for me as either 'self' or 'other'."
I am born alone; I die alone.
No one—neither my own kin nor strangers—removes for me the sufferings of disease, old age, death, and so forth.
Relatives and friends do not follow one beyond the cemetery.
"Dharma alone is my constant companion, never failing"—this reflection is the contemplation on solitude (*ekatvānuprekṣā*). For one who cultivates this in such a way, no attachment to kinsmen arises.
Furthermore, no persistent attachment to hatred toward others arises;
thus, having attained a state of non-attachment, he strives solely for liberation.
The contemplation of otherness (*anyatvānuprekṣā*) is the reflection on the body as being distinct from oneself.

For example: although there is unity with respect to bondage, I am different [from the body] because of the difference in characteristics—the body is perceptible by the senses, while I am beyond the senses; the body is ignorant, while I am the knower; the body is impermanent, while I am eternal; the body has a beginning and an end, while I am without beginning or end. Many hundreds of thousands of bodies have passed away for me as I wandered through the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).
"How much less so, then, toward external possessions?"— for one who thus composes the mind, no longing arises for the body and other such things.
Then, when there is an excellence of dispassion preceded by the cultivation of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), the attainment of the ultimate bliss of liberation occurs.

This body has an utterly impure origin; it is nourished by the impurities of semen and blood, a vessel of filth like a refuse heap, covered merely by skin, with pores and channels from which flows a stream of extreme putridity. Even when one relies upon this physical form as if it were a glowing coal, it quickly brings about [suffering]. Even through bathing, anointing, fumigation, rubbing, clothing, garlands, and the like, its impurity cannot be removed. However, right vision (*samyagdarśana*) and other qualities, when cultivated, manifest the absolute purity of the soul (*jīva*). Thus, the contemplation of the nature of reality is the reflection on the impurity [of the body].
For one who recollects in this way, there arises a sense of revulsion toward the body.
Being revulsed, he composes his mind in order to cross the ocean of birth.

Influx (*āsrava*), restraint (*saṃvara*), and shedding (*nirjarā*), although previously mentioned, are introduced here for the purpose of contemplating their respective virtues and defects. They are as follows: In this context, influxes—consisting of the senses, passions (*kaṣāya*), vows, and so forth—are associated with ruin in this world and the next, and are as sharp as the force of a great river's current. Among these, the senses, such as touch and the rest, cause [beings] like forest elephants, crows, serpents, moths, and deer to plunge into the ocean of worldly existence; likewise, the passions (*kaṣāya*) produce in this life slaughter, bondage, infamy, and affliction.

And by causing one to wander hereafter through various states of existence ablaze with manifold sufferings—such reflection upon the faults of the influxes (*āsrava*) is the contemplation of the influxes (*āsravānuprekṣā*).
For one who reflects in this way, the understanding that forbearance and the other virtues are supreme does not falter.
All these faults of the influxes do not occur for one whose self is withdrawn like a tortoise.

Just as in the great ocean, if the openings of a ship are not closed, the inevitable destruction of those on board will occur when it is gradually overwhelmed by the water flowing in; whereas if the openings are closed, one reaches the desired destination without calamity—so too, when the gates for the influx of karma are restrained, there is no obstruction to spiritual welfare. This reflection upon the virtues of restraint is the "contemplation of restraint. For one who reflects in this way, there arises a state of constant application toward restraint.
And from that, there is the attainment of the state of supreme bliss (*niḥśreyasa*).
It has been stated that *nirjarā* (dissociation) is the ripening of experience (*vedanā-vipāka*).
It is twofold: that which is not preceded by conscious intention (*abuddhipūrvā*) and that which is rooted in the roots of virtue (*kuśalamūlā*).
Among these, that which arises from the ripening of the fruit of karma in the hells and other realms is not preceded by conscious intention; it is accompanied by unwholesomeness (*akuśala*).

When the conquest of the hardships (*pariṣaha*) has been achieved, that which is rooted in the roots of virtue is accompanied by wholesomeness (*śubha*) and is without further consequence (*niranubandha*).
Thus, the contemplation of the virtues and defects of *nirjarā* (dissociation of karma) is the reflection on *nirjarā*.
For one who recollects it in this way, there arises an engagement for the sake of the dissociation of karma.

The rule regarding the configuration and so forth of the world has been explained; that is, the rule concerning the configuration and so forth of the world situated in the vast central region of the infinite non-world-space (alokākāśa) has been explained.
Contemplating its nature is the reflection on the world (lokānuprekṣā).
For one who determines it in this way, there arises the purification of the knowledge of reality.
Within a single *nigoda* body, the living beings (*jīvas*) are infinitely greater in number than the perfected souls (*siddhas*).

Thus, the entire world is densely packed without any gaps by immobile beings (*sthāvaras*); therefore, for a mobile being (*trasa*) to fall there is as difficult as finding a grain of diamond-dust in a sea of sand.
And therein, because those with impaired faculties are so numerous, the state of possessing all five faculties is as difficult to obtain as gratitude is among virtues.
Furthermore, since there are many animals among the beasts, wild animals, birds, reptiles, and so forth, the human condition is as hard to attain as a heap of jewels at a crossroads.
And once that [human state] has passed away, its reappearance is as difficult to achieve as the rebirth of a burnt tree in its former form.

Furthermore, among these gains, being endowed with a favorable country, a noble family, intact faculties, and freedom from disease becomes increasingly more difficult to obtain at each successive stage.
Even if all these are obtained, if there is no acquisition of the True Dharma (*saddharma*), that birth is as useless as a face devoid of sight.
Having thus attained this Dharma which is so difficult to find, to be enamored by the pleasures of the senses is as fruitless as burning sandalwood for the sake of ashes.

For one who is detached from the pleasures of sense objects, however, the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) characterized by the cultivation of austerity, the promotion of dharma, and death at the appropriate time is difficult to attain.
The reflection that "when this [absorption] exists, the attainment of enlightenment becomes fruitful" is the contemplation on the difficulty of attaining enlightenment (*bodhidurlabhānuprekṣā*).
Indeed, for one who cultivates this in such a manner, once enlightenment has been attained, negligence never occurs again.
This Dharma taught by the Victor is characterized by non-violence, established in truth and so forth, and rooted in discipline.
It has patience as its strength, is protected by celibacy, prioritizes tranquility, is defined by certainty, and takes non-possessiveness as its objective support.

Due to the non-attainment of this [Dharma], living beings wander through beginningless saṃsāra, experiencing the suffering born from the ripening of evil karma. Furthermore, the reflection that upon its attainment, the acquisition of supreme bliss (niḥśreyasa) preceded by various forms of prosperity is certain, is the contemplation on the well-expounded nature of the Dharma.
For one who reflects in this way, constant application arises through devotion to the Dharma.
Thus, when there is the presence of reflections on impermanence and so forth, great restraint arises from maintaining supreme forbearance and the other virtues.
The mention of "reflection" in the middle [of the list] serves a dual purpose.

For by cultivating these reflections (*anuprekṣā*), one protects the supreme stages (*kṣamā*) and strives to conquer the hardships (*parīṣaha*). What, then, are those hardships, and for what purpose are they endured? To this he says:
The perfections (parīṣaha) are to be endured for the sake of non-deviation from the path and for the shedding of karmic matter (nirjarā).
Since restraint (saṃvara) is the subject under discussion, the path is thereby qualified by it.
Regarding the "path of restraint":
for the sake of not falling away from that [restraint] and for the sake of wearing away [karma], the *parīṣahas* (afflictions) must be endured.

Enduring hunger, thirst, and so forth, and not falling away from the path taught by the Jina, they close the gateway to the influx of karma through their practice and cultivation of that path; experiencing the results of karma that have already been initiated, they gradually wear away their karma and attain liberation.
To establish the nature and enumeration of these [twenty-two types of parīṣaha], he says:

hunger, thirst, cold, heat, gadflies and mosquitoes, nakedness, lack of pleasure, women, wandering, sitting, lying down, abuse, violence, begging, lack of gain, disease, contact with grass, dirt, lack of respect and honor, and lack of wisdom and knowledge.
There are twenty-two specific types of sensation, beginning with hunger.
One who seeks liberation must endure these.

For example: when a monk seeks blameless food, yet fails to obtain it or obtains only a small amount; when his sensations do not subside and he has turned away from the desire for alms at an improper time or place; when he cannot endure even the slightest necessary decline; when he is devoted to the cultivation of recitation and meditation; when he has frequently practiced both self-inflicted and externally-assisted fasting; when he consumes tasteless food; when his drinking has suddenly dried up like a few drops of water fallen upon a heated frying pan; and even while the sensation of hunger is acute—his victory over hunger consists in considering non-attainment to be of superior merit compared to attainment, and in disregarding the affliction of hunger.

For one who has renounced bathing in water, immersion, and sprinkling; who, like a bird, has no fixed seat or dwelling; and who disregards the remedies for thirst—arisen from excessive saltiness, unctuousness, dryness, or incompatible food, as well as from the summer heat, bile-fevers, and fasting—a thirst that agitates both body and senses—the endurance of thirst is praised when one extinguishes its flames with the cool, fragrant water of meditative concentration (samādhi), which fills the new earthen jar of steadfastness (dhṛti).

For one who has abandoned all covering, whose dwelling is not fixed like that of a bird, and who—having turned away from the desire for remedies when encountering snowfall and cold winds at the roots of trees, on paths, or upon stone slabs—does not recall the objects that served as remedies for cold previously experienced, but dwells instead within the inner chamber of the cultivation of knowledge, his endurance of the sensation of cold is proclaimed.

In a windless and waterless forest interior, where the trees have lost their shade due to fallen leaves dried by the rays of the summer sun, for one who has arrived there by chance and is afflicted by internal heat produced by fasting and other such means; for one whose throat and palate are parched by the harsh winds and heat of a forest fire, yet who does not think of the many remedies he previously experienced, and whose mind is intent on avoiding harm to living beings—the endurance of heat (*uṣṇasahana*) is thus described as the preservation of right conduct (*cāritrarakṣaṇa*).
The mention of "gadflies and mosquitoes" (*daṃśamaśaka*) is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*).

Just as the phrase "let the clarified butter be protected from crows" uses the mention of "crows" as an illustration for any potential destroyer, so too do [the crows] include biting flies, mosquitoes, gnats, wasps, ants, bedbugs, insects, termites, scorpions, and the like.

For one who endures the affliction caused by these without seeking a remedy, who does not retaliate against their harm in any of its three ways, and whose armor is the resolve solely for the attainment of Nirvāṇa—the endurance of those sensations is called the "endurance of the hardship of biting flies and mosquitoes.

The observance of the vow of nakedness (*acelaka*) should be understood as irreproachable for one who bears the stainless gold-like natural state that is beyond the reach of desire, being free from the faults of begging, guarding, and harming; who, due to the absence of possessions, maintains a practice leading individually to the attainment of *nirvāṇa* that does not oppress others; who, because of being devoid of mental agitation and perturbation, contemplates female forms as being utterly impure in the nature of a mass of pus; and who observes unbroken celibacy day and night.

For one who is self-restrained and indifferent toward contact with desirable sense-objects, who delights in the practice of self-study, meditation, and cultivation while dwelling in empty houses, temples, tree hollows, stone caves, and the like—places devoid of song, dance, and instrumental music; whose heart is free from the entry of the arrows of desire through the recollection of pleasures seen, heard, or experienced, or through listening to talk about them; and who is always compassionate toward living beings—for such a person, the victory over the hardship of discontent (*arati-pariṣaha*) is to be understood.

In secluded places such as groves and palaces, when women—intoxicated by the wine of the delusions of fresh youth—are assailing him, he must understand that the endurance of such female assault consists in keeping the fluctuations of his senses concealed like a tortoise, and rendering fruitless the operations of the god of love through charming smiles, gentle speech, playful glances, laughter, and a slow gait languid with intoxication.

The endurance of the hardship of wandering (caryā-pariṣaha) is to be understood as follows: for one who has long observed the celibate life in the teacher’s household; who has realized the true nature of the categories of bondage and liberation; who, for the sake of devotion to the bases of self-restraint (saṃyamāyatana), has been permitted by his teacher to travel to another region; who assumes detachment like the wind; whose body is exhausted by the afflictions of numerous fasts, moderation in diet, restrictions on food, and the renunciation of flavorful tastes; who avoids traveling on roads at improper times or places—which would contradict self-restraint—and who, despite having discarded footwear and suffering pain in his feet from being pierced by harsh pebbles, thorns, and the like, does not recall his former use of vehicles and carriages, but rather maintains his necessary duties without neglect at the proper time.

It is determined that the victory over the hardship of sitting (niṣadyā-pariṣaha) consists of the endurance of the afflictions caused by [the posture] for one who dwells in previously unaccustomed places such as cremation grounds, gardens, empty abodes, mountain caves, and thickets; who has examined the location with the light of the sun and his own sensory cognition; who has performed the prescribed rites; who has maintained the seated posture for a fixed duration; who is free from fear upon hearing the various terrifying sounds of lions, tigers, and other beasts; who does not deviate from the path to liberation by enduring the four kinds of calamities; and whose body remains unmoving from postures such as the hero’s posture (vīrāsana) or the squatting posture (utkuṭikāsana).

The endurance of the hardship of the bed (*śayyā-pariṣaha*) is said to belong to one who is exhausted by the fatigue of the path of recitation and meditation; who experiences sleep for a mere moment on ground-areas that are rough, uneven, crowded with many pebbles and potsherds, and subject to extreme cold and heat; who lies down like a log or in the "one-side" posture to avoid disturbing living beings; who, like a fallen piece of wood, does not turn over as his life-force departs; whose mind is intent upon the cultivation of knowledge; whose body remains unmoved even when various afflictions such as those from intermediate deities (*vyantara*) are inflicted; and who patiently endures the disturbances caused by them for an indefinite period of time.

Even when hearing false views, expressions of resentment, harsh words, contempt, insults, and vulgar speech—which are like flames fanning the fire of anger—the practitioner who has resolved to endure the hardship of verbal abuse is defined as one who, though his mind may not be immediately composed regarding their meaning and who might be capable of retaliating instantly, reflects instead upon the ripening of evil karma; thus, intent on the cultivation of ascetic practice, he leaves no room for even a single atom of the poison of the *kaṣāyas* within his own heart.

When his body is being struck by sharp weapons such as axes, clubs, mallets, and rocks, he who does not experience even the slightest mental agitation toward his assailants reflects: "This is the fruit of evil karma committed by me in the past; what can these wretched beings do? This body, which is by nature as fragile as a water bubble and a cause of calamity, is being tormented by them. My right knowledge, vision, and conduct are not harmed by anyone. Thinking thus, he regards the hardship of execution with equanimity, like one who has been anointed with sandalwood paste at the moment of bathing. § 828.

For one devoted to the practice of external and internal austerities, whose physical form has been rendered sapless by the power of that cultivation—like a tree whose essence has been squeezed out by the heat of a fierce sun and which is devoid of shade, being a mere mechanical frame of skin, bone, and network of veins—it is understood that he endures the hardship of begging; for even when his life is at stake, he does not solicit food, shelter, medicine, or the like through humble speech, changes in facial color, gestures of the body, or other such means, and even at the time of begging, his form is as difficult to discern as a flash of lightning.

One should understand that for a person who, like the wind, moves through many places without attachment; who has accepted eating at a single time; who is a practitioner of silence or one who conforms to that discipline; who depends solely on seeing his own body once [at each meal]; who uses only his cupped hands as a bowl; who, even after failing to obtain alms from many houses over many days, remains with an unafflicted mind; who is indifferent to examining the qualities of specific donors; and who is content—thinking, "For me, non-attainment is the highest austerity even compared to attainment"—there is the victory over non-attainment. § 830.

One should understand the endurance of the hardship of disease as follows: because one has no conceptual attachment to the body—recognizing it as a repository of all impurities, impermanent, and without protection—and because one has undertaken the maintenance of its stability for the sake of increasing and preserving the collection of the "jewel-vessels" of the [bodily] qualities; and because, like the application of ointment to a wound, one accepts food which is of great benefit; and because, even when hundreds of diseases arise simultaneously due to the agitation of the humors (vāta, etc. caused by the imbalance of consuming incompatible food and drink, one abandons subjection to them; and because, despite possessing various supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) derived from many specific austerities such as bathing and the acquisition of medicinal herbs, one remains free from longing for the body and has no need for its remedy. This is the endurance of the hardship of disease.
The mention of "grass" is an illustration for any cause of piercing pain.

Therefore, when one experiences foot-pain caused by being pierced by dry grass, rough gravel, thorns, sharp earth, spikes, and so forth, the victory over the hardship (*pariṣaha*) of the affliction caused by the touch of grass and the like should be understood as occurring when one’s mind is not directed toward those things while walking, lying down, or sitting, and when one is always vigilant in mind regarding the avoidance of injury to living beings.

For one who observes the vow of not bathing until death in order to avoid harming water-bodied beings, and whose head is covered by a mass of dust brought by the wind moistened with perspiration produced by the heat of fanning and scattering [of air], even when itching arises from eruptions of *sidhma*, *kacchu*, or *dadru*—and who avoids scratching, rubbing, or striking [the body]; whose mind is free from the intention to increase the impurities within oneself or to remove the impurities of others; and whose intellect is constantly intent on removing the mud of karmic impurity through the cleansing water of pure knowledge and conduct—the endurance of the affliction of dirt is thus described.

"Honor" consists of worship and praise. "Distinction" means being placed at the forefront or being invited at the commencement of rituals and other such activities; [the opponent says: "In this regard, no one shows me respect. No one performs for me prostrations, acts of devotion, the offering of the *saṃbhrama* seat, and so forth—despite my having long practiced the celibate life (*brahmacarya*), being a great ascetic, a knower of the determination of my own and others' doctrines, and a victor over opposing disputants many times over. Only those with false views possess excessive devotion; honoring even one who knows nothing at all under the presumption that he is omniscient, they promote their own doctrines."

If it were not a false report that in the past the Vyantaras and others performed fresh worship for those of extremely fierce asceticism, why would they not do so now for those like me? Thus, for one whose mind is free from such ill-directed thought, this is understood as the victory over the hardship of honor and hospitality (*satkāra-puraskāra-pariṣaha*).

The conquest of the hardship of wisdom (*prajñā-pariṣaha*) is to be understood as the elimination of the intoxication of knowledge (*vijñāna-mada*), [realized] when one thinks: "In my presence—who am expert in the *Aṅgas*, the *Pūrvas*, and the *Prakīrṇakas*, and proficient in grammar, logic, and the inner self—others do not shine at all, like the glow of a firefly overwhelmed by the radiance of the sun.

One should understand that the victory over the hardship of ignorance (*ajñāna-pariṣaha*) belongs to one who endures such disparaging words as "This man is ignorant, he does not know, he is like a beast," and so forth; who performs most difficult austerities; whose mind is ever-vigilant; and who does not harbor the thought, "Even now, no excellence of knowledge has arisen in me.

[He reflects: "My heart is purified by the cultivation of supreme dispassion; I have known the true nature of all things; I worship the Arhat, the shrine, and the true Dharma; I have long been a renunciant—yet even now, no excellence of knowledge has arisen in me. § 836.
The claim that "extraordinary miracles appeared for those who perform great fasts and other such observances" is mere idle chatter; this life of renunciation is devoid of purpose.

For one who does not find composure in the thought that "the observance of vows is fruitless," the endurance of the hardship of non-perception (*adarśana-pariṣaha*) is to be understood as resulting from the application of purity of vision (*darśana-viśuddhi*).

Thus, for one who endures the hardships that have arisen without volitional construction and whose mind is unafflicted, there occurs a great restraint (*saṃvara*) due to the cessation of the influxes (*āsrava*) resulting from the transformation of passion and the like.

He asks: "Do all these hardships assail one who is striving to cross the great wilderness of *saṃsāra*, or is there some distinction? To this it is replied: These [hardships], such as hunger and the rest, whose characteristics have been explained, are to be classified according to the various types of conduct (*cāritra*).
Furthermore,
these two must necessarily be understood as possessing fourteen [guṇasthānas]: namely, the subtle-passion (sūkṣmasāṃparāya) and the non-omniscient one free from passion (chadmasthavītarāga).
Hunger, thirst, cold, heat, gadflies and mosquitoes, walking, lying down, injury, lack of gain, disease, contact with grass, dirt, wisdom, and ignorance—these are the fourteen.
From the statement "fourteen," it should be understood that there is an absence of other *pariṣahas*.

He asks: It is indeed appropriate to state the restriction to fourteen for a detached (*vītarāga*) *chadmastha* (one still under the veil of ignorance), because of the absence of deluding karma (*mohanīya*) and consequently the absence of the eight *pariṣahas* produced by it which will be mentioned later.

But [one might object]: "In the stage of subtle passion (sūkṣmasāṃparāya), because of the actual existence of the rise of delusion (moha), the restriction that 'there are fourteen' is not tenable. This is incorrect; for it exists merely as a presence.
For in that state, there is only the rise of the kaṣāya of the flickering greed (lobhasaṃjvalana), and even that is extremely subtle.

Therefore, because one is virtually like a detached person (vītarāga) though still in the state of a non-omniscient knower (chadmastha), the restriction that 'there are fourteen' is indeed appropriate there as well.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the designation of "endurance" (*pariṣaha*) regarding the suffering of hunger and so forth is not logically tenable, because there is an absence of the conditions for the arising of delusion (*moha*) and because the arising [of such suffering] is mild, and thus there is no suffering of hunger and so forth to be endured?
[Response: That is not so. What is the reason? Because what is intended is the possession of the capacity [to endure].
It is like the designation of the capacity of a god who has attained all his goals (*sarvārthasiddhi*) to travel to the seventh earth (*pṛthivī*).

He asks: "If the presence of the afflictions (*pariṣaha*) is asserted to exist when the self possesses a body, then how many [afflictions] assail one who has attained absolute knowledge (*kevalajñāna*), yet remains subject to the experience of the fruits of the four types of karma? To this it is replied: "In that case, however—"

Eleven [afflictions] in the Jina: In the Jina, whose four destructive karmas (*ghātikarma*) have been cast away, there exist eleven types of endurance (*pariṣaha*) because of the presence of the karma to be experienced (*vedanīyakarma*).

But is it not the case that, due to the absence of the auxiliary factor of the rising of deluding karma (*mohanīya-udaya*), the designation of "affliction" (*pariṣaha*) is not appropriate when sensations such as hunger are absent? True, this is so; nevertheless, even in the absence of sensation, the metaphorical designation of "affliction" is applied with reference to the continued existence of the substance-karma (*dravya-karman*), just as the metaphorical designation of "meditation" (*dhyāna*) is applied with reference to the result of eliminating karma—even though there is no suppression of thought (*cintā-nirodha*)—in the case of one who has completely cast off all excellence of knowledge (*jñānātiśaya*). Alternatively, the ellipsis of the sentence should be supplied as "the eleven [afflictions] do not exist in the Jina," for the sūtras possess an implicit context (*sopaskāratva*).
For it is accepted that a sentence-remainder (vākyaśeṣa) is to be supplied, and that a sentence depends upon its speaker.
Therefore, because there is an absence of sensations such as hunger which accompany the arising of delusion, the sentence-remainder is "they do not exist.
He asked: "If the *pariṣahas* are distributed among the *sūkṣmasāṃparāya* and other stages, then where are they all together?
[The answer is: "In the *bādarasāṃparāya* stage, all [the *pariṣahas* are present]."§ 843.
*Sāmparāya* means *kaṣāya*. One who possesses coarse *sāmparāya* is called "one with coarse *sāmparāya*" (*bādarasāmparāya*).
This is not a designation for a specific stage of spiritual development (*guṇasthāna*).
What then? It is an explanation of the meaning.
By that, the inclusion of those who are restrained yet negligent and so forth is intended;
for in their case, all [faults] are possible because the defect of their passions (kaṣāya) has not been destroyed.

In which conduct, then, do all [the qualities] occur? They occur in each of the following: the conduct of equanimity (*sāmāyika*), the conduct of re-establishment (*chedopasthāpana*), and the conduct of purification through avoidance (*parihāraviśuddhi*). It is said: "We have understood this determination of the specific locations of the afflictions (*pariṣaha*); however, we do not know which karma is the effect of which primary nature (*prakṛti*. To this, it is replied:
Regarding the obscuration of knowledge (*jñānāvaraṇa*), there is the wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna*);
this [assertion] is untenable.

What is inappropriate here? Since the affliction of ignorance (*ajñāna-pariṣaha*) is possible when there is the obscuration of knowledge (*jñānāvaraṇa*), but the affliction of wisdom (*prajñā-pariṣaha*) occurs upon its removal, how could it exist while the obscuration of knowledge is present? To this it is replied: wisdom that is produced by the subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣāyopaśamikī*) of karma gives rise to pride when some other obscuration of knowledge remains, but not when all obscurations have been destroyed; thus, it is logical that it exists while the obscuration of knowledge is present. Furthermore, in order to specify the particular nature (*prakṛti-viśeṣa*) of two other afflictions, he says:
Regarding the delusion of views and the obstruction [to action], there is a correspondence between them and non-seeing and non-attainment,
respectively.

In the delusion of vision (*darśanamoha*), there is the endurance of non-vision (*adarśanapariṣaha*); in the obstruction to gain (*lābhāntarāya*), there is the endurance of non-gain (*alābhapariṣaha*).
It is asked: if there is one endurance in the first division of delusion, then how many are there in the second? To this it is replied:

in the delusion of conduct (*cāritramoha*), there are [the following]: nakedness (*nāgnya*), lack of pleasure (*arati*), women (*strī*), sitting (*niṣadyā*), abuse (*ākrośa*), begging (*yācanā*), and honor and respect (*satkārapuraskāra*).

Because the hardships such as nakedness (*nāgnya*) have their cause in the arousal of male passion (*puṃveda*) and so forth, we establish that they have the arousal of delusion (*moha*) as their cause.
How is this so for the hardship of sitting (*niṣadyā*)? Even in that case, it is because its purpose is to avoid causing injury to living beings.
"When delusion arises, a transformation resulting in the affliction of living beings occurs. In order to explain the specific natures of the remaining types of *parīṣaha*, he says:
Regarding what is to be felt, the remaining [factors] have been explained;
thus, the eleven hardships (pariṣaha) have been taught.
Other than those, the remaining [afflictions] "exist" when there is that which is to be experienced (*vedanīya*); this is the completion of the sentence.

Which, then, are they? They are the afflictions of hunger, thirst, cold, heat, gadflies and mosquitoes, walking, lying down, standing, disease, the touch of grass, and dirt. It is asked: Since the characteristics of the causes have been explained, how many of these afflictions arise within the individual and persist simultaneously? To this it is replied:
Numbers beginning with one are to be divided simultaneously within a single [group], up to nineteen;
the prefix *āṅ* has the sense of inclusion (*abhividhi*).
From this, it is understood that even nineteen [types of afflictions] may occur simultaneously in some cases.
If one asks, "How so? it is said: within a single self, there can be only one of the two afflictions of cold and heat, and likewise only one of the three—lying down, sitting, or walking.
Why? Because of their mutual contradiction.
When those three have simultaneously disappeared from a single individual, nineteen variations are to be understood as possible for the others. [Objection:

But surely, because wisdom (*prajñā*) and ignorance (*ajñāna*) are also contradictory, they cannot coexist simultaneously? [Response: There is no contradiction, because the "affliction of wisdom" (*prajñā-pariṣaha*) is in reference to scriptural knowledge (*śruta-jñāna*), whereas the "affliction of ignorance" (*ajñāna-pariṣaha*) is in reference to the absence of clairvoyance (*avadhi-jñāna*) and other such forms of knowledge.
He said: The five causes of restraint—namely, the guptis, samitis, dharmas, anuprekṣās, and the conquest of the pariṣahas—have been explained.
Now, that which is designated as conduct (cāritra) must also be stated as a cause of restraint; therefore, in order to demonstrate its divisions, it is said:
conduct consists of sāmāyika, chedopasthāpanā, parihāraviśuddhi, sūkṣmasāmparāya, and yathākhyāta.

Here it is objected: "Since restraint (*saṃyama*) has already been mentioned among the ten-fold dharma, and that very thing is conduct (*cāritra*), its mention again is redundant. It is not redundant; although conduct is included within dharma, it is mentioned at the end for the purpose of making known that it is the direct cause for the attainment of liberation (*mokṣa*).
Equanimity (*sāmāyika*) has been explained.
Where? In the [section] beginning with "abstention from purposeless travel and punishment in all directions" (*dig-deśānarthadaṇḍa-virati-sāmāyika*).
That is twofold: limited by time and unlimited by time.
Study of the scriptures (*svādhyāya*) and so forth are limited by time.
It is not restricted to specific times, such as during the postures (*īryāpatha*) and so forth.
*Chedopasthāpanā* (reinstatement) is either the correct remediation when a continuous stream of harm caused by negligence is destroyed, or the cessation of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
*Parihāra* (avoidance) is the abstention from killing living beings.

That conduct in which there is purity distinguished by that [avoidance] is called *parihāraviśuddhicāritra*. Because the passions (*kaṣāya*) are extremely subtle, it is called *sūkṣmasāṃparāyacāritra*.

Because of the subsidence (*upaśama*) and destruction (*kṣaya*) of deluding karma (*mohanīya*) without remainder, it is designated as *yathākhyātacāritra*, characterized by abiding in the natural state of the self.
It was described by those who practiced former conduct as "not attained" because it had not been reached previously due to the destruction and subsidence of delusion (*moha*).
Because the word *atha* functions in the sense of immediate succession, the meaning is that it manifests immediately after the complete destruction and subsidence of delusion.
Alternatively, it is called "as-described" (*yathākhyāta*), because it exists exactly as it has been described according to its own inherent nature (*ātmasvabhāva*).
The word “iti” should be understood as indicating completion.
Thus, it is made known that from conduct such as that which is called *yathākhyāta*, the complete exhaustion of all karma occurs.
The statement of the sequence beginning with *sāmāyika* is made for the purpose of proclaiming the progressive excellence of the successive qualities.

It has been stated that conduct (cāritra) has been explained. Immediately following that, it was indicated that "through austerity there is shedding" (tapasā nirjarā ca). Now, the prescription of that austerity must be set forth; therefore, this is said:
That is twofold: external and internal.
Each of these is sixfold.
Regarding that, he speaks in order to explain the divisions of the external:
Fasting, reduced intake of food, restriction of diet, renunciation of delicious tastes, dwelling in solitude, and mortification of the body constitute external austerity.
Fasting is for the purpose of attaining self-restraint, success, the destruction of attachment, the eradication of karma, and the acquisition of the scriptures, without regard for visible results.
Moderation in eating (*avamaudarya*) is for the sake of achieving the happiness of self-restraint, wakefulness, the pacification of faults, contentment, scriptural study, and so forth.

For a sage seeking alms, the restriction of intention regarding objects such as a single house and the limitation of one’s livelihood must be understood as being for the purpose of turning away from desire. The fourth austerity is the renunciation of nourishing substances such as ghee, for the sake of subduing the pride of the senses, conquering sleep, and achieving the happiness of scriptural study and other virtues.

The fifth austerity is the practice of lying down and sitting in secluded places such as empty houses—places free from the harassment of living beings—for the sake of achieving self-restraint, the overcoming of afflictions, and the successful accomplishment of the celibate life, scriptural study, meditation, and so forth.

The sixth austerity is bodily mortification, consisting of standing in the heat, dwelling at the foot of a tree, sleeping in an uncovered place, and remaining in various types of meditative postures; and so on.
For what purpose is this? It is for the sake of enduring physical suffering, non-attachment to pleasure, and the glorification of the sacred teaching.

And what is the distinction between this [ascetic practice] and a *pariṣaha* (endurance of hardship)? A *pariṣaha* is one that has befallen one by chance; [this practice], however, is bodily mortification performed by oneself.
Why is this considered external? It is external because it depends upon external substances and because it is perceptible to others.
To demonstrate the divisions of internal austerity, he says:
"Atonement, discipline, service, self-study, renunciation, and meditation are the latter [internal austerities]."
How is this internal? Because it has the purpose of regulating the mind.
The avoidance of the fault of negligence is *prāyaścitta*.
Veneration is respect toward those worthy of honor;
service consists of attending upon them through physical activity and the offering of material goods;
and self-study is the abandonment of laziness in the cultivation of knowledge.
The relinquishment of the conceptualization of self and what belongs to the self is *vyutsarga*.
The relinquishment of mental distraction is *dhyāna*.
In order to demonstrate its divisions, he says:
"There are nine, fourteen, five, and two divisions respectively prior to dhyāna. (860)
By the expression “in due order,” it is intended that penance has nine divisions, discipline is fourfold, service is tenfold, self-study is fivefold, and renunciation is twofold.
The statement “prior to meditation” indicates that meditation will be discussed later, as it requires extensive explanation.
In order to ascertain the nature of the divisions of the first [type], he says:
"inspection, repentance, both together, discernment, renunciation, austerity, severance, avoidance, and reinstatement.
In that regard, *ālocanā* is the reporting of negligence to the guru, free from the ten faults.
*Pratikramaṇa* is the manifestation of counteraction through the utterance of "I have committed a wrong" (*mithyā-duṣkṛta*).
When both are combined, it is called *tadubhaya*, because of the purification resulting from their conjunction.
Viveka is the separation of food, drink, utensils, and other such items that have become mixed together.
Vyutsarga is the practice of kāyotsarga (the renunciation of the body) and so forth.
Tapas consists of characteristics such as fasting (anaśana), reduced intake of food (avamaudarya), and the like.
The loss of the status of renunciation (*pravrajyā*) by means of [a period of] days, fortnights, months, and so forth, is *cheda* (cutting off).
Avoidance from afar through the division of fortnights, months, and so forth, is *parihāra* (exclusion).
Receiving initiation once again is *upasthāpanā* (reinstatement).
To explain the practice regarding the classification of discipline, he says:
"The applications of knowledge, vision, and conduct."
Under the heading of ‘discipline’ (*vinaya*), the following connection is established:
discipline of knowledge (*jñāna-vinaya*), discipline of vision (*darśana-vinaya*), discipline of conduct (*cāritra-vinaya*), and discipline of courtesy (*upacāra-vinaya*).
Discipline of knowledge (*jñānavinaya*) consists of the repeated practice and recollection of acquiring knowledge for the sake of liberation with great reverence.
Discipline of vision (*darśanavinaya*) is faith in the true meaning of reality, free from defects such as doubt.
And discipline of conduct (*cāritravinaya*) is the state of a concentrated mind regarding the conduct of one who possesses those [other two].
When teachers and others are present, respectful conduct (*upacāravinaya*) consists of rising to greet them, approaching them, joining one’s palms in salutation, and so forth.
Even when they are absent, it consists of physical, verbal, and mental acts such as joining the palms, praising their virtues, and recollecting them.
In order to demonstrate the different types of service (*vaiyāvṛtya*), he says:

[service] for the teacher (*ācārya*), the preceptor (*upādhyāya*), the ascetic (*tapasvin*), the student (*śaikṣa*), the sick (*glāna*), the community (*gaṇa*), the family (*kula*), the Saṃgha, the holy man (*sādhu*), and the agreeable person (*manojña*).
Service is divided into ten kinds.
Why? Because of the difference in its objects:
service to the teacher (ācārya), service to the preceptor (upādhyāya), and so forth.

In this regard, one is called an *ācārya* because they practice [the rules] therefrom, that is, because they cause [others] to observe the vows (*vrata*). One is called an *upādhyāya* because, having approached the scripture for the sake of liberation, they study from it. One who performs great fasts and other such observances is a *tapasvin*.
One who possesses the discipline of training is a *śaikṣa*. One whose body is afflicted by illness and the like is "sick" (*glāna*). A "group" (*gaṇa*) is a lineage of elders (*sthavira*).
The assembly of initiators, preceptors, and disciples is the *kula*. A gathering of the four castes and ascetics is the *saṃgha*. One who has long been ordained is a *sādhu*.
It is pleasing and esteemed by the world.

When they encounter the afflictions of disease, wrong views, and so forth, the service that consists of countering them through physical exertion or other substances is *vaiyāvṛtya* (service), for the purpose of manifesting the instilling of concentration, the absence of doubt, affection for the teaching, and so on.

For the purpose of understanding the knowledge of the various forms of self-study (*svādhyāya*), he says: recitation, questioning, reflection, recitation of the scriptures, and instruction in the Dharma.
Recitation (*vācanā*) is the imparting of both the faultless text and its meaning.
Inquiry (*pracchanā*) is questioning others for the purpose of cutting through doubt or for strengthening one's certainty.
Reflection (*anuprekṣā*) is the mental rehearsal of the subject matter already mastered.

Recitation (*parivartana*) is the purity of pronunciation; oral tradition (*āmnāya*) is the practice of preaching the Dharma and so forth; and instruction in the Dharma (*dharmopadeśa*) is [the same].

For what purpose is this fivefold study (*svādhyāya*) intended? Its purpose is the excellence of wisdom, noble resolve, intense spiritual urgency, the increase of austerity, the purification of transgressions, and so forth.
To provide a thorough understanding of the divisions of *vyutsarga* (renunciation), he says:
"Of external and internal acquisitions (*upadhi*)."
*Vyutsarjana* means casting off, relinquishment, or abandonment. It is of two kinds: the abandonment of external requisites and the abandonment of internal requisites.

Unappropriated things such as wealth, grain, and so forth are external *upadhi*. Anger and the like, as well as the physical body (*ātmabhāva*), are internal *upadhi*. The renunciation of the body—whether for a fixed period or for as long as life lasts—is called the renunciation of internal *upadhi*.
For what purpose is this? It is for the sake of achieving non-attachment, fearlessness, and the elimination of hope for life, and so forth.
Regarding that which has been extensively explained as "meditative absorption" (*dhyāna*) and established as a distinct category, the time has now come to state its divisions.
Setting that aside for a moment, it is said [next] in order to determine the nature and the timing of its practitioner:
Dhyāna is the cessation of one-pointed thought for one who possesses the supreme bodily constitution (*saṃhanana*), lasting for at most an *antarmuhūrta*.
The first three types of bodily constitution are supreme: the Vajra-ṛṣabha-nārāca constitution, the Vajra-nārāca constitution, and the Nārāca constitution.
All three of those are means for attaining *dhvani*, but for liberation, only the first one is required.

"One who possesses that supreme constitution" (*uttamasaṃhanana*) refers to such a person; [the phrase] "of him who possesses the supreme constitution" (*tasyottamasaṃhananasya*) constitutes the designation of the practitioner.
The "peak" (agra) is the point of focus.
That which has a single peak is "one-pointed" (ekāgra).

Thought is characterized by movement when it takes various objects as its support; the restriction of that thought away from all other points of focus and its confinement to a single peak is called the "cessation of one-pointed thought" (ekāgracintānirodha).
By this, the essential nature of the grain is stated.
"Muhūrta" refers to a measure of time.
An "antarmuhūrta" is a muhūrta that has gone within [a larger period].
By the phrase “up to an *antarmuhūrta*,” the rule regarding time is established.
Beyond that, because single-pointed reflection (*ekāgra-cintā*) becomes difficult to maintain, [the question arises:

if meditation (*dhyāna*) is the cessation of reflection, and cessation is non-existence (*abhāva*), then would meditation not be like the non-existent horn of a donkey? This is not a fault. It is called "non-existent" in view of the cessation of other reflections, and it is called "existent" because it proceeds with the form of its own object; furthermore, since non-existence is a property of things—due to its being a constituent of a cause and so forth—it is established as a real entity (*vastu-dharma*).
Alternatively, this is not a derivation based on the agent (*bhāvasādhana*), as in "cessation is the act of ceasing" (*nirodhanaṃ nirodhaḥ*).
What then? It is a derivation based on the object (*karmasādhana*): "that which is ceased is cessation" (*nirudhyata iti nirodhaḥ*).
And that [which is] both reflection (*cintā*) and cessation (*nirodha*) is "the cessation of reflection" (*cintānirodha*).
This is what is meant: meditation (*dhyāna*) is simply knowledge (*jñāna*) appearing like a flame of fire that does not flicker.
To demonstrate its divisions, he says:
The [meditations] are the afflicted (*ārta*), the cruel (*raudra*), the virtuous (*dharmya*), and the pure (*śukla*).
Suffering (*ṛta*) is pain; "affliction" (*ardana*) means torment; that which arises therein is the afflicted.
Rudra is one whose disposition is cruel; that which arises from him or pertains to him is *raudra*.
Dharma has already been explained.
That which does not deviate from dharma is *dharmya*.
It is called "white" (śukla) because of its association with the quality of purity.
This fourfold meditation (dhyāna) attains a twofold division.
Why? Because of the distinction between the praiseworthy and the unpraiseworthy.
It is "unpraiseworthy" because it is a cause for the influx of non-meritorious karma;
it is "praiseworthy" because of its capacity to incinerate karma.
If one asks, "What, then, is that? it is said:
"Supreme" means the highest, the further, the ultimate; it is the cause of liberation for others.
The last [of the four stages] is the pure (śukla).
Because of its proximity to that, the stage of duty (dharmya) is also figuratively designated as "supreme" (para).
By the force of the dual-number indication, the secondary [stage] is also included.
From the statement “the others are causes of liberation,” it follows that the former two—the *ārta* and *raudra*—are causes of *saṃsāra*.
Why? Because there is no third thing to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
In that regard, suffering (ārtta) is fourfold.
To explain the definition of the first type of conceptualization, it says:
suffering is the application of mindfulness directed toward the dissociation from what is unpleasant when it is encountered.
That which is unpleasant, disagreeable, such as poison, thorns, enemies, weapons, and so forth, is called "unpleasant" because it causes affliction.

When one encounters such things, the mental application consisting of a continuous stream of thought and recollection—namely, the resolve, "How indeed might this not happen to me?"—is first designated as "afflicted."
In order to provide the definition of the second alternative, he says:
"The opposite of the agreeable."
§ 880. From what is it the opposite? From what was previously stated.

By this, the following is meant: when there is separation from that which is agreeable and desired—such as one’s own children, wife, wealth, and so forth—the mental construction (*saṃkalpa*) for the sake of reunion with them, which is a continuous stream of anxiety (*cintā*), is to be understood as the second type of suffering (*ārta*).
In order to demonstrate the characteristic of the third alternative, he says: "And of sensation..."

Although the word ‘feeling’ (*vedanā*) applies to both pleasure and pain, it here refers specifically to painful feeling because the context concerns one who is afflicted. When that feeling—produced by a disturbance of the humors such as wind (*vāta*) and so forth—occurs, the third type of affliction is said to be the continuous stream of thought and reflection (*cintā-prabandha*) consisting of the resolve: "How indeed might there be an end to this for me? § 883.
He speaks for the purpose of indicating the characteristics of the fourth stage of trance:
"And the causal basis...

The fourth [type of] afflicted thought-construction (*cintā-prabandha*), which is the mental application (*manaḥ-praṇidhāna*) toward the attainment of future objects due to a longing for enjoyments, is called the afflicted *nidāna*.
If it is asked, "To what does this fourfold afflicted state belong? it is said:
These [categories] belong to the non-restrained, the partially restrained, and the careless self-controlled.
The non-restrained range up to those with right view who are not yet self-controlled.
Those who have partial renunciation are the restrained-unrestrained (saṃyatāsaṃyata).
Those who are restrained-with-carelessness (pramattasaṃyata) are possessed of the fifteen types of carelessness and are performers of ritual actions.

Among them, both the non-restrained and those with partial renunciation experience all four types of *ārta* [meditation], because they are possessed of the mental transformation of non-restraint (*asaṃyama*).

However, for those who are partially restrained (pramatta-saṃyata), the other three types of *ārta* [meditation], excluding *nidāna*, may occasionally occur due to the excessive emergence of negligence (*pramāda*).
The *ārta* [meditation] has been explained by means of its designations and so forth.

To determine the name, cause, and master of the second [type of karman], he says: "The *raudra* [karman arises] from violence, falsehood, theft, and the guarding of objects for those who are either non-restrained or partially restrained.
Violence and the others have their characteristics as previously described.
Since these serve as the causes for the arising of *raudra-dhyāna* (fierce meditation), they are understood to be a specification of the cause (*hetu-nirdeśa*).
Following that specification of the cause, the term “recollection and mental application” (*smṛti-samanvāhāra*) is connected [to them].
"Recollection and mental preoccupation with violence," and so forth.
That is to be understood as *raudradhyāna* (fierce meditation) for those who are either unvirtuous (*avirata*) or partially virtuous (*deśavirata*).

While *raudradhyāna* may indeed belong to the unvirtuous, how can it belong to the partially virtuous? For even in the case of the partially virtuous, it can occasionally occur due to the onset of violence and the like, and because of their dependence on the protection of wealth and other possessions.
Furthermore, that [rebirth] is not a cause for those in the hells and so forth, due to the power of right vision (*samyagdarśana*).
For one who is self-restrained, it does not occur at all; because by undertaking such [an act], one would fall away from self-restraint (*saṃyama*).
He said: "The causes of liberation have been taught.

Since it is necessary to provide an instruction regarding the distinctions, essential natures, and masters of the first among those causes of liberation—namely, meditative absorption (dhyāna)—he says:
"For the discernment of the [four] objects—right knowledge, the perils, the ripening of karma, and the structural arrangements—there is that which pertains to the Dharma."
Investigation (*vicayana*) means investigation (*vicaya*), discernment (*viveka*), and examination (*vicāraṇā*).
The investigation of the known, the wretched, the ripened, and the established is "investigation of the known, the wretched, the ripened, and the established" (*ājñāpāyavipākasaṃsthānavicaya*).
The phrase “the application of mindfulness” (*smṛtisamanvāhāra*) is understood to carry over [from the previous context].

It is connected with each [term] individually—as in “the application of mindfulness for the investigation of the authoritative teaching” (*ājñāvicaya*), and so forth. For example: due to the absence of a teacher, due to dullness of intellect, due to the arising of karma, and because categories of reality (*padārtha*) are subtle, when the application of reasons and examples has ceased, one takes as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) the scripture (*āgama*) composed by the Omniscient One. Then, through faith in the profound categories of reality—thinking, “In this very way is it; the Jinas do not speak otherwise”—there arises a determination of the meaning. This is the investigation of the authoritative teaching (*ājñāvicaya*).

Alternatively—*ājñāvicaya* (contemplation of the command) is so called because it consists of the application of reasoning, logic, and valid cognition (*tarka-naya-pramāṇa*) for the purpose of establishing the truth in accordance with one's own tenets by one who, having personally realized the reality of things, desires to make it known to others, and which serves to illuminate the command of the Omniscient One through the recollection of what has been remembered.

*Apāyavicaya* (contemplation of danger) is the reflection upon the loss of the true path, [considering] that those with false views, like those blind from birth, are averse to the path set forth by the Omniscient One; though they suffer the pain of seeking liberation, they stray very far indeed from it due to their lack of knowledge of the correct path.

Alternatively—*apāyavicaya* (contemplation of the states of woe) is the application of mindfulness with the thought: "How might these living beings escape from false view, false knowledge, and false conduct?

*Vipākavicaya* (contemplation of maturation) is the focused attention directed toward the experience of the fruits of actions such as the obscuration of knowledge, which have their causes in substance, place, time, birth, and state.
*Saṃsthānavicaya* (contemplation of structure) is the application of mindfulness for the purpose of investigating the nature of the world's configuration.
Dharma has been described as characterized by supreme forbearance and other such qualities.
Meditation that is not devoid of that [dharma]—which is "conformable to dharma" (dharmya)—should be understood as being fourfold.
It occurs among those who are unrestrained, those who are partially restrained, those who are heedless, and those who are non-heedless.
The examination of the three meditative absorptions has been completed.
Now, the pure meditation (śukladhyāna) must be examined.
That [knowledge] consists of four alternatives which will be explained.
Among those, this is stated for the purpose of indicating the masters of the first two:
"And in the first two pure [knowledges], there is the knowledge of one who knows the previous lives."

Among the varieties of white meditation (*śukladhyāna*) that will be described, in the first white meditation there are those who possess prior knowledge (*pūrvavid*), meaning those who are *śrutakevalins*.
By the word "and" (*ca*), the meditative state characterized by dharma (*dharmya*) is also included.

In this regard, according to the principle that "the specific meaning is understood through the explanation," it is explained that *dharmya* occurs prior to ascending the *śreṇī*, while the two *śukla* [stages] occur upon the *śreṇīs*.
Regarding the question of what remains for whom, it is said here:
The latter two belong to the *kevalins*.

For the *kevalin* whose entire veil of knowledge has been destroyed— whether he be with-vibration (*sayoga*) or without-vibration (*ayoga*)— the latter two types of pure meditation (*śukladhyāna*) occur.

To demonstrate their respective distinctions, this is stated: [the meditative attainments] characterized by the discursive thought of diversity, the discursive thought of unity, subtle activity, the cessation of activity, and the non-returning of activity.

Pure meditation (*śukladhyāna*) is of four kinds: that characterized by discursive thought of diversity (*pṛthaktvavitarka*), that characterized by discursive thought of unity (*ekatvavitarka*), that which leads to subtle activity (*sūkṣmakriyāpratipāti*), and that which brings about the cessation of activity (*vyuparatakriyānivarti*).
With respect to the characteristics to be explained [below], it should be understood that all these names are literal (*anvartha*).
For the purpose of determining the specific nature of its object, he says: "Of those characterized by the three, the one, the conjunction, the body, the yoga, and the non-yoga..."
The meaning of the word *yoga* has already been explained in the passage: "Yoga is the action of body, speech, and mind.
It should be understood that the four previously mentioned varieties of pure meditation (*śukladhyāna*) are to be connected respectively with the four [categories] beginning with the threefold yoga.

The state of discursive reflection on the distinctness of the three yogas; the state of discursive reflection on the unity of one yoga among the three yogas; the subtle movement of the yoga of the body; and the cessation of all movement in the state of non-yoga.
Regarding this, the following is said for the sake of understanding the distinction between the first two:
Regarding "having a single basis and being accompanied by applied thought and sustained investigation" (*ekāśraye savitarkavīcāre*):
those two which have one basis are "having a single basis."
The meaning is that both are undertaken by one who has reached the culmination of the knowledge derived from hearing (*śrutajñāna*).
