"Applied thought" (*vitarka*) and "sustained thought" (*vicāra*) constitute "applied and sustained thought" (*vitarkavicāra*); that which proceeds together with applied and sustained thought is "with applied and sustained thought" (*savitarkasavicāra*).
This means that previously there were the applied thoughts of distinctness and unity.
In this regard, in order to prevent the undesirable consequence that [the second dhyāna] would likewise involve discursive investigation (*vicāra*), this is stated:
"The second [dhyāna] is without discursive investigation."
Of the two preceding [types], that which is the second should be understood as being without investigation (*avīcāra*).
This is what is meant: the first is both with applied thought (*savitarka*) and with investigation (*savīcāra*).
The second is with applied thought (*savitarka*) and without sustained thought (*avīcāra*).
Now, as to what the specific distinction between applied thought and sustained thought is, it is said in this regard:
Vitarka is hearing (śruta).
Specifically, *vitarka* means the act of reasoning (*tarkana*) or deliberation (*ūhana*); its meaning is the knowledge derived from hearing (*śrutajñāna*).
Now, what is investigation? Investigation is the transition from one meaning or one phrasing to another.
The meaning (artha) is that which is to be meditated upon; it is either the substance (dravya) or the mode (paryāya).
The phrasing (vyañjana) is the verbal expression.
Yoga is characterized by the actions of body, speech, and mind.
Transference (*saṃkrānti*) means transformation.
To abandon the substance (*dravya*) and assume a modification (*paryāya*), or to abandon the modification and assume the substance—this is the transference of meaning.
Taking up one spoken word and then taking up another word, and abandoning that as well to take up yet another—this is the transition of syllables (*vyañjanasaṃkrānti*).
Abandoning bodily yoga and grasping another yoga, and abandoning another yoga and grasping bodily yoga—this is the transition of yoga (*yogasaṃkrānti*).
Such a shifting about is called discursive investigation (*vīcāra*).

Therefore, the sage who has performed the preliminary purifications ought to meditate upon this fourfold path of righteousness and purity, which is described in terms of both general and specific categories, and which employs many methods such as the previously mentioned restraints (guptis) for the cessation of saṃsāra.

In that state, meditating upon either a substantial atom (*dravyaparamāṇu*) or a modal atom (*bhāvaparamāṇu*), one who has not yet attained the power of sustained thought (*vitarka*) possesses a mind that shifts separately between the meaning and the expression, as well as between body and speech; like a child’s unsteady and dull enthusiasm, or like cutting a tree with a blunt weapon, he gradually pacifies and exhausts the nature of delusion (*moha*), thereby becoming a partaker of the "meditation with separate thought and discursive investigation" (*pṛthaktvavitarkavicāra-dhyāna*).

Furthermore, desiring to utterly consume the deluding karma (mohanīya) along with its very roots, he relies on a specific excellence of yoga characterized by infinite-fold purity. Restraining the bondage of the many karmic natures that assist the knowledge-obscuring karma (jñānāvaraṇa), and effecting the reduction and destruction of their duration (sthiti), his application of scriptural knowledge (śrutajñānopayoga) is free from the transition of meanings and verbal expressions. With an unwavering mind, his passions (kaṣāya) exhausted, untainted like a lapis lazuli gem, he meditates and does not return; this is called "one-pointedness with discursive thought" (ekatvavitarka).

Thus, having burnt the fuel of karmic matter with the fire of the pure meditation characterized by the discursive thought of unity, the Blessed One—whether he be a Tīrthaṅkara or another Kevalin—shines with the radiant orb of his blazing exclusive knowledge (*kevalajñāna*), like the sun released from the obstruction of a mass of clouds. He is to be approached and worshipped by the lords of the world, and he dwells for a maximum duration of slightly less than ten million *pūrva* years.

When his lifespan has only an antarmuhūrta remaining, and his duration of stay, experience, name, and lineage (nāma-gotra) are equal to that [remaining lifespan], then, having abandoned all vocal and mental yogas as well as the coarse bodily yoga, he becomes capable of entering the meditative absorption characterized by subtle activity (sūkṣmakriyāpratipāti-dhyāna), taking subtle bodily yoga as its object.

When, however, the soul has an Antarmuhūrta remaining of its lifespan and possesses three types of karma with a duration greater than that, it becomes a *sayogī* (possessor of yoga). Then, due to the inherent capacity of the supreme self-absorption (*ātmopayogātiśaya*)—which is assisted by equanimity (*sāmāyika*), characterized by a specific refinement (*viśiṣṭakaraṇa*), constitutes a great restraint (*mahāsaṃvara*), and ripens light karma to the point of shedding the dust of all karma—it performs the expansion of its own spatial units (*pradeśa*) through four moments (*samaya*) to fill the space of a staff, a door-panel, a plane, and finally the entire world; and then, having withdrawn that expansion of spatial units over the same number of moments, it equalizes the four remaining karmas, returns to the size of its former body, and meditates upon the "subtle-motion-descending" meditation (*sūkṣmakriyāpratipāti-dhyāna*) by means of the subtle-body-yoga (*sūkṣmakāyayoga*).
Then, he begins the meditation that turns back all activity (*samucchinnakriyānivarti-dhyāna*).

It is called "turning back all activity" because it involves the cessation of the movement of inhalation and exhalation, as well as all activities and operations of the vibration of every part of the body, speech, and mind.

In that meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) which brings about the cessation of all activity, because it possesses the capacity to arrest all bonds and influxes (*āsrava*) and to eradicate all residual karma, there arises for the one who has attained the state of *ayogakevalin* the complete *yathākhyāta-cāritra*, knowledge, and vision; this directly becomes the cause of liberation, generating the severance of the embrace of the entire web of the sufferings of *saṃsāra*.

Furthermore, that Blessed One, the *ayogakevalin*, having burnt away all stains, blemishes, and bonds by the fire of the excellence of that meditation, attains his true self—like pure gold obtained when dross, ores, and stones have been removed—and enters final liberation (*parinirvāti*).

This twofold austerity is a cause of restraint (*saṃvara*) because it is the cause for the cessation of the influx of new karma; it is also a cause of dissociation (*nirjarā*) because it is the means for shaking off the dust of previously accumulated karma.
Regarding this, one asks: "Do all those with right view possess equal dissociation, or is there some distinction? To this it is replied:

The right-viewed, the śrāvaka-virata, the anantaviyojaka, the darśanamoha-kṣapaka, the upaśamaka, the upaśāntamoha, the kṣapaka, the kṣīṇamoha, and the jina undergo, in successive order, an infinite-fold shedding of karma.
These ten, beginning with the right-viewed, undergo, in successive order, an infinite-fold shedding of karma.

For example—a soul who is capable (*bhavya*), possesses the five senses and mental consciousness (*saṃjñī*), is fully developed (*paryāptaka*), and is aided by the previously mentioned factors such as the attainment of time (*kāla-labdhi*) and so forth—increasing through the purification of its transformation (*pariṇāma-viśuddhi*), gradually leaps up the series of steps beginning with *apūrvakaraṇa* and becomes a destroyer of a vast amount of karma.

Furthermore, when the conditions for attaining the first right conviction (*samyaktva*) are present, that same soul, becoming one of right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), becomes a destroyer of karma by incalculable degrees.

Furthermore, at the time of attaining a transformation characterized by the subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣayopaśama*) of the non-renouncing obscuring (*apratyākhyānāvaraṇa*) karma of the delusion of conduct (*cāritramoha*), that same [soul], through its connection with the excellence of purity, becomes a *śrāvaka* and consequently possesses a destruction of karma [that is] incalculable times greater than before.

Furthermore, through its connection with the purity of transformation caused by the subsidence-cum-destruction of the renouncing obscuring (*pratyākhyānāvaraṇa*) karma, that same [soul], being designated as one who has abstained (*virata*), possesses a destruction of karma [that is] incalculable times greater than that.

When that same person further becomes intent on severing the infinite-bondage (anantānubandhi) types of anger, pride, deceit, and greed, then, through the application of the excellence of purity of transformation (pariṇāma-viśuddhi-prakarṣa), he becomes a shedder of [karmic matter] with incalculable times more merit than before.

Furthermore, when that same person desires to burn away the heap of grass consisting of the three natures of delusion of vision (darśana-moha), through the application of the pre-eminence of purity of transformation, he partakes of the designation "one who destroys delusion of vision" and becomes a shedder of [karmic matter] with incalculable times more merit than what was previously stated.

Thus, having attained right vision through destruction (*kṣāyika-samyagdṛṣṭi*), he becomes intent on ascending the ladder (*śreṇī*) and exerts himself toward the subsidence of the delusion of conduct (*cāritra-moha*). By virtue of his connection with the excellence of purification, experiencing the designation of a "subsider" (*upaśamaka*), he effects a shedding of karma (*nirjarā*) that is incalculably greater than what was previously mentioned.

Furthermore, when the conditions for the complete subsidence of all delusions of conduct are present, he attains the designation of one whose passions are subsided (*upaśānta-kaṣāya*), and his shedding of karma becomes incalculably greater than what was previously mentioned.

Furthermore, that same soul, turning toward the destruction of conduct-deluding karma (*cāritramoha*) and increasing through the purity of its transformation (*pariṇāma*), experiences the designation of a "destroyer" (*kṣapaka*) and undergoes an emission [of karma] (*nirjarā*) that is incalculably many times greater than what was previously mentioned.

When it turns toward the transformation that causes the complete destruction of all conduct-deluding karma and attains the designation of one whose passions are destroyed (*kṣīṇakaṣāya*), it undergoes an emission incalculably many times greater than what was previously mentioned.

That same soul, having burned away the accumulation of destructive karmas (*ghātikarman*) by the fire of the second white meditation (*śukladhyāna*), becomes a possessor of the designation of a Jina and undergoes an emission incalculably many times greater than what was previously mentioned.

He asks: "Even when right vision (*samyagdarśana*) is present, if there is no mutual equality among these [stages] because of the dissipation (*nirjaratva*) of incalculable qualities, then why—like the *śrāvaka*—do these [stages] beginning with 'the restrained' (*virata*) not deserve the state of being a *nirgrantha* due to their differences in qualities? It is said: This is not so.
Why?

Because, despite their mutual distinctions due to differences in qualities, all of them— namely the *pulāka*, *bakuśa*, *kuśīla*, *nirgrantha*, and *snātaka*— are indeed *nirgranthas* through the application of the *naigama* and other *nayās*. § 910.

Those whose minds are devoid of the cultivation of the higher virtues (*uttaraguṇa*) and who, even regarding the primary vows (*vrata*), do not at any time or place attain full perfection, are called *pulāka* because they resemble impure grains of rice.

Established in the state of a Nirgrantha with unbroken vows, yet following after the adornment of body and requisites, having an undisciplined retinue, and possessed of a variegated delusion (*moha-śabala*), they are *bakuśa*.
The word *bakuśa* is a synonym for "variegated" (*śabala*).
Those of bad conduct (*kuśīla*) are of two kinds: those of bad conduct through practice (*pratisevanā-kuśīla*) and those of bad conduct through passion (*kaṣāya-kuśīla*).

Those who do not maintain complete separation from possessions, who possess both [types of conduct] in their entirety, and who somehow fail in the higher virtues, are those of bad conduct through practice.
Those who have brought under control the arising of other passions (*kaṣāya*) and are dependent solely upon the *saṃjvalana* [passions], are those of bad conduct through passion.

The Nirgranthas whose karmic actions of rising are not yet manifest—resembling a line of ripples on water—and who, after a moment, shall possess the emerging *kevalajñāna* and *kevaladarśana*, are those whose destructive (*ghāti*) karmas have been exhausted; these *kevalins* are of two kinds, the *snātakas*.
These are the five types of Nirgranthas.

Even though there are distinctions in the degree of excellence or deficiency of the transformation of conduct (*cāritra-pariṇāma*), all of them are called "Nirgranthas" with respect to the *naigama*, *saṃgraha*, and other viewpoints (*naya*).
In order to further clarify the specific distinctions among those [categories] beginning with the *pulāka*, he says:
They are to be established through the distinctions of restraint, scriptural learning, practice, sacred ford, emblem, coloration, rebirth, and place.
These [categories], beginning with the *pulāka*, are to be established and explained by means of these eight analytical investigations (*anuyoga*), starting with restraint.
For example: the *pulāka*, *bakuśa*, and *pratisevanā-kuśīla* exist in two types of restraint, namely *sāmāyika* and *chedopasthāpana*.
The *kaṣāya-kuśīla* exist in two types of restraint, namely *parihāraviśuddhi* and *sūkṣmasāmparāya*, as well as in the two preceding ones.
The *nirgrantha* and *snātaka* exist in only one type of restraint, namely *yathākhyāta-saṃyama*.
It has been heard: the *pulākas*, *bakuśas*, and *pratisevanā-kuśīlas* at most possess the ten *pūrvas* with unbroken syllables.
The *kaṣāya-kuśīlas* and *nirgranthas* possess the fourteen *pūrvas*.
At the minimum, the scriptural knowledge of a *pulāka* consists of the *ācāravastu*.
The scriptural knowledge of *bakuśas*, *kuśīlas*, and *nirgranthas* consists of the eight *pravacanamātṛkās*.
*Snātakas* are devoid of scriptural knowledge and are *kevalins*.
*Pratisevanā* (practice): By practicing any one of the five root virtues (*mūlaguṇa*) or the abstention from eating at night under the compulsion of another or by force, one becomes a *pulāka*.
The *bakuśa* is of two kinds: the *upakaraṇabakuśa* (defiled in requisites) and the *śarīrabakuśa* (defiled in body).

In this context, one who is "defiled by requisites" (upakaraṇa-bakuśa) is one who desires requisites endowed with many excellent qualities. One who "cultivates bodily grooming" (śarīra-saṃskāra-sevī) is one who is defiled by the body (śarīra-bakuśa).

One who is "defiled by practice" (pratisevanā-kuśīla) is one who, without violating the fundamental virtues (mūlaguṇa), nevertheless practices some form of violation regarding the secondary virtues (uttaraguṇa).
There is no transgression for the *kaṣāyakuśīla*, the *nirgrantha*, and the *snātaka*.
Regarding the "ford" (*tīrtha*), all [these types of practitioners] exist within the fords of all the *tīrthakaras*.
Marks are of two kinds: the material mark (*dravyaliṅga*) and the existential mark (*bhāvaliṅga*).
In dependence upon the existential mark, all five types of Nirgranthas become possessors of the mark.
The *leśyās* are to be classified according to the physical signs (*dravyaliṅga*).
Regarding the *leśyās*: for the *pulāka*, the three higher ones; for the *bakuśa* and the *pratisevanā-kuśīla*, all six.
For one whose conduct is stained by passions (kaṣāyakuśīla), there are four higher [leśyās].
For one whose passions are subtle (sūkṣmasāmparāya), for the one free from bonds (nirgrantha), and for the one who has attained final liberation (snātaka), there is only the pure white leśyā.
Those who are without yoga are without leśyā.
Rebirth—The highest rebirth for the *pulāka* is among the gods of the highest status in the Sahasrāra heaven.
For the *bakuśa* and the *pratisevanā-kuśīla*, it is in the Āraṇa and Acyuta heavens, where the lifespan is twenty-two *sāgaropamas*.
For the *kaṣāyakuśīla* and the *nirgrantha*, the maximum duration is thirty-three *sāgaropamas* in the Sarvārthasiddha [vimāna].
For all [other types], the minimum is two *sāgaropamas* in the Saudharma Kalpa.
For the *snātaka*, it is liberation (*nirvāṇa*).
Regarding the stages (*sthāna*): there are innumerable stages of self-restraint (*saṃyama-sthāna*) caused by the passions (*kaṣāya*).
Among these, the very lowest stages of attainment (*labdhi-sthāna*) belong to the *pulāka* and the *kaṣāya-kuśīla*.
The two travel simultaneously through incalculable stages;
thereafter, the *pulāka* is cut off.
The *kaṣāyakuśīla*, however, proceeds alone through incalculable stages from that point.

Thereafter, those who are stained by defilements (kaṣāya-kuśīla), those who are stained by the practice of [forbidden] conduct (pratisevanā-kuśīla), and those who are stained by being unrefined (bakuśa) proceed simultaneously through incalculable stages.
Thereafter, the bakuśas are extinguished.
Then, after proceeding through further incalculable stages, the pratisevanā-kuśīlas are extinguished.

Having gone from there as well to incalculable places, the one who is stained by impurities (*kaṣāyakuśīla*) ceases to exist. Beyond that, the *nirgrantha* attains the stages free from impurities (*akaṣāyasthāna*).
He too, having gone to incalculable places, ceases to exist.
Thereafter, having gone to one place, the *snātaka* attains *nirvāṇa*; thus, the attainment of self-restraint (*saṃyama*) for these [beings] becomes infinitely greater in quality.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the *Tattvārthavṛtti*, known as the *Sarvārthasiddhi*.
Now begins the tenth chapter.
He said: "Now the time has come to state the essential nature of liberation (mokṣa) which was mentioned at the end.
This is indeed true.
The attainment of liberation and the acquisition of absolute knowledge (*kevalajñāna*) are preceded by this; thus, the cause for the arising of absolute knowledge is stated:
"Absolute knowledge [arises] from the destruction of delusion (*moha*), and from the destruction of the veils of knowledge and perception (*jñānadarśanāvaraṇa*) and the obstructions (*antarāya*).
(Tattvārthasūtra 10.1) § 921.
In this case, it is proper to compose the sūtra in this manner.
Why? Because of its brevity.

How so? By not including the word *kṣaya*, by the absence of a reference to a different case ending, and by the non-employment of the word *ca*, the sūtra becomes concise: "From the destruction of delusion, knowledge-obscuration, perception-obscuration, and obstruction, there is the absolute [knowledge]. (mohajñānadarśanāvaraṇāntarāyakṣayāt kevalam).
This is true; however, the instruction is given through a division of sentences for the purpose of demonstrating the sequence of destruction.

Having first brought delusion (*moha*) to destruction and attained the designation "one whose passions are destroyed" (*kṣīṇakaṣāya*) for an *antarmuhūrta*, one then simultaneously effects the destruction of the veils of knowledge and perception (*jñānadarśanāvaraṇa*) and the obstructive karma (*antarāya*), thereby attaining omniscience (*kevala*).
Thus, its destruction is the cause of the arising of omniscience; therefore, the case-ending is employed to indicate the definition of a cause.

If it is asked, "How is delusion (*moha*) brought to destruction even before that? it is said: A worthy person (*bhavya*) possessing right vision (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), increasing through the purity of transformation, having reached the state of right vision through destruction (*kṣāyikasamyagdṛṣṭi*) by bringing seven types of delusion to destruction at some point within the stages of the uncontrolled-with-right-vision (*asaṃyata-samyagdṛṣṭi*), the partially controlled (*saṃyatāsaṃyata*), the careless (*pramatta*), or the non-careless (*apramatta*), becomes intent on ascending the ladder of destruction (*kṣapakaśreṇī*). Having established himself in the stage of downward-activity (*adhaḥpravṛttakaraṇa*) at the level of the non-careless, and having experienced the designation of the stage of the destroyer with unprecedented activity (*apūrvakaraṇa-kṣapaka-guṇasthāna*) through the application of unprecedented activity, he there thins the duration and intensity of evil dispositions (*pāpaprakṛti*) by means of new pure intentions and increases the experience of auspicious karma. Having attained the stage of non-retrogression (*anivṛttikaraṇa*), he ascends to the stage of the destroyer of gross passions (*anivṛtti-bādara-sāṃparāya-kṣapaka-guṇasthāna*). There, having destroyed the eight [passionate] defilements (*kaṣāya*), he brings about the destruction of the neuter gender (*napuṃsakaveda*), uproots the female gender (*strīveda*), and, having transferred the six quasi-passions (*nokakaṣāya*) into the male gender (*puṃveda*), destroys them; then he transfers the male gender into the active anger (*krodhasaṃjvalana*), the active anger into the active pride (*mānasaṃjvalana*), the active pride into the active deceit (*māyāsaṃjvalana*), and the active deceit into the active greed (*lobhasaṃjvalana*). Having gradually brought these to dissolution through the process of gross extraction (*bādarakṛṣṭi-vibhāga*), and having thinned the active greed, he experiences the state of the destroyer of subtle passions (*sūkṣma-sāmparāya-kṣapaka*). Having destroyed the deluding karma (*mohanīya*) without remainder and having eradicated the passions (*kaṣāya*), he ascends to the state of one whose passions are exhausted (*kṣīṇakaṣāya*). Having laid down the burden of delusion, in the penultimate first moment he brings sleep and drowsiness (*nidrā-pracala*) to annihilation. Then, at the very end, he brings the five types of knowledge-obscuring (*jñānāvaraṇa*), the four types of perception-obscuring (*darśanāvaraṇa*), and the five types of obstructive (*antarāya*) karma to their final end. Immediately thereafter, he attains the state of absolute omniscience (*kevala-paryāya*), which is characterized by knowledge and perception and possesses inconceivable, extraordinary manifestations.
He asked: "For what reason is there liberation, and what is its characteristic? To this it is replied:
Liberation is the complete release from all karma through the absence of the causes of bondage and through the wearing away [of karma].

Due to the absence of causes such as false view (*mithyādarśana*), there is an absence of new karma; and due to the presence of the previously mentioned causes of shedding (*nirjarā*), there is the elimination of accumulated karma.
By means of these two—namely, the absence of the causes of bondage and shedding—there is the indication of the case endings (*vibhakti*) according to their causal characteristics (*hetu-lakṣaṇa*).

Then, for one whose remaining karma has been rendered equalized by the cause of the persistence of existence (*bhavasthiti*), liberation (*mokṣa*) is to be understood as the simultaneous and absolute release from all karma.
The absence of karma is of two kinds: that which is to be accomplished through effort and that which is not to be accomplished through effort.

Among these, the absence of the life-span of hell-beings, animals, and gods in one who possesses his final body is not to be accomplished through effort, because [such a life-span] does not exist [for him].

That which is to be accomplished through effort is now described: among the four spiritual stages (guṇasthāna) beginning with the unrestrained right-viewed (asaṃyata-samyagdṛṣṭi), the destruction of seven types of karma is effected in one of them. At the stage of the "subtle-passion" (anivṛtti-bādara-sāmparāya), the simultaneous destruction of sixteen types of karmic matter is effected: namely, the two sub-classes of sleep (nidrā-nidrā and pracalā-pracalā), drowsiness (styāna-gṛddhi), the two destinies of hellish and animal births, the four classes of beings with one, two, three, and four senses, the two types of migratory chains (ānupūrvya) appropriate for hellish and animal births, heat (ātapa), luster (udyota), immobility (sthāvara), fineness (sūkṣma), and commonality (sādhāraṇa). These sixteen karmic types are destroyed simultaneously at that stage.
Thereafter, right there, the eight primary passions (*kaṣāya*) are destroyed.
The neuter gender (*napuṃsakaveda*) and the female gender (*strīveda*) reach destruction in that very same place, one after the other.
And he casts down the six secondary passions (*nokaṣāya*) together with the remaining one [the male gender] by a single blow.
Thereafter, the male sex-passion (*puṃveda*), the blazing anger (*saṃjvalanakrodha*), pride (*māna*), and deceit (*māyā*) undergo absolute destruction in that very state, one after another.
The blazing greed (*lobhasaṃjvalana*) reaches its end at the conclusion of the stage of subtle passion (*sūkṣmasāmparāya*).

Sleep (*nidrā*) and drowsiness (*pracalā*) reach dissolution in the penultimate moment for the deluded one who has destroyed the passions and is free from attachment (*kṣīṇakaṣāyavītarāgacchadmastha*).

The destruction of the five types of knowledge-obscuring karma (jñānāvaraṇa), the four types of perception-obscuring karma (darśanāvaraṇa), and the five types of obstructive karma (antarāya) occurs at that very same final moment.

In the penultimate moment for an *ayogakevalin*, seventy-two types of karma undergo destruction: any one of the two types of experience (*vedanīya*); the celestial state (*devagati*); the five bodies—gross (*audārika*), transformable (*vaikriyika*), assimilative (*āhāraka*), fiery (*taijasa*), and karmic (*kārmaṇa*)—along with their five bondages (*bandhana*) and five unions (*saṃghāta*); the six figures (*saṃsthāna*); the six limbs and sub-limbs (*aṅgopāṅga*) of the gross, transformable, and assimilative bodies; the five types of bone-joints (*saṃhanana*); the five auspicious colors, five inauspicious colors, two odors, five auspicious tastes, and five inauspicious tastes; the eight types of touch; the celestial-state-qualifying transmigration-body (*ānupūrvī*); lightness (*agurulaghu*); self-obstruction (*upaghāta*); obstruction by others (*paraghāta*); respiration (*ucchvāsa*); the two types of movement through space (*vihāyogati*), namely auspicious and inauspicious; the incomplete (*aparyāptaka*); individual body (*pratyekaśarīra*); firm (*sthira*); non-firm (*asthira*); beautiful (*śubha*); ugly (*aśubha*); unfortunate (*durbhaga*); sweet voice (*susvara*); harsh voice (*duḥsvara*); unattractive (*anādeya*); infamy (*ayaśaḥkīrti*); formation (*nirmāṇa*); and low family-determination (*nīcairgotra*).

In the final moment of an *ayogakevalin*, there occurs the cessation of thirteen types of karmic matter (*prakṛti*): those to be experienced as either [pleasant or unpleasant], human lifespan, human destiny, five-sensed birth, the human-destiny-apt sequence, the subtle, gross, incomplete, fortunate, agreeable, fame-and-reputation, Tīrthaṅkara-name, and high-status families.
He asks: Is liberation determined by the removal of only these material karmic matter types (*dravyakarmaprakṛti*), or also of the karmic state (*bhāvakarman*)? To this it is replied:
And [this applies] to the states of being capable of attaining the subsidential (*aupaśamika*) and other [types of liberation].
What [is the result]? "Liberation" (*mokṣaḥ*) is understood to follow.
The inclusion of the term "capacity" (*bhavyatva*) is for the purpose of excluding other transformative states (*pāriṇāmika*).
By this, it is accepted that liberation occurs through the absence of capacity among the transformative states, as well as the absence of the states such as the subsided (*upaśamika*) and others.

He says: If liberation is asserted to be the cessation of states (bhāva), then would it not follow that for the liberated soul there is the designation of the cessation of all destructive (kṣāyika) states, just as there is the cessation of subsidential (aupaśamika) and other states? This might be so if no distinction were stated. However, since there is a distinction here, this is said in order to establish an exception: [The text continues: "There is a distinction in this matter. Thus, for the purpose of formulating an exception, this is stated: [the verse follows].
"Except for [the states of] pure right view, knowledge, vision, and perfection"—
the designation "what" (kā) is used here in relation to the word "except for" (anyatra).
This rule applies elsewhere than in the case of those who have attained the state of perfection through pure right-conduct, knowledge, and vision alone.

If only these four remain, does it not follow that infinite power (*anantavīrya*) and the other qualities must cease? This is not a fault, because infinite power and the rest are inseparable from knowledge and vision; there is no distinction between them. Furthermore, since there can be no manifestation of infinite awakening for one devoid of infinite capacity, and because bliss consists of knowledge, [these qualities persist].
If it is argued that there is an absence of liberated beings because they lack a physical form, we say no; for they possess the form of the body immediately preceding their liberation.
It might be thought: "If the soul conforms to the body, then in its absence [of the body], it would follow that it expands to the extent of the natural space-points of the world-space (*lokākāśa*).
This is not a fault.
Why? Because of the absence of a cause.
For the connection with name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is indeed the cause of contraction and expansion;
in its absence, there is consequently no further contraction or expansion.

If, due to the absence of a cause, there is neither contraction nor expansion, then, due to the absence of a cause for movement, upward motion would also not occur, as there would likewise be an absence of downward and horizontal motion; consequently, it follows that the soul would remain stationary at the very place where it was liberated.
To this, it is replied:
Immediately after that, it ascends upwards as far as the end of the world.
Immediately following that.
Of what? Of the complete liberation from all karma.
The prefix *ā-* has the sense of inclusion (*abhividhi*).
It goes upward as far as the end of the world.
How can this upward movement, which has no taught cause, be understood? To this it is said:
because of previous practice, because of non-attachment, because of the severance of bonds, and because of the transformation into that [upward] state of existence.
It is said: Even if the meaning of the reason (*hetu*) is complete, it is not sufficient to establish the intended object without the corroboration of an example (*dṛṣṭānta*). To this it is replied:
"It is like a potter’s wheel that has been set in motion, like a gourd from which the pulp has been removed, like a castor-oil seed, and like a flame of fire."
There is a sequential correspondence between the reasons established in the preceding sūtra and the examples stated here.
For instance: the spinning [of a potter's wheel] is preceded by the conjunction of the hand, the staff, and the wheel, brought about by the activity of the potter.
Even after that [body] has ceased, it continues to move due to previous effort until the exhaustion of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).

Thus, even in the absence of the repeated aspiration made by the self while abiding in *bhava* for the sake of attaining liberation, the movement of the liberated one is determined to be preceded by the penetration of that [aspiration].
Furthermore, because of its non-attachment (*asaṅga*).

Just as a gourd vessel, which has sunk to the bottom of the water due to the weight produced by a coating of clay, rises upward immediately once it becomes light as the bond of the clay is loosened by the soaking of the water, so too the self, overcome by the burden of the weight of karma, wanders through *saṃsāra* without fixed regularity under the influence of that immersion;
but when liberated from attachment to that [karma], it ascends upward.
Furthermore, this is because of the severing of its bonds.

Just as the upward movement of a castor seed is observed upon the severing of its bond with the seed-capsule, so too, upon the severing of all karmic bonds—namely those designated as *gati*, *jāti*, *nāma*, and so forth, which procure existence as humans and other beings—the upward movement of the liberated soul is determined.
Furthermore, it is due to the transformation toward such a movement:

just as a lamp flame, no longer desiring connection with the wind whose nature is to blow horizontally, rises upward by its own inherent nature, so too the liberated self, once the karma that causes various downward movements and modifications has been extinguished, ascends upwards alone by virtue of its inherent nature for upward movement.

He asks: "If the liberated soul has the nature of upward motion, why does it not fly upwards even beyond the end of the world? To this it is replied: "Because of the absence of the *dharmāstikāya* (the medium of motion)."

Since the category of existence consisting of motion (dharmāstikāya), which serves as the cause for the support of movement, does not exist above [the world], there is no going in the non-world (aloka).
And in the absence of that, the distinction between the world and the non-world would logically follow as non-existent.

He said: "These [beings] have attained final nirvāṇa; because they lack the causes for distinctions such as the realms of existence and types of birth, they are indeed beyond all conventional designations of difference.
Nevertheless, there is still some kind of distinction."
Why?

Because they are to be established by way of [differences in] field, time, gati, liṅga, tīrtha, conduct, the awakening of a pratyekabuddha, the depth of knowledge, the interval, the number, and the relative magnitude.

The meaning is that those who have attained perfection (*siddha*) and those seeking perfection (*sādhya*) are to be distinguished by twelve applications (*anuyoga*), such as "field" (*kṣetra*) and so forth, according to the intention of the two systems (*tantra-naya*): the system that grasps the present and the system that grasps what has occurred.

For example, first, regarding the field: in which field do they attain perfection? According to the system that grasps the present, perfection occurs in the field of attainment, either in one's own location or in a location of space.

According to the system that grasps what has occurred, with respect to birth, perfection occurs in the fifteen lands of action (*karmabhūmi*); with respect to being summoned (*saṃharaṇa*), perfection occurs in the human field.

At what time does attainment (*siddhi*) occur? According to the perspective of the present method (*pratyutpannanaya*), one becomes perfected by attaining perfection in a single moment. According to the perspective of the method of establishing reality (*bhūtaprajñāpananaya*), one who is born attains perfection without distinction during both the ascending (*utsarpiṇī*) and descending (*avasarpiṇī*) cycles. Specifically, one who is born in the final portion of the *suṣamaduḥṣamā* period and during the *duḥṣamasuṣamā* period of the descending cycle attains perfection.
However, one born in the Duḥṣamā age does not attain perfection in the Duḥṣamā age;
at other times, one certainly does not attain perfection.
By way of being transported [to another time], one attains perfection at all times, both during the Utsarpiṇī and the Avasarpiṇī.
In which destiny (gati) is there accomplishment (siddhi)? In the destiny of accomplishment or in the human destiny.
By what gender (liṅga) is there accomplishment? By the state of being without Veda, or from three Vedas; this accomplishment is through cultivation (bhāvita), not through substance (dravyataḥ).
Substantially, it is only by the masculine gender.

Alternatively, accomplishment (siddhi) occurs through either the mark of a Nirgrantha or the mark of one who has ties (sagrantha), depending on the perspective of the "method of what was previously established" (bhūtapūrvanaya).
Regarding the ford (tīrtha), the accomplishment of a ford is twofold, due to the distinction between being a Tīrthaṅkara and not being one.
The others are of two kinds: those who attain perfection when a Tīrthaṅkara is present, and those who do so when one is not.
By what kind of conduct is perfection attained? Perfection is attained through conduct that is beyond designation, or through conduct consisting of one, four, or five varieties.
The distinction of the enlightenment of a Pratyekabuddha arises from the difference in knowledge caused by either one's own power or the instruction of another.
By what knowledge? Accomplishment is achieved through one, two, three, or four specific types of knowledge.
Penetration (*avagāhana*) consists in pervading the spatial extent of one's own self.
That is of two kinds, distinguished as superior and inferior.
Therein, the superior is five hundred and twenty-five *dhanus* in length;
the inferior is three and a half *aratnis* less than a quarter.
The conceptualizations are in the middle.
They are accomplished within a single immersion.
What is the interval? For those being accomplished and those already accomplished, the minimum interval is two time-units (samaya) and the maximum is eight.
The interval is at its minimum one moment and at its maximum six months.
As for the number, at the minimum one person attains realization in a single moment;
at the maximum, the number is one hundred and eight.
The distinction of fewness or manyness (*alpa-bahutva*) refers to the specific numerical difference among those distinguished by the divisions of fields (*kṣetra*) and so forth.

For example, with respect to the present perspective (*pratyutpanna-naya*), there is no distinction of fewness or manyness regarding those who attain perfection (*siddhi*) in the field of perfection (*siddhi-kṣetra*). However, with respect to the past perspective (*bhūtapūrva-naya*), it is considered as follows: those perfected in a field are of two kinds—by birth and by being transported (*saṃharaṇa*).
Among them, those who have achieved mastery through contraction are few;
those who are perfected by birth are many times more numerous.
The classification of fields consists of the land of karma, the non-land of karma, the ocean, the continent, and [the directions] above, below, and across.
Among them, those who have attained perfection in the upper world are few;
those who have attained perfection in the lower world are many times more numerous;
and those who have attained perfection in the horizontal world are many times more numerous still.
In every respect, those perfected on the oceans are fewest; those perfected on the continents are many times more numerous. Thus much for now, without further distinction.

Those perfected beings in the Salt Ocean are fewest of all. Those perfected in the Kālodaka Ocean are a numerable multiple [of the former]. Those perfected in Jambūdvīpa are a numerable multiple [of the latter].
The perfected beings (siddha) of Dhātakīkhaṇḍa are numerable-fold [more numerous];
the perfected beings of the half of Puṣkaradvīpa are numerable-fold [more numerous].
In this way, even regarding the divisions of time and so forth, the relative smallness and greatness [of numbers] should be understood according to the logic [already established].
For the noble ones who desire to attain the bliss of heaven and liberation, [this treatise] is the essence of the supreme nectar of the Jaina teaching.

Those who have realized the truth of reality should constantly hold in their minds this work titled *Sarvārthasiddhi*, which is so named by the wise because it functions according to the true meaning of reality.
Those who have understood the essence of reality listen to this exposition of the true meaning when it is proclaimed, and those who recite it do so with devotion to the Dharma.
The nectar of the bliss of supreme perfection has been placed in their hands; what more need be said regarding the joys of mortals and lords of the gods?
For by means of the stainless, absolute eye, this unimpeded reality of all objects has been illuminated.

With devotion, I bow to that Hero of wondrous qualities, whose footstool is worshipped by hosts of gods and men from afar; [this work is] the essence of the nectar of the supreme Jaina teaching, sought by noble ones desiring to attain the bliss of heaven and liberation.

"The Attainment of All Aims"—this is the name bestowed upon it by the virtuous; its commentary on the true meaning (*tattvārthavṛtti*) should be constantly held in the mind.

(1) Those who, having understood the reality of the objects of knowledge, listen to this expounded *Tattvārthavṛtti* or recite it with devotion to the Dharma, have placed in their hands the nectar of the bliss of supreme perfection; what more need be said regarding the joys of mortals and the lords of the gods? (2)

I bow with devotion to that Vīra of wondrous qualities, whose footstool is worshipped by hosts of men and gods, and who, with his stainless and absolute eye, has illuminated this entire reality of all objects without obstruction.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the *Tattvārthavṛtti* known as the *Sarvārthasiddhi*.
May it be auspicious for all.
